Its brightest stars form a long, easy cross gliding the misty current.
The swan never tires and never lands; it simply floats on through the dark.
Let it carry you a little, slow as a feather laid upon still water.
And so the pictures turn, all of them, very slowly overhead.
The hunter and his dogs, the bear, the sisters, the princess and her hero, the swan.
They have shone over every night that people have ever known.
Children watched them; their parents watched them; and so on back beyond all counting.
The same stars have steadied sailors, timed the harvest, and pointed the way home.
There is a deep, simple comfort in looking up and finding the old shapes still there.
They were there long before you, and they will be there long after this night.
Tonight you needed only to lie back and let yourself be held by the long telling.
Now let the names grow soft, and the stories blur, and the sky go quiet.
Your breath is slow, your body warm, the dark around you gentle and kind.
There is nothing more to do, and nowhere else to be.
Rest now.
Let yourself drift.

lectures.title: How the World Began
lines: There is nothing to remember tonight, and nothing you need to do.
Let your shoulders grow heavy, and let the bed take all of your weight.
These are only old stories, and old stories ask nothing of you at all.
You can let the words drift past like leaves on slow water.
If your eyes wish to close, let them close; they have carried you far today.
Breathe out, and feel a little more of the day loosen and fall away.
There is rain somewhere beyond the window, soft and unhurried and kind.
You do not have to follow every line, and you do not have to understand.
Let your hands grow warm, and let your jaw go soft and slack.
Whatever you were holding, you may set it down now, gently, in the dark.
We are only going to wander through some very old dreams together.
So sink a little deeper, and let me begin where everything begins.
Nearly every people who ever lived has told a story of how the world began.
These are the oldest poems we have, older than writing, older than walls.
They were told in the dark, around small fires, while children fell asleep.
No one wrote them to be true the way a map is true.
They were told for comfort, and for wonder, and to answer the great quiet questions.
How did all of this come to be here, and why is there something rather than nothing?
And many of these stories begin the same gentle way.
In the beginning, they say, there was only water, dark and vast and formless.
A wide, sleeping sea with no shore, before there was anything at all.
No sky, no land, no light; only the deep and the dark and the slow.
Out of that still water, the storytellers said, everything would one day rise.
And so the first word of the oldest poems is often only this: water.
In another telling, kept by many peoples, the beginning was an egg.
Before there was a world, there floated a single egg in the dark.
Round and whole and patient, it held everything inside its quiet shell.
And in the fullness of time, so the old story goes, the egg began to crack.
Slowly the shell opened, and what was within came pouring softly out.
The upper half curved away and became the great dome of the sky.
The lower half settled down and became the wide and steady earth.
What had been one small thing became a whole world, sky above and ground below.
People in many lands, who never met, dreamed this same tender shape.
A cosmos folded into an egg, waiting in the dark to be born.
It is a kind thing to imagine, that the world hatched gently, like a bird.
And that you live now inside the open halves of that first quiet shell.
There is another old image, just as gentle, of the sky and the earth.
In the beginning, some stories say, they lay close together, pressed as one.
Sky and earth were not yet two; they leaned upon each other in the dark.
There was no room between them, no space at all where life could grow.
And so, in the telling, they were softly parted, lifted away from one another.
Some say a child raised the sky, slowly, the way you might lift a heavy blanket.
The sky rose up to become the high and open air.
The earth stayed below, and between them opened a great breathing room.
Into that new space came the wind, and the light, and at last the living.
It is a tender thought, that the world was made simply by making space.
By lifting two old friends apart, and leaving room enough for everything.
And in that room, made long ago in story, you are lying down to rest.
Far in the north, by colder fires, they told of a great tree.
They called it Yggdrasil, the world-tree, vast beyond all imagining.
Its roots went down through every world, deep into the dark and the spring.
Its branches lifted up and held the high and starlit sky.
All the worlds, they said, were bound and joined within that one wide tree.
The living and the dead, the gods and the dew, all sheltered in its shade.
A small creature ran along its trunk, and an eagle watched from its crown.
And the tree stood through all the ages, holding everything together.
Many peoples have dreamed of such a tree, joining the worlds with root and branch.
A green and patient thing, older than the gods, quietly keeping the whole.
It is good to imagine the world as a tree, growing slowly in the dark.
And to feel yourself a small leaf upon it, safely held, gently swaying.
And there is one more story, told across many lands, that is the softest of all.
In the beginning there was only the endless water, with no land anywhere.
The creatures of that first world swam and floated, looking for a place to rest.
And one small animal, brave and humble, said it would dive down to look.
Down it went, into the cold and the dark, deeper than anyone had gone.
It dived until its breath was nearly gone, all the way to the floor of the sea.
And there, on the very bottom, it found a little mud upon its paws.
Up it swam, slowly, holding that small scrap of earth, and surfaced gasping.
The mud was set down, no bigger than a handful, in the middle of the water.
And gently, gently, it began to grow, and spread, and become all the land.
Every field and forest, the storytellers said, grew from that little diver's gift.
From one small, tired animal, doing one brave thing, in the quiet of the deep.
These were never meant as facts, and you need not believe a single one.
They were humanity's first quiet answers, whispered into the listening dark.
Long before us, by the fire, someone wondered, and made a story out of love.
And here you are, so many years later, held inside those same old words.
You belong to a long-told world, imagined and re-imagined with great care.
Out of dark water, out of an egg, out of parted sky, out of a little mud.
However it began, it ends, for tonight, in this warm and quiet room.
You are a small and welcome part of a story far older than yourself.
There is nothing more to listen for now, and nothing left to hold.
Let the old stories fold themselves away, gently, like a closing shell.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Phoenix
lines: Let the day settle now, like dust drifting slowly down through a quiet evening light.
There is nothing here to remember, nothing to hold, nothing you need to carry into this hour.
Let your shoulders grow heavy, and let the bed take their weight for you.
The words will drift past you like soft rain on a far window, and you can let them go.
You do not have to follow them, or keep them, or do anything at all.
Feel your breath move on its own, slow and easy, in and gently out.
Your hands grow warm and still, and your face softens, and your jaw lets go.
Let the rain outside keep its own gentle time, asking nothing of you.
This is an old, kind story, told only to ease you toward sleep.
So let your eyes rest, and your thoughts loosen, and your whole body grow warm and heavy.
There is all the time in the world, and none of it is yours to keep tonight.
Just breathe, and rest, and let the story carry you the rest of the way.
Long ago, people told of a single bird, more radiant than any other in the world.
Its feathers caught the light like embers and gold, warm as a hearth at evening.
There was only ever one of these birds at any time, living quietly somewhere in the world.
It was said to live for a very long age, far longer than any of us, near five hundred years.
Through all those long years it sang a low and lovely song that few were ever lucky to hear.
And when at last its time drew near, the bird felt no fear at all.
It simply knew, the way we know when evening comes and it is time to rest.
So it gathered fragrant things, sprigs of cinnamon and myrrh, sweet spices and dry twigs.
From these it built a soft and fragrant nest, high in a quiet place, like a bed at the end of a day.
The whole nest smelled of warm spice and sunlight, a gentle place to lie down.
And there the old bird settled in, calm and unhurried, ready for what would come.
For this was never an ending, only the long, slow turning toward something new.
Then, in a gentle warmth, the nest of spices began softly to glow.
The old tale tells it not as a fearful thing, but as quiet as a lamp being lit.
The bird was not lost in that warmth, but eased, the way you are eased into sleep.
And from the warm and fragrant ashes, something tender began to stir.
A new bird rose, young and bright, born of the very one that had rested there.
It was the same phoenix, made new again, with fresh feathers the colour of dawn.
Nothing had truly been lost, you see, only renewed, only made young once more.
Because there was only ever one, the bird was never truly gone from the world.
It simply slipped from old to new, the way morning slips quietly out of night.
And this, the storytellers said, is how the phoenix lives on and on through the ages.
An ending that was really a beginning, soft and certain as the rising sun.
Rest in that thought a while, and let your breath go slow and easy.
Far back in old Egypt, by the wide and patient river, they told of a bird called the Bennu.
The Bennu was joined in their minds to the sun, and to the gentle promise of rebirth.
They said that at the very dawn of the world, when all was still and new, it came to rest.
It alighted upon a single stone that rose from the first quiet waters.
And its soft cry was said to be the first sound, the beginning of all that would be.
Each morning, as the sun climbed warm above the river, people thought of that bird.
For the sun itself was a kind of phoenix, setting only so that it might rise again.
The Greek writer Herodotus, travelling long ago, heard this old story and set it down.
He wrote of the radiant bird and its long life and its gentle renewal, so we would remember.
And so the tale was carried across the years, from one quiet voice to the next.
Down through all the ages it came, gentle and unhurried, until it reached you here tonight.
Let it settle over you now, warm as evening, and let your body grow heavier still.
And it was not only one land that dreamed of a bird of renewal.
Far to the east, in China, they spoke of the fenghuang, graceful and serene.
The fenghuang was a sign of peace, appearing in times of calm and gentle harmony.
Its arrival was thought a quiet blessing, a promise that good and gentle days were near.
In the old Slavic tales there glowed the firebird, with feathers of living light.
A single feather of the firebird could fill a dark room with soft, warm radiance.
And in Persia they told of the simurgh, ancient and patient and kind.
The simurgh was so old it was said to have seen the world begin and end three times over.
It nested high in a faraway tree, and watched over wanderers with a gentle, knowing eye.
Many lands, many names, and yet the same soft idea, told over and over.
That light returns, that what seems to end comes round again, renewed and whole.
Different birds, different voices, all singing the same quiet, hopeful song.
Let that song hum somewhere beneath your breath now, slow and warm and low.
The phoenix has always been a gentle symbol, never a fearful one.
It is like the sun, which sets each evening only so that it may rise again at dawn.
It is like the year itself, turning slowly from the deep of winter back toward spring.
The cold months come, the trees go bare, and still beneath the frost the green is waiting.
And in time the thaw arrives, soft and certain, and the world grows young again.
Nothing is truly lost in all that turning, only carried gently forward into something new.
You know this turning, too, more closely than you might think.
Each night you lay down the long day, and let it loosen and fall away from you.
And each morning you rise renewed, made new by the quiet work of rest.
Sleep is its own small phoenix, a gentle fire that warms and never harms.
It takes the tired weight of the day and, by morning, makes it soft and new again.
So you, too, are quietly renewed each night, made ready for the coming light.
So let the story fade now, the way warm embers settle into a gentle glow.
There is nothing left to follow, nothing to hold, nothing to do at all.
The radiant bird rests in its fragrant nest, and you rest in your own warm bed.
Like the bird, you are not ending tonight, only easing softly into renewal.
Let your breath grow slow and quiet, in and gently out, like a far and falling rain.
Feel how heavy and warm your body has become, sinking deeper with each soft breath.
Whatever the day asked of you is over now, and you may set it down for good.
Trust that the morning will come, gentle and bright, the way it always quietly does.
And you will rise from this rest made new, the way the phoenix always does.
For now there is only the warmth, and the rain, and the soft dark holding you.
Let yourself sink, and soften, and slip away.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Selkie
lines: Settle in now, and let your body grow heavy and warm.
There is nothing here to remember, nothing to hold onto.
The words will drift by like slow water, and you may let them.
Somewhere close, the sea is breathing in and out against the shore.
You can feel that rhythm if you like, the long pull and the soft return.
Let your shoulders soften, and let the back of your neck grow loose.
Each breath out is a little heavier than the last.
You do not need to listen carefully; you only need to rest.
If your thoughts wander off, that is fine, let them wander.
The tide will carry them, and bring you nothing but quiet.
Outside, the moon is rising over the grey and gentle water.
And here, in the warm dark, you are safe, and you are home.
On the cold and rocky shores of the northern seas, people told an old tale.
In Scotland and Ireland, in the Faroes and in Iceland, the story was the same.
They spoke of the selkies, the gentle seal-folk of the deep grey water.
By day and by night, the selkies live as seals, slipping through the cold tide.
They are at home there, among the kelp and the slow swaying light.
But on certain quiet nights, when the moon lays a silver path across the sea, they come ashore.
They haul themselves up onto the smooth wet stones of the empty beach.
And there, in the moonlight, they slip off their soft grey sealskins.
Beneath the skin, each selkie stands in human form, graceful and gentle.
They have dark eyes, deep as the sea itself, calm and full of old kindness.
And on the cool pale sand they dance, slow and easy, while the waves keep time.
When the night thins toward morning, they take up their skins and slip home beneath the waves.
There is one old story that the people loved to tell, soft and a little wistful.
It is the story of a selkie who, one moonlit night, came up onto the sand to dance.
She set her sealskin down upon a stone, as the seal-folk always do.
But that night her skin was lost to her, hidden away, folded and tucked from sight.
Without her sealskin she could not return to the water she belonged to.
So she stayed, and she lived a quiet while among the people of the land.
She was kind, and she was loving, and she was gentle in all her ways.
She learned the small warm things of human life, the hearth and the bread and the lamp.
And yet there was always a stillness in her, a softness that did not quite belong.
Often she would turn, without quite meaning to, to gaze at the grey water.
She carried a longing in her, quiet as the tide, a soft and salt-edged ache for the sea.
It was never bitter, only deep, the gentle pull of a home she had not forgotten.
The years passed kindly, and she was loved, and she gave her love in return.
She walked the shore in the evenings and listened to the long sigh of the waves.
She knew the sea was waiting, patient and wide, the way the sea always waits.
On still nights she thought she could hear the seals singing, far out in the dark.
Their voices came soft across the water, low and sweet, calling her name without words.
She did not feel afraid, and she did not feel sad, only quietly homesick.
For there is a place each of us belongs to, and the heart remembers it always.
Hers was the cool green water, the slow drift, the company of the seal-folk.
And so she waited, gentle and unhurried, the way the moon waits to rise.
She trusted that the sea would not forget her, for the sea forgets nothing.
Every breath of the tide was a small promise, whispered again and again.
Home is still here, it seemed to say, and home is always waiting for you.
Then one quiet day, when the light lay soft and silver on the floor, she found it.
There, folded away in a still and dusty corner, was her own grey sealskin.
She knew it at once, the way you know your own name, the way you know home.
She lifted it with great tenderness, smoothing the soft fur with her hands.
There was no anger in her, and no haste, only a deep and quiet gladness.
She gave her thanks for the kindness she had known among the people of the land.
And then, as the moon rose and laid its silver path across the water, she went down to the shore.
She stood at the edge of the sea, where the waves slipped warm around her feet.
Gently, gently, she drew the sealskin on, and she was herself again, whole and complete.
She slipped beneath the surface, into the cool dark water where she truly belonged.
The sea closed over her like a soft blanket drawn up in the night.
And at last, after the long quiet years, the selkie had come home.
They say the seals swim near that shore still, on the quiet nights when the moon is high.
They linger close to the land they once walked, watching with their dark and gentle eyes.
And softly, softly, they sing, their voices rising and falling with the tide.
It is not a mournful song, but a tender one, full of belonging and of peace.
It is a song that says home is near, that the way back is always open.
This is not a frightening tale, and it was never meant to frighten anyone.
It is a gentle story, about the deep and patient pull of home.
About the quiet joy of returning to the place where you belong.
We all carry a sealskin somewhere within us, a memory of where we are most at ease.
And the sea, wide and patient, is always there, holding our place for us.
The waves go on lapping the smooth stones, slow and steady and kind.
And the moon lays down its silver path, the long road that leads us home.
So let the story settle now, soft as the tide drawing back from the sand.
You do not need to hold any of it; let the words slip away like seafoam.
Your body is heavy and warm, sinking gently into the quiet dark.
The sea breathes on, slow and steady, and your breath is slowing with it.
Far out on the water, the seals are singing low, and all is well.
There is nowhere you need to be, and nothing left to do.
You are home, and you are safe, and the night will hold you kindly.
Let the longing ease, and let the quiet come, soft as moonlight on the waves.
Each breath carries you a little deeper into rest.
The silver path is laid out before you, leading gently into sleep.
You belong here, in this warm and easy dark.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Oak
lines: There is nothing you need to do now, and nowhere else you need to be.
Let the bed take all of your weight, and let your shoulders grow heavy and soft.
Breathe in slowly, gently, and let the breath out longer still.
The dark around you is warm and safe, and it asks nothing of you.
You do not have to remember any of this; you can simply let it wash over you.
If you like, picture yourself walking quietly into an old, still forest.
The light is low and green, and the air is cool and kind.
Somewhere ahead of you stands a single great tree, wide and patient.
You do not have to reach it; you only have to rest here and breathe.
Let your hands grow loose, your jaw unclench, your eyes settle.
Each breath out lets you sink a little further into the quiet.
There is all the time in the world, and none of it belongs to anyone but you.
Let yourself grow heavy, slow, and calm.
The great tree before you is an oak, and oaks belong to a wide old family.
Their family name is Quercus, and there are around five hundred kinds of them.
They grow all across the northern world, in forests cool and warm alike.
The one in old country lanes is the English oak, broad and gnarled and kind.
An oak is in no hurry at all; it grows slowly, ring by ring, year by year.
Each quiet summer lays down a single pale ring beneath its bark.
It does nothing quickly, and it does not need to.
It simply stands, and widens, and waits, season after season.
Imagine that slowness as something you could borrow for a while.
There is no rush in the tree, and there need be no rush in you.
You have nowhere to be and nothing to finish tonight.
Let your breath grow long and slow, like the slow turning of the years.
An oak can live for a very long time, far longer than we do.
Many last hundreds of years, and a few of the oldest pass a thousand.
There is an old country saying about how an oak spends its life.
Three hundred years it spends growing, slowly reaching up and out.
Three hundred more it spends simply living, broad and full and strong.
And three hundred it spends gently, gracefully growing old.
So the tree you are picturing may have stood through long-forgotten lives.
It was here before, and it will likely be here after, and that is a comfort.
It has weathered countless winters without worry, and felt no fear.
You can let it carry that patience for you, just for tonight.
There is nothing to hurry toward and nothing to hold.
Breathe out, and let yourself rest into that long, unhurried calm.
A single oak is not really alone; it is a whole quiet kingdom.
More creatures live upon an oak than upon almost any other tree.
In Britain alone, hundreds of kinds of small lives lean on one oak.
Insects and birds, mossy lichens and soft fungi, mice and small beasts.
Each finds a home in its bark, its leaves, its hollows and its roots.
The tree gives shelter to them all and asks nothing for it.
Imagine all that gentle life, settling down for the night as you are.
The small birds tuck their heads beneath their wings high in the leaves.
Everything in the tree is slowing, quieting, growing still.
You are part of that settling now, one more small life drifting down.
There is room here for you to rest, and you are welcome.
Let the breath fall away from you softly, and sink a little deeper now.
The seed of the oak is the acorn, small and smooth in its little cup.
Most years the tree makes only a few, but now and then comes a special year.
In that year, which is called a mast year, it pours out acorns all at once.
It makes far more than the hungry animals could ever eat.
So a few are always left over, and those few become new trees.
Jays and squirrels gather the acorns and bury them away to keep.
But they are forgetful, and they leave many hidden in the soil.
And so the forgetful jay, without ever meaning to, plants whole forests.
It carries acorns far from the parent tree, and quietly makes more woods.
There is something kind in that, in forgetting, and in letting things grow.
You too may let things slip away now; you do not need to hold them.
Breathe out slowly, and let your thoughts settle like acorns into soft earth.
Beneath the tree, hidden in the dark soil, something gentle is happening.
The oak's roots are joined to fine threads of fungus, finer than hair.
They weave together into a vast, quiet web spread through the ground.
The tree gives the threads a little sugar, and they give it water in return.
Through this hidden web, trees can share, and even softly signal to each other.
So no oak is truly alone underground; it is gently held by all the rest.
Its roots reach down and out, deep and steady, holding it still.
Nothing up above can shake what is rooted so calmly below.
Feel, if you can, that same deep rootedness settling through you now.
You are held, and steady, and there is nothing to brace against.
Let your whole body grow heavy and rooted into the bed.
Breathe out long and slow, and let yourself be held, and sink deeper still.
People have loved and leaned on the oak for a very long time.
Its wood is dense and strong, and it resists rot for years and years.
Long ago it built the beams of great halls and the hulls of old ships.
And the barrels of oak still cradle wine and whisky as they slowly age.
From its bark people once made ink, and softened leather, in the old way.
And many old peoples held the oak as sacred, a tree to gather beneath.
Tall lone oaks are so often touched by lightning that the thunder gods took them.
Now, though, you can let all of that drift quietly away.
You do not have to picture the forest any longer, nor the great old tree.
Let the images soften and dissolve into the warm dark around you.
There is nothing left to think about, and nothing left to do.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Bamboo
lines: There is nothing you need to do now, and nowhere you need to be.
The day is behind you, and you can let it lie there, finished and quiet.
Feel the weight of your body settling down into the bed, heavier with each breath.
Let your shoulders soften, and let them drop a little further than you thought they could.
Breathe in slowly, and then let the breath go, long and easy, like something being set down.
The dark around you is warm and safe, and it asks nothing of you at all.
You are allowed to be exactly as tired as you are.
Imagine, if you like, a green grove of bamboo standing tall in a soft and steady rain.
The tall canes lean a little in the wind, and the rain whispers down through the leaves.
There is nothing to remember here, and nothing to hold.
Let your hands rest open, and let your jaw unclench.
Each breath out lets you sink a little deeper toward sleep.
Stay here a while, in the warm dark, with the rain falling softly on the leaves.
It is a curious thing, that bamboo standing so tall in the rain.
For all its height, it is not a tree at all.
Bamboo is a grass, a giant member of the same gentle family as the grass in a meadow.
There are well over a thousand kinds of it growing across the warm parts of the world.
Some stay small and feathery, and some rise as high as a building, swaying far above your head.
Yet every one of them is a grass, the same soft green family that bends underfoot.
Picture that for a moment, a whole forest made of grass, hushed and dripping in the rain.
The canes lean together and apart, leaning together and apart, in no hurry at all.
There is something restful in a thing so tall that is, underneath, so soft and simple.
You do not need to understand it; you only need to let the picture hold you.
The rain keeps falling, slow and even, and the grove keeps its quiet.
Let your breath grow slow and even too, in time with that gentle rain.
Breathe out, and let yourself sink a little further down toward sleep.
Of all the green and growing things, bamboo grows the fastest of any plant on Earth.
Some kinds can grow most of a metre in a single day, almost fast enough to watch.
A new shoot pushes up out of the ground already as thick as it will ever be.
It does not widen as it climbs; it only rises, taller and taller, in its quiet hurry.
And yet for all that speed, there is no noise to it, only the soft unfolding of leaves.
Imagine standing in the grove at dawn, and the young canes higher than they were the day before.
Everything growing, gently and ceaselessly, while the rain keeps falling on the leaves.
You do not have to keep up with anything; you can simply lie still and let it grow without you.
There is a deep ease in watching something rise so fast and so silently.
The world goes on growing in the dark, and asks nothing of you tonight.
Let that thought settle over you like a soft blanket.
Feel your breathing slow, and feel your limbs grow heavy and warm.
Breathe out, long and easy, and let the night carry you a little closer to sleep.
Lay your hand, in your mind, against one of the tall green canes.
A bamboo stem is called a culm, and inside it is hollow, like a long quiet flute.
It is divided along its length by solid walls at each joint, which are called the nodes.
That hollow, jointed build is the secret of it: astonishingly light, and yet remarkably strong.
So it can bend far over in the wind, lean almost to the ground, and spring back unbroken.
Hidden in its walls are tiny grains of silica, the same stuff as glass and sand.
Those small bright grains stiffen the cane, and some bamboo rivals steel for its strength.
It does not fight the wind; it yields to it, and in yielding it survives.
There is a lesson in that, soft enough to hold while you are falling asleep.
You too can bend tonight, and let the day's weight pass through you and away.
There is nothing rigid you need to keep holding upright.
Let your body go loose and yielding, easy as a cane in the rain.
Breathe out, and bend, and let yourself drift a little nearer to sleep.
When you look across a grove of bamboo, you think you are seeing many separate canes.
But often a whole grove is a single plant, one living thing standing in many places at once.
Beneath the soil it is joined by creeping stems called rhizomes, threading through the dark earth.
So all the tall canes you see may share one quiet root, drinking from the same hidden ground.
What looks like a crowd is really one being, breathing together in the rain.
And bamboo feeds the great gentle panda almost entirely, leaf after patient leaf.
It shelters and feeds countless smaller creatures too, all sheltering under one connected plant.
Picture that one great rooted life, calm and unhurried beneath the falling rain.
You are part of something larger too, held and rooted, even here in the dark.
You do not have to do anything to belong to it; you only have to rest.
Let the picture of that single quiet root spread its calm through you.
Feel yourself rooted in the warm bed, safe and still and held.
Breathe out slowly, and let the grove's deep quiet draw you toward sleep.
Bamboo keeps one strange and beautiful secret across its long, slow life.
Many kinds flower only once, after waiting decades, sometimes a hundred years or more.
And then, all at once, every plant of that kind across the whole world flowers together.
They set their seed in the same season, far apart yet somehow in time, and then they die together.
In parts of India one such bamboo blooms about every half-century, an event long known there.
People have used the gentle cane for almost everything you can imagine over the years.
Scaffolding that holds up tall buildings, and paper, and water pipes, and smooth cool floors.
Hollow flutes, whose breathy notes are simply the wind passing through the empty cane.
The first glowing thread in an early electric lightbulb was a fine fibre of bamboo.
In East Asia it is loved as a sign of humble strength, bending low under snow and rising unbroken.
It is counted among the noble plants, a quiet friend of the cold winter.
Let those soft old stories drift through you and then gently fade.
Breathe out, and let the flute notes and the rain blur into one soft sound that carries you toward sleep.
Now you can let all of it go, the canes and the rain and the long slow stories.
There is nothing left to remember, and nothing more to learn tonight.
Let the green grove soften and dim, and let the rain quiet to a faraway hush.
Let the tall canes fade into the dark, gentle and unguarded.
Feel how heavy and warm your body has become, sinking down into the bed.
Each breath out carries you a little further from the day, a little nearer to sleep.
You have bent enough today, and now you can simply be still.
There is nothing holding you upright, and nothing you must keep.
The dark is soft around you, and you are safe inside it.
Let your thoughts go loose, like leaves drifting down in the rain.
You can let yourself bend, and soften, and sink.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Baobab
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like warm air.
Imagine the day has gone, and a soft African night is settling all around you, dark and kind.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Out in that warm darkness, picture a great wide tree standing alone against a deepening sky.
It is huge and still and patient, and it asks nothing of you at all.
The crickets are singing low in the dusk, and the air is warm against your skin.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the night.
That great tree you are picturing grows in the dry warm country of the world.
You find it across Africa, on the island of Madagascar, and in the far north of Australia.
The grand old African one has a long and gentle name, Adansonia, but you need not keep it.
It is sometimes called the upside-down tree, and there is a soft reason for the name.
In the dry season its bare branches spread thin and bare, like roots clutching gently at the sky.
An old story says the gods planted it upside down, with its roots left waving in the air.
So it stands there in the dusk, looking as though it grew the wrong way round, and somehow content.
There is something tender in that, a tree that wears its roots up against the stars.
Picture it now, that wide dark crown reaching softly into the night above you.
You do not have to remember its name, or where it grows, or any of these small facts.
Let them pass like the warm night breeze, here for a moment and then gone.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Now let your eyes wander down the tree, to its great wide trunk in the dark.
The trunk is enormous and swollen, far thicker than you would ever expect a tree to be.
And inside that vast soft trunk, the baobab is quietly keeping something precious.
Its wood is soft and fibrous, and it holds water, like a great patient barrel made of living wood.
A big old baobab can store many thousands of litres of water inside its swollen body.
When the rains come, it drinks deeply, swelling fuller, taking in all that it can.
Then, through the long dry months, it spends that water slowly, gently, never in a hurry.
So it carries its own quiet drink with it, through season after season of dust and sun.
Imagine all that cool water held softly within the warm dark heart of the tree.
It holds it without effort, the way you are holding your own slow breath right now.
There is no striving in it, only patience, only the quiet keeping of what it needs.
Let that calm keeping settle over you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried.
Feel yourself growing fuller and softer too, as you settle further into the dark.
Now let your mind rest on something stranger still about this great old tree.
The baobab is among the longest-lived of all the flowering trees on Earth.
Some of them reach an age of one or even two thousand years, standing quietly all that while.
Careful scientists, dating the wood with great patience, found some older than almost any broadleaf tree alive.
Think of the long line of nights such a tree has watched over, one after another after another.
It was already old when your great grandparents were young, and older still before them.
Whole lifetimes of people have passed beneath it, while it simply went on standing in the dusk.
Old baobabs often grow hollow inside, opening a great living room within the trunk.
People have sheltered in these hollows, and kept small shops there, and met to talk in their cool dark.
In one strange and wonderful case, a hollow baobab was even made into a tiny bush bar.
Picture that, a room of living wood, holding people gently the way it holds its water.
Let that long, slow age pour into you now, softening your every thought.
There is no hurry anywhere in such a tree; let it teach your breath to slow.
The baobab is known by another kind name, the tree of life, and it earns it well.
It gives so much, quietly, to all the creatures and the people who live near it.
Its large fruit, sometimes called monkey-bread, is rich in the gentle vitamin that keeps us well.
Its leaves can be eaten, and its bark gives strong fibre for making rope and cloth.
It shades whole villages from the heavy sun, and feeds them, and shelters them, year upon year.
So it is not only old and strange, but generous, giving freely and asking nothing back.
And in recent years, sadly, several of the very oldest and largest baobabs have died quite suddenly.
Scientists watching them gently suspect a changing, warming world is troubling these ancient trees.
There is a soft sorrow in that, in the passing of such patient and giving old lives.
But the one you are picturing still stands, dark and whole, against the warm night sky.
Let it stand there for you now, calm and giving, in no danger in this quiet dark.
Let that gentleness hold you, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
There is one last lovely thing the baobab does, and it does it only in the dark.
Its flowers are large and white, and they open only at night, when the world has gone to sleep.
Each great flower lasts but a single night, blooming once in the warm dark and then fading away.
And in that one night, small creatures come softly through the dark to visit them.
Fruit bats drift in on quiet wings, and bushbabies climb close, drawn by the flowers' sweet scent.
They carry the tree's pollen from bloom to bloom under the stars, while the day-world sleeps on.
So even the making of the next baobab happens quietly, in the dark, away from the sun.
Far away on Madagascar, a famous avenue of giant baobabs stands like ancient pillars by an old road.
Some of those great trees are many centuries old, lined up against the dusk like patient guardians.
Picture them now, dark shapes against the last light, holding still as the night comes down.
A tree that holds its water through the drought, and blooms only in the dark, asks you only to rest.
Let that long patience pour into you, slowing your breath, softening your every thought.
Let yourself grow as still and as quiet as a tree that has watched a thousand nights.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the great wide trunk and the upside-down branches fade gently away into the dark.
Let the white night flowers close and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a great old tree is at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that patient tree, holding its water, asking nothing, simply standing still.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the night is soft all around you.
Like the baobab, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no pressure on you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the tree gathers the rain and holds it close.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Cherry Blossom
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to remember.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words; let them pass over you like a soft spring rain.
Imagine the room around you has gone quiet and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the easing along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that darkness, picture pale petals beginning to drift slowly down through the still air.
They fall the way the softest snow falls, without sound, without hurry, asking nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little further, the way a single petal settles gently to the ground.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
Those pale petals you are picturing belong to the cherry tree, the one they call sakura in Japan.
The flowering cherries are a kind of plum tree, close cousins of the cherry that bears fruit.
But these are not grown for any fruit at all; they are grown only for their brief clouds of blossom.
For a few days each spring, a single tree can hold what looks like a soft pink storm among its branches.
The colour is gentle, somewhere between white and the faintest blush of rose.
And then, almost as soon as it has come, the blossom begins to let go and drift down.
There is no need to hold any of these names in your mind; let them settle and fall away.
Picture only the slow falling, the pale petals turning over and over as they sink through the calm air.
Imagine standing beneath such a tree, looking up into a sky softened with blossom.
There is nothing to do there but watch, and breathe, and let the petals come down.
Let that quiet picture rest lightly in you, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, drifting a little, as you settle further into the warm dark.
The most beloved of all these trees is a single old kind called the Somei-yoshino.
Long ago it began as one chance crossing of two cherries, just one tree, found and treasured.
It cannot be grown reliably from its own seed, so every new tree is made by grafting a piece of the old.
That means nearly every Somei-yoshino in the world is a twin of all the others, the same tree many times over.
And because they are all the same, they all feel the spring in the same way.
When the warmth arrives, they open their blossom together, as if at one slow shared breath.
A whole avenue of them can come into flower in the same few days, a single pale wave moving along the street.
Imagine that quiet agreement among the trees, all of them waking to the warmth as one.
There is something restful in it, in all those branches breathing out their blossom at the same moment.
You need not picture it sharply; let it be soft, a pale haze gathering above you in the dark.
Let the image grow gentle and blurred at its edges, the way things do as sleep draws near.
And let your breath grow long and unhurried, falling slowly, the way the petals fall.
The blossom does not last; that is the heart of it, and the whole of its quiet beauty.
A cherry tree holds its flower for only a week or two, and often it falls at its very peak.
Just when it is at its loveliest, the petals begin to let go and come drifting down.
In Japan this passing is not mourned so much as loved, loved for the very fact that it will not stay.
There is a tender old phrase for the feeling it stirs, mono no aware, the gentle sadness of things that pass.
It is the soft ache you feel for something beautiful precisely because you know it is fleeting.
For more than a thousand years, people have gathered beneath these trees simply to watch the blossom.
They call it hanami, the flower viewing, a custom older than almost any other still kept today.
It began long ago in the old imperial court, and it has been carried gently down all the years since.
People sit on the ground beneath the branches, and look up, and let the petals fall around them.
There is a deep peace in loving a thing that does not last, in letting it be enough that it is here now.
Let that thought soften you, and let your breath fall slow, here in this passing quiet hour.
Nothing here needs to stay; let it come, and let it go, and breathe slowly out.
The blossom is woken by warmth, but only after the tree has felt a proper cold winter first.
The tree must feel the chill, and then the slow thaw, before it will open a single flower.
In its own quiet way it is counting the seasons, waiting until the year has truly turned.
When the warmth at last comes north across the land, the flowering follows it like a slow tide.
People speak of a blossom front, a soft wave of flowering that sweeps up the country with the spring.
It begins in the warm south and travels north, tree by tree, town by town, week by week.
And people follow its forecast, waiting for the front to reach their own street, their own park.
Imagine that gentle wave of pink moving slowly across a whole country, in no hurry at all.
In one old city, in Kyoto, people have written down the blossom dates for more than a thousand years.
Those quiet records are among the oldest of their kind anywhere in the world.
And read all together, they show the long slow warming of the world, written in petals across the centuries.
Let that long patient keeping of time settle over you, and let your own breathing slow.
When the wind comes at last and lifts the spent petals, they fall all at once in soft drifts.
People have a name for it, a blossom blizzard, a pale pink snow that fills the air and gathers on the path.
Imagine that now, the petals coming down all around you, settling on the dark ground without a sound.
They drift into the corners and along the water, a gentle pink snow that no one needs to sweep away.
And the trees let them go entirely, holding nothing back, giving the whole of their blossom to the wind.
That letting go is not a loss to them; it is simply the turning of the season, easy and complete.
More than a hundred years ago, as a gift of friendship, Japan sent flowering cherries far across the sea.
They were planted by the water in Washington, and they still bloom there beside it every spring.
So the same pale blossom now opens on the far side of the world, carried there as a kindness.
Picture those petals falling onto still water, drifting out slowly, turning the surface soft and pink.
There is nothing in any of it that clings; everything is given, and everything is let go.
Let your body learn that ease now, the gentle letting go, releasing its weight into the dark.
Let each breath out be a small letting go, the way the tree lets its blossom fall.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the names and the seasons and the far cities fade gently away into the dark.
Let the pale petals slow as they fall, the way the world slows as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere the blossom is drifting softly down, as you are.
There is a deep peace in things that do not last, in letting them come and letting them go.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word that was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the tree in the wind, you have only to let go, and let the quiet carry you down.
Let the warm dark gather you the way the still ground gathers the petals and lets them rest.
You are exactly where you need to be, and the season is turning gently, without any effort from you.
Let the last petals settle.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Atlantis
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like a slow tide.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture, if you like, a wide stretch of calm green water, smooth and unhurried beneath a dim sky.
You begin to sink gently through it, slow and weightless, with nothing to fear and nothing to do.
Far below you, resting on the soft floor of the sea, there is a quiet sleeping city, dim and still.
Each slow breath lets you settle a little further, the way a feather drifts down through still water.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That sleeping city you are picturing has a name you may know, the lost city of Atlantis.
But here is the gentlest secret of it, the soft truth at its heart: it was never a real place at all.
Atlantis began as a story, a tale told by an old Greek thinker named Plato, long, long ago.
He set it down in two of his writings, the Timaeus and the Critias, about two thousand four hundred years past.
He wrote of a great island kingdom, mighty and proud, far out beyond the edges of the world he knew.
It lay, he said, past the Pillars of Hercules, the narrow gate where the inner sea meets the wide ocean.
And in his telling it was vast, larger than the lands of Libya and Asia laid together.
It is a beautiful invention, a city dreamed onto the water by a man with something quiet to teach.
You do not have to decide whether to believe it; you may simply let the lovely picture float by.
There is a deep ease in that, in letting a story be only a story, asking nothing more of it.
Let that ease settle over you now, soft as the water closing gently overhead.
Feel your breath grow slow and long, and let yourself sink a little deeper into the warm dark.
Plato gave a kind name to where the tale had come from, to make it feel old and true.
He said it had been carried home from Egypt by a wise Athenian named Solon, who heard it from the priests there.
From Solon, he wrote, it passed down through the years until at last it reached his own quiet pages.
It is a gentle thread of storytellers, each handing the tale onward, like a candle passed from hand to hand.
Yet most who study these things believe Plato wove the whole of it himself, the Egypt and the priests and all.
He made it, they think, as a teacher makes a parable, a story shaped to carry a single soft idea.
And so the lost city was lost from the very first, lost because it was only ever made of words.
There is nothing sad in that; the most enduring places are often the ones that were only ever imagined.
It has outlasted real cities, this dreamed one, kept alive by nothing but the telling and retelling.
Let that thought rest lightly upon you, that a thing can endure simply by being lovely to imagine.
Picture the dim city below you still, untroubled by whether it is true, content to be at rest.
And let your own breathing slow to match its stillness, easy and unhurried, as you settle further down.
In Plato's story, Atlantis was not destroyed for any small thing; it was a tale about pride.
The people there were once noble and simple and good, and for a long while they lived gently and well.
But over the slow turning of years they grew greedy and proud, and forgot the quiet wisdom of their fathers.
And so, the story goes, the gods turned away, and the sea was allowed to rise and take them.
In a single day and a single night, Plato wrote, the whole great island slipped beneath the waves.
It is less a map than a mirror, this tale, a warning held up softly against the pride of any people.
The real Atlantis, if it lived anywhere, lived in that lesson, not on any shore you could ever find.
There is something almost tender in it, a city sunk not by chance but to teach us to stay humble and kind.
You need carry none of that weight tonight; the lesson can keep, and the story can simply soothe you.
Let the moral loosen its hold, and let the picture remain, calm water closing over a quiet place.
Feel how safe you are here in the dark, with no pride to lose and nothing to be taken from you.
Let your breath fall slow and deep, and let the gentle dark gather a little closer around you.
Plato described his imagined city with great love, and his picture is a soft and lovely one to hold.
He set it in rings, circles of land and water nested one inside the next, calm and orderly.
At the very heart stood a low green hill, and upon it a temple given over to Poseidon, lord of the sea.
Around it ran wide canals where boats moved slowly, and bridges crossed from ring to ring.
He told of springs there, one warm and one cool, rising side by side from the patient ground.
And he spoke of walls sheathed in shining metal, gleaming softly so the whole place seemed to glow.
It is the kind of city you might build in a dream, perfect and unhurried, made only to be beautiful.
You may let your sinking self drift slowly above those quiet rings now, looking softly down.
See the dim temple, the still canals, the faint glimmer of old walls beneath the green water.
Nothing stirs there; it is a place wholly at rest, asking nothing, simply being lovely in the deep.
Let its stillness pour into you, soft and cool, slowing your thoughts to the pace of drifting water.
And let your breath grow long and gentle, each slow exhale carrying you nearer to sleep.
For most of the centuries since, no one thought to go looking for Atlantis at all.
It was read as Plato meant it, as philosophy, a tale to think with, never a treasure to dig up.
Only much later, a little over a hundred years ago, did people begin to dream of finding it for real.
A popular book by a man named Ignatius Donnelly stirred the longing, and soon the search was everywhere.
Since then, dreamers have placed the lost city almost anywhere you could name upon the wide Earth.
In the Atlantic, in the warm Mediterranean, off islands in the Caribbean, even beneath the ice of Antarctica.
And that, gently, is its own quiet answer; a place that can be set everywhere was truly never anywhere.
There is one faint echo some like to follow, an old Bronze Age eruption on the island of Thera, called Santorini.
When it blew, long ago, the gentle Minoan people nearby slowly faded, and some hear Atlantis in that.
But it is only a soft possible echo, not a proof; the deep sea floor holds no drowned and shining city.
No continent has ever sunk in the way the story tells, and the searchers have only found more open water.
There is a deep peace in that too, in letting the looking end, and letting a beautiful tale stay a tale.
Let the searching settle and grow quiet within you, and let your breath slow toward sleep.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the rings of the city soften, and let the shining walls dim into the gentle dark.
Let the old story loosen and float away, the way a tale fades as you slip toward sleep.
You are lying here in the warm dark, drifting easily, held and safe and entirely at rest.
There is a deep calm in still green water, and a deeper calm here in the quiet around you.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Let the lost city sleep on the sea floor, undisturbed, while you sleep here in your own warm peace.
There is nowhere to journey, nothing to find, no story left to tell tonight.
Let the calm water close gently over everything, smooth and dim and still.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Shangri-La
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like a far off bell.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere beyond the dark, picture a great wall of mountains, white with snow against a deep night sky.
And cupped behind those peaks, sheltered from every wind, imagine a hidden green valley, still and warm.
It asks nothing of you; you do not have to find it, only to let yourself rest at its edge.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That hidden valley you are picturing has a name, and the name is Shangri-La.
It is gentle to know, as you lie here, that it is not a real place at all, but a place from a story.
A British writer named James Hilton dreamed it up and set it down in a novel many years ago.
The book was called Lost Horizon, and it came into the world in the early nineteen thirties.
So Shangri-La was never a spot on any map; it was made of words, the way a dream is made of sleep.
And yet, from the moment it was written, people loved it as though it had always existed somewhere.
There is a soft comfort in that, in a valley that lives only in the mind and so can never be lost.
You do not have to travel to reach it; it is already here, wherever the story is gently told.
Let it stay just as it is, imagined and safe, needing nothing from the waking world.
It is a paradise made of longing, and longing is something you may set down for the night.
Picture its quiet meadows once more, knowing they will keep, whether you remember them or not.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
In the story, Shangri-La sits high among the mountains of Tibet, far beyond the reach of any road.
It is a hidden place, a lamasery and a valley together, tucked away where almost no one ever comes.
The travellers who stumble into it find a deep and unhurried peace, the like of which they have never known.
There is no rush there, no hurry, no fretting; the days pass slowly and kindly, one into the next.
And there is a quiet wonder woven through the tale: in that sheltered valley, people age very, very slowly.
Time itself seems to run gently in Shangri-La, the years passing soft as snow, leaving the people calm and whole.
It is the dream of a place where nothing is lost too soon, where the heart is given all the time it needs.
Lying here in the dark, you can feel a little of that slowness yourself, the hours growing wide and soft.
There is no clock in this room that matters now, and nothing that the night is asking of you.
Let the minutes stretch and loosen, the way they do in that imagined valley behind the peaks.
You have all the time you could ever need, and not a single thing you must do with it.
Let your breath grow long and unhurried, slow as the falling of that quiet snow.
It is sweet to know that Hilton did not spin his valley out of nothing at all.
He drew on much older ideas, on real legends that had been told in the high mountains for centuries.
Chief among them is the Tibetan Buddhist legend of a hidden kingdom called Shambhala.
Shambhala is spoken of in sacred texts as a secret land of peace and wisdom, sheltered among the peaks.
It too is hard to reach, hidden from troubled hearts, a refuge of calm and gentle understanding.
Hilton took that old, quiet dream and gave it a new name, and so Shangri-La was gently born.
He may also have heard the tales of explorers and flower hunters who wandered the eastern Himalaya.
They told of secret gorges and lost green valleys hidden deep among the snows, half real and half wonder.
So the story is a new dream resting on much older dreams, the way one soft blanket rests upon another.
It is comforting to think how long people have wished for such a place, all down the patient years.
That wish is very old, and very kind, and tonight you may simply let it carry you toward sleep.
Let those layered legends settle over you, and let your body grow heavier still.
The story arrived at a tender moment, in the quiet years between two great and terrible wars.
The world then felt hurried and uneasy, and many hearts ached for a refuge from all the trouble.
And here came a tale of a hidden valley where the world's noise could not reach, where peace simply was.
Perhaps that is why so many people took it so deeply to heart, and held it close as their own.
The book grew wonderfully popular, and before long it was made into a famous film as well.
The dream spread far and wide, until the very word seemed to belong to everyone who longed for rest.
It is gentle to remember that you, lying here, are part of that same long line of weary hearts seeking calm.
The longing the story names is the same one that softens in you now, as the dark gathers you in.
You do not need a hidden valley tonight; you need only this bed, this breath, this quiet dark.
And the peace the travellers found in the tale is already settling, softly, over you.
Let the troubled world stay outside, far off and small, with no power to reach you here.
Let your shoulders drop, your breath slow, and the last of the day drift away.
The name became so dear that it slipped out of the story and into everyday speech.
Now, when anyone speaks of a far off, perfect, hard to reach paradise, they may simply call it a Shangri-La.
Such was its fame that a mountain retreat in the United States was once nicknamed Shangri-La as well.
That quiet place was later given a different name, and is known today as Camp David.
And in more recent years, a county in Yunnan, in China, chose to rename itself Shangri-La.
They hoped the lovely name would draw gentle travellers to their high and beautiful hills, and so it did.
But there is a soft truth tucked inside that, which you may carry kindly into sleep.
No town on any map can truly be the valley from the book, for the real magic was always the idea.
Shangri-La was never a place to be found; it was a feeling, a longing, a wish given a beautiful name.
And behind that invented name lies something very old and very true within us all.
It is the simple human wish for a sheltered, peaceful place where the heart can finally rest.
You are coming to such a place now, here in the warm dark, with nothing left to seek.
Let that wish be answered tonight, and let your breath grow long and easy.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the high white mountains fade gently away, and the green valley soften into the dark.
Let the old legends and the famous tale grow quiet, the way the world grows quiet as you sink toward sleep.
You do not need a hidden paradise, for the peace it spoke of is already here, all around you.
You are lying in the warm dark, sheltered and safe, with every road and every map far behind you.
There is no journey left to make tonight, and nothing you must find before you rest.
The longing has grown soft and small, and in its place there is only this gentle quiet.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is kind all around you.
You are exactly where you need to be, in a shelter no story could ever name.
Let the warm dark gather you up and hold you close, the way that valley held its quiet days.
There is all the time in the world, and nowhere at all that you need to go.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: El Dorado
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to chase.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like a warm evening wind.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to find, no journey waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that softness, picture a high mountain lake at dawn, round and quiet and still.
Picture green forest rising all around it, the trees breathing slowly in the cool morning air.
The water lies flat and silver, holding the pale sky, and nothing on it stirs at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink, the way the early mist sinks down and settles over still water.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Long ago, far across the warm seas, there grew a story of a man made all of gold.
It is a story people told and retold until it became one of the most famous legends in the world.
His name, in time, became El Dorado, which means simply the gilded one.
And here is the first gentle surprise: at the very beginning, El Dorado was not a place at all.
It was not a city and not a kingdom; it was only this, a single shining person.
The name belonged to a man, the gilded one, and to nothing more than that.
All the great searching that came later, all the long and weary years of it, grew out of these few quiet words.
But that is for another night; for now there is only the gilded man, and the still lake, and you.
You do not have to remember any of this, or carry it anywhere.
Let the story settle over you the way light settles softly on the surface of a calm lake.
There is no hurry in it, and there is no hurry in you.
Let your breath grow long and unhurried, and let yourself sink a little deeper into the dark.
Now let your mind drift back to that high round lake, resting in the mountains.
It is a real place, and its name is Lake Guatavita, a quiet crater lake in what is now Colombia.
It lies in the cool highlands near the city we now call Bogota, ringed by green hills.
And the gilded man was real too, or rather the gentle ceremony that gave him his name was real.
He belonged to the Muisca people, who lived in those highlands long before the searchers ever came.
When a new ruler rose among them, they would honour him at the edge of this sacred lake.
They covered his bare skin in fine gold dust, until he shone in the early light like the morning sun.
Then he was carried out onto the still water on a raft, calm and slow, with no rush at all.
And there, from the raft, he gave the lake its gifts of gold and green emeralds, letting them slip into the deep.
It was an offering, a quiet thank you to the water and the world, and nothing more.
Picture that calm raft on the silver lake, the gold sinking gently down into the dark and peaceful depths.
Let that gentle picture hold you, and let your breath grow slow and soft.
Now from far away came pale strangers in ships, the Spanish arrivals, hungry for gold.
They heard whispers of the gilded man, the one covered in gold beside a mountain lake.
But stories change shape as they pass from mouth to mouth, the way a cloud slowly changes as it drifts.
Each telling added a little more, and a little more, until the small true thing had grown very large.
The gilded man, the single shining person, swelled in the telling into a golden king.
And then the golden king became a golden city, its rooftops bright with treasure.
And then the golden city became a whole golden kingdom, glittering somewhere just beyond the trees.
So a man made of gold dust became, in the dreaming, a country made of gold.
None of it was true in that grand and glittering form, but oh, how the searchers came to believe it.
It is a soft and curious thing, how a true small ceremony can grow into a vast and shining dream.
You can let that dream blur and soften now, the way distant lights blur as your eyes grow heavy.
Let your thoughts grow loose, and let your breath carry you gently down toward sleep.
For more than a hundred years, men went searching for that golden city that was never there.
They pushed through thick jungle and over high cold mountains, certain it lay just ahead.
They were always almost there, always just past the next river, the next ridge, the next green wall of trees.
But there was no city of gold to find, because the city of gold had never truly existed.
Many of the searchers suffered on those long marches, and many of them never came home again.
They had built the shining city inside their own minds, and then spent their lives chasing it.
Far across the sea, an English adventurer named Walter Raleigh caught the same bright dream.
He made two long voyages to South America, hunting for El Dorado, and staked his very life upon it.
And still no one ever walked the golden streets, because those streets were only ever a wish.
There is a quiet sadness in it, but a gentle lesson too, about how much we will chase a glittering thought.
You, though, need chase nothing tonight; the searching can be set down and left behind.
Let it go, the way the searchers could not, and let your slow breath carry the wanting away.
Feel how good it is simply to stop looking, and to rest exactly where you are.
There came a time when people tried to reach the offerings on the bed of Lake Guatavita itself.
If the gold had truly been given to the lake, then perhaps the lake could be made to give it back.
So they tried, with great effort, to drain the quiet water and lay the bottom bare.
They cut a notch in its rim and lowered the level, and they did find some small things of gold.
But they found no city beneath the water, and no kingdom, only the lake and its old mud and its peace.
The lake kept the heart of its secret, and after all the digging it simply filled again and grew still.
Yet the real Muisca gold was never a dream; some of those beautiful old works survive to this day.
In a museum there rests a small golden raft, no larger than your hand, made long ago.
Upon it stand tiny golden figures, and at their centre the gilded ruler, just as the ceremony was.
It shows the very rite that began the whole legend, the small true thing at the root of the great dream.
So the deepest truth is a gentle one: there was real gold, and a real and sacred rite, but the glittering city was only ever a dream the searchers built for themselves.
Let that quiet truth settle over you, and let your breath grow long, and let your body grow heavy.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the golden city fade, that bright dream that was never really there, and let it cause you no more searching.
Let the long marches through the jungle grow dim and slip quietly away into the dark.
Let the gilded man and his raft drift off too, out across the still silver water.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and there is nothing left for you to find.
Picture only the quiet lake at dawn, smooth and silver, holding the soft pale sky.
Picture the gold slipping gently down through the calm water, sinking into the deep and the still.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word that was said.
There is no city to reach, no treasure to win, no journey waiting at the edge of the trees.
Like the lake, you have only to be still, and let the deep quiet hold you close.
Let go of all the searching, the way the water lets the gold sink softly out of sight.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Avalon
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like a soft grey mist.
Imagine the room around you has gone quiet and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the gentle softening along your brow.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this kind and gentle dark.
Out beyond the dark, picture a wide stretch of still grey water, calm and unhurried, going nowhere at all.
And across that water, half hidden in soft mist, imagine a small green island, low and quiet and far away.
You do not have to reach it, or even see it clearly; it is simply there, waiting in the haze.
Each breath lets you sink, the way the evening light sinks slowly over calm and silvered water.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim and far away.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That small green island you are picturing has a name, and the name is Avalon.
It is not a place you could ever sail to and find, for Avalon belongs to a story, and to a legend.
It comes to us from the old tales of King Arthur, those gentle medieval stories of knights and quiet wonders.
So it is a dreamed island, a place of the imagination, and that is exactly why it can be so restful.
No map will lead you there, and no traveller has ever truly stood upon its misty shore.
It lives only where stories live, in the soft country between waking and sleep, where you are wandering now.
And the story it tells is the kindest sort of story, a story all about rest and quiet healing.
You need not believe a word of it; you need only let it carry you, the way still water carries a small boat.
There is a deep comfort in an island that asks nothing and exists only to be a place of peace.
Let it stay there in the mist, untroubled and far off, simply a soft idea on the edge of the dark.
There is no need to hold its shape clearly, or to remember anything at all.
Let that thought rest lightly upon you, and let your breath grow slow and deep and even.
People have long said that the name Avalon comes from an old Celtic word for apple.
And so it is sometimes called the Isle of Apples, a quiet place of orchards and endless mild summer.
Picture it now, if you like, gentle rows of apple trees standing in soft and unfading light.
The evening there never deepens into harsh night, and the warmth never sharpens into heat.
It is always the kind of late summer evening when the air is soft and the day is letting go.
In that mild and golden hush, the trees stand heavy with fruit, and nothing is ever hurried or harsh.
There is no winter coming to that island, and no cold to brace against, only a long and tender calm.
It is the sort of place a tired mind dreams of, a garden where the season never turns and nothing fades.
You do not have to walk among those trees; it is enough to know they are there across the water.
An orchard in endless mild evening is a very old image of peace, and it is yours to rest within.
Let that soft and fruitful stillness settle over you, asking nothing, offering only quiet.
Let your breath grow long and unhurried, as slow as that evening that never quite ends.
Feel yourself loosening, drifting a little nearer to sleep with every gentle breath you let go.
Avalon first appears in writing many hundreds of years ago, in the twelfth century.
It comes to us from a writer named Geoffrey of Monmouth, who gathered up the old tales of King Arthur.
He wrote that Arthur's great sword was forged upon that island, in its quiet and otherworldly air.
From his pages the dream of Avalon spread outward, copied and retold, carried gently down the years.
So the island has been resting in the imagination of people for nearly a thousand years now.
For all that time, in story after story, it has stayed soft and green and half hidden in its mist.
Think of how many tired minds have pictured it across the centuries, in candlelight and in the dark.
How many people, lying down to sleep long ago, have imagined that same still water and that far green shore.
You are joining a very old and gentle company simply by picturing it now in the quiet.
There is something steadying in that, in resting your mind where so many others have found peace.
The island has outlasted them all, calm and unchanging, asking nothing, simply being there.
Let that long and patient calm pour into you, and let your shoulders grow heavy and soft.
Let your breath slow down, as slow as a tale told quietly over a thousand quiet years.
In the heart of the legend, Avalon is the place where the wounded King Arthur is taken to be healed.
After his last great battle, the story says, he is carried gently across the water toward the misty isle.
He is not described as dying there; rather he is borne away to rest, to be tended and to mend.
Picture that slow crossing, the quiet boat upon the still grey water, the soft mist parting before it.
There is no fear in it and no haste, only a wounded man being carried somewhere safe and kind.
On the island he is met by healing women, wise in medicine, chief among them one called Morgan.
She is sometimes named Morgan le Fay, and in the older tales she is a gentle keeper and a healer of harm.
So Avalon becomes a place of tending, where hurt is eased and a weary king is allowed simply to rest.
Perhaps that is the deepest comfort in it, the idea of being carried, when you are tired, to a place of care.
You do not have to row the boat or find the shore; in the dream, you are simply and gently carried there.
Let that be true for you now, the feeling of being borne softly toward rest, asking nothing in return.
Let your body grow heavier, as though you too were being carried, slow and safe, across calm water.
Let your breath grow long, and let the gentle crossing carry you nearer and nearer to sleep.
From the tale of the resting king grew a soft and famous idea, the once and future king.
The legend says that Arthur did not truly die, but only sleeps in Avalon, and may one day return.
Imagine that, a sleeping king upon a quiet island, resting through the long and patient years.
He lies there in deep peace, healing slowly, in no hurry at all to wake, untroubled by the passing time.
Much later, in the Middle Ages, monks at Glastonbury Abbey in England said they had found Arthur's grave.
They claimed to have uncovered the graves of Arthur and his queen Guinevere within their grounds.
And so people began to link the dreamed isle of Avalon with the real green hill of Glastonbury, called the Tor.
Most historians gently believe that the discovery was very likely encouraged, to draw pilgrims to the abbey.
Yet the soft idea took root all the same, and the misty low country of Somerset, once marshy and half flooded, became the place where dreamers placed their Avalon.
So a legend and a real green hill grew quietly together, and the two have stayed entwined ever since.
You need not sort the true from the dreamed; let them lie together, soft as mist over the still levels.
