There is the sleeping king, at perfect rest, and there is the quiet hill in the gentle Somerset haze.
Let that deep and patient sleep be yours as well now, and let your breath grow slow and easy and long.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the still water and the far green shore soften and fade gently away into the dark.
Let the apple trees and the sleeping king and the quiet hill drift off into the mist.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
At its heart, Avalon was only ever an image of safe rest and quiet healing across calm water.
And that gentle peace is here for you too, in the warm dark, without any island to find.
You are lying here, safe and held, and somewhere a tired king sleeps on, deeply and without fear.
Like him, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet tend you and carry you along.
There is nowhere to sail to, nothing to mend, no crossing left to make tonight.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the soft mist gathers and holds the quiet isle.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Nile
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like the current of a quiet river.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your arms and legs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture yourself lying in a small boat on wide, calm water, drifting slowly under a warm and starry night.
The water is dark and smooth, and it carries you without any effort of your own.
Tall reeds stand along the banks, whispering softly to one another as you pass.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed, and feel the gentle rocking of the water.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be carried by the quiet of the dark.
The wide water you are drifting on is a river, and it is one of the longest rivers on all the Earth.
It is called the Nile, and it flows for thousands of miles through the north-east of Africa.
It winds its slow way north, mile after patient mile, until at last it reaches the Mediterranean Sea.
There is something curious and lovely about it, something you can let your sleepy mind turn over.
Most rivers in your imagination might run down a map, but the Nile flows from south to north instead.
So along this river, up the map is downstream, and the water travels gently toward the top of the world.
For thousands of years it has flowed this way, calm and unhurried, never once needing to rush.
It carries no worry and keeps no schedule; it simply goes where the land lets it go.
Imagine all that water, moving so slowly and so surely through the long dark of the night.
It has been flowing like this since long before anyone could write its name.
Let that slow and steady motion settle into you now, the way a river settles into its bed.
Breathe out slowly, and let yourself drift a little further downstream into sleep.
This long river is not born from a single place, but gathers itself from two great branches.
One is called the White Nile, and the other is called the Blue Nile, and they travel a long way to meet.
They come together at a city named Khartoum, in the land of Sudan, and from there they flow on as one.
The White Nile rises far away to the south, among the great lakes of the warm heart of Africa.
People often trace it back toward a vast lake called Lake Victoria, lying quiet beneath the equator.
The Blue Nile rises in the high cool mountains of Ethiopia, and it brings most of the river's water.
It also brings dark, rich earth washed down from those highlands, carried gently along in the flow.
Picture those two waters, one from the southern lakes and one from the eastern hills, finding each other at last.
They mingle softly together and continue north as a single calm and shining ribbon.
For a long, long while, no one in the wider world knew where this great river truly began.
Let that gentle mystery rest in your mind, asking nothing of you, only inviting you to wonder.
And as you wonder, let your breath grow long and slow, and let your body sink deeper still.
Finding where the Nile began was once one of the great questions that travellers longed to answer.
For most of all its history, no one could say with certainty where its first waters welled up.
Searchers went looking through unmapped country, following the river toward its hidden beginnings.
It became one of the famous quests of the nineteenth century, a patient hunt for the source of the Nile.
Long before any of those searches, though, the river was already giving a quiet, faithful gift.
Each summer, in the time before great dams were built, the Nile would gently rise and flood.
It spread soft, dark, fertile mud across the land beside it, a thin layer of new and living earth.
The ancient people who lived there called their country Kemet, which means the black land.
They named it so for that dark and giving soil, the gift the flooding river left behind each year.
Year after year the water came and went, and the land grew rich and green along its banks.
Imagine that slow, dependable rhythm, the river breathing in and out across the seasons.
Let your own breath follow that gentle rhythm now, rising softly and falling soft again.
There is nothing to find tonight; let the searching go, and let yourself rest.
From that yearly gift of dark soil, one of the world's first great civilisations could quietly flourish.
It grew along a narrow ribbon of green that wound through a vast and silent desert.
On either side stretched the dry sands, but beside the water all was living and fertile and calm.
Almost all the life of ancient Egypt gathered close along the river's gentle banks.
The people leaned on the Nile for nearly everything, and it gave to them year after year.
Along the marshy edges grew a tall plant called papyrus, a soft reed standing thick in the shallows.
From that reed they made the first paper-like sheets to write upon, and small light boats to sail.
The river was their road and their calendar; it was, in a true and simple way, their life.
It even shaped where they raised their pyramids and temples, set near the water that gave them everything.
They would sail upstream when the wind blew at their backs, and drift downstream when they let the current take them.
Imagine those small boats, moving so gently on the dark water beneath the same patient stars you see.
Let yourself drift the way those boats drifted, carried softly along, asking nothing of the hours.
For thousands of years that quiet rhythm went on, the flood arriving each summer like an old friend.
People were born and grew old beside the river, and their children after them, all along its banks.
The Nile carried their boats, watered their fields, and marked the turning of their year.
Then, in more recent times, a great wall of stone was raised across the river at a place called Aswan.
This was the Aswan High Dam, and it gathered the river behind it into a vast and quiet lake.
That lake is called Lake Nasser, and it spreads wide and still across what was once dry valley.
The dam tamed the old summer flood, holding the water back and letting it out slowly, as people chose.
And so the ancient yearly flooding, that gift of dark mud, gently came to its end.
Yet the river itself flows on, as it always has, north toward the waiting sea.
It has carried life quietly for thousands of years, and it carries it still, slow and sure in the dark.
Think of all the long ages it has flowed, while countless nights came and softly passed away.
Let that deep, unhurried patience pour into you now, slowing your breath and softening every thought.
There is no hurry anywhere in this; the old river asks you only to rest.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the river and its branches and its long, quiet history fade gently away into the dark.
Let the reeds and the boats and the dark fertile soil soften and blur as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, drifting on calm water beneath a soft and starry sky.
There is a deep peace in that slow current, moving for ages, asking nothing, simply flowing on.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the river, you have only to let go, and let the gentle flow carry you onward.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no current to fight against now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the river gathers its quiet waters and bears them home.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Amazon
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them pass over you like warm rain.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture, if you like, a warm rain falling somewhere far away, on an endless green forest.
It falls without hurry, soft and steady, asking nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink, the way warm rain sinks gently into deep, dark leaves.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet hush of the dark.
That warm rain you are picturing is, somewhere on the Earth, falling onto the largest forest in the world.
Beneath it, gathering all that water, lies a river so great that no other on Earth comes near it.
It is called the Amazon, and it carries more water than any other river there is, by far.
If you took the next several great rivers of the world and added them all together, it would still carry more.
All day and all night it pours toward the sea, more water than you could ever hold in your mind.
And yet it moves without any hurry, broad and brown and patient under the dripping trees.
It is gathered from the rain you are imagining, drop by warm drop, off a million quiet leaves.
There is something soothing in a thing so vast that moves so slowly, so calmly, so sure of its way.
It does not strain or rush; it simply goes, the way water always finds its long way home.
You do not need to remember any of this, only to let it carry you, the way the river carries the rain.
Let that great slow flow move through your mind, and let your breath grow long and easy.
Feel yourself loosening, drifting a little, as you settle further into the warm dark.
Now let your mind travel far away, up to where this great river quietly begins.
It does not begin as a river at all, but as trickling snowmelt high in the Andes mountains.
There, among cold peaks near the very edge of the land, small streams of melting snow begin to gather.
Those mountains stand quite close to one ocean, the Pacific, almost within sight of its waters.
Yet the little stream turns its back on that near sea and sets off the other way entirely.
It flows the whole width of a continent, eastward, mile after patient mile, growing as it goes.
Cool snowmelt becomes a trickle, the trickle becomes a stream, the stream becomes the mightiest river of all.
Imagine that long journey, beginning so small and so high, and never once turning back.
It is fed along the way by more than a thousand smaller rivers, each adding its quiet share.
They wind down out of the hills and through the great green forest, all of them leaning the same way.
There is a deep peace in water that knows its direction, and simply keeps to it, without doubt.
Let that long, sure journey settle over you, and let your breath grow slow and unhurried too.
All that water moves through the largest rainforest in the world, warm and dripping and green.
It is so vast and so full of life that it is sometimes called the lungs of the planet.
Beneath its canopy the air is soft and damp, and the rain you imagined falls and falls and falls.
The forest and the river together hold a great share of all the kinds of living things on Earth.
More sorts of trees and birds and insects shelter there than in almost any place we know.
Many of them have never been counted, and some have never even been named or seen by anyone.
Think of all that quiet life, breathing and growing in the warm green shade, while you lie here resting.
It asks nothing of you, and you need do nothing for it; it simply goes on, calm and unhurried.
The rain falls, the leaves drink, the water gathers, and the great river carries it all gently away.
There is a deep and living peace in that shaded, dripping world, going on without any rush at all.
You do not have to picture it clearly, only to let its warmth and its hush wash softly over you.
Let that warm green stillness gather around you now, and let your breath grow deep and slow.
Each year there comes a wet season, when the rain grows heavier and the great river slowly rises.
It does not flood in a rush, but swells gently upward, day by day, many metres in all.
And then it does something quiet and strange: it spreads out among the trees and floods the forest itself.
The water rises into the woods until the lower trunks stand deep in a calm brown tide.
For a while, the forest becomes a drowned and shining world, half river and half wood.
And in that flooded shade the fish swim out among the tree trunks, moving softly through a sunken garden.
They drift between the roots and over the hidden ground, in a green and watery hush.
Among all this live some wonderful creatures, including pale pink dolphins that move through the river itself.
There are giant fish too, and countless quiet others, many of them still unknown to us.
Picture those dolphins turning slowly in the brown water, gentle and unhurried, in no rush to be anywhere.
When the dry season comes again, the water sinks back, and the forest drains, and all of it waits for the next rain.
Let that slow rising and falling rock you like a tide, and let your own breath rise and fall with it.
Now follow the river all the long way down toward the end of its journey, near the sea.
For its last great stretch the land lies so flat that the river barely falls at all.
Over many, many miles it sinks only the smallest amount, hardly more than the height of a person.
So here the water moves slowly, broad and patient, in no hurry whatsoever to reach the ocean.
It spreads out so wide and so calm that you could stand on one bank and not see across to the other.
And where at last it meets the sea, its mouth is so enormous that whole islands rest within it.
People once argued for a long time whether the Amazon or the Nile was the longest river of all.
But the Amazon is the mightiest beyond all doubt, by the sheer endless volume of its water.
Its fresh, muddy flow pushes far out past the shore, staining the salt sea brown for many miles.
Out where you would expect only blue ocean, the river's brown water reaches on, gentle and unhurried still.
After such a long journey it does not arrive with any rush; it simply pours out, slow and immense and calm.
Let that slow, broad arrival settle over you, and let your breath grow as wide and easy as the river's mouth.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the mountains and the snowmelt fade gently away into the warm dark.
Let the flooded forest and the slow brown water soften and grow dim.
You are lying here in the gentle dark, and somewhere a great slow river is moving, calm and unhurried, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that vast patient water, asking nothing, simply going on, finding its long way home.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the soft hush of rain is all around you.
Like the river, you have only to keep still, and let yourself be carried gently along.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to reach, no current pulling at you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the sea gathers the river at the end of its long journey.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Ganges
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words, or keep them; let them drift over you like warm air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that darkness, picture a wide stretch of still, dark water lying calm and quiet.
And upon that water, picture a few tiny points of light, small flames drifting slowly along.
They move so gently they hardly seem to move at all, carried by a current you cannot see.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed, and watch them go.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
Those little lights are floating on a river, one of the greatest and oldest rivers on Earth.
It is called the Ganges, and in India, where it flows, people have long called it Ganga.
Its long journey begins far away, high among the ice and snow of the Himalaya mountains.
Up there, where the air is thin and cold, the river is not yet a river at all, only ice.
It begins at an ice cave called Gangotri, where meltwater from a glacier first gathers.
Drop by patient drop, the slow melt of ancient ice trickles out and starts to find its way down.
From that single cold mouth of ice, the water sets out on a journey of many hundreds of miles.
It will fall from the high mountains and wander across the wide, warm plains far below.
Picture that long descent, from the silent snow toward the gentle heat of the lowlands.
There is no hurry in it, only the slow, sure gathering of water seeking the distant sea.
Let that slowness settle over you, the patient drift from mountain ice toward warmer ground.
And let your breath grow long and unhurried, like the river feeling its first slow way downhill.
Once it leaves the mountains, the Ganges spreads out across the great plains of northern India.
Here the land grows flat and broad, and the river slows and widens as it crosses the open country.
This wide, level valley is among the most fertile places anywhere on the whole of the Earth.
Year after year the river has laid down rich soil, and on that soil the green fields grow.
It is also among the most crowded places in the world, full of villages and cities and farms.
Hundreds of millions of people live within its broad basin and depend upon its waters.
They drink from it and water their fields with it, and have done so for thousands of years.
Whole lives unfold along its banks, generation after generation, beside the same slow water.
Picture all those quiet lives gathered along one long ribbon of river, far across the dark.
Each evening, lamps are lit in countless homes beside it, small glows along the gentle shore.
There is something restful in that, in so many lives leaning on one patient, flowing stream.
Let the thought drift away now, and let your breath grow slow and deep and soft.
Feel yourself loosening, settling further, as the river settles into its wide and easy bed.
For the people of India, this river is far more than only water crossing the land.
In Hindu tradition the Ganges is revered as a goddess, also named Ganga, and held deeply sacred.
For many people the river is a living blessing, a presence to be loved and honoured and thanked.
It is said in that tradition that to bathe in her waters is a cleansing and a grace for the spirit.
And so, all along the banks, people come down to the water to wash and to pray and to give thanks.
These are beliefs held tenderly for a very long time, woven through countless lives and days.
Whatever you yourself believe, you can feel the gentleness of a people who hold a river so dear.
A river cared for in this way for thousands of years gathers a great quiet weight of love.
Picture the soft devotion of it, the bowed heads and the murmured words along the shore.
There is a deep peace in being held dear, and the river has been held dear beyond counting.
Let that tenderness reach you too, here in the warm dark, asking nothing of you at all.
And let your breath grow slow, as soft and steady as water moving past the bank.
Upon the banks of this river stands an ancient city, one of the oldest still alive in the world.
Its name is Varanasi, and people have lived there, without pause, for thousands upon thousands of years.
Down to the water lead long flights of stone steps, and these steps are called the ghats.
On the ghats, in the cool of evening, a gentle ceremony of light is offered to the river.
It is called the aarti, and it unfolds slowly as dusk falls and the day softens into dark.
Lamps are lifted and circled, and quiet songs rise, and the river is honoured with flame and voice.
The light moves in slow arcs against the gathering night, while the water shines below.
Picture that warm glow upon the old stone steps, and the dark river waiting patiently beneath.
It is the kind of slow, unhurried beauty that has been repeated, evening after evening, for ages.
Nothing in it is rushed, and nothing in it needs you; it simply happens, gentle and sure.
Let your mind rest in that warm and flickering scene, the lamps swinging soft against the dark.
And let your breath fall into the same slow rhythm, easy as the circling of an evening lamp.
As the lamps are lowered, people send their own small offerings out onto the river.
They fold little boats from leaves, and into each they set some flowers and a single tiny flame.
Then they place these gently on the water and let the current carry them slowly away.
And so the dark river fills with little drifting lights, each one a small wish set free.
This is the very scene you have been picturing, the small flames floating off into the night.
Each light carries a hope, or a thank you, or a quiet letting go, sent out upon the stream.
Far downstream, the Ganges meets another great river, the Brahmaputra, and the two flow as one.
Together they spread into one of the largest deltas in the world before they reach the sea.
Like all great rivers it faces real strains today, from cities and from heavy use along its length.
And so many people work gently and patiently to care for it, to keep it clean for those to come.
But tonight, in your quiet dark, only let the little lights drift on toward the distant sea.
Let one of them carry away whatever you have been holding, out onto the gentle current.
And let your breath go with it, slow and soft, releasing a little more with every drift downstream.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the high ice and the long plains and the old stone steps fade gently into the dark.
Let the lamps soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy and still.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a wide river is moving slowly, as you rest.
Upon it the little lights are drifting still, asking nothing, simply floating quietly away.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the river, you have only to move gently and let yourself be carried along.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no current pulling at you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the river gathers its small and drifting lights.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Yangtze
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like water.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture, if you like, a soft mist drifting among steep green mountains, high above quiet water.
The mist asks nothing of you; it only moves slowly, the way clouds move when no one is watching.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink, the way mist settles down into a still valley at the end of the day.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
Far away, in that misty country of your imagining, there is a long and patient river.
It is the Yangtze, the longest river in all of Asia, and the third longest river on the whole Earth.
It crosses the breadth of China from west to east, slipping at last into the sea near Shanghai.
In China it is often simply called Chang Jiang, which means only the long river, the long river.
For thousands of years it has been a highway, a border, and a quiet heart at the centre of the land.
Think of how much time that is, how many evenings have softened to dark along its banks.
Through all of them the water has gone on the same way, moving gently, eastward, toward the sea.
You do not need to remember its name, or where it goes; only let the long river move in your mind.
There is a deep calm in something so old that simply keeps on flowing, without hurry, without end.
Picture moonlight lying soft upon its surface, broken only by the slow turning of the current.
Let that long, unhurried movement carry your own thoughts a little further downstream.
And let your breath grow slow and deep, as patient as the river in the dark.
Now let your mind drift westward, up and up, far from the warm low country and toward the cold heights.
The river is born high on the Tibetan Plateau, in a country of thin air and great quiet.
There it rises from glaciers and from melting snow, gathering itself out of ice and cold streams.
From those high beginnings it falls a very great way, all the long breadth of China, down to the sea.
Imagine the small clear trickles gathering, joining, growing, with no thought of how far they must go.
They do not worry about the journey; they only follow the gentle, downward leaning of the land.
Drop by drop the cold snowmelt becomes a stream, and the stream in time becomes the great long river.
There is something restful in that, in how the largest things are made of the smallest, patiently joined.
You need do nothing to help it; the water has been finding its way down for longer than memory.
Picture the high snow, the slow melting, the quiet beginning of so long a journey.
And as you picture it, let your own breath fall gently, the way the snow gives itself to the stream.
Settle deeper now, as the cold heights soften into mist far behind you.
Down where the land grows steep again, the river gathers all its strength and carves the famous gorges.
These are the Three Gorges, a long stretch of high, misty mountains pressing close around narrow water.
For a very long while poets and painters loved this place, and tried to hold its quiet beauty.
Picture the cliffs rising sheer on either side, their tops lost softly in the morning mist.
The water runs deep and narrow there, dark and smooth, between the great patient walls of stone.
Old Chinese poems speak of this long river carrying boats, and moonlight, and a traveller's thoughts away.
They tell of watching the water slip past and feeling one's cares loosen and drift downstream into the mist.
You can let your own cares do the same now, setting them gently on the water and letting them go.
There is no need to follow where they go; the river is good at carrying things quietly away.
Imagine standing on a high deck at dawn, the gorges hushed, the mist soft upon your face.
Everything is grey and gentle and still, and the only sound is water moving slowly past stone.
Let that stillness fill you, and let each breath out carry a little more of you toward sleep.
For all its beauty, the long river has always been a place of patient, ordinary work as well.
For many centuries, boats could not pass upstream through the swift gorges by sail or oar alone.
So men called trackers walked the narrow cliff paths, leaning into long ropes, hauling the boats against the current.
Picture them moving slowly along the rock, step by patient step, while the water pulled the other way.
It was slow and heavy work, done in mist and rain, the rope taut, the river always pushing back.
And yet, little by little, the boats went on, drawn upstream by nothing but patience and steady weight.
The river has fed that patient life for ages; about one in three people in China lives within its basin.
Its waters give life to a great share of the country's rice and farmland, quietly, season after season.
Think of all those green fields, all that rice, all those quiet meals, fed by the same long river.
There is a deep comfort in something that simply provides, year upon year, asking for nothing in return.
You need not pull against anything tonight; you may let every rope in you go slack and soft.
Let the current have its way, and let your breath grow long, and let your body rest.
The long river is also a home, a quiet refuge for creatures found almost nowhere else.
In its waters still lives the gentle Yangtze finless porpoise, smooth and grey and shy.
It moves slowly through the soft brown water, surfacing now and then with a quiet, easy breath.
There was once another, a pale river dolphin called the baiji, almost a spirit of the stream.
Sadly the baiji has become very rare, perhaps lost altogether, and that is a thing to be quiet about.
But the porpoise lingers still, and people watch over it now, hoping the river will keep it a while longer.
In more recent times a great wall was built across the river, the enormous Three Gorges Dam.
It is one of the largest dams in all the world, made for power and to calm the river's great floods.
It changed the old valley and moved many people, and the water now lies deeper and stiller behind it.
So the river holds both the old and the new, the ancient porpoise and the great quiet dam, side by side.
You do not have to weigh any of it tonight; you may simply let it all rest in the soft dark.
Let the gentle porpoise rise and breathe in your mind, slow and calm, and breathe slowly with it.
And as it slips back beneath the surface, let yourself sink a little deeper too.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the high snow and the cold glaciers fade gently away into the dark.
Let the misty gorges soften and dim, and let the trackers set down their ropes and rest.
Let the porpoise go quiet beneath the water, and let the great dam stand silent and far away.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a long river is still slipping toward the sea.
There is a deep peace in that quiet water, moving without hurry, asking nothing, simply going on.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the river, you have only to keep moving gently, with no effort, toward your own quiet rest.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the sea gently gathers the long river at the end.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Everest
lines: There is nothing you need to do now, and nothing you need to keep in your mind.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or hold them; let them drift over you like cool clean air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are warm and safe within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet easing along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere far beyond the walls, picture an immense mountain standing alone under a deep starry sky.
It rises far above the clouds, vast and silent and utterly still, asking nothing of you at all.
Up there the snow lies hushed and untouched, and the cold blue air does not stir.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink lower, the way evening sinks slowly over a high and quiet peak.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
That great mountain you are picturing is the highest place on all the Earth above the sea.
It stands on the long border between Nepal and Tibet, among the high snows of the Himalaya.
It is older in name than in any measuring, for it was held sacred long before it was ever counted.
In Nepal it is called Sagarmatha, and in Tibet it is Chomolungma, often understood as the Goddess Mother of the World.
Imagine all the prayers and quiet reverence given to it across the ages, simply for being so vast and high.
In English it carries another name, given after a surveyor of long ago called George Everest.
It is a small and gentle truth that he himself did not wish the mountain to be named for him.
But the mountain is far older than any name, and is not troubled by what we choose to call it.
It has stood through every word ever spoken about it, unchanged and serene.
Picture that calm indifference, that great stone presence that needs nothing from anyone.
There is rest in a thing so settled and so sure, so far above all our naming and counting.
Let that stillness settle over you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
Now let your mind sink back through an almost unimaginable span of time, gently and without effort.
The whole of the Himalaya was born from the slowest collision the world has ever known.
Long ago the land of India began to drift north, across an ancient sea, toward the body of Asia.
Over tens of millions of years it pressed onward, slow as a dream, until the two great lands met.
Where they touched, the ground had nowhere left to go, and so it crumpled and folded upward into mountains.
Picture that vast, patient crumpling, the earth rising fold upon fold, slower than any eye could follow.
It is a strange comfort to know that the mountain is still rising even now, a little more each year.
All that lifting happened too slowly to see, the way the hand of a clock seems never to move.
There was no hurry in it, no sudden force, only the deep and steady patience of the Earth itself.
The highest place in all the world was made not in a moment but across ages beyond counting.
Let that slowness pour into you, the long unhurried making of a mountain.
Feel yourself loosening with each breath, settling deeper into the warm and quiet dark.
There is a wonder hidden in the pale stone near the very top of the mountain, and it is this.
High on the summit, miles above the sea, the rock holds the fossils of small sea creatures.
Picture them, the faint shells and curls of things that once lived in shallow water long ago.
For that pale limestone was once the floor of an ancient ocean, lying quietly beneath the waves.
The slow collision of the lands lifted that old sea floor up and up into the freezing air.
So the highest point on Earth was once the bottom of a warm and forgotten sea.
Imagine the patience of that journey, stone carried from beneath the water to the roof of the world.
What was once sunk in the deep now stands nearer the stars than anything else on the planet.
There is a deep gentleness in that thought, the rising of the lowest place into the highest.
Nothing was lost or hurried; the old sea floor simply waited and slowly climbed the sky.
Let that thought rest lightly upon you, and let your eyes grow heavier still.
Breathe out slowly, and let yourself be carried as gently as that ancient stone.
Let your mind drift now to the very top of the mountain, where the air grows thin and clear.
It rises so high that planes themselves cruise at about the height of its summit.
Up there the great winds called the jet streams blow, sweeping past the peak in long ribbons of cold.
There is so little air to breathe in that high place that climbers call its top the death zone.
Yet the mountain itself is at peace there, needing nothing, breathing not at all.
From the summit the sky above looks dark even in the middle of the day, deep and quiet and vast.
Imagine standing in that thin bright cold, with the curve of the world falling away beneath you.
The sacred Sherpa people live in the valleys below, and their kindness and skill have made the climbing possible.
It was Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary who first reached the top, in nineteen fifty-three, after many earlier tries.
Picture them resting at the summit in the great silence, the whole world spread out far beneath their feet.
But you do not need to climb anywhere tonight, only to lie still and let the mountain be.
Let the thin high air settle your thoughts, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Remember, as you drift, just how vast and how ancient this quiet mountain truly is.
It rose from the floor of a vanished sea, lifted across ages no one was there to count.
It carries the shells of old sea creatures in its pale crown, miles above the waves they once knew.
It has been sacred to the people of its valleys far longer than it has had any measured height.
The deep hush at its summit has held through countless nights, undisturbed and serene.
Up there the snow lies in a stillness older than memory, gathering quietly under the dark blue sky.
There is no rush in any of it, no impatience, only the long calm of stone and snow and time.
The mountain asks nothing, keeps nothing, holds only its great and peaceful silence.
It simply stands at the top of the world, ancient and unhurried, content to be still.
Let that old patience pour into you now, slowing your breath, softening your every thought.
There is nothing in all that height and age but rest, and it offers that rest to you.
Let yourself grow as still and as quiet as the deep snow at the top of the world.
Breathe out slowly, and let the great calm of the mountain hold you.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the high snows and the thin clear air fade gently away into the dark.
Let the ancient sea floor and the slow rising of the mountains soften and dissolve.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a vast still peak is at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that quiet mountain, asking nothing, simply standing calm and high.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the mountain, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to climb, nothing to reach, no height left to gain tonight.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the deep snow gathers in the silence above the clouds.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Mount Fuji
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to remember.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely; let them drift over you like a soft evening mist.
Imagine the room around you has gone quiet and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the gentle settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this peaceful dark.
Somewhere far off in that darkness, picture a single mountain, calm and perfectly still.
It rises in a smooth and even cone, pale and serene, its summit dusted with quiet snow.
Below it lies a lake so calm that the mountain is mirrored there, a second peak resting upside down on the water.
The air is hushed, the surface unbroken, and nothing stirs but the slow turning of the dawn.
We are only going to gaze upon it together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That serene mountain you are picturing has a name, gently spoken, Mount Fuji.
In Japan it is often called Fujisan, and it is the highest mountain in all that land.
It stands on the largest island of Japan, the island of Honshu, rising alone above the gentle country around it.
Because it stands so apart, it can be seen from very far away, a pale cone floating on the horizon.
On a clear day it can even be glimpsed from the great city of Tokyo, hovering quietly beyond the rooftops.
It is famous most of all for its shape, an almost perfect cone, smooth and even on every side.
Few mountains in the world are so balanced, so calm and symmetrical against the open sky.
Snow rests upon its summit for much of the year, giving it that soft pale crown you are imagining.
For a long, long time, people have simply turned to look at it, and felt something in them grow still.
There is no need to journey there; it is enough, tonight, to hold its quiet shape in your mind.
Let that calm and even mountain settle gently behind your eyes.
And let your breath grow as slow and unhurried as the mountain is still.
Now let your mind sink down beneath that pale cone, into the patient body of the mountain itself.
For Mount Fuji is a volcano, though it has slept quietly for a very long time.
It is not a dead thing, but a resting one, calm now, with its old fires gone gentle and still.
Its last great waking was around the early seventeen hundreds, an eruption remembered as the Hoei eruption.
Since then it has been silent, generation upon generation, watching over the land in peace.
Picture all those long years of quiet, the slow turning of seasons over a mountain at rest.
It was not always so calm; the very shape you love was built by fire, slowly and over ages.
Layer upon layer of eruptions, one after another, piled the mountain up and smoothed its sides.
Each cone rose over the older ones beneath it, and that patient building gave Fuji its even form.
So the serenity you see is the gift of a great and ancient making, now grown gentle and quiet.
There is a deep peace in a sleeping volcano, all its old heat hushed and folded away.
Let that long stillness settle over you, and let your body grow heavier as you breathe slowly out.
There is a reason a mountain of fire rises in just that place, and it lies far beneath the ground.
Deep below, the great plates of the Earth's surface drift and meet, slowly, over countless ages.
Mount Fuji sits where three of these vast plates come together, pressing gently against one another.
Where they meet, the deep heat finds its way upward, and so a volcano was born in that very spot.
It is a slow and patient meeting, nothing hurried in it, the plates moving slower than you could ever see.
From that quiet pressure far below, all the long building of the mountain once began.
Around its broad base lie cool forests and a scattering of calm and quiet lakes.
In the stillness of those lakes the snowy peak is mirrored, just as you have been imagining it.
For ages, people in Japan have loved that reflected calm and woven it into their art and poetry.
The mountain became a gentle symbol of endurance and peace, standing unmoved through all the years.
Let that image of patient stone and still water rest softly in your mind.
And let your own breathing grow long and quiet, like the unbroken surface of the lake.
Mount Fuji is not only admired from afar; it has long been held sacred and dearly loved.
In the old Shinto tradition of Japan, the mountain has been revered for a very long time.
For many centuries, pilgrims have climbed its slopes slowly, as a quiet act of devotion.
They went not to conquer the peak, but to honour it, step by patient step toward the summit.
Even now, in the short warm season of summer, many people make the long climb to the top.
Often they walk through the night, moving softly upward in the cool and the dark.
They climb so that they may stand on the summit as the sun first appears over the world.
That arrival of light at dawn has its own gentle name, Goraiko, the coming of the light.
Imagine standing high above the clouds, in the hush before dawn, waiting for the sky to warm.
Then the first soft glow spreads across the horizon, and the long night quietly ends.
There is a deep stillness in that waiting, a peace held by everyone upon the mountain.
Let that gentle coming of light wash over you, and let your eyes grow heavier still.
Because it is so beautiful, Mount Fuji has been painted and pictured more than almost any mountain on Earth.
Its snow-capped cone has drawn the eyes of artists and poets for age upon age.
Long ago an artist named Hokusai made a famous series of pictures of it, called Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.
In each one the mountain appears, sometimes near and clear, sometimes small and pale in the far distance.
His most famous picture of all shows a great curling wave, with little Fuji resting calmly far behind it.
The wave rises and rears, full of motion, while the mountain sits perfectly still beyond.
That stillness behind the storm is part of why the image has been loved for so very long.
Today Mount Fuji is honoured as a place of deep cultural and spiritual meaning.
People come from all over the world simply to look upon it, asking nothing more than to see.
It remains what it has always been, a calm and enduring presence above the quiet land.
Let that famous, peaceful shape soften now, the way the day softens into evening.
And let your breath grow slower and deeper as the picture gently fades.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the high summit and the still lake fade gently away into the dark.
Let the snowy cone soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a quiet mountain rests, as you are resting now.
There is a deep peace in that calm and sleeping peak, asking nothing, simply standing still.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the mountain, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to climb, nothing to reach, no summit waiting for you tonight.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the dawn light gently gathers the sleeping land.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Kilimanjaro
lines: There is nothing you need to do now, and nowhere at all you have to be.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not need to follow the words closely, or hold onto them; let them drift over you like a warm evening wind.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nothing to finish, nothing to remember, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Far off in that darkness, picture a great mountain rising alone over a wide and quiet plain.
The day is ending, and the evening light is warm and gold, and the air is soft and still.
The mountain is calm and patient and old, and it asks nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest now, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little further, the way the warm land sinks slowly into dusk.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
That great mountain you are picturing has a name, and the name is Kilimanjaro.
It rises in the far north of Tanzania, in eastern Africa, close to the border with Kenya.
It is the highest mountain in all of Africa, lifting up toward the sky above the warm plains below.
What makes it so striking is that it stands quite alone, not gathered into a long chain of peaks.
It is what people call a free-standing mountain, lifting straight up from flat and open land.
Because nothing else rises near it, it seems immense, a single shape filling the whole horizon.
On a hazy evening it can appear to float, its broad snowy top resting above a soft band of mist.
From far across the plain it looks less like solid stone and more like a quiet dream of a mountain.
Picture it there, vast and gentle and still, glowing faintly in the last of the light.
There is something deeply restful in a thing so large that simply stands, and waits, and is.
It has stood like that for longer than you can easily imagine, in no hurry, going nowhere.
Let that stillness settle over you, and let your breath grow long and slow and unhurried too.
Kilimanjaro was not always there; it was made, slowly, by fire deep within the Earth.
It is a volcano, though a quiet one now, a sleeping mountain that has rested for a very long time.
Long ago, melted rock rose from far below and built the mountain up, layer upon patient layer.
It grew not in one place but as three great cones, three gentle summits gathered into one body.
The highest of the three is called Kibo, and Kibo carries the very top of the mountain.
That highest point has a name of its own, Uhuru Peak, and Uhuru is a word that means freedom.
It is a soft and open word to leave resting at the summit of so calm and ancient a place.
The fires that built it have grown quiet, and the mountain has settled into a long, deep sleep.
Now it only stands, warmed by the day, cooled by the night, dreaming above the plain.
Picture all that slow building, all that patient work, now come at last to perfect rest.
There is no fire in it now, only stillness, only the long calm of a thing that is finished and at peace.
Let your body share in that calm, growing heavier, sinking softly toward sleep.
The strangest and most beautiful thing about Kilimanjaro is what it holds upon its top.
Although it rises in the warm heart of Africa, very close to the equator, its summit is capped with snow.
High above the green and sunlit plains, there is ice and cold and a quiet crown of white.
Glaciers and fields of ice have rested up there for many thousands of years, far older than any city.
Imagine that, a cap of snow gleaming under warm African stars, almost upon the equator itself.
It is so high that the air at the top grows thin and cold, while the land below stays gentle and warm.
In recent times those ice fields have been slowly shrinking, growing thinner with the passing years.
But for now a soft white crown still rests up there, far above the heat of the day.
Picture the warm dark plain below, and that quiet glimmer of snow floating high above it all.
It is a meeting of warmth and cold, of summer and winter, held gently in a single mountain.
There is a deep peace in that high, cold stillness, so far above everything, touched only by the stars.
Let that cool quiet drift down over you now, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
To walk up Kilimanjaro is to pass through many different worlds in only a few quiet days.
Because it stands near the equator yet climbs so very high, its slopes hold many climates at once.
It is a little like walking from the warm tropics all the way to the cold poles, but going only upward.
Low down there are farms and villages, green and warm, where people tend their fields in the sun.
Higher up the path enters a belt of rainforest, cool and dim, watered by mists that gather on the slopes.
That forest is alive with birds and flowers, and small monkeys move softly through the dripping trees.
Above the forest the land opens into heath and moorland, with strange tall plants and wide grey skies.
Higher still it becomes a cold and stony desert, a quiet land of bare rock and thin clear air.
And at the very top there is only snow and ice, the cold white crown beneath the open sky.
So in a single gentle journey upward you pass through nearly all the worlds the Earth can hold.
Picture moving slowly through them, from warm fields to cool forest to high and silent snow.
Let that long, gentle climb carry you onward, and let your body grow heavier with every step.
What is rare and lovely about Kilimanjaro is that so many ordinary people can reach its top.
Unlike most of the world's great peaks, it needs no ropes, and no skill at climbing, only time and care.
It asks only for a slow and steady pace, so the body has time to grow used to the thin high air.
Those who hurry grow weary and unwell, but those who go gently, breath by breath, can walk all the way up.
The mountain rewards patience above all, the simple willingness to move slowly and to wait.
It rose long ago near the great rift where Africa is, very slowly, beginning to pull itself apart.
Along that vast slow seam in the land, the deep fires gathered and lifted these mountains into the sky.
Many who climb it walk the final stretch in the dark, through the cold night toward the summit.
They reach the high rim just as the sun is rising, the light spreading over the great curve of Africa.
Imagine standing at the top in that first soft light, the whole warm continent waking far below.
There is nothing to prove up there, only the quiet reward of having gone slowly, and arrived.
Let that same slow patience fill you now, breath by breath, easing you down toward sleep.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the wide plain and the great mountain soften and fade gently away into the dark.
Let the green forest and the cold high snow dim quietly, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a vast still mountain is at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that quiet peak, standing alone, asking nothing, simply being calm and old.
You do not have to understand any of it, or hold onto a single word that was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the mountain, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to climb, nothing to reach, no summit waiting for you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the night gathers the gentle plain.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Matterhorn
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like cool evening air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere far off in that darkness, picture a single great peak rising alone above a quiet valley.
It stands above a small village whose lights are growing dim, and it asks nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little lower, the way the last warm light sinks slowly down a mountainside.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That great peak you are picturing has a name, soft to say: the Matterhorn.
It rises in the Alps, on the long border between Switzerland and Italy, high above the village of Zermatt.
On the Italian side they call it by another gentle name, Cervino, the same mountain seen from another valley.
It does not lie among a crowd of other peaks; it stands a little apart, alone, easy to know at a glance.
Its shape is what you remember most, a steep four-sided horn leaning up into the sky.
Of all the mountains in the world, few have an outline so clear and so simple to hold in the mind.
Picture that lone dark pyramid against a pale evening sky, still and patient above the sleeping land.
It has stood there far longer than any village, far longer than any name we have given it.
There is no hurry in it, no restlessness; it is only there, quiet and enormous in the dusk.
You do not need to climb it or measure it; you have only to let it stand in your mind and rest.
Let that calm shape settle over you, dark and unmoving against the fading light.
Feel your breath grow long and slow, as steady as a mountain at the close of the day.
Now let your mind wander gently back through time, to how that sharp peak came to have its shape.
It was not carved by any hand, but slowly, over countless ages, by ice.
Long ago the high places were wrapped in glaciers, great slow rivers of ice that never rushed at all.
These rivers of ice clung to the mountain on several sides, and each one quietly ground away at the rock.
Year upon year, age upon age, each glacier wore down its own face of the mountain, patient and unhurried.
As the faces were ground back from many directions, they began to meet at steeper and steeper angles.
Where all those slopes finally met, a single sharp point was left, lifting into the air.
A peak shaped this way, with steep faces rising to a point, is called a horn by those who study the Earth.
And the Matterhorn is the most famous horn of all, the one others are quietly compared to.
So its bold shape is really the work of vanished ice, slowly carving while the world looked away.
Picture that slow patient sculpting, going on for ages with no one to watch and nothing to hurry it.
Let that slowness ease into you, and let your breath grow long and soft and unhurried too.
There is a stranger wonder still, hidden in the very rock at the mountain's top.
Long before the ice came, the Alps themselves were raised when two great pieces of the Earth pressed together.
Whole continents drew slowly toward each other, and where they met the land buckled and rose into mountains.
In that vast slow collision, a sheet of rock from the far side was lifted and laid across the top.
So the stone at the very summit of the Matterhorn came from what was once the African side of that meeting.
It travelled a long way and was stacked high, and now it crowns the peak as older, far-carried stone.
Beneath your feet the world is always moving, only far too slowly for any of us to feel.
Mountains rise and wear away again over spans of time too long to hold inside a single mind.
There is something restful in that, in how the great Earth takes its time and is never in a hurry.
You do not have to remember which rock came from where, or hold any of these facts at all.
Let them drift past like clouds crossing the high faces in the last of the evening light.
Breathe out slowly, and let your body sink a little deeper toward sleep.
For a long time people believed this peak could never be climbed at all.
Its faces are so steep that it seemed to lean back from anyone who tried, and many turned away.
It was one of the very last of the great Alpine peaks to be reached, long thought impossible.
Then, in the year eighteen sixty-five, a party led by a man named Edward Whymper at last stood upon its summit.
For a moment there was triumph, high above the valleys, with the whole world of the Alps spread below.
But the descent turned to sorrow, for on the way down four of the climbers fell from the heights.
That mingling of triumph and grief travelled far, and it made the Matterhorn famous all around the world.
From then on its lone horned shape became known to people who would never go near a mountain.
In time it grew into a symbol of the whole range of the Alps, and even of Switzerland itself.
Yet the peak itself stands as it always has, untroubled by any story we tell about it.
Let those old tales soften now, the climbing and the falling alike, and let them fade into the dark.
Breathe slowly, and let your thoughts grow quiet beneath that enormous, indifferent calm.
Picture the mountain now in the last clear hour of the day, as the sun slips low.
Its sides are so steep and sheer that snow can find no place to settle on its faces.
So while gentler slopes turn soft and white, the Matterhorn keeps its dark stone bare and sharp against the sky.
That is part of why its outline cuts so cleanly, a black horn standing plain above the snow.
As the sun goes down, the valleys below fall first into a deep blue shadow and grow dim.
But the high summit still catches the very last of the light, and for a little while it glows.
It turns a warm rose and gold while everything beneath it has already settled into evening.
People have a soft name for that quiet fire on the heights; they call it the alpenglow.
Imagine that glow now, gentle and slow, the highest stone warm with light while the world below sleeps.
Then the light lets go, the colour fades, and the peak goes grey and then dark and still.
And the whole valley breathes out into night, the village lights small and warm far below.
Let that last warm light fade behind your eyes, and let yourself sink down into the dusk.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the high horn of stone fade gently away, dark and quiet against a darker sky.
Let the ice and the slow collisions and the old stories soften and slip out of your thoughts.
Let the last warm glow on the summit dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a great peak stands quietly at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that still mountain, carved over ages, asking nothing, simply being there.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the mountain, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to climb, nothing to reach, no height before you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you in the way the night gathers the valleys below the peak.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Crane
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like soft mist.
Imagine the room around you has gone quiet and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the gentle easing along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this peaceful dark.
Picture, if you like, a wide quiet wetland at dawn, with a low mist lying soft upon the water.
Somewhere in that stillness stands a tall, grey, elegant bird, calm and patient, asking nothing of you.
Let your eyes rest now, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little further, the way the mist sinks slowly over the still marsh.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That tall grey bird you are picturing is a crane, one of the most graceful birds in all the world.
Cranes are among the very tallest of flying birds, long of leg and long of neck, standing serene and still.
They make their homes on wetlands and marshes and wide open grasslands, across much of the world.
Picture one standing in shallow water, unhurried, its long neck curved like a soft question into the mist.
It can stand so quietly, for so long, that it seems almost a part of the reeds and the still grey water.
There is a deep patience in a crane, a stillness that has nothing restless in it at all.
It waits the way the dawn waits to brighten, in no hurry, certain the light will come.
All across the world, in many lands, cranes stand like this at the edges of quiet water.
Imagine the soft sounds of the marsh around it, the small ripples, the rustle of reeds in a low breeze.
There is something in that calm grey figure that asks only to be watched, and to be at peace.
Let that stillness settle over you, and let your breath grow slow and unhurried too.
Feel yourself growing as quiet and as patient as a tall bird at rest in the dawn mist.
Now imagine the mist beginning to lift, and the marsh waking softly into the new day.
For cranes are famous, above all, for their dancing, which is one of the loveliest sights in nature.
When a crane dances, it bows low, and it leaps lightly into the air, and it spreads its great wings wide.
It tosses up bits of grass with its long bill, and bobs, and steps, with a grace that seems almost gentle joy.
Often two cranes dance together, turning and bowing to one another in the soft early light.
This dancing helps a pair grow close, and to know one another, and to bind themselves together.
For many crane pairs stay together for years and years, and some of them stay together for life.
Picture that, two faithful birds, returning to one another season after season, dancing in the dawn.
There is a quiet tenderness in it, two long-lived creatures keeping faith across the turning years.
Let your mind hold that gentle image, the slow bow, the soft leap, the wide and patient wings.
And let your own body grow softer still, your hands unclenching, your breath drawing long and deep.
Breathe slowly out, and let the dancing fade gently, like figures glimpsed through lifting mist.
Some cranes are great travellers, and this is one of the quiet wonders of their lives.
When the seasons turn, they fly enormous distances between their summer homes and their winter ones.
Certain cranes cross great mountain ranges on their journeys, flying among the highest of all known birds.
Picture them passing far overhead, tiny against the cold blue, patient wings carrying them over the peaks.
They fly in long lines, and in wide drifting shapes like a letter V written softly across the sky.
And as they go, they call out, a loud, far-carrying, bugling cry that can be heard from a great distance.
Imagine that sound rolling down from high above, faint and wild and lovely, then fading into the quiet.
Sometimes, on their long journeys, great numbers of cranes gather at certain rivers and wetlands to rest.
It is one of nature's grand quiet gatherings, thousands of tall birds standing together in the shallows.
Think of all those patient travellers, paused along the way, resting before they journey on.
There is no hurry in it for you tonight; you have no mountains to cross and no distance to fly.
Let that long patient journeying carry your thoughts gently away, and let your breathing slow.
Breathe softly out, and rest, as the travellers rest at the river in the fading light.
The world holds many kinds of crane, and each has its own quiet beauty.
In the wetlands of east Asia lives the red-crowned crane, white and grey, with a patch of bare red skin on its head.
In the Americas there are sandhill cranes, soft grey and many, gathering in their great seasonal flocks.
And there is the whooping crane, tall and white and very rare, watched over and carefully protected by many caring hands.
Picture them all, across the wide world, standing in their quiet waters at the edge of the day.
In Japan the crane is much beloved, held as a gentle symbol of long life, and of luck, and of faithfulness.
An old folk belief there holds that the crane lives for a thousand years, a lovely thought, even if it is only a story.
Cranes have stepped into the art and the tales of many lands, as emblems of grace and watchfulness and good fortune.
It is easy to see why, watching that calm and elegant bird stand patient in the mist.
Let those soft symbols rest lightly on you, long life and luck and faithfulness, like a quiet wish.
You need not hold any of it; let the names and the meanings drift away into the warm dark.
Breathe out slowly now, and let yourself grow heavier, and more peaceful, and more still.
There is one more gentle story about cranes, and it is woven of folded paper.
The origami crane, folded from a single square of paper, is one of the best known paper folds in all the world.
Perhaps you have seen one, or made one, its small wings and slender neck rising from a flat sheet.
There is a tender tradition that says folding a thousand paper cranes is a way of making a wish.
This folding of a thousand cranes has a name, senbazuru, and the wish is often one of healing, or of peace.
Picture the slow patience of it, one careful fold after another, a thousand small quiet cranes taking shape.
It is only a tradition, only a gentle custom of the heart, yet there is something deeply soothing in it.
A thousand small paper birds, each folded slowly, each carrying a soft hope toward healing and toward peace.
Across the world the crane has come to stand, in many hearts, for that very thing, for peace and for calm.
Let that quiet wish settle over you now, a wish for peace, for healing, for soft and easy rest.
You do not have to do anything with it; only let it rest on you, light as a folded paper wing.
Breathe slowly out, and let the thousand small cranes drift gently away into the dark.
Let yourself grow as still and as peaceful as a paper bird laid quietly down.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the wide misty marsh and the tall grey bird fade gently away into the dark.
Let the slow dance soften, the bow and the leap and the wide patient wings, all dimming now.
Let the long high journeys and the far bugling calls grow faint, and then grow still.
Let the folded paper cranes settle and rest, their quiet wish carried softly off into the night.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a calm grey bird stands at rest, as you are.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the crane in the dawn mist, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no distance to cross at all.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Raven
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like wind through trees.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Far away in your mind, picture a pale winter sky, wide and still and faintly glowing.
And across it, slow and unhurried, imagine a pair of dark wings turning on the wind.
They ask nothing of you; they simply ride the cold air, rising and falling, far above the quiet ground.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the hush of the dark.
That dark bird you are picturing, turning on the pale sky, is a raven.
It is a big and glossy black bird, with feathers that catch a soft blue and purple sheen in the light.
Though it seems a creature of wild and open places, it is, of all things, a songbird.
It is in truth the largest of all the songbirds, the great gentle giant of the perching birds.
But it does not sing the way a small bird sings; its voice is a deep and rounded croak.
That low, rich croak is quite unlike the harsh caw of a crow, and it carries far over quiet country.
Across snow and forest and empty hill, you might hear it as a slow knocking, gurgling call.
There is nothing frightening in it; it is only a large dark bird, talking softly to the wind.
Picture it now, wheeling far above, calling out across the cold and the quiet for the simple joy of it.
It is calm and unhurried, at ease in the wide air, with nowhere it needs to be.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, sinking gently, as the slow dark bird turns far overhead.
Now let yourself wonder, softly, at how clever this quiet bird truly is.
Ravens are among the most intelligent of all the birds in the whole wide world.
They can work out puzzles, and even use simple little tools to reach what they cannot otherwise touch.
They seem to plan a little for the future, tucking food away in hidden places to find again later.
And, perhaps most lovely of all, they appear to play, simply for the fun of it.
They have been seen sliding down snowy slopes again and again, the way a child might sled in winter.
And they tumble and roll through the air, turning over and over, for no reason but delight.
They can learn to copy sounds, too, even a few human words, in that deep and gentle voice.
And they remember faces; a raven can know one person from another, and recall them long after.
Imagine that bright, playful mind at rest now, the cleverness gone quiet, the wings folded and still.
There is something soothing in such a clever creature simply tumbling through the air for joy.
Let that gentle wonder settle over you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried.
These dark birds live across the whole northern half of the world, in nearly every kind of land.
You will find them in hot deserts and on lonely coasts, and high up in the cold and shining Arctic.
Wherever they go, they are masters of the wind, riding it with an easy, effortless skill.
They soar and glide and tilt on the air, reading every gust the way you might read a familiar room.
In their high spirits they will sometimes even roll right over and fly upside down for a moment, in play.
And ravens often stay together, a pair of them, for many long years, faithful and fond of one another.
Picture two of them now, wheeling side by side, performing slow rolls and tumbles in the open sky.
They turn and dive together, calling softly, two dark shapes playing on the same patient wind.
Then they settle, wing to wing, on some high branch above the hushed and snowy forest.
There is a quiet tenderness in it, two old companions resting close against the cold.
Let that closeness warm you, and let your shoulders soften further into the dark.
Breathe out slowly, and let yourself grow as still as a bird at rest on a winter branch.
Because they are so clever and so dark, people have told stories about ravens for a very long time.
In old Norse myth, it is said that the god Odin kept two ravens, who flew out across the world each day.
Their names were Huginn and Muninn, which mean, very gently, Thought and Memory.
The story tells that they soared over all the lands and seas, then returned to whisper the news in his ear.
Remember, this is only an old, old story, a way that people once imagined the wide and watchful sky.
And far away, among many peoples of the Pacific north-west of North America, others tell of Raven too.
In their tales, Raven is a clever shaper of the world, and in some old stories, a bringer of light.
These are stories, mind, not facts, but they are warm and kindly ones, told for the wonder in them.
It is a lovely thought, that a real bird, so bright and so playful, should carry such gentle stories with it.
Let the tales drift through you now, the way a dark wing drifts across a pale and quiet sky.
You need not keep a single name or word of them; let them pass and grow dim.
Breathe slowly, and let the old soft stories carry you a little closer toward sleep.
There is one more gentle tradition, kept far away in the city of London, that you might like to hold lightly.
By long custom, a small group of ravens is cared for at the old Tower of London, by the river.
And there is a kindly old saying that goes along with them, told for hundreds of years.
The saying is that the kingdom will be safe for as long as the ravens stay at the Tower.
So the birds are tended gently there, fed and watched over, honoured guests in their grey stone home.
It is only a tradition, of course, a fond old story, but a peaceful and rather lovely one.
Picture those dark birds at rest in their ancient courtyard, settled and calm in the falling dusk.
And think again of all the wild ones, far from any city, soaring over quiet forests and snow.
Their deep calls carry far across the hush, and they ride the wind, it seems, for the sheer joy of the air.
Cared for in old stone towers, or free above the empty north, they are all sinking now toward rest.
Let the day's last light go grey and soft, and let the wide sky empty and grow still.
Breathe out, long and slow, and let yourself drift down with the settling dark.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the wide pale sky fade gently away, and let the dark wings come slowly down to rest.
Let the old stories soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a dark bird is at rest, as you are.
Its wings are folded now, its bright mind quiet, its deep voice fallen still beneath the stars.
