You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the hush is soft all around you.
Like the raven on its winter branch, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to fly, nothing to remember, no wind to ride and no place you must be.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the still night gathers the sleeping forest.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Swan
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like mist over water.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that darkness, picture a wide still lake at the close of the day, its surface smooth as glass.
A low mist rests upon the water, soft and grey, and the air is cool and very quiet.
And gliding across that calm water, slow and white and untroubled, is a single swan.
It moves without sound, leaving only the gentlest ripple, asking nothing of you at all.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be carried by the quiet of the dark.
That white bird gliding over your still imagined water is one of the largest of all flying creatures.
A swan has a long and graceful neck, and broad white wings that span a surprising width.
The one you are most likely picturing is the mute swan, the familiar bird of parks and gentle rivers.
It carries an orange bill, marked with a soft black knob above, and it holds its neck in a tender curve.
For all its great size, it moves with an ease that looks like nothing at all, smooth and unhurried.
There is no haste in it, no struggle that you can see, only that slow and floating grace.
It seems to belong to the water, as though it had never known any other way to be.
Watch it cross the lake in your mind, white against the grey, leaving the faintest silver trail.
Let the size of it not trouble you; it is gentle, and it glides without a sound.
There is a deep calm in something so large that moves so softly and so slow.
Let that calm settle over you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
Feel yourself loosening as you watch, sinking a little further into the warm dark.
Now let your eyes follow that gliding bird, and notice how perfectly serene it seems.
Above the water it is all stillness, all grace, scarcely seeming to move itself along at all.
But beneath the calm surface, where you cannot see, the swan is paddling steadily on.
It has large dark webbed feet, and they push at the water with a quiet and constant effort.
So the serene gliding you see is held up by a hidden, patient work below.
It is a gentle image, that one, of grace upon the surface and quiet labour underneath.
There is no strain that shows, no sign of how the smoothness is made; it simply appears to drift.
And perhaps that is a kindly thing to carry into sleep, that calm can rest upon steady effort.
You need not paddle now; you may let all that effort go, and simply be carried.
Let your own hidden striving grow still, the small constant work of the day come to rest.
Let it sink beneath you, the way the swan's effort sinks below the quiet water.
And let your breath grow slow and deep, smooth as the surface of that misty lake.
There is nothing left to push against; let yourself simply glide.
Swans are among the most faithful of birds, and there is a tenderness in how they live.
A pair will often stay together for many years, returning to one another season after season.
When a swan is courting, the two will face each other on the water and curve their necks together.
Their two necks bend and meet, and the white shapes form, between them, the soft outline of a heart.
It is a real thing, that gesture, and it is one of the gentlest sights the quiet water holds.
They are devoted parents too, watchful and patient with their young.
The little ones are not yet white but a soft and dusky grey, and they are called cygnets.
Sometimes a cygnet grows tired upon the water, and climbs up onto a parent's broad back.
There it nestles down among the warm white feathers and is carried, safe, across the lake.
Picture that, a small grey bird tucked among the feathers, riding peacefully along.
There is a great safety in that image, of being carried, of being kept warm and close.
Let yourself feel held in just that way, and let your breath grow soft and slow.
You are carried now, as the cygnet is carried; you have only to rest.
Not all swans are as quiet as the white one drifting through your mist.
Some kinds are great travellers, crossing long distances when the seasons turn.
The whooper swan and the smaller Bewick's swan fly far between their summer and winter homes.
They call to one another as they go, with bright bugling voices that carry across the cold sky.
Imagine that sound, faint and far away, a soft wild music high above sleeping fields.
The mute swan, the one you are watching, is the quietest of them all.
It does not bugle; it makes only soft grunts and gentle hisses, low and close.
And when it flies, its wings give out a slow and rhythmic throb, a steady beating of the air.
That heartbeat of wings is, for the mute swan, almost its truest song.
But the one upon your lake is not flying now; it is at rest upon the still water.
It has folded its great wings and settled, quiet and white, into the gathering dusk.
Let those far bugling voices fade now into the distance, and let your breath grow long.
For all their grace, swans have gathered many old stories around themselves over the years.
There is an ancient belief that a swan stays silent its whole life, then sings once, beautifully, as it dies.
People called this the swan song, and the words still mean a last and lovely act.
But that is only a poetic legend, a tender old idea, and not something that truly happens.
A real swan lives and grows quiet old, and there is no single dying song; the tale is only a story.
In a well loved fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen, a plain grey bird is mocked for being homely.
It is called the ugly duckling, until one day it grows, and finds it was a swan all along.
It is a gentle story of becoming what you quietly were, of growing into your own true shape.
And in the ballet called Swan Lake, with its music by Tchaikovsky, a maiden is enchanted into a swan by day.
It is one of the best loved of all the stories ever danced upon a stage.
In the myths of many lands the swan stands for love, for faithfulness, for light and for change.
Let those old tales drift over you now, as soft as the mist, asking nothing, keeping nothing.
Let your breath grow slow, and let the stories settle gently into the dark.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the old tales and the far bugling voices fade gently away into the dark.
Let the misty lake grow dim, and the white bird upon it grow soft and indistinct.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a quiet swan rests upon still water, as you rest.
There is a deep peace in that calm bird, gliding without effort, faithful and untroubled.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the swan upon the water, you have only to be still, and let yourself be carried.
There is nowhere to glide to, nothing to make, no hidden effort left to give.
Let the warm dark gather you up, the way the quiet lake holds the sleeping bird.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Owl
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like a soft night wind.
Imagine the room around you has gone dark and quiet, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the gentle slackening along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture, if you like, a quiet wood at night, the trees still and the moon pale above the branches.
Somewhere in that wood, a soft-feathered bird sits calmly on a bough, watching the dark with kind round eyes.
It asks nothing of you at all, and you have only to lie here and grow heavier.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the night.
That calm bird you are picturing is a creature wholly at home in the dark, where you and I would be lost.
An owl is a bird of the night, and the night is no trouble to it at all.
Its eyes are large and face forward, the way ours do, gathering what little light there is.
With those great gentle eyes it can see in the dim where we would only stumble.
Its eyes are so big within its head that it cannot really roll them about as we do.
So instead, when it wants to look around, it simply turns its whole head, slowly and far.
An owl can turn its head much further than we ever could, easing it around to watch behind itself.
Picture that soft round head turning gently in the moonlight, patient and unhurried, taking in the quiet wood.
There is no startle in it, no rush, only a calm and steady looking.
It is content to sit and watch, and to let the long night pass slowly by.
Let some of that stillness settle into you now, the calm of a creature at ease in the dark.
Feel your breath grow slow and deep, and let your own head rest, heavy and still.
Now, in your mind, let that owl lift quietly from its branch and open its broad soft wings.
And here is the loveliest thing about it: an owl flies almost in perfect silence.
Where other birds beat the air with a rush and a flutter, the owl makes hardly a sound.
The edges of its feathers are soft and finely fringed, like a comb worn down to velvet.
Those gentle fringes hush the air as it slips past, so the wings whisper instead of beating.
It glides low and slow through the dark, a pale shape passing without a single sound.
Imagine it drifting over the still wood, silent as a shadow, calm as a held breath.
Nothing below ever hears it coming; it moves through the night like a soft secret.
There is something deeply peaceful in that hush, in a thing that can move so quietly.
Let your own breathing grow that soft, that smooth, that nearly silent.
Picture yourself gliding too, weightless and quiet, sinking gently down toward sleep.
Breathe out slowly, and let every sound in you grow faint and far away.
If the owl sees so well and flies so softly, its hearing is more wonderful still.
It listens to the night the way you might listen for a familiar voice across a quiet house.
In some owls, one ear sits a little higher on the head than the other, just slightly out of line.
That small unevenness helps the owl place a sound exactly, telling near from far and high from low.
With such ears it can find the faintest rustle in the dark, even the stir of something beneath the snow.
And that round flat face you have been picturing is not only gentle to look upon; it is useful too.
The face works like a soft shallow dish, gathering the smallest sounds and easing them toward the ears.
That is part of why owls have such calm, moon-like faces, all curved to catch the quiet of the night.
Imagine that soft face turned toward the wood, listening to the whole still dark at once.
It does not strain or worry; it simply listens, patient and unhurried, content to wait.
Let your own listening grow that gentle, taking in the quiet around you without holding to any of it.
Breathe slowly, and let the small sounds of the night drift past you and away.
There is not just one owl in the world, but many kinds, each suited to its own quiet corner of the dark.
The barn owl is pale and ghostly, with a face shaped like a soft white heart.
It drifts low over the fields on hushed wings, a gentle glimmer passing in the dusk.
The great horned owl and the tawny owl are the voices you may know best from the night woods.
Theirs are the deep, soft hooting calls that float between the trees when the world has gone to sleep.
That low hoot is a calm and steady sound, less a cry than a question asked gently of the dark.
And smallest of all is the tiny elf owl, no bigger than a sparrow, a little round handful of feathers.
It tucks itself into hollows in the dry country and watches the desert night with bright small eyes.
Great or small, pale or dark, each one is at home in the hours when we lie down to rest.
Picture them all out there now, scattered through the gentle dark, each one quiet and content.
There is room in the night for every one of them, and room in it for you to rest as well.
Let that soft chorus of distant hooting carry you a little deeper toward sleep.
Breathe out, slow and long, and let the night hold you the way it holds them.
People have always looked up at the watching owl and felt something quiet and wise in its gaze.
Because it sees in the dark and sits so still, the owl has long seemed a thoughtful, knowing thing.
In ancient Greece the owl was the companion of Athena, the goddess of wisdom.
And so, across many lands and many years, the owl became a symbol of wisdom and quiet watchfulness.
This is the gentle meaning people gave it, a story laid softly over a calm and ordinary bird.
The owl itself knows nothing of being wise; it simply sits and waits and listens to the night.
Yet in the folklore of many peoples it became a keeper of the night and a gentle guardian of secrets.
Many cultures saw it as a quiet watcher over the dark hours, harming no one, simply keeping watch.
These are legends, soft old stories, not facts, and there is comfort in them all the same.
There is something restful in the thought of a patient, watchful presence over the sleeping world.
You can let yourself be one of the sleeping ones now, with a calm watcher somewhere in the dark.
Picture that quiet guardian on its branch, asking nothing, simply keeping the long night for you.
Breathe slowly, and let yourself be watched over, safe and warm, as you sink toward sleep.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the wood and the moon and the pale gliding wings fade gently away into the dark.
Let the soft hooting grow faint and far, the way all sounds soften as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a calm owl is at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that quiet bird, watching the night, asking nothing, simply being still.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the night is soft all around you.
Like the owl on its branch, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to fly, nothing to watch for, no listening left to do at all.
Let the warm dark gather you the way the gentle wood gathers the sleeping bird.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Taiga
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like a soft wind.
Imagine the room around you has gone quiet and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the gentle settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this kind and quiet dark.
Picture, if you like, an endless forest of dark evergreen trees, stretching away to the far horizon.
Picture deep snow lying soft and unbroken between them, and a low northern light over everything.
It is still out there, and patient, and it asks nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That great still forest you are picturing has a name; it is called the taiga, or the boreal forest.
It is the largest land forest on all the Earth, a vast green belt ringing the far north of the world.
It runs in a wide soft band just below the cold edge of the Arctic, all the way around the top of the globe.
It crosses the north of Canada, and reaches over Scandinavia, and stretches on and on across Siberia.
Think of how far that is, how unimaginably far, mile after quiet mile of trees with no end in sight.
You could travel for days within it and see only more of the same hushed and snowy evergreen woods.
There is something restful in a thing so vast and so calm, so far beyond any need to be counted.
It does not hurry, and it is not going anywhere; it simply rings the cold north, year upon year.
Let your mind wander out into that endless forest, and let it grow quiet there.
There is room in it for all your thoughts to spread out thin and slow until they fade.
You do not have to hold any of this; the forest will keep it for you while you rest.
Let your breath grow long now, slow and even, like a soft wind passing through far trees.
The trees of the taiga are mostly conifers, the evergreens that wear needles instead of broad leaves.
They are the spruce and the pine, the fir and the larch, standing dark and narrow against the snow.
Their shape is gently pointed, tapering up like a quiet flame, so the snow slides softly from their branches.
Their needles are slender and waxy, made to hold onto their moisture through the long and bitter winters.
Most of them keep their needles all the year round, never letting go, never standing bare.
And so, when the brief summer finally comes, they are ready in an instant to drink the low northern sun.
They do not have to grow new leaves and wait; they only have to wake, and quietly begin again.
There is a calm patience in that, in trees that simply hold on and stay green through all the cold.
Picture them now, dark and still, dusted with snow, breathing slowly in the long northern night.
Picture how the wind moves through their needles with a soft and endless sigh.
Let that sound settle over you, the gentle hush of wind in a thousand quiet trees.
And let your own breath fall into time with it, slow and soft, growing heavier with each release.
There is one tree among them that is a little different, and it is called the larch.
The larch is an unusual conifer, for unlike its evergreen neighbours, it does let its needles go.
Each autumn its soft needles turn a warm and glowing gold, lighting up the dark woods for a while.
And then, gently, it lets them fall, standing bare and patient through the deepest of the cold.
Picture whole stands of larch turning to gold across the north as the short summer fades away.
Picture that quiet gold against the dark green of the spruce, and the white of the coming snow.
Then the needles drift down, soft and slow, and the tree rests bare until the light returns.
It is a small and lovely thing, this golden letting go before the long winter settles in.
There is no sadness in it, only a gentle releasing, a making ready for the quiet months ahead.
Perhaps you can borrow a little of that ease, and let go of the small weights of your own day.
There is nothing you need to carry into the dark with you tonight.
Let it all turn gold and drift down, soft and slow, as your breath grows long and deep.
The winters in the taiga are long, and deeply, quietly cold, and the whole forest grows slowly.
Nothing rushes here; a tree may take many years to add even a little to its height.
On the ground, a thin soft layer of fallen needles carpets the floor, springy and hushed underfoot.
That carpet is gentle and a little acidic, and so beneath the trees little else chooses to grow.
The forest floor is quiet and clean and bare, cushioned with needles, waiting under the snow.
And it is home to creatures that are built for the cold, who live in the long stillness of the north.
There are moose moving slowly among the trees, and lynx with their wide soft feet upon the snow.
There are wolves that pass like shadows, and bears that sleep the whole of the deep winter away.
There are small birds, and there are hares that quietly turn white as the snow comes down.
Imagine the bear curled deep in its den, breathing slow, while the snow falls soundless overhead.
Picture the white hare gone still and hidden, and the lynx asleep in the long blue dusk.
Let yourself grow as still as the wintering forest, your breath slow, your body warm and heavy.
This great cold forest does a quiet and important thing, simply by standing where it stands.
It holds within it a vast share of all the world's trees, more than you could ever begin to count.
And down in its cold dark soils, in its slow wet peat, it locks away an enormous store of carbon.
It breathes with the seasons, slowly, taking in and holding fast, year after patient year.
And yet, for all its long winters, the taiga has its brief and shining summer too.
When summer comes the days stretch long and bright, and in the far north the light barely fades at all.
The soft bogs hum and shimmer with insects, and the slow rivers gleam beneath an endless sky.
Birds arrive from far away, crossing whole continents to nest among the trees while the warmth lasts.
For a little while the quiet forest fills with song, and then, gently, the cold and the calm return.
Picture that brief bright summer, and then picture the snow returning, soft and slow and silent.
Through all of it, the forest only breathes, slowly in and slowly out, with the turning of the year.
Let your own breath join it now, unhurried and deep, in and out with the patient north.
There is no rush in any of this; the forest asks you only to grow still, and to rest.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the vast forest fade gently, and the snow, and the long cold dark of the north.
Let the dark spruce and the golden larch soften and blur as your eyes grow heavy.
Let the moose and the lynx and the sleeping bear settle into the quiet and be still.
You are lying here in the warm dark, safe and held, while somewhere a great forest rests as you do.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the wintering woods, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no weight upon you now at all.
Let the soft sigh of the wind in the needles fade into your own gentle breathing.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Black Forest
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like soft rain on a window.
Imagine the room around you has gone quiet and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the gentle softening along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this kind and easy dark.
Picture, if you like, deep green wooded hills, rolling away under a soft and steady rain.
The hills are dark with trees, and a fine grey mist hangs low among them, asking nothing of you.
Let your eyes rest now, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little lower, the way mist settles slowly into a quiet valley.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the deep peace of the woods.
The place you are picturing has a name; it is called the Black Forest, and it lies in the south-west of Germany.
It is a large and hilly region, thickly covered with trees, in the gentle corner of a faraway land.
The trees are mostly fir and spruce, dark and close-growing, standing patiently shoulder to shoulder.
They grow so near to one another that very little light ever reaches the soft ground below.
And that is how the forest came by its name, for under those close dark branches the woods seem nearly black.
It is a place of deep green hills and misty valleys, of quiet lakes and small old towns.
For a very long time it has been known simply for its peace, and for the deep stillness of its woods.
People have wandered there for ages, and felt the hush of it settle over them like a soft blanket.
There is no hurry anywhere in such a place; the trees keep their own slow and patient time.
Let that stillness reach you here, in your own warm dark, far from any forest at all.
Let the picture of those dark green hills grow soft at the edges, dim and quiet.
Breathe out slowly now, and feel yourself sink a little deeper toward sleep.
Among those quiet hills, something small and gentle begins, though you would hardly notice it at all.
From little springs hidden in the slopes of the Black Forest, a great river is born.
It is the river called the Danube, one of the longest in all of Europe, and it starts here, very small.
It begins as no more than clear water seeping from the ground, trickling between the roots and stones.
These first small springs gather and join, and slowly the trickle becomes a stream.
From this hushed and humble place, that water sets out on a journey of many hundreds of miles.
It will wind across much of a continent, growing wide and broad, passing many lands before it reaches the sea.
But here, in the forest hills, it is only a quiet beginning, soft and unhurried in the rain.
Picture that small bright water, slipping out of the ground in the green and misty dark.
There is something restful in a thing so great beginning so gently and so quietly.
Let your own breath be like those first small springs, soft and slow and easy.
Sink a little further now, and let the long journey of the river carry your thoughts away.
In this same forest, through the long dark winters, the people kept their hands busy by the fire.
Snow lay deep outside, and the days were short, and there was little to do but stay warm and work indoors.
And so, over many years, the forest families grew famous for what they carved and made by lamplight.
Here is the traditional home of the cuckoo clock, patiently hand-carved through those long quiet winters.
Each clock holds a little wooden bird, hidden away behind a small door of carved wood.
When the hour comes, the small door opens, and the little bird leans out and softly calls.
It calls the hours one by one, with a gentle wooden voice, and then withdraws again into the dark.
There were other crafts too, born of those still winters; woodcarving, and the blowing of glass.
By firelight, with snow at the windows, careful hands turned long evenings into lovely things.
Imagine that quiet work, and the soft and steady ticking of an old clock in a warm room.
Let that gentle, even ticking slow your own breathing, soft and regular, in and out.
There is no need to count the hours now; let them pass you by while you rest.
Sink into the warmth, and let the slow tick of the clock carry you toward sleep.
The deep woods of Germany, like these, have always lived quietly in the stories people tell.
Long ago, two brothers named Grimm wandered such regions, listening to the old tales people knew.
They gathered the folk stories of the land, and wrote them down so they would not be lost.
The dark forest of fairy stories, the kind you may half remember, owes a great deal to woods like these.
An old story might begin with a child lost among the close dark trees, far from any path.
But these are only stories, gentle and old, told to pass the long evenings by the fire.
The forest itself is kind; its slopes are crossed by countless soft and gentle footpaths.
In some places the firs stand so tall and so close that the wood grows hushed and cathedral-like.
You can stand among them in that quiet and feel the deep calm of the place settle into you.
It is the same calm the storytellers must have felt, walking home beneath the tall dark trees.
Let the old tales fade now, soft and harmless, into the dim of your own quiet room.
Breathe out slowly, and let the hush of those great still woods gather around you.
For all its old dark stories, the Black Forest has long been a place where people come simply to rest.
Its air is clear and clean, and there are gentle spa towns tucked here and there among the hills.
For a very long time, people have travelled to these towns only to walk among the trees and grow well again.
They come to breathe the fresh air, to take the quiet waters, and to let their cares fall away.
Streams tumble down the valleys, and after rain a soft grey mist rises slowly from the trees.
The forest gives its name to a well-loved cake, made of cherries and dark chocolate and cream.
It is a homely, comforting thing, born of a region that knows how to be warm in the cold and the dark.
And everywhere among the hills run those gentle paths, where there is nothing to do but walk and breathe.
Imagine yourself on such a path now, with the mist soft around you and the rain falling lightly.
There is no destination, no hurry; the walking itself is the whole of the peace.
Let that ease move through you, the deep rest that brings people across the world to these woods.
Breathe in the clear imagined air, and let the long breath out carry you gently down.
Sink a little deeper now, as easy and as quiet as mist drifting through the trees.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the dark green hills and the misty valleys soften and fade gently into the quiet.
Let the small river and the little wooden bird and the old stories drift away into the dim.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and the deep peace of the forest is all around you.
There is no path to walk now, no hour to count, no tale to remember at all.
You do not have to understand any of it, or hold onto a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft on every side.
Like the still woods after rain, you have only to be quiet, and let the hush hold you.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the mist gathers softly among the trees.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let the forest grow quiet, and let your thoughts grow quiet too.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Daintree
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them fall on you like a soft warm rain.
Imagine the room around you has gone dim and green and gentle, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture, if you like, a great green forest in the warm night, its wide leaves dripping softly long after the rain.
The air there is warm and wet and easy to breathe, and a low mist drifts among the trees.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath out lets you sink, the way a single drop slides down a leaf and is gone.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the warm green dark.
That forest you are picturing is a real place, far away on the warm north-east coast of Australia.
It is called the Daintree, and it lies in the tropical north of a state named Queensland.
It is one of the oldest rainforests anywhere on Earth, far older than the great forest of the Amazon.
Some of its corners have grown green and unbroken for well over a hundred million years.
That is older than you can easily hold in your mind, so let the thought stay soft and far away.
All that time, the rain has fallen, the leaves have dripped, and the forest has simply gone on being green.
There is no need to imagine the years; only the patience, the slow and gentle keeping of one place.
You are lying still in your own warm dark while that ancient forest breathes its warm wet air.
Nothing about it is in a hurry, and nothing about it needs anything from you.
Let that deep age settle over you, calm and unhurried and kind.
Feel how small a single night is beside a forest a hundred million years old.
Let your breath grow long and slow, and let yourself sink a little further into rest.
Long ago, all the southern lands were joined into one great country, which people now call Gondwana.
It was a vast super-continent in the age of the dinosaurs, slow and warm and covered in green.
Over unimaginable ages the lands drifted apart, and the seas opened between them.
But here and there, a patch of that first ancient forest simply carried on, unbroken, through all the change.
The Daintree is one of those patches, a living remnant of that lost green world.
When you picture its trees, you are picturing a forest that knew the footsteps of the dinosaurs.
It has watched the world rearrange itself around it, and it has only kept on growing.
There is something deeply restful in a thing that simply endures, quietly, without struggle.
It did not have to do anything clever; it only had to remain, season after season, rain after rain.
Let that long survival be a comfort to you in the dark.
You too may simply remain here, breathing, asking nothing of the hours.
Let your breath slow, and let the old green forest hold the weight of all that time for you.
The Daintree does a rare and lovely thing, found in very few places in the whole world.
It grows right down to the edge of the sea, the tall green forest meeting the warm shallow water.
And just offshore, beneath the gentle waves, lies a living coral reef.
So in this one place an ancient rainforest and an ancient reef lie almost side by side.
Picture the trees leaning out over the sand, their roots near the tide, the reef glimmering beyond.
Clear cool streams run down through the forest from the high ground, all the way to the coast.
At dawn a soft mist hangs in the high green canopy, and the leaves drip quietly into the hush.
It is the meeting of two old worlds, the green and the blue, with nothing rushed between them.
You do not need to travel there; you have only to let the picture grow soft and dim.
Imagine the warm sea breathing slowly against the shore, in and out, like your own quiet breath.
Let the sound of that distant water carry you a little further toward sleep.
Breathe out slowly, and let the tide draw your last small worries gently away.
Within that warm green dimness lives an extraordinary richness of quiet creatures.
There are countless kinds of ferns, and butterflies, and frogs, and birds, some found nowhere else on Earth.
Among the most ancient of all are its flowering plants, some of the oldest kinds we know.
They offer gentle clues to how the very first flowers in the world may once have looked.
Tall fan palms spread their wide leaves like soft green hands, catching the light as it filters down.
Strangler figs rise slowly through the canopy, and everything is patient, and everything is green.
Through this forest walks the cassowary, a tall flightless bird with a tough crest upon its head.
It moves quietly among the trees, swallowing large fruit whole as it goes.
Later it scatters the seeds across the forest floor, and so it gently helps to plant the forest anew.
In its slow wandering way, this one bird helps the whole green world keep growing.
Let that quiet image of a forest tending itself settle softly over you.
Breathe slowly now, and let your body grow as still as a leaf with no wind to move it.
This forest has not been alone in its long keeping, for it has been cared for by people too.
Its Aboriginal custodians are the Kuku Yalanji, who have known and tended this country for many thousands of years.
They hold deep and patient knowledge of its plants, its seasons, and its quiet ways.
They know which fruits are kind and which must be carefully prepared, and when the rains will come.
For them the forest is not a place apart, but home, and kin, and a story still being told.
It is right to feel a quiet respect for that long and living care, kept faithfully across so many lifetimes.
The forest you are picturing has been loved and understood for longer than almost any city has stood.
There is a deep peace in knowing a place can be held so gently, and for so very long.
You are only borrowing the picture of it for a little while, here in the safe warm dark.
Let your gratitude be soft and wordless, and let it ask nothing of you.
The forest is well cared for, and tonight, so are you.
Breathe out slowly, and let yourself rest within that long and gentle keeping.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the ancient trees and the warm rain fade gently away into the dark.
Let the mist in the high canopy soften and thin, the way the world thins as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a great green forest is at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that quiet forest, ancient and patient, asking nothing, simply being green and still.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the forest, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no need to know anything at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the green canopy gathers the falling rain.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Cloud Forest
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like soft moving mist.
Imagine the room around you has gone quiet and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the gentle softening along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this kind and quiet dark.
If you like, picture a high mountain forest somewhere in that darkness, wrapped in slow drifting cloud.
See the mist moving softly between the trees, and the moss hanging green and damp from every branch.
The air is cool and still, and the whole place is hushed, and it asks nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little further, the way cloud sinks slowly down a quiet hillside.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
The forest you are picturing is a real kind of place, high up where the mountains meet the sky.
A cloud forest is a mountain rainforest that sits so high it lives much of the time inside the clouds.
Day after day, the slow cloud comes drifting through the trees, wrapping them in near-constant mist.
So the forest does not always wait for rain to fall; instead it drinks its water straight from the air.
Moisture gathers on every leaf and every strand of moss, beading and pooling until it grows heavy.
Then it falls, drop by gentle drop, dripping steadily down through the green, even when no rain is falling.
Imagine that soft and endless dripping, quiet all around you, never hurried, never loud.
The whole forest is wet and cool and breathing slowly inside its drifting cloud.
There is nothing dramatic in it, only the patient gathering of water out of the passing mist.
It is one of the gentlest ways a forest can be fed, simply by standing still and letting the cloud arrive.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself softening too, settling further into the warm and quiet dark.
Because the cloud touches the trees so constantly, the branches become gardens all their own.
They are draped thickly in mosses and ferns, and in orchids and bromeliads, layer upon soft green layer.
These hanging plants are called epiphytes, and they perch upon the branches rather than rooting in the ground.
They take no soil at all; instead they gather their water and their dust quietly from the passing air.
So the trees wear whole small forests on their limbs, green and dripping high above the forest floor.
All of this makes the cloud forest one of the lushest, greenest, most dripping places on the whole Earth.
It is soft and hushed and cool, every surface furred with moss, every branch heavy with gentle life.
Picture the deep green of it, the way the mist moves slowly between the laden trees.
Nothing here is bare; everything is cushioned and softened and softly alive.
There is a deep peace in a place so green that even the trees are clothed in growing things.
Let that green softness settle over you, cool and quiet and kind.
And let your breath grow long and unhurried, in time with the slow drip of the moss.
These forests grow in the high places of the world, where warm lands climb up to meet the clouds.
Famous cloud forests rise in the mountains of Central and South America, lush and cool and green.
There is Monteverde, high in the hills of Costa Rica, and there are the cloud forests of the long Andes.
And there are others scattered across the tropics, wherever warm air rises against high ground and cools.
When that moist air climbs the mountainsides, it cools as it rises, and its water turns to drifting cloud.
So the cloud forms again and again upon the slopes, and settles into the trees, and the forest drinks.
It is a slow and faithful cycle, the warm air rising, the cloud gathering, the moss catching every drop.
Picture those green mountainsides far away, half hidden in cloud, breathing mist into the sky.
You do not need to find them on any map; only let the high green places drift through your mind.
They have stood like that for a very long time, quietly gathering water from the air.
There is no hurry anywhere in them, only the slow turning of cloud into water and water into cloud.
Let your body share in that slowness, growing heavier, asking nothing of the hours.
Within all that green and dripping quiet live some of the rarest and loveliest creatures on Earth.
Here is the home of the quetzal, a bird of brilliant green, with long soft feathers like trailing leaves.
Here too are the glass frogs, so clear in the belly that you can almost see the small life within them.
And here are tiny hummingbirds, no bigger than a thumb, moving like sparks through the cool green air.
Many of the plants and creatures here are found nowhere else in all the world, only on these few high slopes.
Even the little bromeliads become small worlds, holding pools of rainwater cupped within their leaves.
Those tiny pools are gardens and ponds high above the ground, where insects and small frogs live whole lives.
Imagine that, an entire small life lived out in a teaspoon of water held in a leaf in the mist.
All around them the moss drinks, the ferns drip, and the cloud drifts slowly through.
It is a place crowded with quiet, jewel-like life, and yet it feels deeply and gently still.
You do not have to remember any of their names; only let them shimmer softly and fade.
And let your breath grow slow and deep, as quiet as a frog asleep in a leaf of rain.
Notice, as you drift, how very quiet such a forest is, and how gently sound moves through it.
All the moss and all the water soften every sound, so the forest feels deeply and tenderly hushed.
There is little here but the slow dripping of the trees, and now and then one distant unseen bird.
The mist itself seems to muffle the world, wrapping the green in a soft and patient silence.
And all that gathered water does a quiet and generous thing as it trickles slowly downward.
The constant mist and the dripping trees feed the small mountain streams that run far below.
Drop by drop, the cloud forest fills those streams, and the streams become the rivers of the lower lands.
So the high green forest quietly waters the valleys and the fields and the people who live beneath it.
It does this without sound or hurry, simply by standing in the cloud and letting the water fall.
Picture that gentle giving, the high mist becoming a stream, the stream becoming a river far away.
There is a deep kindness in it, a whole forest serving the land below just by being still and green.
Let that long quiet pour into you now, slowing your breath, softening your every thought.
Let yourself grow as still and as hushed as a forest deep inside its drifting cloud.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the high green forest soften and grow dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
Let the cloud drift slowly away, and the dripping moss fall quiet, and the distant bird go still.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a cool green forest is at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that quiet place, gathering water from the air, asking nothing, simply being green.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the forest in its cloud, you have only to be still, and let the gentle quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no task waiting for you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the slow cloud gathers softly around the trees.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Sahara
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like warm air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that darkness, picture a wide stretch of soft sand, smooth and pale and endless.
Above it hangs a huge quiet sky, deep and dark and scattered all over with faint stars.
The air is cool and still, and there is no sound at all but your own slow breathing.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That wide pale sand you are picturing belongs to the Sahara, the largest hot desert on all the Earth.
It lies spread across the whole top of Africa, from one far sea to another far sea.
It is so vast that it covers a stretch of land about the size of a great country like China, or the United States.
Imagine that, a desert nearly as wide as a continent, and almost all of it still and empty.
You could travel for days and days across it and meet nothing but sand and stone and sky.
There is a deep and ancient quiet over all of it, a silence that has lain there for a very long time.
No crowd, no clamour, no hurry; only the slow turning of day into cool night into day again.
It is far too large for any one mind to hold, and you do not need to try.
Just let it be enormous and peaceful out there beyond you, going on and on under the stars.
There is something restful in a space so wide that nothing in it ever has to rush.
Let that vast stillness settle over you, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, growing as quiet and unhurried as that great open land.
It is easy to picture a desert as nothing but rolling dunes, soft golden hills of sand without end.
But the truth, gently, is that much of the Sahara is not sand at all.
A great deal of it is bare rock, and gravel, and wide flat plains of stone.
The famous seas of dunes do exist, and they are called ergs, but they are only a part of the whole.
So picture not just soft sand but also long open tablelands, and dark hills, and stony ground worn smooth.
Across all of it the days can grow fiercely hot, scorched by a high and steady sun.
But the dry air holds little moisture, and so it cannot hold the heat once the sun goes down.
When night comes, the warmth slips quickly away, and the desert turns surprisingly cold.
On some nights the temperature falls so far that it comes close to freezing under the stars.
Picture that cool clear night settling over the stone and the sand, calm and deep and still.
There is a great peace in that cooling dark, a quiet that comes down with the falling heat.
Let the cool of that imagined night settle over you, and let your breathing grow long and slow.
Now here is a gentle and astonishing thing, the kind to wander through as you grow sleepy.
The Sahara has not always been a desert; not so very long ago, it was green.
Only a few thousand years past there was a time we call the African Humid Period.
In those days rain fell across the land, and there were lakes, and rivers, and wide soft grasslands.
People lived there too, among the grass and the water, in a country we would hardly know today.
We can be sure of this, because ancient paintings remain on the rocks from those greener years.
On the bare stone, people long ago painted hippos in the water, and herds of cattle grazing.
Imagine that: hippos and cattle, where now there is only quiet sand and sun-warmed stone.
The same wide land that lies so dry tonight once held reeds, and pools, and the calls of animals.
It is a soft reminder that even the greatest, stillest places are slowly, slowly changing.
Let that thought rest lightly in your mind, asking nothing of you, only wonder.
And let your breath grow slow and deep, as the green fades gently back into the warm dark.
You might wonder how a green and watered land could ever turn to such an enormous desert.
The answer lies in a slow and gentle wobble, far out in the way the Earth moves through space.
Over many thousands of years the Earth tilts and turns just a little differently as it journeys.
That tiny, patient shift changes where the great rains fall, and how the seasons reach the land.
And so, across ages too long to feel, the Sahara slowly dries, and then slowly greens again.
It has done this many times over, breathing in and breathing out across deep and unhurried time.
There were green Saharas long before the last one, and there may be green Saharas again.
Think of the desert as something that breathes, ever so slowly, over thousands upon thousands of years.
One enormous breath in across the ages, and one enormous breath out, and no hurry in any of it.
There is a deep calm in that, in changes so slow that no single life could ever watch them happen.
Let that slowness pour into you now, the long patient breathing of the land matching your own.
Breathe in gently with the green ages, and breathe out softly with the long dry years.
Let your own breath grow as slow and as patient as the deep breathing of the desert.
Even now, the Sahara reaches out across the world in ways you would never guess from its stillness.
When the wind lifts the fine dry dust from its plains, that dust rises high and travels far.
It crosses the whole wide Atlantic Ocean, carried on the wind for thousands of miles.
And it comes down at last on the other side of the world, upon the green Amazon rainforest.
There, the desert dust feeds the soil, scattering the minerals the great forest needs to grow.
So the driest place helps to nourish the wettest, the empty sand quietly feeding the deep green trees.
And the people of the desert have always reached outward too, by old and patient ways.
For centuries, long caravans of camels have crossed the sand, trading salt and gold along ancient routes.
They found their way by the stars overhead, and by a deep, handed-down knowledge of the land.
The Tuareg and other desert peoples have long made their home here, moving with the seasons and the scarce water.
And beneath the sand lie vast old stores of water, laid down in wetter ages, feeding green oases where date palms grow.
Picture one such oasis, the palms and the still water hidden in all that sand, calm in the cool night.
Let that quiet picture soften now, and let your breath grow slow and your eyes grow heavy.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the wide sand and the bare stone fade gently away into the dark.
Let the green ages and the dust on the wind and the long camel routes drift softly out of thought.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and far away the great desert lies still beneath its stars.
There is a deep peace out there, a silence laid down over the sand across thousands of patient years.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the desert under its huge quiet sky, you have only to be still, and let the long night hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no hurry anywhere at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the cool night gathers the wide and sleeping sand.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Gobi
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like a far wind.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that darkness, let an immense open plain begin to spread out before you, flat and endless and still.
The horizon is a long, calm line, very far away, and it asks nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little further into the wide, quiet stillness of that place.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, across that open land, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That vast open plain you are picturing has a name; far from here, it is called the Gobi.
It is one of the great deserts of Asia, spreading across the south of Mongolia and the north of China.
It is enormous, a sweep of land so wide that you could travel for many days and see only more of the same calm distance.
And here is the first gentle surprise of it; it is not a hot desert at all.
The Gobi is a cold desert, lifted high above the sea and far inland, away from any softening ocean.
Its winters are bitter and long, and sometimes a thin dusting of snow settles quietly over its sands.
Picture that for a moment, snow lying soft and silent on a desert, the cold so still it seems to hold its breath.
It is a place of great patience, where the seasons turn slowly under an immense and open sky.
There is nothing harsh in it tonight, only a wide, cool, peaceful emptiness.
You are warm and safe, watching it all from far away, with nothing asked of you.
Let that cool, quiet distance settle over you like a soft blanket.
And let your breath go slow and deep, easing out into the calm.
Let your gaze wander now across the ground of this place, slowly, in no hurry at all.
Much of the Gobi is not soft golden dune as you might imagine a desert to be.
Instead it is bare rock and gravel plains, and wide stretches of pale, dry grassland.
The word Gobi itself comes from the Mongolian tongue, and it means something close to a waterless place.
It is dry because it lies in what is called a rain shadow, far behind the great mountains of the Himalaya.
Those huge mountains stand in the way of the moist winds, and wring the rain from them long before it can ever reach here.
So the clouds arrive empty, and the land below stays still and dry and open, year after patient year.
There is a quiet honesty to a place like this, asking for nothing, holding only stone and grass and sky.
Imagine the small sounds of it, the faint whisper of wind over gravel, and then a deep and settling silence.
It is a silence so wide and so soft that it could carry you gently down into sleep.
Let it carry you a little now, this vast and waterless quiet.
Breathe out slowly, and let your thoughts grow as still as that open plain.
Now let your mind drift toward the red cliffs that rise here and there from the floor of the Gobi.
They glow a soft, warm red in the low light, and within them sleeps a wonderful secret.
For the Gobi is one of the great resting places of the dinosaurs, who lived and died here unimaginably long ago.
Locked deep in the rock are their bones, lying patient and undisturbed for many tens of millions of years.
Some of the very first dinosaur eggs ever found in all the world were uncovered here, in this quiet land.
Imagine them, small rounded eggs turned to stone, cradled in the rock through age after silent age.
Whole creatures lie here too, curled where they came to rest, sleeping in the cool of the cliffs.
There is something deeply restful in that, in such a long and undisturbed sleep within the patient earth.
Nothing hurries them, and nothing wakes them; they simply rest, held gently by the stone.
You can let yourself rest in just that way tonight, easy and unhurried and safe.
Let the warm red cliffs and their sleeping bones soften and fade into the dark.
And let your own breathing slow, drifting down toward that same deep and easy rest.
Across the long edges of this desert, picture now a faint and ancient path winding through the haze.
Long ago, the old trade route called the Silk Road skirted the borders of the Gobi.
Slow caravans of camels crossed this hard, open country, moving between China and the lands far to the west.
They carried silk and tea and small precious goods, swaying gently along over the gravel and the sand.
Picture the camels themselves, the two-humped Bactrian camels of these cold plains, calm and shaggy and patient.
They walked for days through the stillness, their soft feet quiet on the ground, in no great hurry to arrive.
And the Gobi is home to other gentle, rare creatures, who wander it far from any path.
There are wild asses and slender gazelles, and the very rare Gobi bear, one of the rarest bears in all the world.
They move quietly across the immense land, asking little, content in the wide and open space.
There is no hurry anywhere in this scene, only the slow and easy passing of patient living things.
Let yourself move with that same unhurried calm, soft and slow and untroubled.
Breathe out gently, and let the long, dreaming caravan carry you onward into sleep.
Now imagine the day fading over the Gobi, the light going soft and golden and then a deep and gentle blue.
Scattered across the open land, picture the round felt tents of the herding people who have always lived here.
For longer than anyone can remember, they have moved with their animals across this country, following the grass.
Their tents are warm and round and snug, holding a small glow of light against the cool of the evening.
And as the dark comes down, the sky above grows vast beyond all telling.
The silence here is immense, so deep and so wide that it feels like a soft hand laid over the whole plain.
Then the stars come out, and they crowd thick and bright over the cold, dark land.
There are more of them than you could ever count, scattered close and shining in the clear high air.
You are lying safe and warm beneath all of that quiet brightness, small and held and peaceful.
There is nothing to do but watch, and breathe, and let yourself grow heavy and still.
Let the great crowd of stars wheel slowly above you, calm and silent and endless.
And let each slow breath out carry you a little deeper toward sleep.
Now let the desert begin to soften and grow dim, the way a far landscape fades at the close of the day.
Let the red cliffs and the sleeping bones drift gently out of mind, asking nothing of you at all.
Let the camels and the round tents and the bright crowded stars grow faint, and then quietly let them go.
There is nothing more to picture now, and nothing left to hold; you may set it all softly down.
Feel only the warmth around you, and the slow, easy rise and fall of your own breathing.
Your limbs are heavy and loose, your shoulders soft, your thoughts grown slow and dim.
You are safe, and warm, and there is nowhere at all you need to be.
The vast quiet of that far plain is in you now, calm and wide and deep.
Let your breath grow slower still, with each gentle one carrying you down.
There is nothing left to do.
Let yourself drift.
Let go now, into the soft dark.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Atacama
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like the night air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture, if you like, a vast dark sky thick with stars, spread wide above a still and silent ground.
The air is cool and clear and utterly calm, and the land below lies quiet, asking nothing of you.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath out lets you sink a little further, the way the dusk settles slowly over an open plain.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That still and silent ground you are picturing is a real place, far away in the south of the world.
It is called the Atacama, a long high desert that lies in the north of a country named Chile.
Of all the deserts on the Earth that are not locked in ice, it is the very driest one we know.
In some corners of it the rain almost never comes, and the air stays clear and dry day after day.
There are weather stations there that have waited for years and never once measured a single drop of rain.
It is a land of dust and pale stone and wide open sky, with very little to break the quiet.
You do not need to remember its name, or where it lies; just hold the feeling of that dryness and that calm.
Imagine standing on that ground in the cool of the evening, with nothing moving and no sound at all.
There is a deep and ancient stillness in such a place, the stillness of a land long undisturbed.
It has been quiet there for so very long that the silence itself seems to have settled into the stones.
Let that wide calm spread softly through you now, and let your breath grow slow and unhurried.
Feel yourself loosening, settling, drifting a little further into the warm and gentle dark.
It is worth wondering, gently, how a place could ever grow so dry and so still.
The Atacama lies caught between two great walls of mountains, with the sky stretched wide between them.
To one side rise the high peaks of the Andes, and to the other a lower range near the coast.
Those mountains stand like patient guardians, holding back the rain clouds before they can ever reach the land.
And out beyond the coast, a cool ocean current drifts by, which keeps the sea air calm and dry.
Between the mountains and the cool sea, the rain is gently turned away, again and again, year upon year.
So the desert lies sheltered in the middle, in a deep and lasting calm, almost untouched by storms.
You do not need to hold the shape of it; just feel that quiet, that long stillness between the hills.
Some of the dry riverbeds there have not felt flowing water for hundreds, even thousands, of years.
Their pale channels wind across the ground, patient and empty, waiting in a silence older than memory.
There is no hurry anywhere in such a land, only the slow turning of the days beneath a wide sky.
Let that ancient patience settle over you, and let each breath grow longer and softer than the last.
Sink a little deeper now, into the calm, the way the dusk sinks slowly over the silent plain.
Now let your mind lift gently upward, away from the ground, into the wide and darkening sky.
Because the air here is so dry, and so clear, and the land lies so high and so far from any city, the nights are very dark.
There are almost no clouds to soften the sky, and almost no glow of lamps to wash the stars away.
And so the Atacama holds some of the darkest, clearest night skies anywhere on the whole of the Earth.
When the sun goes down, the stars come out in their thousands, sharp and steady and very bright.
The great band of the Milky Way arches overhead, so bright that it can cast the faintest shadow on the ground.
Imagine that, lying out there in the cool dark, the soft light of countless stars falling all around you.
It is the kind of sky that people travel a long way to see, the sky as it was before our cities grew.
There is nothing between you and the depth of the universe but clear and silent air.
You do not have to name a single star, or trace a single shape; only let the wide dark sky hold you.
Let your gaze drift gently out into that depth, with no effort at all, the way thoughts drift before sleep.
Breathe out slowly, and let the vastness of that sky feel calm and kind, rather than far away.
Let yourself grow heavier, held beneath the stars, sinking softly toward sleep.
It is because of those clear and steady skies that people have brought their great instruments to the Atacama.
High on its quiet ridges stand observatories, with their wide telescopes turned patiently toward the night.
From these calm heights, watchers peer deep into the universe, gathering the faint old light of distant stars.
They are gazing gently out across unimaginable distances, into the soft glow of galaxies far away.
The dryness and the dark that make the desert so still are the very things that make it so good for this looking.
You can picture the great domes resting on the high ground, silent and patient under the turning stars.
And the ground itself is so dry and so red, in places, that it looks a little like the planet Mars.
Because it is so dry and so bare, scientists come here to test their Mars rovers and their Mars experiments.
They drive small machines across the pale earth, rehearsing journeys to another world entirely.
So this quiet desert becomes a doorway, both upward into the stars and outward toward the red planet.
But none of that asks anything of you now; it is only happening, gently, far away in the calm.
Let those distant domes and quiet machines fade softly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Sink further into the warm dark, as still as the high ground beneath the watching stars.
It would be easy to think that nothing at all could live in a place so dry and so still.
And yet, even here, life clings on quietly, in small and patient ways, where it can.
There are tiny, hardy microbes hidden in the soil and within the stones, living slow and sheltered lives.
There are lichens that drink the rare coastal fog when it rolls softly in from the cool sea.
Now and then, very rarely, after an unusual rain, the desert does something quiet and astonishing.
All across the pale ground, flowers open in their countless thousands, and the bare land blooms.
For a little while the dry earth is carpeted with soft colour, and then, gently, it fades again to calm.
High in the desert there are pale lagoons and wide flats of salt, shining faintly in the still air.
Tall flamingos wade there in the shallow water, feeding slowly, calm against the pale and quiet ground.
And at dawn, in places, fields of geysers breathe slow columns of steam into the cold morning sky.
So even in the driest land, there is a soft and patient kind of life, asking little, resting much.
You do not need to keep any of it; just let those gentle pictures drift slowly across your darkening mind.
Breathe out, and let yourself grow as still and as patient as that quiet, far away land.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the wide dry land and the high quiet mountains fade gently away into the dark.
Let the great band of stars soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a vast still desert rests quietly beneath its sky.
There is a deep peace in that wide silence, that long calm, that gentle gazing into the depth of the night.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like that still high ground, you have only to be quiet, and let the long calm hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no hurry anywhere at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the night gathers softly over the silent desert.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Namib
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like a soft tide.
Imagine the room around you has gone warm and dark, and that you are safe within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
If you like, you may picture a great sweep of red sand, glowing soft and warm under a wide quiet sky.
And far at its edge, a cool grey mist drifting in off a distant sea, slow and silent and kind.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little further, the way warm sand settles when no one walks across it.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
The warm red sand you are picturing has a name, and it lies in a true place far away.
It is called the Namib, a desert that runs along the western coast of southern Africa.
It lies in the land of Namibia, which took its own gentle name from this very desert.
And here something rare and strange happens, something that exists in almost no other place on Earth.
For here a great dry desert comes right down to meet a wide and cold ocean, the Atlantic.
Picture that quiet edge of the world, where endless warm sand simply reaches the cool grey water.
There is no struggle in it, no hurry; the dunes and the sea have lain side by side for a very long time.
It is a meeting of two enormous calm things, the patient sand and the patient sea.
You are only resting at the edge of it now, the way you rest at the edge of sleep.
There is nothing for you to do here but breathe and be still.
Let your breath grow long and unhurried, in and slowly out.
And let your body sink a little deeper into the warm dark with each one.
Now let your mind wander out across that red sand, and rest there a moment in the stillness.
It is thought that the Namib is the oldest desert on all the Earth.
It has been dry, they believe, for tens of millions of years, far longer than nearly any other.
Try to let that long age settle softly over you, without trying to grasp it.
This sand was already old and dry when creatures we have never seen walked the world.
It has simply lain here, warm and patient, through unimaginable stretches of quiet time.
There is no rush anywhere in such a place; it has all the time there ever was.
Nothing about it is hurried, and nothing about it needs to be.
Picture the slow stillness of sand that has waited longer than memory itself.
Let that ancient patience pour gently into you now, slowing everything within you.
You have all the time in the world, and you have nowhere at all to be.
Breathe slowly, and let yourself grow as still and as old as the patient sand.
Some of this sand has come a very long way to lie here in the warm and waiting dark.
Over countless ages, rivers far to the south carried grains of it down toward the sea.
And then the cold ocean current and the steady wind gathered it up and bore it slowly north.
Picture that, the sea and the wind passing the sand along, grain by grain, over endless years.
And here, at last, the wind has gently piled it into dunes, in a place named Sossusvlei.
These dunes are among the very tallest in all the world, rising hundreds of metres into the sky.
They glow a deep orange and a soft warm red, with crests drawn sharp and clean against the blue.
Imagine standing small and quiet at the foot of one, looking up its long curving slope.
It took the wind ages upon ages to raise it, one patient grain laid upon another.
There is no force in it now, only the long slow work of time, finally come to rest.
Let that slow rising settle you too, and let your breath rise and fall as gently as the dunes.
Feel yourself growing heavier, sinking softly, asking nothing of the passing hours.
You might think a desert this old and this dry could hold no life at all.
Almost no rain falls here, season upon season, year upon patient year.
And yet there is a quiet secret, and it comes in softly off the cold sea each morning.
For most mornings a cool fog rolls in from the chilly ocean and drifts across the sand.
It moves slow and grey and silent over the great red dunes, and it carries gentle water within it.
This soft fog is the secret of all the life that lingers here, a breath of moisture in a dry land.
Some small beetles have learned its quiet gift, and they wait for it in the cool of dawn.
They climb the dunes and tip their little bodies upward, so the fog gathers in tiny beads upon their backs.
And then the water trickles slowly down to their mouths, and they drink the morning air.
It is a tiny, gentle, ingenious thing, gathering a sip of water from the passing mist.
Picture that soft fog drifting over the sand, bringing its quiet life to a patient place.
Let it drift through your mind the way it drifts over the dunes, cool and slow and kind.
And let your breath grow soft and misty too, slow on the way in, slower on the way out.
There is a strange and ancient plant that lives here, drinking from that same soft fog.
It is called the welwitschia, and it grows in a way no other plant on Earth quite does.
For its whole long life it grows only two leaves, just two, that lengthen slowly across the sand.
And it lives a very long time; some welwitschia alive today are well over a thousand years old.
Imagine a single quiet plant that has rested in one place since before your great cities were built.
Nearby, at a place called Deadvlei, stands something stranger and more still again.
There a pale white pan of cracked clay holds the dark skeletons of camel-thorn trees.
Those trees died many centuries ago, yet in the dry air they cannot rot, so they simply stand.
They wait there, black and silent against the glowing red dunes, keeping their ancient shapes.
And along the cold coast, old shipwrecks lie half buried in the sand, where the desert meets the sea.
Picture all of it resting together in the quiet, the old plant, the still trees, the patient wrecks.
Let those calm and ancient things keep watch while you let go, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
There is nothing to do here but rest, the way they have rested for so very long.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the great red dunes soften and grow dim, fading gently into the warm dark around you.
Let the cool fog drift away, and the still trees, and the long quiet edge of the sea.
You do not have to remember a single word of any of it; let it all settle and be still.
You are lying here in the warm dark, as old and as patient as the oldest sand.
There is a deep peace in that quiet desert, asking nothing, simply waiting beneath its wide sky.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the sand, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no pressure on you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the desert gathers the soft grey mist at dawn.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Lake Baikal
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them move past you like cool water.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
