Somewhere in that darkness, let yourself picture a great lake lying perfectly still under a wide night sky.
Its water is dark and clear and deep, and not a single ripple troubles its calm.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink, the way a smooth stone settles slowly through still and silent water.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That still lake you are picturing has a name, and its name is Baikal.
It lies in the south of Siberia, far away in the cold heart of Russia, ringed by quiet mountains.
Of all the lakes upon the Earth, this is the deepest, sinking down more than a mile beneath its calm surface.
Think of all that water, layer upon dark layer, growing colder and stiller the deeper it goes.
Above it the sky is vast, and the mountains stand patient all around, and the air is clean and cold.
There is no need to imagine reaching the bottom; only to feel how deep and how quiet it is.
It is so deep that the lowest waters lie in a darkness that the daylight has never once touched.
Down there, all is slow and silent and undisturbed, as it has been for an unimaginable age.
You do not have to hold any of these things in your mind; let them simply drift by.
Let the depth of that water settle into you, vast and dark and calm.
Feel yourself sinking gently along with it, growing heavier with each breath.
Let your breath grow slow and deep, as deep and unhurried as the still lake itself.
This lake is not only the deepest in the world; it is also the oldest, by far.
Most lakes are fleeting things, slowly filling with silt until they vanish within a brief stretch of time.
But Baikal is around twenty-five million years old, far older than almost any other lake on Earth.
It was already an ancient lake when creatures we have never seen walked the young and changing land.
Picture that long quiet age, all those millions of years of still water lying patiently in its place.
It does not vanish, and it does not fill in, because it sits in a deep and slowly widening crack in the world.
Far below, the crust of the Earth is gently pulling apart, and so the lake stays deep, and slowly grows.
Over ages too long to feel, this great basin is opening wider, the way a sleeper's chest rises and falls.
There is no hurry anywhere in this; the lake measures its life in millions of unbothered years.
Let that immense slowness pour over you, asking nothing, hurrying nothing.
There is all the time in the world here, and none of it belongs to you tonight.
Let your breath lengthen, slow and patient, as ancient and calm as the lake.
Now let your mind rest on the water itself, which is famous for being clear and pure.
On a still day you can look down through it and follow your gaze a long, long way into the deep.
Part of the reason is a great deal of quiet, unseen work, going on day and night in the water.
Countless tiny shrimp-like creatures drift through the lake, grazing as they go, gently cleaning it.
They graze and graze, never resting, sweeping the water clean so that it stays bright and clear.
It is a soft and tireless labour, going on far beneath the surface, asking for no thanks at all.
Because of them, and the cold, and the depth, the lake keeps that rare and glassy clearness.
Imagine looking down into water so clear it seems there is nothing between you and the deep blue dark.
There is something restful in that work being done, quietly, without you needing to lift a hand.
You can let everything be tended for you now, the way the small creatures tend the lake.
Nothing here needs your attention; it is all looked after, all gently kept.
Let go a little more, and let your breath grow soft and slow.
In the long cold of the Siberian winter, the surface of the lake freezes over completely.
The ice grows thick enough to walk upon, and to bear great weight, stretching white to the far shore.
And yet, in places, this ice is so clear and so pure that you can seem to look straight down into the deep.
Imagine kneeling on that glass-clear ice and gazing through it into the dark and patient water below.
On the coldest mornings, mist rises softly from the open water, drifting low against the ringing mountains.
The frozen lake is not silent, though; the thick ice groans and cracks with strange, booming sounds.
These deep singing notes travel far across the still white surface, rolling out into the cold and quiet.
It is a slow music, made by the ice alone, with no one needed there to hear it.
Picture that vast white expanse, the rising mist, the far booming song of the ice in the cold.
The local peoples have long held this lake to be sacred, and have loved its great stillness.
Let that hush of cold and clear ice settle gently over you now.
Let the booming song fade soft and far away, and let your breath grow slow.
Because Baikal is so old, and so deep, and so cut off from every other water, it is a world of its own.
Most of the creatures that live within it are found nowhere else upon the whole of the Earth.
They arose here, slowly, over the long millions of years, and they belong to this one ancient lake alone.
Among them is the nerpa, a small and gentle seal, one of the only freshwater seals in all the world.
Picture it resting on the ice, or drifting through the clear cold water, calm and unhurried and at home.
No one is quite sure how its ancestors came to this lake so far from any sea, long and long ago.
But here it has lived for ages, in waters that hold about a fifth of all the fresh surface water on Earth.
That is more unfrozen fresh water than all the great lakes of North America hold together.
Imagine all of it, gathered into one deep still basin, holding its own small private world.
There is a deep peace in a thing being so entirely at home, asking for nowhere else.
You are at home here too, in the warm dark, with nowhere else you need to be.
Let yourself rest in that belonging, and let your breath grow slow and easy.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the great depth and the long ages fade gently away into the dark.
Let the clear ice and its far booming song soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a vast still lake is resting too, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that quiet water, ancient and clear and calm, asking nothing, simply being still.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the lake, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to keep, no depth you need to reach tonight.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the great basin gathers its deep and patient water.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Caspian Sea
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like a slow tide.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that darkness, picture a great calm body of water at dusk, wide and still and grey.
Its surface is smooth and unhurried, and you cannot see across it; there is no far shore at all.
The light is fading softly over it, and the air is warm, and the small waves breathe in and out.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little, the way the evening light sinks slowly down into still water.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That wide and quiet water you are picturing has a gentle secret to it.
It is the largest enclosed body of water on the whole Earth, and people have always called it a sea.
Yet it has no opening to any ocean; it is a sea that touches no other sea at all.
It lies entirely surrounded by land, ringed by deserts and grassy steppes and far blue mountains.
In truth it is the world's largest lake, the greatest still water held within the land.
But it is so very vast, and its water is so faintly salty, that no one ever thinks to call it small.
So it has carried the name of a sea for as long as anyone can remember, and the name suits it well.
It rests between Europe and Asia, where two great parts of the world lean quietly toward each other.
Five different countries gather around its long shores, sharing its calm grey water between them.
Imagine standing at its edge, looking out, and seeing only water meeting the soft evening sky.
There is something restful in a sea with no way out, holding itself gently in the cradle of the land.
Let that wideness settle over you, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, growing calm and enclosed and safe, as you settle further into the dark.
Now let your mind drift far back, long before any of us, into the deep patience of time.
This great water is the quiet remnant of a much larger sea that once spread across this whole region.
Ages ago an ancient sea reached far across these lands, wide and open under a different sky.
Then, slowly, over spans of time too long to picture, the land itself rose and shifted around it.
Little by little the old sea was closed off, cut away from the wider ocean by the lifting earth.
What was left behind, gathered in a great low hollow of the land, is the calm water we see today.
It is the last still pool of a vanished sea, kept and cradled where the ocean once had been.
None of this happened in a hurry; it was the work of an unimaginably slow and gentle world.
The mountains pushed up grain by grain, and the sea was enclosed almost without anyone noticing.
Picture that slow shaping going on quietly through the ages, with no need to rush at all.
And so the water you are imagining is very old, an ancient sea held softly inside the land.
Let that slowness pour into you now, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
There is no hurry anywhere in this old water; it asks you only to rest.
Many rivers feed this great enclosed sea, flowing down to it from across the lands around.
They come from far away, gathering rain and snow, and pour their waters quietly into it.
Greatest of them all is the mighty Volga, a long and patient river winding down from the north.
It brings the gift of fresh water down through the plains and lays it gently into the sea.
Yet here is the strange and lovely thing: though so many rivers flow in, not one flows out.
There is no river leaving, no channel running off to the ocean, no outlet anywhere along its shores.
Instead the water leaves only by rising slowly into the warm and thirsty air, vanishing into the sky.
Day by day, under the wide sun, a little of the sea lifts gently away as unseen vapour.
So the sea is forever filling and forever evaporating, a slow breath of rivers in and air out.
It is the quietest of balances, the long tides of rain and river answered by the patient sun.
Picture that gentle exchange going on without end, the water arriving and softly rising again.
Let your own breath match that slow rhythm, flowing in, drifting out, asking nothing.
Breathe in like a river, and let it go like vapour into the warm dark.
Let your mind rest now on the deep low place where all this water gathers.
The surface of this sea lies below the level of the world's far oceans, down in a great low basin.
It is one of the lowest places on all the continents, a deep calm hollow holding its ancient water.
Imagine the land sloping gently down and down to meet it, the sea settled in the lowest seat of the earth.
Far from any ocean, in this great low cradle, the water rests deeper than the seas of the world.
And in its dim depths live creatures found in few other places, quiet and old and at home there.
The sturgeon swims here, an ancient armoured fish that has changed little across long ages of time.
From its roe comes the famous caviar, but in the dark of the deep it simply drifts and feeds and rests.
Here too lives the small Caspian seal, a gentle creature that is found in this one sea and nowhere else.
Picture that little seal turning slowly through the cool grey water, unhurried, perfectly at peace.
All of them are held in the same low calm basin, sheltered far from the open ocean's reach.
Let yourself rest in that low quiet place too, settling down to the very bottom of the dark.
Sink gently, like a seal drifting down through still water, and let your breath grow soft.
For all its quiet, this sea has long known the slow passage of people across its waters.
For many centuries its surface has carried small boats, ferrying goods from one shore to another.
Branches of the old Silk Road, those ancient threads of trade, once touched along its distant shores.
Caravans and traders came down to its edges, and bundles of goods were carried out across the water.
Imagine those slow journeys long ago, sails leaning softly into the wind, in no great hurry at all.
Silks and spices and quiet news passed from hand to hand around this enclosed and patient sea.
Its level rises and falls gently over the years, lifting with the rains and the swelling rivers.
In wetter years the water creeps a little higher up the shore, and in dry years it eases softly back.
And always its far shore is lost beyond the horizon, too distant ever to be seen from where you stand.
You could sail a long while across it and still find only water meeting the soft and quiet sky.
There is a deep peace in that, a sea so wide it hides its own far edge in the gentle haze.
Let that wide horizon blur and soften now, and let your eyes grow heavier still.
Let the slow boats and the slow rivers carry your thoughts off into the warm dark.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the wide grey water and the far lost shore fade gently away into the dark.
Let the slow rivers and the rising vapour soften and dim, the way the world dims as you grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a great calm sea is at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that ancient enclosed water, holding itself quietly within the land.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like that quiet sea, you have only to be still, and let the long calm hold you.
There is nowhere to sail, nothing to carry, no far shore you need to reach tonight.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the low land cradles its ancient and patient water.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Dead Sea
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like warm air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture yourself lying back on calm, still water, the surface so smooth it barely moves.
The water holds you up easily, without any effort, the way a warm hand cradles something small.
You float as though resting in a chair made of water, your weight given up entirely to it.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
The water you are floating on lies in a real place, far away and very low.
It is called the Dead Sea, a long lake of still water resting between Jordan and Israel.
Of all the dry land on Earth, its shore is the very lowest, sunk far below the level of the world ocean.
If you walked down to its edge, you would be standing lower than anywhere else on solid ground.
All around it the desert lies open and warm, and the air is calm and very still.
There is a great quiet in such a place, the hush of the lowest, stillest land there is.
Imagine the warmth of that air, soft on your skin as you lie back on the heavy water.
Nothing hurries here; the sun moves slowly, and the surface barely stirs.
It is the kind of stillness that asks nothing of you, only that you let yourself rest.
You are floating at the bottom of the world, in the most peaceful of low and quiet places.
Let that lowness settle into you, drawing your body down into the warmth beneath you.
And let your breath grow slow and long, slipping out gently into the still desert air.
The reason this water can hold you so easily is hidden within it, dissolved and unseen.
The Dead Sea is not like the ocean; it is many times saltier, heavy with salt and minerals.
So much salt is folded into it that the water itself grows dense and strong and buoyant.
That is why no one sinks here; people lie back on the surface and simply float, as you are floating now.
You could not go under if you tried; the water lifts you up and keeps you gently afloat.
It is so salty that almost nothing can live in it, no fish, no plants, scarcely anything at all.
That is how it earned its name, the Dead Sea, a sea too salt for living things.
Yet there is no harm in that stillness, only a deep and ancient quiet within the water.
Imagine resting there, held up without effort, in water that asks nothing and lets nothing struggle.
All that weight of salt beneath you is what keeps you so safely, so easily, afloat.
Let yourself be carried by it, your whole body loose and unresisting on the calm.
And with your next slow breath out, let yourself sink a little deeper into rest.
You may wonder how the water came to hold so much salt, and the answer is a slow and patient one.
A river called the Jordan flows down into the sea, bringing fresh water from the hills above.
But no river ever flows back out again; the water arrives, and then it stays.
Over the warm slow ages, the fierce desert sun draws the water upward into the dry air.
The water rises away as vapour, but the salt and the minerals it carried are left behind.
Year upon year, that quiet leaving has gathered the salt, making the sea ever more dense.
So the heaviness that holds you up was made slowly, by sunlight and time and patience.
There is no rush in any of it, only the long, unhurried breathing of water into warm air.
Picture that slow work going on, the sun lifting the water, the minerals quietly staying.
It is the gentlest kind of making, accomplished over more years than you could ever count.
Let that slowness move through you now, unhurried as the sun upon the still water.
And let your own breath rise and fall as softly, growing longer and quieter with each one.
Along the shores of this sea, the leftover salt does strange and lovely things.
White crystals of salt build up at the water's edge, gathering into odd and delicate shapes.
They grow slowly, pillar and ledge and glittering crust, pale against the dark still water.
The mud along the shore is rich with minerals, soft and grey and faintly warm.
Since ancient times, people have prized that mud and water, believing them gentle and healing.
They came from far away to rest beside the sea, to float, and to be eased by it.
Imagine the smoothness of that mineral mud, and the soft white salt shining at the brink.
For thousands of years this quiet shore has welcomed the weary and let them rest.
You are in good company, then, lying back on this old and patient water.
Many have floated here before you, easing their tired bodies on the buoyant calm.
Let that long company of rest gather around you like the warmth of the desert evening.
And let your breath ease out slowly, leaving you a little lighter, a little more still.
This whole low place lies within a great crack in the surface of the Earth.
It rests in a vast rift valley, part of a long split in the ground that runs far to the south.
That same deep crack reaches on and on, down into the wide warm lands of Africa.
The Dead Sea settled into the lowest fold of it, gathering its quiet water there.
Near its shore stands the town of Jericho, among the oldest places people have ever lived.
People have made their homes there, without pause, for longer than almost anywhere on Earth.
And in dry caves nearby, hidden away, ancient writings were found in the last century.
These were the Dead Sea Scrolls, kept secret in the stone for two thousand years.
The dry desert air preserved them wonderfully, holding their words safe through all that time.
Imagine that great patience, the words waiting in the dark, the town enduring through the ages.
Such deep time lies all around this still and quiet water, asking nothing, simply lasting.
Let that long endurance settle over you, steady and calm, slowing every thought.
And let your breath grow slow and unhurried, as patient as the old caves in the cliffs.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the desert and the salt and the long slow ages fade gently away into the dark.
Let the still water soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, held up as easily as if you floated on calm water.
There is no effort anywhere in this, nothing to grasp, nothing to do at all.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the still sea at the bottom of the world, you have only to be quiet and at rest.
Let the warm dark hold you the way the heavy water holds whatever lies upon it.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Lake Titicaca
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or remember them; let them drift over you like a soft wind.
Imagine the room around you has gone dim and still, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet easing along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
If you like, you might picture a vast and still blue water, lying high among great mountains.
The air above it is thin and clear, and a huge calm sky stretches out from edge to edge.
The water does not stir; it only waits, smooth and patient, and it asks nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink, the way evening light settles slowly down over quiet water.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
That wide blue water you are picturing lies high in the mountains called the Andes.
It rests along the border of two countries, Peru on one side and Bolivia on the other.
It is so high among those peaks that it is the highest large lake in the world that boats can sail upon.
Up there the air is thin and cool, and the sun is bright by day while the nights turn quietly cold.
The water itself is a deep and steady blue, still and clear under that great open sky.
It is one of the largest lakes in all of South America, broad enough to feel like a small inland sea.
It is fed by mountain rains, by snow melting on the high peaks, and by rivers that wander down from above.
Slowly, season by season, those waters gather here and rest in this high blue bowl.
Imagine how clear and pure the light must be, so far up, with the thin air letting it through.
There is no need to hold any of this; let the facts drift past like clouds over the water.
Let your breath grow long and unhurried, in and slowly out, as the lake lies still in your mind.
Feel yourself loosening, sinking gently, as quiet as that high and patient water.
Now picture the shallows near the lake's edge, where tall reeds grow up out of the water.
These reeds are called totora, and they rise in soft golden stands wherever the water runs shallow.
Among those reeds live a people called the Uros, who make their home upon the lake itself.
They live not on the shore but out on the water, on islands they weave and build by hand from the reeds.
They cut and gather the totora and lay it down in layers, until a soft floating ground holds them up.
As the reeds beneath slowly soften and rot away, they simply add fresh reeds across the top.
So the island is always being gently remade, layer upon layer, year after year.
From these same golden reeds they make their boats, and their houses, and much of the island under their feet.
It is a way of living that has been carried on quietly for many, many generations.
Imagine the soft give of a reed island underfoot, floating on the deep blue water.
There is something restful in that, in a home that drifts so lightly upon the lake.
Let that softness come into your own body now, and let your breathing slow and deepen.
Breathe out slowly, and feel yourself float, held gently as a reed island on still water.
This high blue lake has been held sacred for a very long time.
Long ago the Inca built a great empire across these mountains, and the lake lay near its heart.
In Inca tradition the lake is a sacred place of origin, the place where their people are said to begin.
An old story tells that the first Inca, the children of the sun, rose up out of these very waters.
From the lake, the tradition says, they came forth to found their people and their line of rulers.
It is a story, gently held, not a fact to be measured, but a belief carried down through the ages.
Out on an island in the lake stand old sacred stones and quiet ruins linked to these tales of origin.
People have come to honour this water for longer than anyone can clearly say.
Picture those worn stones standing in the thin bright air, in a silence that is very old.
There is a deep calm in places like that, in a quiet that has been kept for so long.
You do not need to remember the story; let it settle softly and then slip away.
Let that old quiet reverence move through you, and let your breath grow slow and easy.
Breathe out, and let yourself rest in that ancient stillness, as still as the sacred stones.
There is more to this lake than the wide blue surface that you can see.
Down beneath the water, where the light grows dim, the past lies quietly waiting.
Over many centuries, people came to the lake to leave gifts to the water itself.
Divers and patient archaeologists have searched below the surface and found these ancient offerings.
They have found old ruins down there too, quiet shapes resting in the cool and silent deep.
These were gifts given long ago, lowered into the water in reverence and then let go.
Imagine them resting in the still dark below, undisturbed through all the long years.
The lake has kept them gently, the way deep water keeps things, slow and undisturbed.
You do not need to know the details; only picture that calm, deep, sheltering dark.
There is a peace in things laid down and left, asking nothing, simply at rest.
Let your own thoughts settle in the same way, sinking softly out of sight.
Let the day's small worries drift down and come to rest, far below, in the quiet.
Breathe slowly out, and let yourself sink toward sleep, as gentle as a gift to the deep water.
Lift your gaze now, in your mind, back up to the wide and shining surface of the lake.
It lies so high and so still that it holds the whole great sky upon its face.
The clouds drift across it, and the blue above is doubled in the blue below.
The light up here is clear and pure, with so little air between the water and the sun.
By day the surface gleams, and by night the cold sky leans down close above the water.
All around stand the high peaks, watching over the lake in patient silence.
The Uros still gather their golden reeds, and the old stones still stand on their island.
The water still waits, deep and blue, mirroring the sky as it has for ages past.
There is no hurry in any of it, only a long, calm, high stillness.
Let that stillness be yours now, the wide quiet of still water under a vast sky.
You do not have to keep a single fact; let them all drift off like mist over the lake.
Let your breath grow as slow and as smooth as that mirrored, sky-filled water.
Breathe gently out, and let the high calm of the lake settle deep within you.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the high mountains soften and fade gently away into the dark.
Let the golden reeds and the floating islands drift quietly out of sight.
Let the old stones and the offerings in the deep sink back into the calm.
You are lying here in the warm dark, as still as that wide blue water far away.
There is a deep peace in that high quiet lake, asking nothing, simply lying still beneath the sky.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the lake under its great sky, you have only to be still, and let the quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no task waiting for you now at all.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Great Pyramid
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to remember.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like warm desert air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere out in that darkness, picture a great pale shape resting calmly on a wide and silent plain.
It is enormous and still and patient, and it asks nothing of you at all.
Above it spreads a huge quiet sky, soft with stars, holding everything in a deep and steady hush.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That great pale shape resting on the plain is the Great Pyramid of Giza, standing in Egypt.
It rises from a wide desert plateau, not far from the slow green waters of the Nile.
It is the oldest of the seven wonders of the ancient world, the ones the old travellers loved to name.
And it is the only one of those seven still largely standing today, quietly outlasting all the rest.
The others have crumbled or vanished, but this one remains, patient and enormous, where it has always been.
People have come to gaze at it for longer than almost any story can hold.
Even in ancient times it was already ancient, already old enough to fill its visitors with wonder.
Picture it now, vast and calm in the early dark, the desert spreading flat and silent all around.
There is no hurry in it, and there never has been; it simply rests, as you are resting now.
It has seen more nights than you could ever count, and each one has settled softly over its stone.
Let that great stillness settle over you too, the way the night settles over the plain.
And let your breath grow slow and deep, as easy as the wind moving over the sand.
Let your mind drift back now, very far back, across an almost unimaginable stretch of time.
The Great Pyramid was raised around four and a half thousand years ago, in the deep past of the world.
It was built as a tomb for a pharaoh, a king of ancient Egypt whose name was Khufu.
It was meant to be his resting place, a great stone house to keep him safe for all the ages to come.
Try to feel how long ago that truly was, longer ago than nearly anything you have ever been told.
Whole peoples have come and gone, whole languages have been born and forgotten, since the stone was laid.
And through all of that, the pyramid has simply stood, holding its quiet on the plain.
For more than three and a half thousand years it remained the tallest thing human hands had ever made.
Nothing anywhere on Earth rose higher, for span after span of years, than this single calm mountain of stone.
Picture all those centuries passing over it like slow clouds, while it stands unchanged beneath the stars.
There is a deep peace in something so old and so patient, asking nothing, simply enduring.
Let that long patience pour gently into you now, and let your breath grow long and unhurried.
Sink a little deeper into the warm dark, as steady and as still as the stone itself.
Now let your mind move closer, and picture the great body of the pyramid up near.
It is built of millions of stone blocks, each one heavy, some as heavy as a few cars together.
Block upon block they were laid, rising in a slow and orderly slope toward a single high point.
And they were fitted together with astonishing care, so closely that the joins are fine and true.
We are still not certain exactly how such a thing was raised, so long ago, with no machines as we know them.
For a long while people told dark stories of countless slaves driven to build it, but that does not seem to be true.
Most scholars now believe it was raised by a large and well organised workforce, skilled and willing.
These were workers who were fed and housed and cared for, laboring together in their thousands.
They likely used long ramps, and levers, and wooden sledges to move and lift the heavy stone.
Imagine that great patient effort, going on year upon year under the wide and burning sky.
And imagine the deep quiet that fell when the last stone was set, and the work was finally done.
There is no labour left in it now, only that old stillness, settled deep into every block.
Let your body share in that stillness, growing heavier, asking nothing of the hours.
There is one thing about the pyramid that has always filled people with quiet wonder.
Its four great sides are aligned almost perfectly with the points of the compass.
One side faces true north, and one true south, and the others true east and west.
To set such an enormous thing so precisely, so long ago, was a remarkable feat of careful measurement.
The builders must have watched the sky with great patience, reading the stars and the path of the sun.
Picture them standing on the plain in the cool of the night, looking up to find their way.
From the slow turning of the heavens they drew the lines that the great stone would follow.
So the pyramid is not only resting on the Earth; it is quietly turned to face the whole sky.
It stands squared to the world, settled and certain, pointing softly toward each far horizon.
There is something deeply calming in that, in such vast care taken to set a thing just right.
Let that sense of careful order rest over you, steady and reassuring in the dark.
And let your breath grow slow and even, turning gently like the patient stars above.
Long ago, the Great Pyramid did not look as it does now; it was even more beautiful then.
Its whole surface was once cased in smooth white limestone, polished and gleaming bright.
Under the desert sun that pale casing would have shone, a great bright shape pouring light across the sand.
Imagine seeing it from far away, glowing soft and white on the plain, almost too bright to look upon.
Most of that smooth white casing is long gone now, worn away or carried off across the ages.
So today its stepped grey stone is bare, but once it was clad in shining white from base to peak.
And deep within the pyramid run narrow passages, leading inward to chambers hidden in the stone.
The air inside is cool, and still, and silent, far from the heat and brightness of the open day.
Picture that deep inner quiet, the cool dark held safe at the very heart of the stone.
No wind reaches there, and no sound, only a stillness that has lasted for thousands of years.
It is a place made entirely of quiet, untroubled and calm, holding its silence patiently.
Let your mind rest in that cool still dark, and let your own breath grow soft and faint.
Feel yourself settling, deeper and deeper, into a quiet as old and gentle as that.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the great pale stone soften and grow dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
Let the wide desert and the huge starry sky drift gently away into the warm dark.
You are lying here, safe and held, while somewhere a great quiet thing rests as you are resting.
It has stood through the rise and fall of countless kingdoms, watched over by the desert and the stars.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the pyramid, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to build, no pressure on you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up, the way the silent desert gathers the ancient stone.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Hanging Gardens
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like warm air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that warm darkness, picture green terraces rising one above another, leaf upon leaf.
Imagine cool water trickling down them, falling softly from level to level, a sound that asks nothing of you.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink, the way a slow drop of water sinks gently through still green leaves.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
Those green terraces you are picturing have a name, and a very old one.
They are called the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, and they are counted among the seven wonders of the ancient world.
They were said to have stood in the great city of Babylon, in a warm and distant land.
That land lies in what we now call Iraq, beside the slow brown waters of the river Euphrates.
Picture a city of mud brick and painted gates, shimmering in the heat of a long ago summer.
And rising somewhere within it, a great mound of growing things, climbing toward a wide pale sky.
It was spoken of as a rising mountain of terraces, planted with trees and vines and flowers.
The greenery was said to spill and hang down from the heights, as if the whole hill were softly draped in leaves.
That is where the lovely name comes from, gardens that seemed to hang in the warm air.
You do not need to remember any of this; let the picture simply rest in your mind.
Let the image of that green and falling water settle over you like a soft cloth.
And let your breath grow slow and deep, easing out a little longer each time.
There is an old story told about why such gardens might ever have been made.
It is said that a king built them, long ago, as a gift to comfort the wife he loved.
The king in the story is often named Nebuchadnezzar, a ruler of great Babylon.
His queen, the tale says, had come from a faraway country of green hills and cool mountains.
In the flat and dusty plain of Babylon she grew homesick for the slopes of her childhood.
So, to ease her longing, the king is said to have raised a green mountain within the city for her.
He filled it with the trees and flowers of her distant home, so she might walk among them again.
Whether it truly happened that way, no one can say, but it is a tender thing to imagine.
A whole hillside of gardens, raised out of love, so that one homesick heart might rest.
Picture her walking those shaded terraces in the cool of the evening, content at last.
Let that gentle story drift through you, and let your own longing grow quiet.
Breathe out slowly, and let your shoulders sink a little further into the warmth.
To keep such a garden alive, there was a quiet problem to be solved.
Babylon lay in a hot and thirsty land, where rain was scarce and the summers were long and dry.
Trees and flowers piled high upon terraces would need a great deal of water to stay green.
And all that water would have had to be lifted up, somehow, from the river far below.
It would have to climb from the low banks of the Euphrates to the topmost leafy heights.
People who told of the gardens spoke of clever hidden machines that raised the water up.
Perhaps great screws turning in the dark, or long chains of buckets dipping and rising endlessly.
Up the water would go, level by level, to spill down again through the waiting green.
It was, if it was real, a quiet marvel of patience and cleverness, water taught to climb.
Imagine that soft endless trickle, water rising and falling, rising and falling, never hurried.
Let that gentle rhythm match your breath, the slow rise in, the long fall out.
And let each falling breath carry you a little deeper toward sleep.
Now here is the gentle mystery at the heart of these gardens, and you may simply let it be.
Of all the seven wonders of the ancient world, the Hanging Gardens are the one we are not even sure were real.
No certain trace of them has ever been found, no clear ruin we can point to and name.
Even the scribes of Babylon itself, who wrote down so very much, do not clearly speak of them.
They recorded their kings and their temples and their walls, yet of these famous gardens they are nearly silent.
All the lovely descriptions we have come to us second hand, written far away and long after.
They were set down by Greek and Roman authors who may never have seen Babylon with their own eyes.
So the gardens we picture may be a memory of a memory, a story passed gently from hand to hand.
If they existed at all, they have left us only their image, and almost nothing else.
There is no need to solve this; some lovely things are meant to stay softly uncertain.
Let the mystery rest beside you, unhurried, asking nothing, like the dark itself.
Breathe out, and let the not knowing be as easy as the falling of leaves.
Some thoughtful people have wondered, gently, where the truth of the gardens might lie.
Perhaps they were quite real, but stood somewhere other than where the old tales place them.
Some scholars think the famous gardens may have been confused with great terraced gardens at another city.
That city was called Nineveh, far up the rivers, where a different king built green and watered slopes.
Over the long centuries, two beautiful places may have softly blurred into one in people's minds.
Others believe the Hanging Gardens were simply a lovely story, told and retold until it felt true.
And yet, whether they truly stood or not, the image of them has never faded.
For more than two thousand years, people have closed their eyes and seen those green and falling terraces.
Green and cool and impossibly lovely, watered against the heat, a hill of leaves in a dry land.
An image can endure far longer than any wall, and soothe far more minds than any single garden could.
So perhaps the wonder was never really the stone and the soil, but the dream that outlived them.
Let that enduring green dream hold you now, asking nothing, only that you rest.
Breathe slowly, and let yourself sink toward sleep among those imagined leaves.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the green terraces soften and fade, level upon level, gently into the dark.
Let the trickling water grow quieter and quieter, until it is only the sound of your own slow breath.
It does not matter now whether the gardens were ever real, and it never needs to matter.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and a lovely uncertain dream is allowed simply to be.
There is a deep peace in letting a mystery rest unsolved, like a light left softly dimmed.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is warm all around you.
Let the falling water, the green leaves, the old king and his far away queen all drift away.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to build, no water left to lift, nothing at all to do.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Colossus of Rhodes
lines: There is nothing you need to do now, and nothing you need to remember.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely; let them drift past you like a warm tide going out.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere beyond the dark, picture a calm blue sea, breathing slowly against a quiet shore.
Above that harbour, picture warm light resting on bronze, golden and still and asking nothing of you.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little lower, the way the evening light sinks slowly into the sea.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That warm bronze light you are picturing once belonged to a true and famous thing.
Long ago there stood, above a calm harbour, a giant statue called the Colossus of Rhodes.
Rhodes is a Greek island, set in a warm blue sea, and the statue rose beside its sheltered port.
It was a figure of Helios, the sun god, the bright one who was said to draw the day across the sky.
People counted it among the seven wonders of the ancient world, the great marvels worth a long journey to see.
It was made of bronze, and in the soft light of morning and evening that bronze would gently glow.
Picture it now, calm and golden above the water, a great quiet giant simply watching the sea.
It did nothing and asked nothing; it only stood there, patient, catching the day's first and last light.
There is something restful in that image, in a vast and gentle figure keeping watch over calm water.
You do not need to hold any of these names; let them settle softly and then let them go.
Let that warm glow rest lightly in your mind, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, settling further, as the imagined sea breathes in and out below.
Let your mind drift back, gently, to why such a giant came to stand above that quiet harbour.
More than two thousand years ago, the island of Rhodes had come safely through a long and weary siege.
A great enemy had pressed against the city for many months, and at last that enemy gave up and went away.
The people of Rhodes were so glad to have survived that they wished to give thanks to their sun god.
And so they decided to raise a statue of Helios, taller than anything anyone had seen.
There is a lovely, true detail here, soft enough to drift to sleep upon.
The enemy, in leaving, abandoned their great machines of war, the towers and engines built to break the walls.
The people sold off all that abandoned iron and bronze, and used the money to pay for their giant.
So the very metal of war was melted down and made instead into a calm figure of light.
Picture that quiet turning, the weapons of a siege becoming a gentle bronze giant watching the sea.
There is a deep peace in that, in something fearful being remade into something serene.
Let that peace settle over you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
Now imagine, slowly, just how large this quiet giant truly was.
It stood about as tall as a building of ten storeys, rising high above the harbour and the ships.
If you have ever pictured the Statue of Liberty, lifting her torch above another harbour far away, you are close.
The Colossus stood about that same height, from the soles of its feet to the crown upon its head.
And that is no accident, for the people who later made the Statue of Liberty thought of this ancient giant.
So a little of the Colossus lives on, gently echoed, in a newer figure standing above newer water.
It was built of bronze plates, hammered and fitted over a strong framework of iron within.
A sculptor named Chares led the slow work, raising the great figure plate by plate, year upon year.
It was not done in haste; the giant rose patiently over about twelve quiet years.
Picture that unhurried building, the scaffolds climbing higher each season, the bronze slowly catching the sun.
There was no rush in it at all, only steady hands and the long patience of making something vast.
Let that slowness pour into you now, softening your shoulders, lengthening each gentle breath.
Feel your own weight settling, plate by plate, deeper into the warm and quiet dark.
Now let us gently set right an old story, in the way one smooths a wrinkle from a blanket.
Many people picture the Colossus standing astride the mouth of the harbour, one foot on either side.
In that famous image, the great ships sail in beneath it, passing between its enormous legs.
It is a striking picture, and it has charmed people for a very long time.
But it is only a later legend, a lovely invention, and not the way the giant really stood.
No single bronze figure could have stood splayed across a harbour mouth without breaking under its own weight.
In truth it almost certainly stood to one side, calm and upright, as a single great upright figure.
Picture it that way instead, a tall serene giant on the shore, gazing out over the open water.
There is no need for it to straddle anything; it only stands, and watches, and gleams in the soft light.
Let the old straddling legend drift off like a boat slipping quietly out to sea.
Keep only the gentle truth: one calm bronze figure, upright above a quiet harbour, at peace.
Let your body grow heavier with that calm, and let your breath slow to match the slow water.
Now, as you drift, let us follow what became of the great gleaming giant.
For all the years it took to raise, the Colossus stood for only a few short decades.
Then, one day, the earth itself shifted, and a strong earthquake shook the island of Rhodes.
The giant could not bear the trembling, and it snapped at the knees and slowly toppled to the ground.
And yet, even fallen, it lost none of its power to amaze the people who came to see it.
For centuries afterward, the broken bronze pieces lay along the shore, vast and quiet in the sun.
Travellers journeyed from far away simply to stand beside the ruin and wonder at its size.
It is said that few of them could wrap their arms even around a single one of its fallen fingers.
From this giant, and others like it, we keep a word still used today for anything enormous.
When we call a thing a colossus, we are remembering, without knowing it, this gentle bronze giant by the sea.
Picture it now, the great calm pieces resting along the warm shore, the blue water lapping near.
There is a deep peace even in the ruin, in a giant laid down at last to rest beside the sea.
Let that restfulness fill you, slowing your breath, softening your every fading thought.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the harbour and the giant and the long siege fade gently away into the dark.
Let the bronze dim, the way the evening light dims as your own eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a calm sea is breathing slowly against a quiet shore.
There is a deep peace in that old giant, raised slowly, fallen slowly, resting at last in the sun.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the giant by the sea, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to journey, nothing to build, no weight resting on you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you the way the calm sea gathers the last of the evening light.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Temple of Artemis
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like a warm breeze.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
If you like, you might begin to picture rows and rows of tall pale columns standing quietly in soft light.
They rise around you in long calm lines, patient and still, asking nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little further, the way evening light sinks slowly toward the ground.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
Those tall pale columns you are picturing once stood together in a single, famous place.
Long ago, beside the sea, there was a great temple built for the goddess Artemis.
It stood at a city called Ephesus, on the gentle coast of what we now call Turkey.
In its day it was counted among the seven wonders of the ancient world, the most marvellous things people knew.
It was a temple far larger than most, wide and high and open to the soft sea air.
But of all its many glories, the one most spoken of was its forest of tall marble columns.
There were more than a hundred of them, standing in long and patient rows, white in the morning light.
Imagine walking slowly between them, the cool stone rising far above you on every side.
It must have felt like wandering through a quiet woodland made all of pale and gleaming marble.
You did not need to hurry there; the columns simply stood, as they had stood for years.
Let that vast calm space open softly in your mind, the rows going on and on into the light.
And let your breath grow long and easy, as slow and unhurried as that quiet marble forest.
Now let your mind rest gently on how patiently that great temple came to be.
It was not raised all at once, but built and rebuilt several times over the long centuries.
An earlier temple on that spot was once swept away by a flood, the waters quietly carrying it off.
And so, in time, the people built it again, and a later temple rose grander than the one before.
Picture the slow and steady work of it, stone laid upon stone across many seasons.
There was no rush in such building; it was the work of years, of patience handed down.
Each column was shaped and lifted with great care, then set into its place among the rest.
Little by little the long rows grew, until the marble forest stood complete once more.
It is a soft and reassuring thing, to think of something made so slowly and so well.
What the water took, the people gently gave back, larger and more lovely than before.
There is a quiet kindness in that patience, in the long willingness to begin again.
Let that patience settle over you, and let your breath grow slow and unhurried too.
Now imagine the temple in its fullest glory, with the morning sun warming its stone.
Sunlight would have streamed between its great columns, falling in long soft bands across the floor.
At dawn and at dusk the marble itself would glow, pale and faintly gold, like a low and gentle fire.
The temple was richly adorned, with fine sculpture and bronze gleaming softly in that light.
It was not only a place of worship, but a gathering place, alive with quiet voices.
It served even as a kind of treasury, where people left their gifts and valuables in its care.
They trusted the temple to hold what was precious to them, safe within its calm and watchful walls.
Pilgrims and traders came to it from across the ancient world, drawn by all they had heard.
They journeyed great distances simply to stand among those columns and feel the stillness there.
Picture them arriving footsore and weary, and growing quiet and easy in that soft golden hush.
It was a place that gathered people in and let them rest, the way you are resting now.
Let that warm glow fill your mind, and let your body grow heavier as you breathe slowly out.
There is one more chapter to the temple's story, and we will tell it softly.
One of the great temples that stood there was, long ago, destroyed by a fire in the night.
It was set, the old accounts say, by a single man who only wished to be remembered.
The city was so grieved and so angry that it forbade anyone ever to speak his name aloud.
And so his name was let go, allowed to fade quietly into the dark, just as a name should.
But the temple itself was not let go; the people gathered once more and rebuilt it.
They raised it again, more beautiful than before, the marble forest standing tall and bright.
What one restless night had taken, the patient work of many hands gently gave back.
There is comfort in that, in how a loved thing can be made whole again after the dark.
The fire passed, and was forgotten, and the calm white columns stood once more in the light.
Let the small trouble of that night drift away from you now, harmless and far off.
And let your own breath grow soft and steady, as quiet as marble standing in the dusk.
For a long time the temple stood, gathering travellers and sunlight, year upon gentle year.
But all made things, even the greatest, soften slowly back toward the earth in time.
Over the long centuries the temple slowly fell into ruin, with no single ending to its days.
Its fine marble was carried away, stone by stone, to be used in other walls elsewhere.
There was nothing violent in this last fading; it was only the slow, patient turning of the years.
The columns came down one by one, and the rows grew quiet, and the grass came creeping in.
Today, on that calm site, little remains but the worn foundations and a single rebuilt column.
That one tall pillar stands alone in the open air, where a whole forest of them once rose.
The traveller Antipater, who first named the seven wonders, wrote of this temple with the deepest awe.
Of all the wonders he had seen, he said, this one filled him with the most wonder of all.
And even now, standing among its quiet stones, you can feel a little of that old hush remain.
There is a soft peace in such slow turning, in the gentle passage from glory into stillness.
Let that stillness pour into you now, slowing your breath and softening your every thought.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the great temple and its long story fade gently away into the warm dark.
Let the tall columns soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You do not have to remember the city, or the sea, or a single word of what was said.
Let the morning light between the pillars grow dim, and let the marble forest fall quiet.
You are lying here in the soft dark, safe and warm, with nowhere at all to go.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the night is gentle all around you.
Like the quiet stones in their calm field, you have only to rest, and to be still.
There is nothing to build now, nothing to guard, no journey left to make.
Let the warm dark gather you up and hold you, the way the temple once held the weary and gave them rest.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Trans-Siberian
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them pass over you like the dark beyond a window.
Imagine the room around you has softened into a small warm berth, gently swaying as it carries you on.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no station you are hurrying to reach.
Picture lying tucked beneath a blanket while a great forest slips by unseen in the night.
The dark outside is endless and cold, but here, where you are, it is warm and close and safe.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Beneath you there is a slow and steady rocking, the kind that lulls a child to sleep.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be carried gently through the quiet dark.
The train that carries you tonight runs along the longest railway line in all the world.
It crosses the whole breadth of Russia, from Moscow in the west to Vladivostok far away on the Pacific shore.
From end to end it stretches more than nine thousand kilometres, a thread laid clear across a continent.
To ride the whole of it takes about a week of days and nights, a slow unhurried passage over the sleeping land.
You need not measure any of it; only feel how far there is to go, and how gently you are being carried.
The land is so vast that the journey crosses eight time zones, one after another, hour by quiet hour.
As you travel, the clocks themselves shift slowly beneath you, the hours sliding by like the dark trees.
There is no need to keep the time tonight; let the hours come loose and drift where they will.
You are only a small warm thing being carried across an enormous and patient land.
Far ahead the rails run on through the night, and far behind they fade into the dark.
And here in the middle of it all, you are held, swaying softly, going gently nowhere you must reach.
Let that great distance settle over you, and let your breath grow long and slow.
This railway was not always here; once there was only the wide land and no road across it at all.
More than a hundred years ago, people set out to lay a line of iron clear across the whole of it.
It was an enormous undertaking, the work of many years and many thousands of patient hands.
The rails were laid through deep forests and over wide rivers, across ground that lay frozen much of the year.
In the cold the very earth turned hard as stone, and still, slowly, the line crept onward, mile by mile.
Picture them working through the short days and long nights, laying down one length of rail and then the next.
It was slow and heavy labour, and it took far longer than a single lifetime feels.
But little by little the two far ends of the land were drawn together by that thin and steady thread.
And now, long after, you ride upon their patient work without a thought, carried smoothly through the dark.
All that effort settled long ago into this quiet, ordinary rocking beneath your resting body.
There is no labour left for you tonight; it was all done, gently, long before you were born.
Let that old patience hold you, and let your breath grow soft and unhurried too.
For days at a time, the train runs on through the taiga, the great forest of the Siberian north.
Out beyond the window stand birch and pine and larch, ranked close together, going on without end.
Mile after mile it is the same gentle scene, the dark trees passing, the open sky above them pale.
You could watch it for an hour, or two, or three, and the forest would only deepen and continue on.
There is a great peace in that sameness, in a green and silent country that asks nothing of you.
The forest does not begin or end while you are watching; it simply is, vast and calm and old.
It is one of the largest forests on the whole of the Earth, and the train slips through it like a small bright thread.
Snow may lie soft between the trunks, and the air beyond the glass is cold and clean and still.
But inside the warm carriage there is light, and quiet, and the gentle swaying of your berth.
Let your eyes follow the trees a moment longer, until they blur and soften into one dark band.
There is nothing to find out there, and nothing you must look for; you may simply let it pass.
Let the endless forest carry your gaze away, and let your eyelids grow heavy and slow.
Breathe out slowly now, and let the dark green country lull you further toward sleep.
After many days, the line draws near the shore of a great and ancient lake called Baikal.
It is the deepest lake on all the Earth, holding more still water than you could ever picture.
The rails curve along its edge, around high cliffs and through one tunnel after another, hewn into the rock.
This was one of the very hardest stretches to build, where the mountains came down sharply to the water.
Imagine the train threading slowly between the dark stone and the wide, calm, silver lake.
In the tunnels the world goes black for a moment, and then the great lake opens out again, vast and quiet.
Its water is so clear and so cold and so old that it seems to hold a stillness all its own.
The line was so difficult here that for a time, before the tunnels, boats carried the carriages across the ice.
But tonight you need not cross anything; you have only to lie still and watch the dark water slide by.
There is a deep peace beside that ancient lake, a quiet older than any railway or any name.
Let the calm of all that still, deep water gather around you in the warm dark.
Breathe slowly, and let the stillness of the lake settle into your resting body.
Aboard the train, life slows down until it keeps only the gentle rhythm of the rails.
At the end of each carriage a samovar holds warm water, and you may have tea at any hour of the night.
The day softens into long blue hours of dusk and dawn, when the land glows pale and the lamps burn low.
Now and then the train pauses at a quiet station in the night, and stands a while in the cold and the dark.
Then it moves on again with a gentle lurch, and the steady rocking of your berth resumes.
In the warm carriages, strangers share bread and tea and slow, low stories as the hours drift past.
There is no hurry in any of it; the train will arrive when it arrives, and the night is long and kind.
And underneath it all is the sound: the soft and even clicking of the wheels along the rails.
Click and click and click, hour after hour, steady as a slow heart, across the sleeping land.
That patient clicking becomes a kind of lullaby, asking nothing, simply carrying you on.
Let it move into your breathing now, slow and even, in and gently out.
There is nothing to do but lie still and be rocked, warm within, the cold dark far without.
Let the long sound of the rails carry you down, slow and soft, toward sleep.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the long forest fade gently away, and the great lake, and the quiet stations in the night.
Let the rails grow faint beneath you, the clicking soft and far, like a sound remembered in a dream.
You are lying here in the warm dark, carried gently onward, asking nothing, holding nothing.
There is no distance left to cross, no time to keep, no station waiting anywhere ahead.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Let the warm berth hold you the way the long train holds its sleeping travellers through the night.
There is nowhere to arrive, and nothing to make, and no hurry anywhere at all.
You are exactly where you need to be, rocked gently across a vast and quiet land.
Let the swaying carry you down into the deep warm dark.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Orient Express
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them pass over you like the dark countryside passing a window.
Imagine you are lying in a snug little berth, deep inside a warm carriage, safe and held in the night.
The walls around you are panelled in soft old wood, polished by many quiet hands and glowing faintly in the lamplight.
A small lamp burns low beside you, the colour of honey, and beyond the glass the rain streaks gently down.
Feel the slow, easy sway of the carriage, rocking you a little this way and a little that, the way a cradle rocks.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you anywhere along the line tonight.
Beneath you the wheels keep up their soft and steady clack, a quiet heartbeat carrying you onward through the dark.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed against the gentle light.
Each breath lets you sink a little further into the warm bed, the crisp sheets cool and smooth around you.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let the rocking of the carriage carry your thoughts slowly away.
The train you are lying in is a very old and famous one, and it has been carrying sleepers like you for a long, long time.
It is called the Orient Express, and it first began to run in the eighteen eighties, more than a hundred years ago.
Night after night, it gathered up its travellers in Paris and carried them slowly across the whole of Europe.
Its long journey reached all the way to the east, toward the city of Istanbul, which was then called Constantinople.
Picture that quiet thread of light slipping across the dark map of the continent, one small warm train among the sleeping fields.
From the very beginning it was famous for its comfort, for the gentle care taken of everyone aboard.
The sleeping cars were lined with fine wood, just like the one around you now, and the berths were deep and soft.
It was a place made for resting, a moving room of warm light gliding through the night.
You do not need to remember the name, or the year, or the city; let them drift past like stations in the dark.
There is only this: a famous old train, running gently through the night, made for sleep.
Let that thought rest lightly upon you, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, settling further into the berth as the carriage rocks you on.
The journey aboard this train was never a hurried thing; it took several long and unhurried days.
It crossed many countries and many quiet borders, easing from one land into the next while the travellers slept.
It wound through high mountains and across wide plains, and the sleeper would wake, and sleep, and wake again.
You might close your eyes among the fields of one country and open them among the hills of another.
All through the day the world drifted past the window, slow and green and golden, with nothing to chase.
And all through the night the same gentle clack of the rails went on beneath you, country after country.
Imagine how easy it was to lose track of time, to forget which border had been crossed or which would come next.
There was no need to know; the train knew the way, and carried you onward whether you waked or slept.
Think of all those sleepers, in all those years, rocked gently through the dark just as you are now.
Each of them safe in a warm berth, the rain on the glass, the lamp turned low, the wheels singing softly below.
You are one more traveller in that long quiet line, with nowhere to be and all the night to rest.
Let the slowness of the journey settle over you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
There is no station you must reach tonight; let yourself simply be carried.
In its grandest years, the Orient Express became a byword for romance and for elegant, gentle travel.
It carried all manner of travellers between the west and the east, drawn by the comfort and the quiet adventure of it.
Diplomats rode it on their slow errands, and royalty, and writers, and wanderers of every gentle kind.
There was a dining carriage, and you may picture it now, glowing softly at the heart of the train.
The tables were dressed in white linen, and there was crystal that caught the lamplight and held it.
Passengers would dress for dinner and sit at those bright tables as whole countries drifted past the window between the courses.
Imagine watching a far hillside slip slowly by while a quiet meal is set before you, the lamps warm and low.
And then, when the evening was over, each traveller would retire to a berth made up with crisp clean sheets.
They would lie down, just as you are lying now, and let the rocking of the carriage carry them off.
All that elegance, in the end, came down to the same gentle thing: a warm bed, moving softly through the dark.
You do not need to dress, or dine, or do anything at all; you have only to rest in your berth.
Let those soft images of linen and crystal grow dim, and let your eyes grow heavier still.
This famous old train found its way into stories too, the way beloved things often do.
The writer Agatha Christie once set a mystery novel aboard it, called Murder on the Orient Express.
Now that tale is only a story, a work of fiction dreamed up for the pleasure of readers, and nothing more.
No need to wonder at it or follow it; it is a made thing, gentle as any bedtime tale.
But the story was loved by so many that it made the train more legendary still, the name known all over the world.
People who had never ridden it came to picture its lamplit carriages and its long journey through the night.
It is a lovely thing, that a warm old train should live on in stories as well as in iron and wood.
And yet the real train asks nothing of those tales; it only ran on, carrying its sleepers east through the dark.
Let the story be just a story, drifting at the edge of your mind, asking nothing, keeping nothing.
You are not in any tale tonight; you are simply here, warm and safe, rocked gently on the rails.
Let the imagined pages soften and close, the way a book slips from the hands of someone falling asleep.
Let your breath grow slow, and let the quiet of the carriage gather you in.
And so, night after night, the train would climb the mountains in the dark while its travellers slept.
It eased across the high passes under the stars, the cold peaks all around, the carriage warm and bright within.
And by the end of the line it reached the shores where Europe at last meets Asia, at the edge of the world it knew.
There the waters of Istanbul were waiting, and the slender minarets standing quiet against the sky.
Over the long decades the route changed many times, and one grand service was traded for another.
In the end the famous old run came gently to its close, the way all long journeys must.
Yet its name and its style did not vanish; luxury trains still echo it today, still carry sleepers softly through the night.
So the gentle idea of it goes on: a warm lamplit berth, the rain on the glass, the sway of the carriage on the rails.
You are part of that long unhurried story now, lying in your berth as the dark country slides by.
There is no peak left to climb tonight, no shore you must reach, no border left to cross.
Let that long, easy travelling pour into you now, slowing your breath, softening your every thought.
There is no hurry anywhere in this; the old train asks you only to rest.
Let yourself grow as still and as quiet as a sleeper rocked through a hundred quiet nights.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the long journey and the lamplit carriages fade gently away into the dark.
Let the mountains and the borders and the far waiting shore soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in a warm berth, rocked softly on the rails, and the rain is gentle on the glass.
There is a deep peace in this slow travelling, asking nothing of you, carrying you on through the quiet night.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the lamp is low and warm beside you.
Like a traveller long asleep, you have only to be still, and let the carriage carry you on.
There is nowhere to travel to, nothing to do, no station waiting in the dark.
Let the warm carriage gather you up and rock you the way it has rocked sleepers for a hundred years.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the night, and all the world, in which to rest.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Darjeeling Railway
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like mist.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no journey waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere far away, picture green mountain slopes, and soft white mist drifting slowly through them.
And winding up through that mist, picture a small train, climbing gently, in no hurry at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little lower, the way the cool air settles into a quiet valley.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
