So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be carried by the quiet of the dark.
That little train you are picturing is climbing in the far north of India, into the foothills of the Himalaya.
It begins down on the hot, flat plains, where the air is heavy and warm.
And from there it climbs, slowly and patiently, up into the cool green hills toward a town called Darjeeling.
It is a small railway, the smallest sort, with a track far narrower than the great wide lines below.
Its engines and its carriages are so little that people call it, with great fondness, the toy train.
There is something tender in that name, in a tiny train working its way up a vast mountain.
It does not rush, and it does not strain; it simply climbs, hour by hour, into the cooler air.
Below it the plains grow distant, and above it the misty slopes rise on and on.
Imagine that small train far away in the hills, puffing softly, asking nothing of you at all.
You do not need to remember its name, or where it goes; only let it climb.
Let the picture of it soothe you, the way a slow moving thing in the distance soothes the eye.
Breathe out gently now, and let your body sink a little further into the warm dark.
This little railway was built a very long time ago, well over a hundred years past.
It is one of the oldest mountain railways still running anywhere in the world.
Think of all the years it has been climbing these hills, patiently, again and again.
Generation after generation of small engines have made the same slow journey up through the mist.
For all that long faithful service, the railway is now honoured as a treasure of the whole world.
It is held as a World Heritage place, kept safe and cared for, as something rare and precious.
And yet it does its gentle work just as it always has, in no greater hurry than before.
There is comfort in a thing that has gone on quietly for so long, unchanged and unhurried.
It has climbed through more mornings of mist than anyone could ever count.
Picture all those countless quiet journeys, layered one upon another, like soft falling years.
You are held by something just as patient now, the slow steady rhythm of your own breath.
Let that rhythm carry you, slow and even, deeper toward sleep.
Climbing a mountain is not an easy thing for a train, for a train cannot go straight up a slope.
If the hill is too steep, the wheels would only slip, and the little engine could not hold.
So this railway does something clever and gentle to gain its height without ever straining.
In places it curls right around upon itself, in great slow loops, like a ribbon spiralling upward.
It comes around in a wide circle and crosses softly over its own track, a little higher each time.
And in other places it climbs by going back and forth, a zig and then a zag, easing up the slope.
It runs forward for a while, then gently reverses, then forward once more, gaining a little height with each turn.
In this way it never has to rush the climb; it gathers its height slowly, a small rise at a time.
There is a deep patience in that, in choosing the long winding way rather than the steep one.
It is the same patience your breath is learning now, rising and falling without any haste.
Picture the train looping softly through the mist, climbing without effort, climbing without hurry.
And as it gathers its gentle height, let yourself sink, lower and softer, toward rest.
Breathe slowly out, and let the slope of sleep carry you down.
Higher and higher the little train climbs, until at last it reaches a small station called Ghum.
Ghum sits high among the hills, so high that it is one of the highest railway places in all the world.
Up there the train is wrapped in clouds, with the cool thin air drifting in soft and damp.
Along the way the line winds past wide green tea gardens, spread out gently over the slopes.
It slips through small mountain towns, and runs so close to the houses and shops that you could almost reach out and touch them.
The narrow track threads right through the middle of daily life, quiet and familiar, like an old friend passing by.
Little steam engines, lovingly cared for, still puff and chuff along parts of the line.
Each one trails a soft white plume of steam that hangs for a moment in the cool mountain air, then fades.
Picture that gentle plume drifting up among the trees, soft as a breath let slowly out.
The town and the tea gardens and the clouds all pass by slowly, in no hurry to be anywhere.
There is nothing for you to do here but watch it go, and let your eyes grow heavy.
Breathe out, soft and long, and let the high quiet air settle around you.
On a clear morning, something wonderful floats above these hills in the far distance.
It is the great snow peak of Kanchenjunga, one of the very highest mountains anywhere on Earth.
It seems to hover above the green slopes, pale and immense, as though it were resting upon the clouds.
From the little train it looks soft and far away, a quiet giant watching over the gentle climb.
The train moves so slowly along these stretches that people sometimes step on and off as it goes.
Someone may climb gently aboard a slow moving carriage, or step down again, with no need to wait for a stop.
And as it eases along, the mist drifts in through the open windows, cool and faintly sweet.
Imagine that cool air moving softly over you, and the great pale mountain floating far off in the calm.
Everything here is unhurried, the slow train, the drifting mist, the patient old mountain.
There is no clock that matters, no place you must reach; there is only the gentle going on.
Let that unhurried feeling fill you, the deep ease of travelling slowly through a quiet land.
Breathe out once more, slow and complete, and let yourself drift a little closer to sleep.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the little train fade gently into the mist, still climbing softly somewhere far away.
Let the tea gardens and the small towns and the high station dissolve quietly into the dark.
Let the great pale mountain sink back behind its clouds, calm and unwatched, at rest.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and the climbing is done, and there is nowhere left to go.
You do not have to remember any of it, or hold a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the soft dark is all around you.
Like the train at the end of its long quiet climb, you have only to come gently to rest.
There is no slope left to climb, no height to gain, no hurry anywhere at all.
Let the warm dark carry you, slow and patient, the way the little train carried its quiet load.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Ghan
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to remember.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely; let them pass over you like the soft sway of a train.
Imagine you are lying snug in a warm berth, safe in the dark, while the world carries you gently along.
Feel the quiet rocking beneath you, a slow and steady motion that asks nothing of you at all.
Beyond the dark glass, picture endless red desert sliding by, flat and calm to the far horizon.
Above it all hangs a huge dark sky, scattered with more stars than you could ever hope to count.
There is nowhere to be and nothing to finish, only this gentle journey through the quiet night.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the soft settling along your jaw.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed against the dark.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let the long quiet of the night carry you onward.
The train that holds you tonight is called the Ghan, and it is a famous traveller of the night.
It crosses the whole of a great wide land, running from the south of the country all the way to the top.
It begins in a city called Adelaide, near the cool southern sea, and sets out toward the warm and distant north.
Slowly, over several unhurried days, it makes its way to Darwin, near the tropical edge of the land.
Between those two far places lies a vast red heart, an outback so wide it seems to have no end.
The whole journey runs about three thousand kilometres, straight through that quiet desert centre.
There is no need to rush such a crossing, and the train does not try; it simply rolls on, day after day.
You are somewhere in the middle of all that distance now, held safe between the south and the north.
Picture the long line of carriages stretched out beneath the stars, moving softly across the empty land.
There is something deeply restful in being carried so far while you do nothing at all but lie still.
All the great distance is the train's to cross, not yours; you have only to rest within it.
Let that thought settle over you, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, sinking further into the warm dark as the desert slides by.
The train carries an old and gentle name, and the name itself is a small and tender story.
It is called the Ghan in honour of the Afghan cameleers, men who came long ago to this dry country.
Before any railway crossed the desert, they led long trains of camels across the harsh and empty land.
Camels could go where almost nothing else could, patient and strong in the heat and the waterless miles.
These men and their camels carried goods deep into the outback, to places no cart could ever reach.
They opened quiet ways through the red centre when there were no roads, only sand and scrub and sky.
For their long labour in that hard country, the great train across the desert still carries their name.
So every night the Ghan rolls north, it gently remembers those patient travellers who went before.
Picture them now, moving slowly through the same red land, under the same enormous bowl of stars.
There is a kindness in a name that keeps such quiet, faithful work alive across the years.
Let that old story rest lightly in your mind, asking nothing, only softening as you drift.
Breathe in slowly, breathe out longer, and let your thoughts grow dim and warm.
Sink a little deeper now, carried gently through the dark by a train with an old and gentle name.
Near the very middle of the journey, the Ghan passes through a small town called Alice Springs.
It sits almost exactly in the centre of the whole continent, far from any sea in every direction.
All around it spreads the open outback, wide and dry, with the nearest coast many days away.
It is a quiet place in the heart of an enormous land, ringed by ancient hills and endless red plains.
For hour after hour beyond the window, the world is red earth and low scrub and pale dry grass.
The land stretches flat and calm to the horizon, with only a far ridge or a lone tree to break it.
There is a deep and gentle emptiness to it, a vastness that somehow feels peaceful rather than lonely.
Picture that open country slipping past, mile after quiet mile, under the slow turning of the sky.
You are crossing the very middle of a great land tonight, held safe in the warm hush of the train.
There is nothing out there that asks anything of you, only space and stillness and far horizons.
Let that wide emptiness ease your mind, smoothing every thought out flat and calm.
Breathe out slowly into the quiet, and let your body grow heavier still.
Let the deep peace of that empty land settle over you as you drift toward sleep.
The land the Ghan crosses is far older in story than any railway or any town.
It is the ancient home of many Aboriginal peoples, who have lived with this country for a very long time.
For tens of thousands of years they have known these red plains and quiet hills as home.
They have read the land and its sky, its waters and its seasons, through countless gentle generations.
Long before any train, this was a living country, deeply known and quietly cared for.
So the desert sliding past your window is not empty at all, but rich with stories far older than memory.
Every ridge and waterhole out there has been seen and named and loved across the long ages.
There is a deep dignity in that, a sense of belonging that runs deeper than anything built of steel.
Picture the same stars above you tonight, watched over this land for thousands upon thousands of years.
You are only passing through, a guest carried softly across a country far older than you can hold in mind.
Let that great age of the land steady you, the way deep roots steady a tree in the wind.
Breathe slowly now, and let your thoughts grow quiet and reverent and dim.
Rest in the keeping of a country that has held the night for longer than you can imagine.
It may surprise you that the full railway across the land was only finished in modern times.
For many years the line reached only partway, climbing slowly up from the south into the desert heart.
Travellers and goods could ride the rails to the middle, but not yet all the way to the warm north.
Only in recent years was the last great stretch laid down, joining the centre at last to the top.
And so the bottom of the continent was finally linked to the top by a single unbroken line.
Now the Ghan can run the whole long way, from the southern sea to the tropical edge in the north.
By day the desert shimmers in the heat, the red ground baking under a wide and burning sky.
But by night the air grows cool, and the great dark fills with more stars than you can imagine.
They lie thick and bright from horizon to horizon, a vast soft river of light spilled across the dark.
Picture that enormous starry sky above the cooling desert, and the train rocking gently beneath it.
The carriages are warm and snug, carrying you safely across the empty land while you sleep.
Let the cool night and the bright stars and the gentle rocking fold together into one soft calm.
Breathe out long and slow, and let yourself sink toward sleep beneath that enormous sky.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the great distance and the old names and the far horizons fade gently away into the dark.
Let the red desert soften, let the bright stars dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, carried safely onward through the long and quiet night.
There is a deep peace in that gentle motion, in being held and carried while you simply rest.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the warm dark is soft all around you.
Like the land out there, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere left to travel, nothing to finish, no distance you must cross yourself.
Let the gentle rocking carry you the way it has carried so many gently into sleep.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Iceland
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like steam.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that darkness, picture a still pool of warm water out under an open winter sky.
Soft white mist rises slowly from its surface into the cold, calm air, and then is gone.
All around the warm water lies quiet snow, and nothing moves, and nothing asks anything of you.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
The warm water and the quiet snow you are picturing belong to a real place, far in the north.
It is an island, set out alone in the cold Atlantic, just touching the edge of the Arctic.
People call it the land of fire and ice, for there the volcanoes and the glaciers lie side by side.
Fire sleeps beneath the ground, and ice rests upon it, and somehow the two share the same quiet country.
It is a hushed and open land, mostly treeless, with only a small and scattered few living there.
Picture wide moss and old lava and distant white peaks, all of it still beneath a soft grey sky.
There is so much room in such a place, so much silence between one small town and the next.
You do not need to hold any of this; just let the wide quiet land settle gently into your mind.
Fire and ice, resting together, asking nothing, the way you are resting now.
Feel how much space there is, and how little there is to do in all of it.
Let that openness ease across you, loosening your chest, softening your breath.
Breathe out slowly, and let your body grow as still as that quiet northern land.
Now let your mind sink down, far below the snow, into the warm dark body of the Earth.
This island sits upon a great seam, a long crack that runs beneath the floor of the ocean.
There, two of the Earth's vast plates lean slowly away from one another, pulling gently apart.
Because of this, the island is very quietly splitting, and growing a tiny bit wider each year.
The change is far too slow to see or feel; it is the patient work of unhurried ages.
In some places you could stand in the very gap, with one drifting plate to your left and one to your right.
It is a strange and peaceful thought, a whole land slowly opening like a held breath let go.
There is no hurry in it, only the long, calm widening of the deep, year upon year upon year.
Let that slowness reach you, the sense of something enormous moving too gently to disturb the quiet.
You do not have to picture it clearly, or remember a word; let the deep work go on without you.
Feel your own body loosen, as if you too were very slowly, gently easing open.
Breathe in softly, breathe out longer, and let yourself sink with the slow widening dark.
Because that great seam runs beneath it, much heat lies close under this island's skin.
And so the warm water you imagined is no rare thing here; it rises almost everywhere.
Hot springs steam in quiet hollows, mud pools bubble slowly, and gentle vents breathe out warm air.
Much of the whole country is warmed and lit by this clean, steady heat from below.
Whole towns draw warm water up through pipes from the hot ground, and that water keeps the houses snug.
And people bathe outdoors in broad warm pools, easy and unhurried, while soft snow falls around them.
Imagine resting in that warm water in the falling snow, the cold on your face, the warmth all through you.
The steam lifts slowly past you, white against the dim sky, and there is nothing at all to do.
Fire below, snow above, and you held gently between them in the warmth, perfectly at ease.
There is a deep kindness in heat that simply rises on its own, asking nothing, given freely.
Let that warmth seep through your imagined body now, down your arms, down your slow heavy legs.
Breathe out into the steam, and let every muscle soften toward sleep.
Now and then, in such a land, the warm ground does something quiet and wonderful with its heat.
Deep below, water gathers and grows very hot, hotter than boiling, held down by the weight of the rock.
Then, all at once, it can rush upward and fountain into the cold air in a tall plume of steam and spray.
A hot spring that does this, now and then, is what we call a geyser.
And that very word, geyser, comes from this island, from a famous old spring there named Geysir.
So whenever anyone, anywhere, speaks of a geyser, they are gently borrowing this quiet land's name.
Picture one of them rising in the distance, a soft white tower lifting slowly, then sinking back to stillness.
It comes when it comes, in its own time, and then the ground falls quiet again and waits.
There is no rush in it; it simply breathes out its heat, then rests, then breathes again.
You need not hold the name, or the why of it; let the white plume rise and fall in your mind.
Let your own breath move like that, rising slowly, then easing all the way down into rest.
Breathe out long and soft, and let the steam in your mind settle back to the warm still ground.
Upon this same warm island lie great glaciers, slow rivers of ancient ice, white and immense.
Ice caps rest across the land, and from beneath them cold meltwater slips quietly out and away.
It gathers into rivers and pours down in waterfalls, falling clear across black volcanic sand.
Fire made that dark sand long ago, and now the cold glacier water runs gently over it; ice upon fire's work.
And in the long dark of the northern winters, the sky itself sometimes comes softly alive.
The northern lights, the aurora, ripple overhead in slow curtains of green and faint violet.
They drift and fold without a sound, lighting the snow below, then fading gently away.
Picture lying there in the warm water, watching that soft light move slowly across the dark sky.
People first came to this island more than a thousand years ago, mostly Norse seafarers from across the sea.
They gathered to make laws at an old meeting they called the Althing, among the oldest such gatherings in the world.
But you need not keep any of that; let the green light and the falling water blur softly together.
Let the quiet aurora drift behind your heavy eyes, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Breathe out once more, and let the long dark and the soft light hold you gently toward sleep.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the seam in the deep and the slow widening land fade gently away into the dark.
Let the geyser sink back, and the glaciers soften, and the black sand grow dim and far.
Let the green aurora dissolve, the way the world dissolves as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, held between an easy warmth and a deep and gentle quiet.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Fire and ice rest side by side, and you rest too, asking nothing, needing nothing.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no task waiting for you at all.
Let the warm water hold you, and let the still snow settle, and let the long quiet gather you in.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Hawaiian Islands
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like a warm tide.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Far away, in that darkness, picture a calm and endless ocean, lit only by the soft light of the stars.
Somewhere upon it there is a warm green shore, and small slow waves are folding onto the sand.
They come in and slide back, in and back, patient and unhurried, asking nothing of you at all.
Let your breath fall into the same easy rhythm, in and out, slow as the gentle waves on that far sand.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That warm green shore you are picturing lies far out in the very middle of a vast ocean.
The Hawaiian islands sit alone in the wide Pacific, among the most remote islands anywhere on Earth.
They are thousands of miles from any continent, with nothing but open water on every side.
Picture how small they seem, a handful of green peaks rising from a sea that goes on and on.
All around them the water stretches to the horizon, calm and dark and almost endless.
There is a deep peace in being held so gently by so much quiet ocean.
No noise of the wider world can reach a place that far away across the water.
It is a kind of softness, that distance, a long blue stillness wrapped around the land.
Let yourself feel that same remoteness now, far from anything that ever asked anything of you.
You are as safely apart from the day as those small islands are from every distant shore.
Let that vast calm water settle around you, holding you up the way it holds the islands.
And let your breath grow slow and deep, in time with the long swell of the sea.
Now let your mind sink gently downward, past the islands, into the warm body of the Earth.
These islands were not always here; each one was slowly built, one by one, from fire deep below.
Far beneath the sea floor there is a hotspot, a quiet plume of heat rising from deep within the Earth.
It stays in one place, patient and steady, melting rock and feeding it slowly up toward the surface.
Over millions of years that rising stone piled up and up, until at last it broke gently into the open air.
That is how each island was born, layer upon layer, with no hurry in it at all.
The great plate of the sea floor drifts slowly along, carrying each finished island away with it.
So the islands lie in a long line, the oldest and most worn at one end, the newest land at the other.
One by one they were lifted into the light, then carried off to grow old and soft beneath the rain.
Picture that slow procession, island after island, made over spans of time too long to hold in your mind.
There is no rush anywhere in it, only deep heat, deep time, and the patient drift of the Earth.
Let that slowness pour into you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
On these far green islands rise some of the largest mountains anywhere on the planet.
One of them is called Mauna Kea, and it is taller than you might ever guess.
Measured from its base on the deep sea floor, Mauna Kea stands taller even than Mount Everest.
But most of it lies hidden, far below the waves, so only its calm summit shows above the water.
Picture the whole great mountain in the dark, its huge slow shoulders resting on the deep sea floor.
Near it stands Mauna Loa, another of the gentle giants, one of the largest mountains on Earth by sheer bulk.
It does not rise in a sharp peak, but spreads out broad and low, like a vast resting shield.
You could walk its slopes for a very long time and barely feel that you were climbing at all.
There is something restful in a mountain that rises so gently, so patiently, so quietly broad.
Imagine lying somewhere on that long slope under the stars, the warm earth holding you up.
Let your body feel as heavy and as settled as one of those great patient mountains.
And with each slow breath out, let yourself sink a little further toward sleep.
Long ago, these lonely islands were found and settled by the Polynesian voyagers.
They crossed enormous stretches of open ocean in canoes, with only the wide sea around them.
They carried no maps and no instruments, yet they found these tiny islands in all that water.
Instead they read the stars, learning the paths the lights take softly across the night sky.
They read the long ocean swells, and the way the water moves, and the flight of distant birds.
Picture them out there in the dark, calm and watchful, the canoe rocking gently beneath them.
Above them turned the same slow stars you might see, steady and patient and bright.
By that quiet knowledge, gathered and shared with great care, they came at last to these green shores.
There is a deep wonder in that, in finding a home so far away by the light of the stars alone.
Let yourself be guided now the way they were guided, gently, by something steady in the dark.
You need not steer or search; you have only to drift, and let the night carry you.
Breathe slowly, and let the quiet stars look down on you as they once looked down on the voyagers.
Life, too, had to journey a very long way to reach these islands so far out in the sea.
At first there was only bare new rock, warm and quiet, with no plant and no creature upon it.
Then, slowly, life arrived, a single seed carried on the wind, a bird blown gently off its course.
Each arrival was rare, scattered across long ages, a small soft gift drifting in from far away.
And from those few patient beginnings, the islands bloomed into living things found nowhere else on Earth.
Warm trade winds blow softly over them, and gentle rains fall, and the valleys turn deep and green.
There are lush forests and quiet waterfalls and bright flowers opening in the warm still air.
All of it grew, slowly and tenderly, from those few seeds and wanderers that found their way across the sea.
And the islands are not yet finished, for new land is still being born far beneath the waves.
Even now, deep under the water, a young volcano is building patiently toward the surface, for some distant day.
Picture that quiet making going on in the dark, unhurried, with all the time in the world.
Let that same calm patience fill you, and let your breath grow soft and slow.
There is nothing to wait for and nothing to finish; like the islands, you may simply rest and grow still.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the wide ocean grow dim, and the green islands soften, and fade gently into the dark.
Let the great slow mountains sink away, and the stars blur, and the warm winds fall quiet.
You are lying here in the soft dark, far from everything, safely held as the islands are held by the sea.
There is a deep peace in that, in being so quietly apart, asking nothing, simply being still.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is warm all around you.
Like a far green island under the stars, you have only to be still, and let the night hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no distant shore you need to reach.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the calm sea gathers and cradles the islands.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Krakatoa
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like a warm tide.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture a quiet tropical sea at dusk, the water smooth and dim, the last warmth fading from the sky.
Small waves lap at nothing in particular, slow and even, asking nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink, the way the evening sinks gently down onto a calm and sleeping sea.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the warm dark.
That calm sea you are picturing lies in a far and gentle part of the world.
It is in Indonesia, in a narrow stretch of water called the Sunda Strait.
The strait runs quietly between two great islands, Java on one side and Sumatra on the other.
Somewhere in that warm water there once stood a small volcanic island called Krakatoa.
Some people knew it by another soft name, Krakatau, which means much the same thing.
For a very long time it simply sat there, green and steaming faintly, a mountain rising from the sea.
Ships passed it on their slow way through the strait, and the years went gently by.
Picture it at rest in the evening light, its slopes dark against a darkening sky.
It is only a far away place and a far away time, and none of it can reach you here.
There is nothing in this story you need to remember, and nothing you need to fear.
Let the warm water and the quiet mountain settle softly into your mind.
Breathe in slowly, and let a long breath out, and let your body grow heavier still.
Mountains like Krakatoa are made where the great plates of the Earth's crust meet far below.
Down in the deep, slow rock grows hot enough to soften and rise, gathering quietly over ages.
Now and then it finds its way upward and builds an island, patient layer upon patient layer.
For most of its long life Krakatoa was calm, the way it is calm in your picture now.
But the Earth beneath it was restless, the way the Earth so often is, breathing slowly far below.
In the year eighteen eighty-three, after a long quiet, the old mountain began to stir.
There were soft tremors first, and gentle plumes of steam drifting up into the bright tropical air.
Picture those slow white clouds rising over the warm sea, soft as breath in cold morning air.
It was the deep heat of the world, gathering itself with the unhurried patience of stone.
You do not need to follow any of it closely; let it move at the edge of your drifting mind.
There is something soothing in how the Earth keeps its own slow time, far below all hurry.
Let that slowness pour into you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
Sink a little further now, and let the warm dark hold you close.
Then, on a day in late August, the gathered heat of the deep reached its great release.
Krakatoa erupted, in one of the most powerful eruptions in all of recorded history.
Much of the island broke apart and sank quietly beneath the waves, until the sea closed over it.
Try to hold it gently, with a kind of quiet awe, the way you might watch lightning far out at sea.
It was the vast power of the Earth itself, the same power that lifts mountains and lays them down again.
We are very far from it here, in our warm dark room, with the whole calm world between us and that day.
When it was over, the sea grew still again, smoothing slowly over the place where the mountain had stood.
The water settled, and the strait fell quiet, and the great heat sank back down into the deep.
All of that was long, long ago, and all of it is at peace now, resting under a gentle sea.
You do not have to carry any of it; let the power of that far day soften and grow distant.
There is only stillness left there now, smooth water over a sleeping deep.
Let your own breathing slow to match that calm, easing out long and even.
Breathe out slowly, and let your shoulders sink, and let yourself grow still.
The sound of that great eruption is among the loudest noises the world has ever known.
It rolled out across the sea and was heard thousands of miles away, across a large part of the globe.
People on distant shores, in lands far from the strait, heard a faint far rumble like a low drum.
Imagine that one deep sound, spreading out softly over oceans, growing gentler with every mile.
By the time it reached those distant places it was only a murmur, a soft thunder on the edge of hearing.
And high above, fine ash drifted out into the upper air and wrapped itself around the world.
For months afterward, the sunsets everywhere turned to extraordinary reds and deep glowing oranges.
All across the world, people stepped outside in the evening to watch skies they had never seen before.
Painters and artists tried to hold those strange and beautiful colours in their pictures.
Picture those quiet evenings, the whole sky glowing warm and rose and amber, soft as embers.
So far away, the Earth was painting the dusk in gentle fire, and the world simply stood and watched.
Let those warm sunset colours fill your mind, soft and fading, dimming toward night.
Let your eyes grow heavier still, and breathe slowly out into the dark.
So much fine dust drifted in the high air that it gently dimmed the sunlight for a time.
For a while it cooled the whole planet, only a little, the way a thin cloud cools a summer afternoon.
It was a quiet sign of how the air carries things softly, all the way around the turning world.
And on the bare remnants left behind, life began to return, with the most patient kind of grace.
At first there was almost nothing, only cooled rock and ash, washed by the warm sea.
Then spiders drifted in on threads of silk, and ferns took hold, and seeds arrived on the wind and waves.
Birds came, and carried more seeds, and slowly, year by year, the green crept gently back.
The bare ground softened into living things again, quietly, with no one needing to tend it.
And then, decades later, a new island rose from the sea in the very same place.
They named it Anak Krakatau, which means the child of Krakatoa, and it is gently building still.
It is a soft reminder that the Earth is restless and alive, forever making anew what it takes down.
Today the strait is calm again, the sea quiet over the place where the old mountain stood.
Let that quiet renewal settle over you, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the far away strait and the old quiet mountain fade gently away into the dark.
Let the great sound soften to nothing, the way all sounds soften as you slip toward sleep.
Let the rose and amber sunsets dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, safe and far from any far away day.
Somewhere a calm sea is resting over a sleeping deep, smooth and still, just as you are.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like that quiet sea, you have only to be still, and let the long calm hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no power pressing on you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the gentle sea has gathered the strait into peace.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Galapagos
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like a warm tide.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture a still, warm shore somewhere far away, where the night has come and the sea breathes slow.
On that quiet shore there are creatures resting, unafraid, dozing in the soft and easy dark.
They are not watching for danger, and neither are you; there is nothing here that means you harm.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That warm shore you are picturing belongs to a small and lonely group of islands.
They are called the Galapagos, and they sit out in the wide Pacific, right upon the equator.
They lie far off the coast of Ecuador, in South America, alone in a great stretch of open sea.
These are young islands, raised up slowly by volcanoes rising from the floor of the ocean.
Imagine that, the dark sea, and out of it a quiet rim of land lifting into the light.
They sit at a meeting place, where a cool current and a warm current gently come together.
So the air is mild and the water is strange and rich, and life has gathered there in its own way.
There is no crowd of land around them, no neighbours close by, only the patient sea on every side.
Picture them small and dark and still, scattered across the water under a wide and open sky.
It is a far and peaceful place, asking nothing of you, simply resting out there in the warm dark.
Let that distance soothe you, the long quiet miles of sea between you and any hurry.
Let your breath grow slow and deep, as slow as the tide moving around those lonely shores.
Because the islands are so remote, life reached them only rarely, and only the patient ever arrived.
A seed carried on the wind, a creature drifted on a raft of branches, a bird blown far off its course.
And once they were there, on those quiet shores, almost nothing was waiting to hunt them.
There were no great predators on the islands, no large beasts prowling to bring them fear.
And so, over a very long time, the animals there simply forgot how to be afraid.
To this day many of them are famously unafraid, even of people who come walking quietly among them.
A bird may sit calmly as you pass, a sea lion may sleep on the sand without stirring at all.
There is a deep gentleness in that, a whole world of creatures with no need to flee.
Picture them now, dozing easily on the warm rocks and the soft sand, fearless in the falling dark.
Nothing is chasing them, and nothing is chasing you, and the night is calm on every side.
Let that fearlessness settle over you, that ease of a creature with nothing left to dread.
Soften your shoulders, and let each breath out carry a little more of your weight into the dark.
Among the gentlest of these unhurried creatures are the giant tortoises that gave the islands their name.
They are enormous and slow, some of them as heavy as a few grown people standing together.
They graze quietly in the cool green highlands, moving so slowly that they seem hardly to move at all.
And they live a very long time, well over a hundred years, far longer than you or I will live.
Imagine one of them now, ancient and calm, lowering its great old head to rest as the day fades.
It has seen a hundred years of these islands, and it is in no hurry whatsoever to do anything more.
There is a marvelous slowness in it, a creature that measures its days in seasons and not in minutes.
It carries its shell like a quiet home, and it sleeps without worry beneath the gathering stars.
Picture its slow breathing, its heavy stillness, its long and patient ease in the warm dark.
Let yourself borrow that slowness now, that calm of something that has all the time in the world.
There is no rush anywhere in this; the old tortoise asks you only to grow still and rest.
Let your breath grow long and unhurried, as slow as a tortoise settling down to sleep.
Along the dark rocks of the shore live the marine iguanas, found nowhere else on all the Earth.
They are small dragon-like creatures, and they have learned to swim out into the cool sea.
There they graze on the soft green seaweed that grows beneath the moving water.
And when the cold of the sea has crept into them, they climb back out onto the dark warm rocks.
There they lie still, basking, letting the warmth soak slowly back into their patient bodies.
Picture them now, a quiet crowd of them, resting on the rocks as the last of the light goes.
Nearby the sea lions doze on the sand, and the blue-footed boobies settle for the night.
Penguins live here too, small ones, right by the equator, which seems a wonder and yet it is true.
And some of the birds have no need to fly at all, and have given their flying up entirely.
All these gentle neighbours share the same quiet shores, each one drifting toward its own rest.
Let that whole calm shore hold you, the warm rocks, the soft sand, the breathing of the tide.
Let your body grow as heavy and as still as an iguana warming on the dark rocks at dusk.
Long ago, in the year eighteen thirty-five, a young naturalist named Charles Darwin came to these islands.
He wandered slowly among the tortoises and the iguanas and the fearless little birds.
And he noticed something small and quiet, a thing easy to miss, in the finches from island to island.
On one island the little birds had one shape of beak, and on the next a slightly different one.
Each island, in its long isolation, had gently shaped its own forms of life, a little apart from the rest.
Many creatures here live nowhere else, each lonely shore quietly making something all its own.
And from that small and gentle observation, Darwin slowly came to a very large idea.
He began to understand how living things change over time, slowly, as the diamond is slowly made.
He did not rush to it; the thought formed in him gently, over many quiet years.
Now the islands are carefully protected, a living museum of how life unfolds when left to itself.
There is a deep calm in that, life finding its own slow way, with no one to hurry it along.
Let that slowness pour into you now, softening your thoughts, lengthening your breath.
Let yourself grow as still and as patient as life quietly shaping itself across the ages.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the islands and the currents and the slow old tortoises fade gently away into the dark.
Let the warm rocks and the quiet sea soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere those creatures are at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace on that distant shore, unafraid, unhurried, simply being still beneath the stars.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the dozing tortoise, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no fear anywhere in you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the gentle sea gathers those lonely shores.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Great Wall
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like a soft wind.
Imagine the room around you has gone dim and quiet, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the gentle softening along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this peaceful dark.
Far off in that darkness, picture a long low wall, winding slowly over hill after misty hill.
It climbs and dips with the land, following the ridges into the distance, until it fades into the haze.
It is old and quiet and patient, and it asks nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink, the way the evening mist settles slowly into a sleeping valley.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
That long wall you are picturing is older and gentler than it first seems.
It is not really one single wall at all, but many walls, laid down over a very long time.
Different dynasties built and rebuilt it across the north of China, for more than two thousand years.
Each age added its own stretches, mended what had crumbled, and let other parts quietly fall away.
So when we say the Great Wall, we are speaking of a whole family of walls, raised by many hands.
Some sections stand close together, some run far apart, and some have softened back into the hills.
It was never finished all at once, the way you might finish a single careful drawing.
It grew slowly, in pieces, over more generations than you could easily hold in your mind.
Picture all those long centuries of patient building, with no hurry in any of it.
There is something restful in that, in a thing made so slowly that no one alive saw it all.
Let that slowness settle over you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
Feel yourself loosening, sinking gently, as the quiet of the dark gathers around you.
Now let your mind follow that wall as it travels, far across the wide north of the land.
Together its branches and sections wander for many thousands of miles over the face of the country.
It crosses green mountains, dry deserts, and broad open grasslands, going wherever the land allows.
It is one of the longest things people have ever made, laid end to end across half a world of hills.
Yet it is also very narrow, only wide enough for guards to walk along the top of it.
So think of a thin grey thread, drawn out over an enormous land, stitching the ridges together.
It does not march in a straight line; it climbs and bends and follows the shape of the ground.
Along its spine it seems to ripple, rising with each hill and dipping into each quiet valley.
Mile after mile it goes, over the high places and down into the low, never once in a rush.
Imagine walking that long top in the cool of evening, with the hills falling away on either side.
There is no end to reach tonight, and no distance you must cover; the walking is only for rest.
Let your body grow heavier with each slow step you imagine, and let your breath grow soft and deep.
For all its great length, the wall was made for a simple and patient purpose.
It was raised mostly to watch over the open north, and to slow the riders who came from the steppes.
Far beyond it lay wide grasslands, and from there came swift horsemen the builders wished to keep watch on.
So the wall was less a thing to stop the world than a long, quiet line from which to see it coming.
Along its length stood gates where travellers passed, and towers where small garrisons kept their watch.
Soldiers lived out there in the lonely towers, tending fires, looking north over the empty land.
Most nights nothing came at all, and the watch was only the wind, the stars, and the slow turning hours.
Picture one such guard, leaning on the cool stone, listening to the quiet, his eyes growing heavy.
The wall did not have to do very much; it only had to wait, and watch, and be patient.
It is restful to think of all that quiet watching, going on through so many calm and ordinary nights.
There is nothing for you to guard tonight, and no horizon you must keep your eyes upon.
Let that long, gentle watch fade now, and let your own eyes grow heavier still.
When at last a watch did stir, the wall could pass the word along astonishingly fast.
All down its length stood signal towers, set within sight of one another across the hills.
By day a guard would send up smoke, and by night he would light a fire on the tower top.
The next tower, seeing it, would answer with its own, and the next, and the next after that.
So a single warning could race from tower to tower, leaping the ridges faster than any rider.
Picture those small fires waking one by one along the dark spine of the mountains, a chain of soft lights.
A message could travel the length of the wall while most of the country still slept beneath the stars.
And then, the word passed on, each fire would gutter low and the towers fall quiet once more.
The hills went dark again, and the long wall settled back into its patient waiting.
There is something gentle in that image, of light passed quietly along in the deep of night.
Let those small fires fade out one by one, the way the day fades softly into sleep.
Breathe slowly out, and let each breath dim a little more of the waking world.
The grand stone wall that most people picture is, in truth, the youngest part of all.
Those high stretches of brick and cut stone were largely raised by the Ming dynasty, only a few hundred years ago.
It is the Ming work that climbs so proudly over the hills near the old capital, in the form we know best.
The far older walls were humbler things, made of rammed earth, of wood, and of bundled reeds.
Those early sections never had the fine grey brick; they were the colour of the very ground they rose from.
Much of that ancient earth has quietly returned to the hills, worn down by the long centuries of weather.
And it is a gentle myth, often told, that the wall can be seen from the Moon, or even from low orbit.
It cannot; though it is long, it is far too narrow and too like the land around it to pick out from so high.
The wall was the slow labour of countless soldiers, peasants, and prisoners, over many long generations.
Much of it now stands quiet and half wild, with grass and small trees growing along the old stones.
Picture it weathered and softened, the wind moving through the pines that have taken root in its cracks.
There is a deep calm in a made thing returning so gently to the earth that made it.
Let that calm pour into you now, slowing your breath, softening your every thought.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the long wall blur and soften, fading into the mist that drifts along the sleeping ridges.
Let the small fires dim, and the quiet towers, and the cool stone underfoot, all gently slip away.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a long old wall is at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that patient stone, made over ages, asking nothing, simply lying still on the hills.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the old wall, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to guard, no distance left to cross at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the mist gathers softly over the sleeping land.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Appian Way
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them pass over you like a warm evening breeze.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no journey waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that darkness, picture an old straight road, its worn paving stones glowing faintly in the dusk.
Tall pines lean over it, their broad crowns spread like umbrellas against a warm and fading sky.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little further, the way the light sinks slowly out of an evening.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That old road you are picturing is one of the oldest and most famous of all the roads the Romans ever made.
They called it the Via Appia, and we know it now as the Appian Way.
It was begun more than two thousand three hundred years ago, in the early days of Rome itself.
It was started by a Roman official named Appius Claudius, and it still carries his name down to this day.
From the gates of Rome it set out, running south and east, reaching at last all the way to Brindisi on the distant coast.
Think of that, a single road stretching from the heart of the city to the edge of the sea.
It was so admired that the Romans came to call it the queen of roads.
They gave it that name because it was wide, and remarkably straight, and built to last.
Picture it now, that long stone road laid down so very long ago, still patient beneath the pines.
There is no need to remember the names; let them drift past like leaves on the warm air.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, settling further into the dark, as the old road waits quietly in your mind.
Now let your mind move closer to those worn stones, and see how carefully the road was made.
The Romans did not simply lay a path upon the ground; they built it up in careful layers, like a slow piece of work.
First they dug down and set a deep bed of stone and gravel, firm and patient beneath everything else.
Upon that bed they fitted the paving stones, tightly and snugly, each one settled neatly against the next.
It was laid with such care that the rain would run off it and the road would not sink or wander.
So well was it built that parts of it still survive today, after all these many centuries.
You can still walk, even now, on stones that Roman feet once crossed, smoothed and polished by the ages.
Imagine kneeling to lay one such stone, fitting it gently into its place with no hurry at all.
There is something restful in that, in work done slowly and well, meant to outlast the ones who made it.
Picture the road running on ahead of you, stone after fitted stone, fading softly into the evening light.
Let that quiet care settle over you, the calm of a thing made to last.
And let your breath grow long and unhurried, as steady as the laying of those patient stones.
The Roman roads ran famously straight, and the Appian Way was the straightest and most admired of them all.
Where they could, the Romans cut their roads across the land as directly as a line drawn by hand.
They would press on over hill and marsh, keeping to their straight course rather than wandering aside.
This is part of an old saying you may know, that all roads lead to Rome.
For the city sat at the heart of a great web of roads, and the Appian Way was the first and the queen of them.
Along the road, slender stone pillars once stood to mark the distances, the old mileposts of the empire.
A traveller could read how far they had come, and how far there still was to go.
And spaced out along the way were inns and changing-stations, where the weary could rest and find fresh horses.
Picture stopping at such a place in the warm dusk, the long straight road behind you, the night drawing gently in.
There is no further to walk tonight; the road can wait until morning, or longer still.
Let that ease pour into you, the deep relief of a journey set down for the night.
Let your body grow heavier, your breath slow and soft, as the road sleeps under the darkening pines.
For many long centuries this road did its patient work, carrying the life of the empire upon its stones.
Marching armies went out along it, their feet falling in time upon the paving, off toward the far frontiers.
Traders came and went with their loaded carts, and messengers hurried with word from one distant place to another.
Ordinary travellers walked it too, pilgrims and wanderers and folk simply going home.
All of them, year upon year, helped knit the sprawling empire gently together along this one great road.
Think of how many feet have passed where you are picturing, more than anyone could ever count.
Countless footsteps, century after century, each one wearing the stones a little smoother.
And yet on a still evening now it is the most peaceful of places, quiet and slow and kind.
The hurry has long since drained out of it, and only the long calm of old age remains.
Picture the last light fading, the road empty and at rest, the traffic of ages all gone quietly to sleep.
There is no one left to pass tonight; the road belongs only to the dusk and to you.
Let that emptiness be a comfort, and let your breath grow slower with the falling light.
Along the edges of the road, just outside the old city walls, there once stood rows of tombs and monuments.
For it was the Roman custom to bury their dead beside the roads, out in the open air, beyond the walls of the city.
So a traveller leaving Rome would pass between quiet stone tombs, lining the way on either hand.
Many of these ruins still stand along the Appian Way even now, gentle and broken in the long grass.
They are not fearful places, only old and still, softened by time and shaded by the leaning pines.
Tall umbrella pines spread their broad green crowns above the worn stones, casting their cool and dappled shade.
On a still evening it is a deeply peaceful place to walk, where so many feet have passed before.
Picture the ruins glowing faintly in the last of the light, patient and unhurried, asking nothing of you.
The road has outlived empires and armies and all the haste of the living, and it rests on, quietly.
There is a deep calm in that long patience, in stones that have seen everything and now simply abide.
Let that calm settle into your own bones, the calm of a thing that no longer needs to hurry.
And let your breath grow long and slow, as quiet as the dusk gathering over the old straight road.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the long road and the marching armies and the old mileposts fade gently away into the dark.
Let the tombs and the ruins soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere an old road lies at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that quiet road, worn smooth by ages, asking nothing, simply lying still beneath the pines.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the old road, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to carry, no distance left to cross tonight.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the dusk gathers softly over the worn and patient stones.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Hadrian's Wall
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like wind over grass.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere out in that darkness, picture a wide stretch of rolling green moorland, soft with mist.
Let your eye wander along a low ridge, where an old line of stone runs quietly over the hills.
The wall rises and falls with the land, patient and weathered, asking nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of that misty green country.
That low line of stone you are picturing is older than you might think, and gentler now than it once was.
It is a wall the Romans built across the north of Britain, nearly nineteen hundred years ago.
They laid it across the narrowest neck of the land, running all the way from one coast to the other.
From the cold grey sea in the west to the cold grey sea in the east, the stone made one long quiet line.
It was ordered by an emperor named Hadrian, a careful man who liked to know where his world ended.
Rather than push his empire ever wider, he chose to mark a firm and steady edge, and to hold it.
So he set down a clear boundary in the hills, a line between what was within and what lay beyond.
Picture the workers laying course upon course of stone, in no great hurry, under the wide northern sky.
There is something restful in a thing built simply to be still, to stay, to mark a quiet limit.
The wall did not wish to conquer the world; it only wished to hold one calm and certain line.
Let that thought rest lightly upon you, asking nothing, settling like mist along the ground.
Feel your breath grow slow and deep, and let yourself sink a little further into the dark.
Let your mind walk softly now along the top of that long wall, mile after gentle mile.
It once ran some eighty Roman miles, a great length of stone threading over the open hills.
Beside it lay a deep ditch, dug into the earth, so the wall rose above a long quiet trench.
And it was never only the wall; a string of small posts was set all along its patient length.
There were forts where soldiers lived, and between them smaller milecastles, like little gateways in the stone.
Between those, in turn, stood slender turrets, low towers where a watcher could stand and look north.
Picture them spaced out along the ridge, each one quiet, each one keeping the same long view.
From those towers the soldiers watched the misty hills, where the land rolled away into the unknown north.
Imagine the wind moving over the moor, and a lone figure leaning on cold stone, looking out at nothing in particular.
It was a calm sort of watching, hour upon hour, with little to do but mark the turning weather.
There is a deep peace in that slow keeping of watch over an empty and beautiful land.
Let that quiet watching settle your thoughts, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
Breathe out slowly, and let the misty hills grow softer in your mind.
Think now of the men who stood along that wall, far from the warm places where they were born.
Soldiers came here from many corners of the empire, drawn to this damp green edge of the world.
Some had grown up under warmer suns, in lands of dry hills and bright open skies.
And now they found themselves here, among the mists and the rain, watching the grey northern weather roll in.
Picture them wrapped against the cold, far from home, keeping the same long view from the same cold stone.
They were ordinary people, in the end, with ordinary lives going on quietly behind the wall.
There were kitchens and stables and small warm rooms, the murmur of voices, the smell of woodsmoke.
Whole little towns gathered close against the forts, families and traders living their days in the lee of the stone.
It is easy to forget that history was lived by people much like you, who grew tired and longed for rest.
Imagine them at the end of a long watch, setting down their cares, drifting toward their own sleep.
The same dark that holds you now once held them too, on those same windswept hills.
Let that gentle thought loosen your shoulders, and let your body grow heavier still.
At one of those forts, a place called Vindolanda, something small and wonderful was kept by the wet ground.
There, thin slips of wood, no thicker than a leaf, lay buried in the cold damp earth for many centuries.
On them, in faded ink, people had written the small ordinary letters of their daily lives.
One is an invitation to a birthday party, sent warmly from one woman to another, long, long ago.
Another is a simple request for warm socks, and for sandals, to keep out the cold of the northern winter.
These are not the words of emperors or great battles, only small human voices speaking quietly across the years.
Someone shivered in the damp and wished for dry socks; someone hoped a friend would come to share a happy day.
Imagine those soft voices, almost lost, kept safe in the dark earth until they could be gently read again.
There is great tenderness in that, in how the smallest kindnesses outlast the strongest stone.
The wall was also a doorway, you see, a place where goods and people crossed and were watched and counted.
Through its gates moved traders and travellers, paying their dues, passing from one land into the other.
Let those small old voices murmur softly at the edge of your mind, asking nothing, only wishing you well.
Breathe out, and let yourself sink toward sleep on the comfort of their kindness.
In time, the Romans gathered up their things and went away, back toward the heart of their fading empire.
The watchers came down from the towers, the gates fell still, and the long wall was left to the weather.
Slowly, gently, over many hundreds of years, the unattended stone began to crumble and to settle.
And the people who lived nearby carried much of it away, for cut stone is a useful and welcome thing.
Its blocks went into the walls of farms, and churches, and small houses scattered across the land.
So the wall lived on, quietly, hidden inside the homes and the lanes of the country it once divided.
Yet long stretches of it still remain, running over the green hills, rising and falling with the land.
It is a quiet line of old stone now, threading through wild and open country, soft with moss and grass.
Today it is cared for and protected, and people walk its whole length, from one sea to the other.
They follow the old path over the ridges, with the wind on their faces and the mist in the hollows.
There is a deep calm in a thing that has weathered so many years and simply grown quieter with each one.
Let that long settling enter you too, the slow easing of stone back into the soft green earth.
Let your breath grow slow as the years, and let your body settle as gently as the wall.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the long wall and the misty hills fade gently away into the warm dark around you.
Let the watchers and the soldiers go, and let the small old voices soften into silence.
You are lying here in the quiet, and far away an old line of stone is at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in that weathered wall, asking nothing now, simply lying still upon the green.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the old stone, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, no watch to keep, no line to hold tonight at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the green hills have gathered the patient stone.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Inca Roads
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like cool mountain air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no journey waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that darkness, picture a narrow path of fitted stone, climbing slowly among high green peaks.
Cloud drifts across the mountains above it, soft and grey, and the path simply waits, patient and still.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath out lets you sink a little, the way a traveller eases down to rest after a long, gentle climb.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That stone path you are picturing is part of something very old and very large.
Long ago, high in the Andes of South America, a people called the Inca built a great network of roads.
They gave it a name in their own tongue, the Qhapaq Nan, which means the great road, or the royal road.
All together those roads ran for many thousands of miles, threading through the mountains like quiet veins.
They linked a vast empire, reaching from what is now Colombia in the north down through Chile and Argentina.
At the heart of it all stood the city of Cusco, and from there the roads spread outward in every direction.
Picture them now, those long stone ways, winding over ridges and along high green valleys.
They were not built in a hurry, but laid down patiently, stone by careful stone, over many years.
You do not need to remember any of these names; let them pass over you like the drifting cloud.
It is enough to know that, far away and long ago, careful hands joined the mountains together with roads.
There is something calming in that, in roads laid down so slowly and meant to last so long.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep as you settle further into the dark.
Think for a moment of all that the Inca did not have when they made these roads.
They had no wheel to roll along the paths, and no horses or carts to carry loads across the high country.
They had no iron tools, no hard metal blades to cut and shape the stone.
And yet the paths, the steps and the walls they made were beautiful, fitted close and true.
They worked the stone with patience and with skill, with simpler tools and with steady, knowing hands.
Much of what they built has stood for centuries, weathering rain and frost and the long passing of years.
Picture those fitted stones, smoothed by the feet of travellers, still holding their shape after all this time.
There is a deep quiet in such work, the quiet of people who were not in any hurry at all.
They built as though they had all the time in the world, and in a way, the mountains gave them that time.
You can let your hands grow as still as theirs once were after a long day of patient work.
Imagine resting beside that old path now, the cool stone steady beneath you, the peaks soft with cloud.
Let that patient stillness settle over you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
In the high mountains the land is broken by deep gorges, with rivers running far below.
To cross them, the Inca did something gentle and clever: they wove bridges out of grass and fibre rope.
They twisted slender grasses into cords, and the cords into thick, strong ropes, and the ropes into bridges.
Hung high above the rushing water, these woven bridges swayed softly and carried people safely across.
It seems a delicate thing, a bridge of grass, and yet made well it could bear a great deal of weight.
In some mountain communities, people still come together each year to rebuild such a bridge by hand.
They gather the grass, twist the ropes, and weave the bridge anew, just as their ancestors did long ago.
Picture that quiet work, many patient hands turning soft grass into something strong enough to trust.
It is a gentle kind of keeping, this remaking, holding an old skill alive across the generations.
There is no rush in it, only care, and the slow rhythm of hands that know what they are doing.
Let yourself imagine that soft swaying bridge, high above the water, holding steady in the mountain air.
And as you picture it, let your body grow heavier, your breath softer, asking nothing of the hours.
Along these roads the Inca sent messages, not by writing, but by running.
Swift relay runners called chasquis carried news and orders up and down the mountains.
Each runner sprinted only a short way, from one small waystation to the next, then passed the message on.
In this way word could travel a very long distance, handed gently from one runner to another.
They carried more than words; sometimes they even brought fresh fish up into the high mountains.
Picture a runner moving lightly along the stone path, the cool air in his chest, the peaks all around.
And to hold their records, the Inca did not use letters at all, but knotted cords called the quipu.
Colours and knots tied into the cords could hold numbers, counts and careful accounts.
It is a quiet thought, a whole memory held in soft cord, in knots tied by patient fingers.
You do not have to keep any of this; let the runners and the knots drift softly out of mind.
Imagine the message passing on into the distance, growing fainter, until it fades away among the peaks.
Let your own thoughts fade like that now, and let your breath grow slow and easy in the dark.
Here and there along the roads stood quiet shelters, storehouses and rest-houses called tambos.
Travellers and the running chasquis could stop at a tambo to shelter, to eat, and to sleep.
Picture a small stone rest-house at the end of a long day's path, warm and steady against the cold.
The roads themselves climbed high, often with long staircases of stone over the great passes.
They rose through cloud forest, where mist hangs in the trees, and up onto bare cold uplands.
Much of the way lay far above the line where trees can grow, in the wide, hushed country of the heights.
Up there the air is thin and clear, and the silence is deep, and the mountains seem very old.
Even now, much of that great network still survives, worn but standing, after all these years.
People walk parts of it today, going between mountain villages, as their families have for generations.
Imagine resting in one of those old tambos tonight, the long climb finished, nothing more to do.
There is a deep calm in the high country, a stillness that asks only that you lie down and rest.
So let that calm pour into you now, slowing your breath, softening your every thought.
Let yourself grow as quiet and as still as a tambo at nightfall, high among the sleeping peaks.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the long stone roads and the high passes fade gently away into the dark.
Let the woven bridges and the running messengers soften and grow distant, like cloud drifting off the peaks.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a quiet path of stone is at rest, as you are.
There is a deep peace in those old roads, laid down so slowly, asking nothing, simply waiting in the hills.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the mountains, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, no message to carry, no climb left to make at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the high country gathers the mist and holds it close.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Dragon
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like warm air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
