There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere far off in that darkness, picture a great calm creature, curled and fast asleep.
It is vast and ancient and still, breathing slowly in a quiet cave, and it asks nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath you let go slips out long and unhurried, the way that great sleeper breathes in the dark.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That great sleeping creature you are picturing has never lived anywhere but in our stories.
The dragon is a legend, a beast we dreamed up long ago and have carried in our tales ever since.
And yet it is one of the strangest and loveliest legends we have, for it appears almost everywhere.
Across the whole world, in lands that never met, people imagined some version of the same great beast.
From Europe to the Americas to the far East, the dragon coils through one folklore after another.
Few imagined creatures are shared so widely, dreamed up again and again by people who lived worlds apart.
It is a wonder, really, how many separate peoples reached for a single vast and ancient beast.
No one ever found one; the dragon lives only in the telling, passed gently from voice to voice.
Perhaps that is why it feels so old, this creature woven through so many quiet evenings of stories.
You do not need to remember any of these places, only to let the sense of them settle softly.
Picture all those distant firesides, all telling of one great beast asleep somewhere in the dark.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep as you sink a little further.
The stories do not all agree on what the dragon is, and that is part of their gentle charm.
In the West, people often pictured a winged beast, breathing fire, guarding a hoard of gold.
It was imagined coiled over its treasure in some deep mountain hall, watching, half asleep.
But far to the East, especially in old China, the dragon was dreamed quite differently.
There it was usually wingless and serpentine, long and supple, more like a great river than a flame.
And it was not a monster at all, but wise and noble, a gentle bringer of rain and of good fortune.
In Chinese tradition the dragon was an auspicious creature, long linked with emperors and with water.
It was thought to move through the clouds and call down the life-giving rains upon the fields below.
So in one telling the dragon hoards and burns, and in another it blesses and quietly gives.
Both are only stories, two faces of one old dream, and tonight we will keep to the calmer one.
Picture a great kindly beast turning slowly through soft clouds, asking nothing, harming nothing.
Let that easy image carry you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried as you drift.
It is worth wondering, as you sink, where such a dream might first have come from.
The dragon was never real, yet the idea had to begin somewhere, in something people truly saw.
Scholars think it may have grown, in part, from great bones the old peoples found in the ground.
Now and then the rock would weather away and reveal the huge skull or limbs of some ancient creature.
These were the remains of dinosaurs and other long vanished beasts, though no one then knew it.
To those who found them, they looked like the bones of giant reptiles, sleeping in the stone.
And from such great bones, it is easy to see how a tale of a vast lizard might gently grow.
Living animals may have added to the picture too, in their own quiet way.
Giant snakes and crocodiles, and the large monitor lizards we now call Komodo dragons, all played a part.
Out of old bones and real reptiles, the imagination slowly built one great beast that never was.
There is something soothing in that, in how a legend can be stitched so softly from real and quiet things.
Let that slow stitching of the story settle over you, and let your breath grow long and easy.
The very word we use carries the same old sense of a watching, sleeping guardian.
Dragon comes down to us from an old Greek word that meant a great serpent.
And that word, in its turn, seems to have meant something like the one who watches.
It is a fitting name for a guardian, a creature set to keep watch over something precious.
Picture a beast that never quite closes both its eyes, always half keeping the long watch.
Through countless tales the dragon does just this, coiled around a hoard of gold in the dark.
It sleeps over its treasure beneath the mountains, patient, asking only to be left in peace.
In some stories it circles protectively through the clouds, watching over the land below.
Whether it guards gold or rain or simply the quiet of its cave, it is always keeping watch.
But tonight the watch is gentle, for there is nothing here that needs guarding against.
Let the great beast keep its slow watch in the dark, and let you have no watch to keep at all.
There is nothing to guard now; let your breath go soft, and let yourself sink toward sleep.
Most often, in the oldest tales, the dragon is not raging at all, but simply sleeping.
It is imagined lying vast and patient for hundreds of years at a time, deep in the quiet earth.
Picture all that slow time passing while it sleeps, the seasons turning far above its cave.
It does not stir, it does not hurry; it only breathes, long and deep, in the warm dark.
Whatever shape the dragon takes, it has always gathered up something old within us.
Into one great imagined beast we folded our sense of the wild, the ancient and the powerful.
All that was too large to name we gave to the dragon, and laid it down to sleep in the earth.
And so the legend rests, as it has rested through so many tellings, vast and calm and still.
You are lying here in your own warm dark, and the great beast is sleeping in its cave.
Its breathing is slow and its body is heavy, and slowly your breathing is slowing to match.
There is no fear in any of it, only the deep peace of something ancient gently at rest.
Let that long patience pour into you now, slowing your breath, softening your every thought.
Let yourself grow as still and as quiet as a great beast asleep for a hundred years.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the far off firesides and the old tales fade gently away into the dark.
Let the winged guardian and the gentle rain-bringer soften and dim and drift apart.
Let the great bones in the rock and the long watch in the cave fade quietly out of mind.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a great calm creature is at rest, as you are.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the sleeping dragon, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to guard, no watch to keep, no task at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the deep cave gathers the great sleeper and holds it close.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Unicorn
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with each slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like a soft wind through trees.
Imagine the room around you has gone quiet and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the gentle softening along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this kind and easy dark.
Far off in that darkness, picture a quiet glade in a forest, hushed and silvered by the moon.
Among the still trees, imagine a soft pale shape standing very calmly, doing nothing at all.
It is gentle and unhurried, and it asks nothing of you whatsoever.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little further into the warm and patient quiet.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
That soft pale shape you are picturing is a unicorn, and the unicorn is a legend.
It is a creature people imagined long ago, never one you could ever truly have found in the woods.
Most often it is pictured as a graceful white horse, gentle and slender, standing calm in the green hush.
Upon its brow there is a single horn, long and slender, with a soft spiralling twist along its length.
No such animal has ever walked the Earth, and yet people have loved the thought of it for thousands of years.
The real wonder is not the beast itself, but the long and tender story of how people came to believe in it.
For the unicorn was not first dreamed up as a thing of magic; it was once described as a real, if distant, animal.
It lived at the far edges of the known world, in lands too far away for anyone to go and look.
And so it grew quietly in the imagination, gathering grace and gentleness as the centuries passed.
There is something soothing in that, in a kindly idea handed softly from one age to the next.
You do not need to hold any of it; let the thought rest as lightly as mist among the trees.
Let your breath grow slow and deep, and feel yourself settle further into the dark.
Let your mind wander now to a writer who lived in ancient Greece, very long ago.
His name was Ctesias, and he set down one of the oldest accounts we have of a one-horned beast.
He never saw it himself; he wrote down stories that travellers had brought back from distant India.
He described it plainly, as though it were simply a real animal living in far-off lands.
He wrote of a swift wild creature with a single horn upon its head, fleet and hard to catch.
To him it was no spirit and no magic thing, only an exotic animal at the edge of the maps.
From those few travellers' tales, repeated and softened over the years, the legend slowly grew.
Picture how a story passes from one mouth to another, each teller adding a little gentleness of their own.
What began as a far-off animal became, in time, a creature of grace and quiet wonder.
It is a soft thing, the way a tale can travel further than any traveller ever did.
There is no need to remember the name, or the writer, or the far country; simply let them drift.
Let your breath lengthen, and let your body grow heavier against the warm and waiting dark.
For a great many centuries, people believed the unicorn's horn held a wondrous power.
The horn was given its own name; they called it alicorn, and they treasured it above almost anything.
It was said that the alicorn could purify water that had been poisoned, and could heal the sick.
Kings and great lords paid astonishing fortunes for a single horn, prizing it more than gold.
They kept them in their treasuries, dipped them in their cups, and trusted them to keep them safe.
Yet here is the gentle truth at the heart of it, quiet and rather lovely once you know it.
Nearly all those treasured horns were in truth the long spiralled tusks of the narwhal.
The narwhal is a small whale of the cold Arctic seas, and its single tusk twists just like the storied horn.
Northern sailors traded the tusks far to the south, and kept the secret of where they truly came from.
So the prized unicorn horn was a whale's gentle tooth, carried quietly down from the icy waters.
Let that soft secret settle over you, no burden in it, only a small and pleasant wonder.
Breathe out slowly now, and let your thoughts grow as dim as a candle burning low.
In the Europe of long ago, the unicorn grew gentler still, and became a symbol of purity and peace.
People wove it into beautiful tapestries, large and soft, hung upon the cool stone walls.
In those old hangings the unicorn rests quietly in a flowering garden, among small blossoms and green leaves.
It lies at ease, calm and unafraid, a picture of stillness you could gaze at for a long while.
An old legend told of how the wild unicorn could be tamed, and it is the gentlest of stories.
It was said the creature could not be taken by force, by hunters or by hounds or by any chase.
Instead one had only to sit down peacefully in the forest and wait, very quiet and very still.
Then, the legend says, the unicorn would come softly from the trees, trusting and unhurried.
And it would lay its head down to rest, calm at last, in the quiet of the woods.
Picture that now: the pale creature stepping gently near, and lowering its head to sleep.
There is such peace in that image, a wildness made calm simply by stillness and quiet.
Let your own head grow heavy too, and let yourself be as still as the waiting forest.
There are other gentle threads in the long story of the unicorn, woven from real things glimpsed afar.
Some believe the idea was fed by true one-horned animals, half seen or described from a great distance.
Travellers spoke of the rhinoceros, a heavy beast with a single horn upon its nose, in far-off lands.
Others may have caught sight of the oryx, a pale desert antelope with two long and slender horns.
Seen from the side, in profile, the oryx can seem to carry only one horn, the two lined up as one.
So glimpses of real creatures, half understood, may have quietly fed the dream of the single horn.
The unicorn is also the national animal of Scotland, chosen long ago as a proud and untamed emblem.
It was taken as a creature wild and free, never truly captured, and yet gentle at heart.
Through all these many threads, woven softly together, it became a beast of healing and quiet grace.
It stands alone in the green hush of the woods, calm and pale, asking nothing, harming no one.
Let all those gentle strands gather into one soft image and rest there, in the moonlit glade.
Breathe slowly out, and let the last of your thoughts grow faint and warm and far away.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the old writer and the far country fade gently away into the dark.
Let the treasured horns and the soft tapestries dim and soften, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a gentle pale creature is at rest, as you are.
It stands calm and unafraid in its quiet glade, and slowly it lowers its head to sleep.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the soft green quiet is all around you.
Like the gentle creature in the moonlight, you have only to be still and let the peace hold you.
There is nowhere to go, nothing to tame, no task waiting for you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up as softly as the forest gathers the sleeping unicorn.
You are safe, and you are still, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Mermaid
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like the tide.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture, if you like, a calm sea under the moon, the water moving slowly, silver and unhurried.
Somewhere far off across that water, a soft song seems to drift, too distant to make out the words.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath rocks you a little, the way the sea rocks a small boat at its quiet mooring.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the gentle dark, as the sea holds the moonlight.
The song you are imagining out on the water belongs to a creature that has never truly lived.
For the mermaid is a legend, a being half woman and half fish, dreamed up long ago and never real.
And yet that dream is one of the oldest we have, told and retold by seafaring people the world over.
Wherever there were boats and tides and long nights at sea, someone told a tale of the mer-folk.
They appear in the stories of distant shores and far countries, in voices that never met one another.
It is a gentle wonder, how a creature that was never real could swim through so many separate dreams.
Perhaps the sea is so vast and so strange that the mind reaches out and fills it with company.
So as you lie here, you can hold the mermaid lightly, the way you hold any old and lovely story.
There is nothing in her to fear and nothing to believe, only something soft to wonder at.
She is a legend, no more and no less, and legends ask only to be listened to as you fall asleep.
Let that thought rest easy, asking nothing of you, true or untrue, it does not matter now.
Breathe out slowly, and let yourself sink a little further into the warm and quiet dark.
Some say the legend reaches back thousands of years, to a goddess of the ancient world.
Her name was Atargatis, told of in the old Assyrian myths, far back at the dawn of written stories.
In some of the oldest tellings she was shown with the tail of a fish, slipping between woman and sea.
Whether or not she was truly the first, she is among the earliest such figures that we know.
It is a strange comfort, to think the dream of the mermaid is older than almost anything you can name.
People were imagining her long before your great grandparents, long before their great grandparents too.
For as long as there have been sailors, there have been tales of shapes half seen beneath the waves.
Sometimes the mer-folk lured, and sometimes they warned of coming storms, and sometimes were simply glimpsed and lost.
A flash of pale shoulder, a turn of a tail, and then only the water, smoothing itself over again.
You do not need to picture her clearly; let her stay soft and uncertain, far off in the dim.
There is no edge to this story, nothing sharp to hold, only the slow roll of the sea.
Let your breath grow long and even, and let the old dream carry you gently downward.
Now here is the tender part, the part where the legend brushes up against the real world.
For many sober and honest sailors truly believed they had seen mermaids out on the water.
They were not lying, and they were not foolish; they had simply seen something gentle and strange.
It is widely thought that what they saw were real sea creatures, the manatees and the dugongs.
These are large, slow, peaceable animals, plant eaters that drift through warm and shallow seas.
They are sometimes called sea cows, for they graze quietly on the meadows of the seabed.
Now and then one rises to the surface, and a mother will cradle her young as she nurses it close.
From a distance, in a haze of sun and longing, a sailor might glimpse that shape and think of a woman.
So the mermaid was perhaps born partly from these soft, harmless creatures, mistaken in the light.
There is something kind in that, that so great a legend grew from so gentle an animal.
Hold that quiet thought, the sea cow drifting and the sailor wondering, both at peace on the water.
And let your own breath slow, drifting like the creature, asking nothing, hurrying nowhere.
These gentle sea cows belong to a group of animals with a name borrowed straight from legend.
They are called the sirenians, named for the sirens of the old sea tales, the singers of the deep.
So even the careful people who study them could not help but reach back to the old stories.
The legend, you see, had soaked so deep into us that it crept even into the names we give to the real.
There is a famous tale, too, of the explorer Columbus, sailing strange waters long ago.
He wrote in his log that he had seen mermaids out among the waves on his voyage.
But he added, plainly and honestly, that they were not nearly so beautiful as the stories had promised.
It is a small and human moment, that note, a man meeting a legend and finding only a gentle animal.
You can almost feel his quiet disappointment, and smile softly at it, here in the dark.
The stories had set the bar so high that the warm and living sea could not quite match them.
Let that little scene drift away now, the old ship, the calm water, the honest disappointed words.
Breathe out slowly once more, and let yourself settle deeper, heavier, nearer to sleep.
In the kindest of the tales, the mermaids sang songs of an unearthly sweetness.
Sailors spoke of music drifting over calm water at dusk, when the light grows low and soft.
You can imagine it, that faint melody you heard at the very start, carried in over the slow waves.
And in time the legend found its way into a story you may know, written down with great tenderness.
The writer Hans Christian Andersen gave us the little mermaid who longed for the world above.
It is a story of love and the sea, of a creature gazing up toward a life she could not reach.
All down the years the mermaid has carried our deep wonder at the sea itself.
Its beauty, its mystery, and the strange longing it stirs in those who watch it from the shore.
She is, in the end, the shape we gave to that longing, half of us and half of the deep water.
Let that longing soften now, settling into peace the way the evening sea settles into glass.
There is nothing more to reach for; the song can fade, and the wonder can lie down to rest.
Breathe slow and deep, and let the gentle rocking of the sea carry you further down.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the old goddess and the honest sailors fade gently away into the dark.
Let the slow sea cows drift off, and the little mermaid sink quietly back beneath the waves.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and the far off song is growing softer, almost gone.
There is a deep peace in the sea at night, the moon laid across it, the water moving slow.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the calm water under the moon, you have only to be still, and let the quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to sail, no shore to reach, no longing left to follow now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way the gentle sea gathers the last of the evening light.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Griffin
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like cool mountain air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture, somewhere far above the world, a range of high and quiet peaks at dusk.
The air up there is still and clean, and the last warm light is fading from the highest stone.
On one of those high crags rests a great calm guardian, watchful but wholly at peace.
It asks nothing of you at all, only keeps its quiet vigil while you let yourself grow still.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That calm guardian on the crag is a creature of legend, dreamed up long ago and called the griffin.
It is a made thing, a beast of story, never truly walking the hills of the waking world.
And yet for thousands of years people have pictured it just as you are picturing it now.
In the old tellings, the griffin has the strong body of a lion and the head and wings of an eagle.
It joins the king of beasts to the king of birds, the great cat below and the proud eagle above.
So it has a lion's heavy paws and tawny flanks, and an eagle's curved beak and broad feathered wings.
Because the lion and the eagle were each seen as noble and royal, the griffin became a sign of both.
It stood for strength joined with watchful, far-seeing vision, the power below and the keen eye above.
Remember, as you rest, that none of this is fact, only a beautiful old story that people loved to tell.
There is no need to weigh it as true or false; let it simply be a gentle picture in the dark.
The wonder is not that the beast was real, but that so many people, for so long, imagined it together.
Let that quiet thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening a little more, settling further into the soft dark.
This dreamed creature is very, very old, far older than most of the tales you know.
The griffin appears in art and stories from the ancient lands of the Near East, from Egypt, and from old Persia.
It was carved and painted thousands of years ago, long before the stories were ever written down for us.
Often it was shown as a proud and majestic figure, dignified and still, a guardian set to watch.
Later the Greeks took up the griffin and told their own stories of where it was said to live.
They believed it dwelt in far-off mountains and deserts somewhere to the east, beyond the edge of the known world.
These were lands they had only heard of in rumour, wild and distant and wreathed in mystery.
Picture those far mountains the old storytellers imagined, high and golden in a country no Greek had seen.
All of this was legend, of course, a tale passed from mouth to mouth across the long centuries.
But hold how patient that idea is, how it endured through so many lands and so many lifetimes.
A single quiet creature, carried in the mind from one people to the next, never once changing its calm.
Let that long endurance settle over you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
There is no hurry in any of it; let the old story keep its slow and steady pace, and follow it down.
In the Greek tellings, the griffin was given a single faithful task, and it kept that task forever.
It was said to guard great hoards of gold in the far mountains and deserts of the east.
The stories told that griffins dug their very nests in the goldfields, among the bright and buried treasure.
So the beast lived among the gold, watching over it, never wandering far from what it kept.
Picture that: a noble creature curled upon a hidden hoard, eyes half closed, perfectly at rest.
It is not a fierce image, not really; it is the image of something steadfast, settled, quietly keeping watch.
The griffin asked for nothing and went nowhere; it simply stayed, guarding, through all the long years.
Imagine the still air of those high places at dusk, and the gold growing dim as the light fades.
And the guardian among it, breathing slowly, content to keep its long and patient guard.
This is still only a story, remember, a thing the old people dreamed and loved to repeat.
But there is deep peace in it, in a creature that wants only to stay where it is and rest.
Let your body share in that stillness, growing heavier, asking nothing of the hours.
Let your breath flow out slowly, and let yourself settle, as the guardian settles, into the quiet.
Now here is the most curious part, a gentle idea about where this old story may have begun.
A modern historian named Adrienne Mayor offered a thought about how the legend might first have grown.
She suggested it may have started not with imagination alone, but with something real, found in the ground.
Long ago, travellers crossed a great dry land in the east called the Gobi desert, a place of golden sand.
And there, weathering slowly out of the sand, lay the old bones of a creature called Protoceratops.
It was a dinosaur, sheep-sized and long vanished, with four legs and a sharp, hooked, beaklike face.
Its pale bones and beaked skulls lay scattered in that golden, gold-bearing ground, plain for any eye to see.
Now imagine an ancient traveller finding such bones: a four-legged skeleton with a fierce beak, lying near gold.
It might well have looked like the remains of a beaked, lion-bodied beast that guarded treasure in the sand.
So perhaps the griffin was the old world's gentle reading of bones it could not yet name.
We cannot be certain it happened so, but what a soft and lovely idea it is to drift upon.
Let that quiet thought of bones in golden sand grow dim now, and let your eyes grow heavier still.
Breathe out slowly, and let the desert and its sleeping bones fade gently into the dark.
Across all the long ages that followed, the griffin kept its faithful place as a guardian.
It was carved upon temples and palaces, set to watch over thresholds and doorways and sacred ground.
Wherever there was something precious to protect, the old builders might place a griffin to keep it.
It stood at the edges of holy places, dignified and still, a steadfast keeper of what lay within.
And in much later ages, it found a new home upon the coats of arms of families and of cities.
There it stood again as it always had, a steadfast guardian, proud and watchful and calm.
Through every one of these tellings, across so many lands and centuries, its nature never truly changed.
It remained a watchful, dignified creature, keeping its long and patient guard over what it treasured.
All of it imagined, all of it legend, and yet the same gentle spirit held through every age.
There is something deeply restful in that, in a guardian so steady that the years could not unsettle it.
You need not remember any of these names or places; let them blur softly together in the dark.
Only keep, for a moment longer, the feeling of something calm and watchful, settling now to rest.
Let your breath grow slow and long, and let yourself sink toward sleep beside that quiet keeper.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the high peaks and the golden sand and the old carved temples fade gently away into the dark.
Let the lion's body and the eagle's wings soften and grow dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a calm guardian is at rest, just as you are.
Its long watch is ended for the night; it has folded its wings and laid its great head down to sleep.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the guardian on its high quiet crag, you have only to be still, and let the long quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel now, nothing to guard, nothing at all to keep watch over.
Let the warm dark gather you up and hold you close, safe and still through the night.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Cinnamon
lines: There is nothing you need to do now, and nothing you need to remember.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or hold onto them; let them drift over you like warm air.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dim, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your arms, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Picture, if you like, a warmth in the air, faintly sweet, the kind of scent that makes a place feel like home.
It asks nothing of you; it only drifts in and softens the edges of the dark.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each slow breath lets you sink a little further, the way warmth sinks into tired hands.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That warm sweet scent you are imagining comes from a quiet and ordinary thing: the bark of a small tree.
Far away, in warm green places, there grows a modest evergreen, no taller than a kindly old garden tree.
Cinnamon is nothing more than the dried inner bark of that tree, gently peeled away in long thin strips.
When the strips are set out to dry, they slowly curl in upon themselves, rolling into the little quills we call sticks.
So each cinnamon stick is simply a curl of bark, dried and rolled by the warm air all on its own.
There is something soothing in that, in how something so comforting begins as plain bark from a plain tree.
The whole of its sweetness was waiting there quietly in the bark, asking only to be peeled and left to dry.
Picture a quiet grove of these small trees, their leaves still in the warm and fragrant air.
No one is hurrying among them; the bark dries in its own slow time, curling gently as it goes.
Let that image rest lightly in your mind, soft and warm and green.
There is nothing here you need to learn or keep; let the words simply pass through you.
Feel your breath grow slow and deep, and let your body settle further into the dark.
The very finest cinnamon, the most delicate kind, comes from a warm island far out in the sea.
That island is called Sri Lanka, which long ago people knew by the older name of Ceylon.
The true cinnamon grown there is light and gentle, its sweetness soft rather than sharp.
It has a coarser, stronger cousin called cassia, which grows in China and in other warm lands.
Cassia is bolder and more fiery, and a great deal of the everyday cinnamon in the world is really this hardier cousin.
So when a warm sweet smell rises from a kitchen, it may be the gentle true kind, or its stronger relative.
Both come from the bark of small evergreen trees, close kin to one another across distant warm places.
Picture that far island again, ringed by quiet sea, its groves breathing out their soft fragrance into the air.
Think of warm rain on green leaves, and the slow patient drying of bark in the sun.
You do not need to keep these names; let them drift away as soon as they are spoken.
There is no hurry in any of this, no need to hold a single thing.
Let your breath grow long and unhurried, and let yourself sink a little deeper into rest.
Cinnamon is one of the oldest spices that people have ever known and loved.
It was prized in the ancient world, long before the cities you have heard of had even begun.
The people of old Egypt valued it greatly, thousands of years ago, in a world now long vanished.
They used it among their fragrant oils and resins, even in the careful work of preparing their dead.
It was thought a precious thing, fit to be offered to kings and laid before their gods.
For a long stretch of time it was so treasured that it was counted worth more than its weight in many things.
Imagine how far it must have travelled to reach those ancient hands, carried over sea and desert.
Picture the small dried curls of bark passing quietly from one trader to the next across the warm world.
All of that long journey, only so that a little warmth and sweetness might reach a far-off home.
You do not have to picture it clearly; let the old image blur softly at its edges.
There is a deep calm in such old and patient things, made long ago and carried gently down the years.
Let that calm settle over you, and let your breath grow slow and soft.
Feel yourself loosening, growing heavier, as you drift a little nearer to sleep.
For a long while, the people who carried cinnamon kept its true home a careful secret.
The traders of old Arabia brought it from the east, and they did not wish others to know where it came from.
To guard their trade, they let strange and wonderful stories grow up around it instead.
The old Greek writer Herodotus passed along one such tale, gathered from the merchants of his day.
He told how great birds were said to gather cinnamon for their nests, high on cliffs no one could climb.
In the story, people had to leave out heavy pieces of meat, which the birds carried up to their nests.
The weight, it was said, would break the nests, and the cinnamon would tumble down to be gathered below.
It was only a story, of course, perhaps spread on purpose to hide the real and simpler truth.
There were no such birds, only small trees on a far green island, and traders keeping a quiet secret.
Still, it is a lovely thing to imagine, drifting between the true and the made up as you fall asleep.
Let the great birds and the high cliffs fade now, gently, into the soft dark.
Let your breath grow long, and let your thoughts grow as light and as drifting as an old tale.
The warm sweetness of cinnamon comes mostly from an oil that lives within the bark.
That oil is rich in a substance with a long name, cinnamaldehyde, but you need not keep the word.
It is simply the thing that gives cinnamon its comforting and familiar scent.
When the bark is warmed, that scent rises into the air, and somehow it feels like warmth itself.
The tree is often cut back low, so that it sends up many slender young shoots instead of one tall trunk.
It is the bark of these gentle young stems that is most carefully and tenderly harvested.
So the spice comes not from old hard wood, but from young growth, fresh and soft and full of scent.
Today that same warmth flavours warm drinks and slow baking in kitchens all over the world.
For many people its scent is tied forever to comfort, to warmth, to the feeling of being home.
Perhaps it carries some such memory for you, half remembered, soft at the edges.
Let that warm familiar feeling fill the dark around you, gentle and asking nothing.
There is nothing to do with it but breathe it in and let it soothe you.
Let your breath grow slow and deep, and let yourself sink further toward sleep.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the far green island and the warm sea fade gently away into the dark.
Let the old traders and their secrets, and the great birds of the story, drift softly out of sight.
Let the small curled sticks of bark grow dim, and the warm sweet scent grow faint and far.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and there is nothing now that needs your attention.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to carry, no secret to keep at all.
Let the warmth gather you up the way a quiet home gathers everyone in at the end of the day.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let the last faint sweetness fade, and let your thoughts grow still.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Saffron
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to remember.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to listen closely, or keep a single word; let them drift over you like a warm breeze.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dim, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the gentle easing along your brow.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no errand waiting for you in this quiet dark.
Picture, if you like, a wide still field at the edge of morning, hushed and grey and calm.
Across that field a low mist is lifting, and a soft golden light is just beginning to spread.
And scattered through the grass, opening their petals to the dawn, are countless small violet flowers.
They sway only a little, asking nothing of you, glowing faintly purple in the early light.
We are only going to wander among them for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and warm and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the soft quiet of the dark.
Those small violet flowers you are picturing are a kind of autumn crocus, low and delicate.
From this humble little blossom comes saffron, the most costly spice in all the world by weight.
It is a precious thing, and yet it begins in something as plain and tender as a flower in a field.
Each crocus opens a small cup of soft purple petals, no taller than the grass around it.
And the flower blooms for only a short season, opening its violet cups for a few precious weeks each year.
When that brief season passes, the field falls quiet again, and the long waiting begins anew.
So everything that becomes saffron must be gathered in that small window, while the flowers still stand.
There is a gentle preciousness in that, in how the whole year leans toward those few short weeks.
Picture the patient field, holding its purple bloom for just a little while before letting it go.
Nothing about it is hurried; the flowers simply open when their time comes, and rest when it ends.
Let that unhurried rhythm settle over you, and let your breath grow slow and long.
Feel yourself softening, sinking a little further into the warm dark with every breath out.
Now look closer, in your mind, at one of those small open flowers in the morning light.
Deep inside each violet cup lie only three slender threads, fine and crimson red.
These tiny red threads are called the stigmas, and these threads, once dried, are the saffron itself.
That is all there is: just three thin crimson strands hidden in the heart of each bloom.
So all the saffron in the world is gathered three small threads at a time, flower by flower.
It must be picked by hand, one blossom at a time, in the cool and quiet of early morning.
Imagine patient hands moving softly through the field, lifting each flower, drawing out its threads.
There is no machine for this, only gentle fingers and the calm of the dawn.
And because each flower gives so little, it takes many thousands of flowers to make a single ounce of the spice.
That is why saffron is so precious, and why a small jar of it holds the work of a whole quiet field.
Picture those soft and patient hands at their gathering, unhurried in the cool grey light.
Let your own hands grow still and heavy now, and let your breathing deepen and slow.
And yet, for all its preciousness, only a little of this spice is ever needed.
A little goes a very long way, so that just a few of those crimson threads can colour a whole pot.
Drop a few threads into warm water or warm milk, and let them rest, and watch what they do.
Slowly, gently, they turn the liquid a glowing golden yellow, warm as the morning light itself.
From three small red threads comes a colour like soft sunlight, spreading quietly through the bowl.
And as it steeps, it gives off a gentle fragrance, honeyed and earthy and faintly sweet.
It is a warm and soothing scent, the kind that seems to settle the room and quiet the mind.
People have long stirred these threads into rice and bread and sweet warm drinks before rest.
Picture that golden glow blooming slowly in the warm liquid, unhurried, soft, and kind.
Imagine the gentle honeyed scent drifting up and filling the dim and quiet room around you.
Let that warmth and that golden colour gather you in, the way a warm drink soothes you toward sleep.
Breathe it in slowly, and let your breath flow out longer still, deeper into the dark.
This small golden gift is far older than you might think, older than almost anything we keep.
Saffron has been grown and treasured for thousands of years, long before our own time began.
It was loved in ancient Greece and in old Persia, the land we now call Iran, and far beyond.
On the walls of very old buildings there are paintings of people gathering these very flowers.
Picture those long ago hands, in fields much like the one you are imagining now, doing the same gentle work.
For all those years, across all those lands, the spice has been gathered the same patient way.
It was used not only to flavour and colour food, but as a soft dye to warm a cloth with golden light.
It was pressed into perfumes for its honeyed scent, and steeped as a soothing, calming medicine.
Its glowing colour and its warm fragrance made it, in many places, a quiet symbol of light and of luxury.
So when you picture that golden glow, you are seeing a colour that has comforted people for ages.
There is something restful in that long unbroken thread, hand to hand across the centuries.
Let that deep, gentle history hold you now, and let your thoughts grow slow and far away.
Feel yourself drifting back through all that quiet time, growing heavier, easing into rest.
Even today, that same ancient work goes on, in fields not so different from the one you see.
Much of the world's saffron is now grown in Iran, where the purple crocus still opens each autumn.
There are famous crops, too, from Kashmir, high among the mountains, and from sunny parts of the Mediterranean.
In all those places, when the season comes, the small violet flowers rise again across the fields.
And in all those places, in the cool of the morning, patient hands still gather them one by one.
Picture fields of violet blooms glowing softly at dawn in Kashmir, in Iran, in the warm Mediterranean light.
The flowers do not know how precious they are; they simply open, and wait, and are gathered.
Three crimson threads at a time, the golden spice is gathered, just as it always has been.
It is a slow and gentle craft, unchanged by all the hurry of the world around it.
There is a quiet comfort in knowing that somewhere, even now, those calm hands are at their work.
Let that patient, ancient gathering carry you gently, the way a slow stream carries a leaf.
Breathe out slowly, and feel the last of the day loosen and drift away from you.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to hold in your mind.
Let the old paintings and the far fields and the gathering hands fade softly into the dark.
Let the golden glow grow dim, the way the world grows dim as your eyes turn heavy with sleep.
Let the honeyed scent thin to nothing, and let the violet flowers close and settle in their field.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a quiet field is at rest, as you are.
You do not have to understand any of it, or keep a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the field after its short bright season, you have only to grow still and let the quiet hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to gather, no work waiting for you now at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up as gently as patient hands once gathered the smallest of threads.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Black Pepper
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like warm rain.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere far off in the warmth, picture green hillsides under a soft and steady rain.
See the leaves shining wet, the slow drops gathering and falling, the air close and warm and kind.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath out lets you sink, the way warm rain sinks quietly into soft and waiting earth.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the warm dark.
Out there on those rainy green hills, picture a slender vine climbing patiently upward.
It is the vine that gives us black pepper, and it grows in warm and well watered places.
It is native to the lush, rainy Malabar coast of southern India, in what is now called Kerala.
There the great monsoon rains come and soak the green hills, season after season, year upon year.
The vines climb up trees or tall poles, reaching gently toward the dappled light above.
Along their stems hang small round berries, called peppercorns, gathered in slender clusters.
They cluster like tiny green grapes strung along a stem, plump and quiet in the warm air.
There is no hurry in any of it, only the rain, and the green, and the slow growing of the vine.
Picture the soft drumming of the rain on broad leaves, steady and unhurried and calm.
Imagine the warm wet air, the smell of green growing things, the patience of the climbing vine.
There is nothing for you to do here but rest, and breathe, and let the rain go on falling.
Let your breath grow slow and deep, and let yourself sink further into the quiet dark.
It is a gentle wonder that one single vine can give us three different kinds of pepper.
Green, black, and white pepper all come from the very same plant on the very same hill.
The difference lies only in when the small berries are picked, and in how they are dried.
For black pepper, the unripe berries are gathered while they are still firm and green.
Then they are spread out and left to dry in the open air, under the warm and patient sun.
As the days pass, each little berry slowly wrinkles, and darkens, and shrinks toward black.
Picture them lying in the sun, drying gently, while somewhere nearby the warm rain waits to return.
The clusters are picked by hand, one by one, and laid out to dry beneath the open sky.
It is slow and simple work, the kind that has gone on quietly for a very long time.
There is something restful in that slowness, in berries left to wrinkle in their own good time.
Let that unhurried drying soften your thoughts, the way the sun softens the small dark berries.
Breathe out slowly now, and feel yourself drying into stillness, settling deeper into the dark.
It is hard to believe, lying here, that such a humble little berry was once worth a fortune.
Long ago black pepper was so prized that people called it black gold.
In the ancient world it was traded for vast sums, far more than its small size could suggest.
It was so valued that it was sometimes used to pay rents, and even to pay ransoms.
Imagine handing over small dark berries the way one might hand over gold or silver coins.
For a long, long time it was the most widely traded spice in all the world.
It was the everyday king of the spice trade, the humble little berry that everyone desired.
And all of it began on those rainy green hillsides, on a slender climbing vine.
Picture the small clusters drying in the sun, never knowing they were thought as precious as gold.
There is a quiet wonder in that, in how much longing could gather around so plain a thing.
But none of that worth need weigh on you now; let the gold and the trading drift away.
Let your breath grow long and unhurried, and let the warm dark hold you close.
Because it was so prized, people carried black pepper across enormous distances to reach it.
The Romans prized it greatly, and brought it the long way from India to their faraway tables.
Picture those old journeys, by land and by sea, all for the sake of a small dark spice.
Ships rode the monsoon winds across wide waters, laden with peppercorns from the rainy coast.
Long after, the desire for pepper and other spices helped drive the great age of sea exploration.
People set out across unknown oceans, in part, simply to find an easier road to this humble berry.
Imagine the slow creak of old ships, the dark sea, the patient stars, the long way home.
All that distance, all that danger, all that longing, gathered around a single fragrant spice.
Picture a tropical evening at the end of such a voyage, the warm air, the quieting of the day.
There is a deep stillness in those old crossings now, long finished, long since come to rest.
Let that long quiet pour into you, the calm that follows when a great journey is finally done.
Breathe out slowly, and let yourself drift, the way old ships once drifted gently into harbour.
All that longing, in the end, was for something quite small and simple and warm.
When a peppercorn is freshly ground, its scent rises up bright and fragrant into the air.
Its gentle warmth and its mild bite come from a substance within it called piperine.
It is that quiet warmth that people travelled so far, for so long, to bring to their tables.
And how strange and lovely it is that today it sits on nearly every table in the world.
It has grown so common now that it is easy to forget it was ever worth a fortune at all.
The everyday spice beside your plate was once the prize of empires and the cause of voyages.
Picture that small dark grinding, that bright warm scent, born of rain and sun and patient hands.
There is a soft comfort in a thing so humble and so common, asking nothing, simply being itself.
Let that warmth settle over you now, gentle and fragrant and asking nothing in return.
Let the rain go on falling somewhere far away, on the green hills where it all began.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and there is nowhere at all you need to go.
Let yourself grow as still and as patient as a small berry drying in the warm sun.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the rainy green hills and the climbing vine fade gently away into the dark.
Let the drying berries and the old ships soften and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and far away the rain is falling, soft and steady and kind.
There is a deep peace in that quiet, in green hills and slow rain and a humble little spice.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your limbs are heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the berries drying in the sun, you have only to be still and let the warmth hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to gather, no longing on you now at all.
Let the warm dark fold around you the way the rain folds gently over the green hillsides.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Vanilla
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past you like a warm breeze.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that warm darkness, picture the faintest sweetness drifting in the air around you.
It is soft and familiar and comforting, the kind of scent that makes a room feel kind.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each slow breath lets you sink a little further, the way warmth spreads gently through a quiet room.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That soft sweetness you are imagining comes, in truth, from one of the gentlest of all the spices.
It is the only spice in the whole world that comes from an orchid, that most delicate family of flowers.
Vanilla is the cured seed pod of a climbing vine, a slender orchid that winds its way upward through the trees.
Picture that quiet green vine in a warm forest, reaching softly from branch to branch in the dappled light.
It does not stand tall and proud; it leans and climbs, finding its way slowly toward the gentle sun.
Among its leaves it opens pale, simple flowers, each one quiet and unhurried and lovely.
There is something soothing in the thought of it, a sweetness that begins as a single tender bloom.
Long before it was a scent you know, it was only a flower, growing patiently in the green and the warmth.
Let that picture rest lightly in your mind, the soft vine, the warm forest, the quiet pale flowers.
You do not need to remember any of it; let it simply float there, gentle and dim.
Feel your breath grow slow and deep, in time with the slow growing of that patient vine.
Let yourself loosen and settle a little further into the warm and welcoming dark.
This gentle orchid first grew in the warm forests of Mexico, far away and long ago.
There, the Totonac people cared for it and first coaxed it into cultivation, ages before our time.
They knew its secret long before the rest of the world had ever caught its sweetness on the air.
In those same warm forests lived a particular small native bee, who alone knew the flower well.
That little bee would visit the pale blooms and carry their pollen softly from one to the next.
Picture that quiet partnership, the small bee and the simple flower, keeping company in the green shade.
Each flower opens for only a single day, and sometimes only for a few brief hours of the morning.
If no one comes to pollinate it in that short while, it simply closes and withers, asking nothing more.
This is what makes the vanilla orchid so delicate, so tender, so patient and demanding to grow.
There is a soft wonder in a flower that asks so little and waits so quietly for its one short day.
Let that quietness settle over you now, the hush of a warm forest at the edge of morning.
Let your breath grow long and slow, and let the day's small worries close and wither away.
For a long time, this orchid could only truly thrive in its own warm homeland.
People carried the vine far away, to other warm and distant lands, hoping it would grow for them too.
And grow it did; the vine climbed happily, and opened its pale flowers just as it always had.
But the flowers, once open, set no pods at all, and so brought forth no fragrant spice.
The reason was a quiet one: the little native bee did not live in those faraway places.
Without its old companion to carry the pollen, each flower simply opened and faded, alone.
So for many years, the precious vanilla could only be gathered from the forests of its first home.
Picture all those distant vines, flowering year after year in lands too far from their gentle bee.
There is something tender in that, a flower waiting faithfully for a friend who would never come.
It is a small reminder of how gently the living things of the world are woven together.
Let that soft thought drift and dim, and feel no need to hold it as it goes.
Let your body grow heavier still, and let your breath slow into the quiet of the dark.
The puzzle of the faraway flowers was solved at last by a child, on an island in the Indian Ocean.
His name was Edmond Albius, a young enslaved boy with quick eyes and patient, clever hands.
In the year eighteen forty-one, he found a wonderfully simple way to do what the bee once did.
With a small sliver of bamboo and a gentle press of his thumb, he could pollinate each flower by hand.
He would lift a tiny fold inside the bloom and softly join its parts, one quiet flower at a time.
Picture those patient hands, moving slowly from blossom to blossom in the warm island air.
His clever method was so good that it is still used by growers all over the world today.
Because of that small discovery, vanilla could at last be grown far from its first home.
Now much of the world's vanilla comes from the island of Madagascar, warm and green and far away.
It is a gentle thought, that a child's careful hands could spread such sweetness across the world.
Let your own hands grow soft and still now, resting heavy and at peace.
Let your breath grow slow and easy, and let the warm dark draw a little closer.
Even once a pod is grown, its famous sweetness does not come to it all at once.
The freshly picked green pods have almost no scent at all, just a plain and quiet greenness.
Their warm fragrance only appears slowly, over weeks of careful and unhurried tending.
The pods are gently blanched, then left to sweat in soft warm wraps, then dried slowly in the sun.
Day after day they are set out in the morning light and folded away again as evening falls.
Picture that slow ritual, the pods darkening and softening, growing fragrant in their own quiet time.
Only after all that patient curing does the deep, comforting sweetness finally rise from them.
That warm scent comes largely from a single molecule, gently named vanillin, soft and round and kind.
It is said to be one of the most loved and most comforting smells in all the world.
Because the growing and the curing ask so much patience, real vanilla is among the most precious of spices.
Only saffron is counted dearer, and so this gentle sweetness is a small and patient treasure.
Let that slow patience pour into you now, the unhurried warmth of pods drying in the sun.
Let your breath grow long and deep, and let yourself cure slowly into rest.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the warm forests and the quiet vines fade gently away into the dark.
Let the small bee and the patient hands and the slow sun-drying soften and dim.
You are lying here in the warm dark, with the faintest sweetness still drifting somewhere near.
There is a deep comfort in that soft scent, gentle and familiar, asking nothing of you at all.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the quiet vine in its warm green shade, you have only to rest and be held.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no hurry on you now at all.
Let the warm sweetness gather you up the way the slow sun gathers the fragrance from the pods.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Piano
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like rain on a windowpane.
Imagine the house around you has gone quiet and dark, and that you are warm and safe within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the soft easing along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere down the hall, in another room, picture a piano standing quietly in the shadows.
Someone is playing it softly, so softly the notes seem to fall like rain, slow and unhurried.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each note that drifts to you settles and fades, and another follows, gentle as breathing.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be carried by the quiet music in the dark.
Listen, in your imagining, to how soft those notes can be, and then how full they grow.
A piano can whisper or it can swell, all from how gently or how firmly a hand touches the keys.
That is the heart of its name, for its full name was once the pianoforte, meaning soft and loud.
The instruments before it could not do this; a harpsichord plucked its strings and played at one steady level.
But the piano let a player lean into a note or barely brush it, and the sound would follow the hand.
So a single instrument could murmur a lullaby or rise into something grand, and choose between them freely.
Picture that soft and loud living in the same quiet keys, waiting under gentle fingers.
The player down the hall is choosing only the softest end of it now, the merest brush of sound.
Each note arrives small and warm and then lets itself fade away into the dark of the house.
There is no need to hold any of it; the music does not ask to be kept, only heard.
Let that softness settle over you, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, growing heavier, as the gentle notes drift on without you.
This soft and loud was a kind of puzzle once, and someone patient had to solve it.
Long ago, around the year seventeen hundred, a man named Bartolomeo Cristofori worked it out.
He lived in Italy, and he was a keeper of instruments, caring for harpsichords and the like.
He wanted a keyboard that could feel the touch of a hand, growing soft or loud with it.
His answer was the hammer, a small soft hammer that a key would throw against the strings.
The clever part, the part that took such care, was that the hammer must strike and then spring away at once.
If it leaned on the string it would deaden the sound, so it had to fly, touch, and fall back free.
And so the strings, struck and then released, were left to ring on quietly into the air.
From that one gentle idea, the whole singing voice of the piano slowly came to be.
Picture that little hammer, rising and falling away, leaving each note to shimmer and fade.
There is something restful in a thing made so carefully, by patient hands, so long ago.
Let that long-ago quiet settle into you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried.
Now let your mind drift inside the piano itself, into the dark warm space beneath its lid.
There you would find the strings, row upon row of them, stretched tight and waiting in the gloom.
They are held by a great frame of cast iron, strong and heavy, because the strings pull so hard.
All together they strain with the weight of many tons, an enormous pull held calmly in place.
Yet none of it strains you; it is held and balanced and still, asking nothing, simply ready.
The longest strings, the ones for the deepest notes, are wound about with fine copper wire.
That winding makes them heavier, and so their voice sinks lower, into a soft and gentle growl.
And here is a quiet secret of the piano: most notes are not one string but two or three, tuned together.
Those strings, sounding as one, lend the piano its full and shimmering and slightly trembling voice.
Imagine all those strings resting in the dark, ringing only when a soft hammer comes to touch them.
There is no hurry in any of it, only a great calm readiness waiting under the lid.
Let your body share in that stillness, growing heavier, asking nothing of the hours.
Breathe slowly out, and let the deep low notes hum somewhere far beneath your drifting thoughts.
Now picture a hand laid gently across the keys, and how many there are beneath it.
A piano has eighty-eight keys, the white ones and the black ones together, spanning more than seven octaves.
That sweep runs from a deep and rumbling growl at one end to a tiny bright tinkle at the other.
The hand could wander anywhere along that range, but tonight it lingers low and soft and warm.
And under the foot of the player there are pedals, and one of them is doing something lovely now.
Inside, when a key is let go, a soft felt damper settles down onto the string to quiet it.
But press the pedal on the right, and all those dampers lift away from the strings at once.
Then every note, once played, rings on and on, and the sounds blur softly into one another.
So the room fills with a warm haze of held notes, each one blending gently into the next.
Picture that soft blur of chords, hanging in the dark of the house, slowly fading into silence.
The rain is still at the window, and the notes drift through it, neither one in any hurry.
Let those held notes loosen you, and let your breath grow slow and deep and long.
There is one more quiet wonder to the piano, and it is the whole of its wooden body.
The trembling of a thin string alone would be far too faint for you to hear across a room.
So beneath the strings lies a great thin sheet of wood, the soundboard, and it does the gentle work.
It takes the small shivering of the strings and spreads it out into the air all around.
The whole body of the piano becomes a voice, breathing the sound softly into the room.
It is why a piano played in another part of the house can reach you, warm and full, even faint.
For centuries this instrument has sat at the heart of homes and great halls alike.
It is just as much at home with a simple lullaby as with the grandest sweeping symphony.
Tonight it asks for nothing grand, only the softest notes, drifting through the quiet rooms to you.
Picture it standing there, patient in the dark, its wide wooden body humming low and warm.
The sound it gives is gentle and round, gathered and softened by all that quiet wood.
Let that warm and rounded sound wrap around you, and let your eyes grow heavier still.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the hammers and the strings and the soft pedal fade gently away into the dark.
Let the warm blur of the held chords loosen and dim, the way the world dims as your eyes grow heavy.
The player has slowed, and the last soft notes are drifting through the quiet house toward you.
One note, and then another, each softer than the last, settling slowly into silence.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the rain is gentle at the window.
Like a held chord left to ring, you have only to fade softly, with nowhere to go.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to play, no need to hold any note at all.
Let the warm dark gather you in, the way the wood gathers the sound and lets it fade.
You are exactly where you need to be, and the last note is dissolving into quiet.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Harp
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift over you like falling water.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere in that darkness, picture a soft cascade of notes, each one tumbling gently after the last.
They fall like quiet rain, like water slipping over smooth stones, asking nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little further, the way a slow note fades into the hush behind it.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
Those soft notes you are picturing come from one of the oldest of all the instruments we know.
The harp is so ancient that pictures of it survive from the early days of Egypt and Mesopotamia.
People were plucking gentle strings on open frames thousands and thousands of years ago.
Long before there were books, or clocks, or cities much like ours, there were harps and the soft sounds they made.
Imagine those faded carvings, the slender frames, the quiet hands resting upon the strings.
Across so many ages and so many lands, people have sat and let these strings ring softly in the evening.
There is something gentle in that, in how old and how patient this small sound truly is.
It has soothed people to sleep for longer than almost anything you could name.
You are listening, in a way, to a sound that has comforted countless others before you, all of them now at rest.
Let that long quiet company settle around you, as if the years themselves were keeping you warm.
There is nothing to remember of all this; let it pass through you and away.
Let your breath grow slow and deep, and sink a little further into the dark.
Picture the harp itself now, standing quietly in the soft dark of the room.
Its strings are stretched across an open, triangular frame, leaning gently against the shoulder.
There is nothing between the fingers and the strings, nothing at all; they are plucked directly, skin against string.
That is why the sound is so soft and so intimate, so close and so kind to the ear.
No hammer strikes it, no bow draws across it; only the quiet touch of a fingertip releases each note.
And the strings are of many different lengths, rising in a long and gentle row.
The long strings give the low, deep notes, and the short ones give the high and shining ones.
So the rising row of strings is itself a kind of ladder of sound, a thing you could almost see.
Low at one end, high at the other, the pitches climb the frame like a slow, soft staircase.
Imagine a hand drifting across them, letting each string in turn ring softly into the air.
There is no hurry in it, only the gentle falling of one note after another.
Let your shoulders loosen, and let your own breath fall as softly as those notes.
Sink a little deeper now, and let the slow music carry you down.
Let your mind rest now on a large concert harp, tall and curved and patient in the dark.
Such a harp may carry around forty-seven strings, a great gentle fan of them rising up the frame.
And down at its base sit seven pedals, quiet beneath the player's feet.
When a pedal is gently pressed, it shortens the strings a little, and softly changes their notes.
In this slow and quiet way the harpist can reach into any key, any colour of sound.
With so many strings to find, the harpist gives some of them a gentle colour to follow.
The C strings are coloured red, and the F strings are blue or black, like small guides among the rest.
So the hands can find their place among the many, the way you might find a familiar path in the dark.
Imagine all those strings waiting in their long pale row, with a few softly coloured to lead the way.
It is a calm and orderly thing, this quiet ladder of sound, made plain and easy for the wandering hand.
You do not have to hold any of it; let the numbers and the colours drift away.
Only let the picture soothe you, the long row of strings, patient and still.
Breathe out slowly now, and let yourself grow heavier in the warm dark.
When a harp string is plucked, the sound does not stay only in the string itself.
The harp has a hollow wooden body, and that body is the soundboard, the part that truly sings.
The plucked string sets the wood gently humming, and the wood spreads the soft ringing out into the room.
So the whole quiet instrument trembles a little, breathing the sound outward like a long, slow sigh.
And because the bare strings keep ringing on after they are touched, the notes begin to overlap.
One note has not yet faded before the next is sounded, so they blur and shimmer softly together.
That is why a harp can sound so much like flowing water, like a small stream slipping over stones.
The notes overlap and shimmer, and pool together, and slide gently one into the next.
It is the loveliest sound for falling asleep, this soft cascade that never quite ends.
Imagine it filling the dark room, gentle and rippling, with no hard edges anywhere.
Let the shimmering notes wash over you, rising and overlapping and slowly fading away.
There is nothing to listen for; just let the soft water of the sound carry you.
Let your breath grow long and unhurried, and drift on that quiet, rippling tide.
In the old myths and the old stories of many lands, the harp was the instrument of poets and of peace.
It was said, in those gentle tales, to soothe troubled hearts and to quiet the restless mind.
Kings were calmed by it, and sorrows were eased, or so the legends softly tell.
These are only old stories, of course, but there is a kindness in them that feels true even now.
For a soft string, gently plucked, does seem to settle the heart and slow the breath.
And the harp is loved enough that one whole country has taken it for its own.
The harp is the national emblem of Ireland, the only land in the world to choose a musical instrument as its symbol.
Imagine that, a whole green country whose quiet sign is a thing that makes gentle music.
Of all the emblems a place might choose, this one was made only to soothe and to sing.
There is a deep peace in that idea, a country resting beneath the sign of a gentle instrument.
Let that peace pour softly into you, the way the old stories say the harp eased every weary heart.
You do not have to keep any of it; let the tales and the names fade into the dark.
Let your breath grow slow, and let the quiet music settle you toward sleep.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the ancient frames and the coloured strings and the seven quiet pedals fade gently away.
Let the soft cascade of notes grow fainter, overlapping and shimmering and slowly slipping into silence.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and the last gentle note is fading into the hush.
There is a deep peace in that fading sound, asking nothing of you, simply softening into quiet.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like a string that has finished ringing, you have only to rest, and let the silence hold you.
There is nowhere to travel, nothing to make, no music left to play at all.
Let the warm dark gather you up, gentle as falling water, gentle as a fading note.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Flute
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them drift past like a far off tune.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere out in that darkness, picture a soft and breathy melody, carried to you on a slow breeze.
It is quiet and airy and unhurried, and it asks nothing of you at all.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little more, the way a long note fades gently into the evening air.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
