So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
That soft melody you are picturing is made of something as simple as your own breathing.
A flute makes its sound from breath alone, with nothing more than moving air.
You blow gently across the edge of a hole, and there the stream of air splits and begins to flutter.
That small fluttering of air sets the column of air inside the tube quietly singing.
There is no reed in it, no little wooden tongue to buzz, as there is in so many other instruments.
The player's breath striking the edge is the whole source of the tone, and that is all.
Perhaps that is why a flute sounds so pure and breathy, so close to a sigh or a soft word.
It is breath made into music, plainly and gently, with nothing standing in between.
There is something soothing in that, in a song born so simply out of moving air.
Your own breath, slow and even, is the same gentle thing, going out into the dark.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, your chest softening, as you settle further into the dark.
Now let your mind wander far back, far past anything you can easily picture.
The flute is one of the very oldest instruments there is, older than almost anything we have made.
In quiet caves, people have found flutes carved long ago from the hollow bones of birds.
Others were shaped from the pale ivory of the mammoth, patiently hollowed and pierced with holes.
These small flutes are around forty thousand years old, made by hands in a world long vanished.
Picture someone, all those ages ago, sitting in the firelight and breathing a tune into the dark.
The same simple act you are imagining now, that splitting of air across an edge, is that old.
Long before writing, before cities, before nearly everything, there was breath becoming song.
It is the oldest of tunes, the soft airy voice that has kept us company through all those years.
There is a deep comfort in being part of something so gentle and so old.
You are one more quiet listener in a line that stretches back beyond all memory.
Let that long stillness settle over you, and let your breath grow long and unhurried too.
Now picture the slender tube of the flute itself, lying easy across a pair of hands.
Along its length there is a row of small holes, waiting quietly under the fingers.
When the player covers and uncovers these holes, the singing column of air grows shorter or longer.
And as that column of air changes its length, the note it sings changes too.
A longer column of air gives a lower sound, deep and round and soft.
A shorter column gives a higher one, brighter and lighter, lifting up into the air.
So the melody simply rises and falls as the fingers lift and settle, slow and patient.
There is no force in it, only breath and the gentle covering of holes, one after another.
Picture those fingers moving softly, the tune drifting up and down like a breeze through grass.
Each note flows into the next, unhurried, with nowhere it needs to hurry to.
You can let your own thoughts rise and fall just as gently, asking nothing of them.
Let that slow melody carry you, and let your breath grow soft and even.
Now and then, a flute player wants to reach the bright high notes that float far above.
And they reach them not with new fingers, but simply by breathing a little harder.
When the breath grows a touch stronger, the column of air leaps to a higher way of singing.
It jumps up a whole octave at once, to a clear and shining note above the one before.
It is a small and lovely thing, this leap, as easy as a slightly firmer breath.
Almost every culture on Earth has some kind of flute, found and made and loved many times over.
There are bamboo flutes and flutes of clay, and the bound reeds of the panpipes, all breathed into.
For thousands of years, in countless places, people have lifted a hollow tube and made it sing.
It is as if the flute were waiting in every reed and bone, ready to be found again and again.
Imagine all those airy melodies, drifting up across the centuries, each one made of nothing but breath.
You are held within all that gentle music now, far away and very soft.
Let those distant tunes blur into one quiet sound, and let your eyes grow heavier still.
Now picture a flute of bright silver, slender and gleaming softly in the dim.
The shape of this modern flute was settled long ago, in the eighteen hundreds.
A patient craftsman named Theobald Boehm, in Germany, arranged its keys and holes with great care.
He laid them out so the fingers could move easily, and every note would sound clear and even.
His gentle design was so good that flutes are still made much the same way today.
And though so many flutes now are made of metal, the flute is counted among the woodwinds even so.
It keeps that older name because its ancestors were wooden, hollowed from cane and from branches.
And because its sound is still made the woodwind way, from breath alone and never from a string.
So the bright silver flute carries the memory of all those quiet wooden ones that came before.
Its tone sits close to the human voice, and close to the soft sound of the wind itself.
Perhaps that is why it falls so easily on the ear, so calming and so natural to us.
Let that gentle, voice like sound wrap around you, and let your breath grow long and slow.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the caves and the old bone flutes fade gently away into the dark.
Let the silver and the careful keys soften and dim, as the world dims when your eyes grow heavy.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a soft breathy tune is drifting on the breeze.
There is a deep peace in that simple song, made of nothing but slow and gentle air.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Like the flute, you have only to let the air move gently and ask for nothing more.
There is nowhere to travel, no melody to finish, no breath you need to hold.
Let the warm dark gather you up the way a tune fades softly into the evening air.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Drum
lines: There is nothing you need to hold onto now, and nothing you need to understand.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words closely, or keep them; let them pass over you like warm smoke.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be, nothing to finish, no task waiting for you in this gentle dark.
Somewhere far off in that darkness, picture the faintest warm glow of a distant fire.
And from that direction, very softly and very slowly, imagine a single low beat.
It comes again, unhurried, then again, calm and even, like a heartbeat heard from a long way off.
It asks nothing of you; it only keeps its slow, patient time while you rest.
Let your eyes grow heavy, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let that soft far beat carry you down.
That low beat you are picturing comes from one of the oldest things our hands have ever made.
The drum is among the very oldest of all instruments, and likely one of the first we ever knew.
Long before written words, before bronze or wheels, people were already keeping a beat in the dark.
And it is found in nearly every culture across the whole world, from one far shore to another.
In Africa and in Asia, on the high plains and the cold north, somewhere a drum has always sounded.
It is one of the few things that almost every people on Earth, across all the ages, has made and loved.
Perhaps it came so easily because we already carried a beat within us, before we made one outside.
A hollow log, a stretched skin, a patient hand: that was nearly enough, and it was enough for a very long time.
So the soft beat in your imagining is an old, old sound, far older than almost anything you could name.
Countless people, long gone now, have rested to that same slow pulse beside their own fires.
There is something gentle in that, in belonging to so old and so wide a thing.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, settling further into the warm and patient dark.
Let your mind drift now to the simple shape of the thing that makes that sound.
Most drums work the same plain way, and it is an easy thing to picture as you lie still.
A skin is stretched tight across the mouth of a hollow body, and held there firm and even.
That skin is called the membrane, or the drumhead, and it is the part that sings.
When the drumhead is struck, it trembles, quivering up and down faster than the eye can follow.
And the hollow space within the body catches that trembling and booms it softly back out into the air.
That is the whole of it: a skin that shivers, and a hollow that answers with a low warm voice.
For most of our long history that skin was made from animal hide, stretched over wood, or clay, or metal.
Today many drumheads are made instead from plastic, smooth and pale, but they sound in the very same way.
Hide or plastic, ancient or new, it is still only a trembling skin over a patient hollow.
Picture that gentle quiver, and the soft boom that follows, fading slowly back to quiet.
Let your own breath be like that fading sound, easing out long and slow and unhurried.
There is nothing to do but rest, and let the soft beat keep its time.
Now let yourself wonder, very gently, why one drum sounds high and another sounds deep.
It turns out the answer is simple, and there is no need to hold it tightly in your mind.
The tighter the skin is stretched across the body, the higher the note it gives when struck.
And a looser, softer skin gives back a lower, deeper, more comfortable voice.
This is why, in the old days, players would warm their drums by the fire before they played.
The warmth of the flames would tighten the skin a little, and lift the drum's voice up brighter.
On a damp and rainy night the air would loosen the skin again, and the drum would speak lower and softer.
So a drum is a living thing in its way, changing its voice with the warmth and the weather around it.
Picture that distant fire once more, its glow keeping the far drum's skin warm and its low beat steady.
The size matters too; a bigger drum, with more air held inside, gives a deeper and slower-sounding boom.
That is why the largest drums always seem to be speaking gently to you from very far away.
Let that deep, far, comfortable boom settle over you, low and slow and warm.
And let your breath sink down to meet it, slower with each soft beat.
There is something else these old drums could do, across the great distances of the world.
In many lands, long ago, drums were used to carry messages far beyond where a voice could reach.
From hilltop to hilltop, from one village to the next, a pattern of beats could pass along through the dark.
A waiting drummer would hear the far beat, and take it up, and pass it gently onward through the night.
And in some places there lived what people came to call the talking drums.
These drums could be made to rise and fall in their pitch, higher and then lower, as they were played.
By rising and falling that way, they could echo the very tones of speech, almost like a low spoken word.
So the drum could nearly talk across the miles, its meaning carried on a slow and rolling beat.
Imagine those soft messages crossing the quiet land at night, from one warm fire to another, far away.
No words you needed to know, only a low patient voice moving gently through the dark.
It is a calming thought, that even our distances were once crossed by something so slow and soft.
Let those far beats fade into the night, one by one, growing fainter as you grow heavier.
Breathe out slowly, and let yourself sink a little deeper still.
Now let us rest with the gentlest thing the drum can do, the thing it has always done best.
A slow, steady, soft drumbeat is one of the most calming sounds there is, anywhere in the world.
Some believe this is because it echoes the soft, even beating of a heart.
The heartbeat is the very first sound any of us ever hears, long before we are born, in the warm dark.
So a slow drum may reach something very old and very deep, a memory older than memory itself.
Struck softly and slowly, a drum does not excite at all; instead it quietly settles and soothes.
It is like a calm and patient heartbeat, keeping time for you in the gentle dark.
For thousands of years, around fires and in quiet ceremonies, people have gathered to such a pulse.
A single shared, gentle beat can draw many hearts into one slow and easy rhythm together.
Imagine that now: a soft circle of warmth, a far fire, and one low beat that everyone breathes to.
You are part of that old, wide, gentle circle, simply by listening to the slow beat in your mind.
Let the steady rhythm ease you down, the way it has eased countless people down to sleep before.
Let your breath slow to match it, until you can hardly tell the beat from your own quiet heart.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the far fire dim, and let its warm glow soften and fade gently into the dark.
Let the talking drums fall silent, their messages long since carried safely home.
Let the low boom grow fainter, slower, softer, until it is only the quietest pulse.
You are lying here in the warm dark, and somewhere a slow beat keeps its patient time, as your heart does.
You do not have to understand any of it, or remember a single word that was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
There is nowhere to travel, no message to send, no fire to tend, nothing at all to do.
Let the old shared rhythm hold you the way it has held so many before, gently, and let it carry you down.
You are exactly where you need to be, and there is all the time in the world.
Let the last soft beat fade away into the quiet.
Let yourself drift.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Golden Gate
lines: Let the room grow soft and dark around you, and let the day loosen its hold.
There is nothing to do now, nothing to fix, nothing to carry into this quiet hour.
Feel the weight of your body settling, your limbs growing heavy and warm where they rest.
Each breath out can be a little slower than the last, with no effort at all.
Let your shoulders sink, and let your jaw unclench, and let your hands lie open and still.
Somewhere far off the water moves in the dark, a slow and patient breathing of its own.
A cool mist drifts past, soft as smoke, and you do not need to follow it anywhere.
Out in that mist a great calm shape stands quietly, holding still while the fog moves through.
You do not have to see it clearly; let it stay dim and gentle at the edge of your mind.
There is all the time in the world here, and none of it asks anything of you.
Let the sound of the words carry you, and let yourself grow heavier with each one.
If your thoughts wander off, that is fine, for wandering is its own soft kind of rest.
You are safe, and you are held, and you will drift off to sleep.
Long ago, where the open sea meets a wide and sheltered bay, there is a narrow gap in the land.
Through that gap the cold ocean pours in and out with the tides, restless and gray and deep.
A traveler once stood and looked at that opening and thought of a famous harbor on the far side of the world.
In the year eighteen forty six he gave the strait a name, calling it the Golden Gate.
He chose the word for a passage of gold, a doorway, long before any gold was found in those hills.
Almost every day, a pale fog gathers over the cold water and rolls quietly through the gate.
It moves like a slow river of cloud, softening the headlands and hushing the shore.
The water itself is rarely still, churning where the tide and the ocean meet and pull against each other.
For a long time this was only a place where the land parted and the sea came through.
Picture that quiet strait now, the fog drifting, the tide breathing in and out.
Let your own breath fall into that slow rhythm, in and then gently out.
There is nothing to reach for here, only the easy turning of the tide in the dark.
For many years people dreamed of crossing that gap, of laying a calm line across the restless water.
Some said it could never be done, that the strait was too wide and too deep and too wild.
They spoke of the strong tides, the fog, the wind, and the cold gray swell beneath.
Many doubted that any bridge could stand in such a place and not be swept away.
But a few held to the dream anyway, the way you might hold a small warm coal through a long night.
They believed a single graceful span could reach from one shore to the other.
A bridge, after all, is only a quiet promise that the two sides can be joined.
It is a calm line drawn across a place that will not hold still, a steady answer to a restless question.
The dreamers studied the depths and the currents, patient through years of waiting and arguing.
Slowly, the doubt began to soften, the way fog thins as the air grows still.
You do not need to hold any of these worries tonight; let them drift off the way the doubters' fears did.
Let the idea of the bridge rest lightly in you, an easy promise that two shores can meet.
Breathe out, and let the dream settle quietly into the dark water.
The work of imagining the bridge fell to a chief engineer, a determined man named Joseph Strauss.
He carried the dream and pushed it forward, year after year, through every doubt and delay.
But a bridge is too large for any one mind, and many quiet hands shaped it beside him.
An engineer named Charles Ellis worked through much of the deep mathematics, the patient sums that made it stand.
He calculated the great cables and towers in careful detail, though for a long time his work went unthanked.
Another, named Leon Moisseff, brought a way of thinking called deflection theory.
It allowed the long span to bend a little in the wind, to sway and yield rather than break.
A bridge that can move gently is stronger than one that tries to hold itself perfectly rigid.
There is a soft lesson in that, in the strength that comes from being able to give a little.
They drew the towers in the clean lines of the time, slender and rising, with stepped and graceful crowns.
Let your own body learn that gentle strength now, soft and yielding, sinking deeper as you breathe.
There is nothing to hold rigid here; let everything ease and sway and settle toward rest.
When at last the building began, two great towers rose from the water, one near each shore.
They climbed high into the fog, taller than almost anything around them, anchored deep in the seabed and the rock.
Then came the slow and patient making of the cables, the two huge ropes from which the road would hang.
Each great cable is not one thick wire but thousands upon thousands of slender ones, gathered together.
Workers ran the thin wires back and forth across the gap, again and again, in a process called spinning.
Wire by wire the bundles grew thicker, until each cable was as wide as a barrel and far stronger.
From those two cables the deck would hang, the long road floating quietly above the tide.
It is a wonder to think of so much strength made from so many small and gentle strands.
One thin wire is nothing, but woven together they can hold a road across the sea.
There is comfort in that, in how the smallest patient things can add up to something that holds.
Let each slow breath be one such strand, gathering quietly into a deep and easy calm.
Wire by wire, breath by breath, let yourself grow heavier and more still.
Building so high above the cold water was dangerous, and in those days many took such danger for granted.
But the engineers tried something kinder, hanging a great safety net beneath the deck as the men worked.
It stretched along under the roadway, a wide soft web ready to catch anyone who slipped.
Over the course of the work, that net caught and saved nineteen men from the long fall.
Those nineteen formed a little fellowship and gave themselves a wry and grateful name.
They called themselves the Halfway to Hell Club, men who had fallen and yet been caught.
It is a gentle thing, that net, a quiet promise that someone has thought to break your fall.
Imagine being held like that, caught softly out of the air, set down safe and whole.
You are held like that now, cradled by whatever you rest upon, in no danger at all.
Nothing can fall here, and nothing needs catching; you are simply and completely held.
Let that safety sink all the way through you, soft as the net beneath the high road.
Breathe out, and trust the quiet that is holding you.
There is nowhere to fall, only deeper into rest.
At last the great line was finished, and the bridge opened to the world in the year nineteen thirty seven.
Its main span reached about four thousand two hundred feet between the towers, the longest in the world at the time.
They painted it a deep warm color called International Orange, chosen in part to glow softly through the fog.
Against the gray mist and the blue water it stands out gently, neither harsh nor cold.
The salt air is hard on the metal, so the painting never truly ends; it is repainted patiently, always.
Crews move slowly along it through the years, tending the color the way you might tend a garden.
And still, almost every day, the old fog rolls in through the gate and drifts among the towers.
The bridge simply waits within it, a calm warm line holding steady over the restless strait.
It has stood now for many quiet decades, swaying a little in the wind, never breaking, always there.
You do not need to remember any of this; let the names and numbers drift away on the tide.
Keep only the soft picture of that warm line in the fog, holding still while the water moves.
Let your breath be that steady span now, calm above all the day's restless currents.
There is nothing left to do, and nowhere to go; let yourself drift, and rest now.

lectures.title: Ponte Vecchio
lines: There is nothing you need to do now, and nowhere at all that you need to be.
Let your body grow heavy where it rests, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow these words; let them drift over you like warm air over slow water.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet easing along your jaw.
There is nothing to finish tonight, nothing waiting, no task left over from the day.
Somewhere in that gentle dark, picture a wide river moving slowly, its surface glowing faintly in the dusk.
Hear how unhurried it is, that soft and patient sound of water sliding past in the half light.
And over the water, picture an old stone arch, low and worn, reflected dim in the slow current.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you settle a little further, the way the light settles slowly out of an evening.
We are only going to wander a little while together, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words become a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
That slow river you are picturing has a name, and it is called the Arno.
It winds through the heart of an old Italian city, the city of Florence, on its long way to the sea.
At one quiet place the river narrows, drawing its banks gently closer together than anywhere else nearby.
And at that narrow place, for as long as anyone can remember, there has been a bridge across the water.
People have crossed the Arno here since the days of ancient Rome, long ago.
Bridge after bridge stood at this spot, each one giving way in time to the next.
The bridge that stands here now is so old that its very name simply means the old bridge.
Think of that, a crossing so ancient that people have called it old for hundreds of years.
Picture the river slipping past beneath it, the same slow water, patient through all those long centuries.
There is no need to hold the names; let them drift past like leaves on the gentle current.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, settling further into the dark, as the old crossing waits quietly in your mind.
Now let your mind move closer to the bridge itself, and see how it rises from the water.
It is built of pale stone, and it crosses the river on three low and gentle arches.
The arches are wide and shallow, curving softly down to meet the water rather than leaping high above it.
An earlier bridge once stood in this same place, but long ago a great flood came down the Arno.
The river rose and rushed and swept that older bridge away into the dark water.
And so, around the year thirteen forty five, the people of Florence raised this one in its place.
They built it low and strong, with those three quiet arches meant to let the flood waters pass beneath.
It has stood now for nearly seven hundred years, watching the same river flow under the same stones.
Floods have come again over the centuries, and still the old bridge has remained.
There is something deeply restful in a thing that simply endures, asking nothing, only staying.
Picture those three gentle arches reflected in the dim water, holding steady in the falling light.
Let that quiet steadiness settle over you, the calm of a thing built to last.
And let your breath grow long and unhurried, as steady as the slow river beneath the stone.
On the back of the bridge, all along its two sides, there have always stood little shops.
The bridge is not bare stone alone, but lined with small workshops leaning out over the river.
In the early days, those shops belonged to butchers and to tanners, the workers in meat and hides.
It suited them to be out over the water, for they could let their waste fall down into the river below.
But this made the bridge an unpleasant place, full of smells the passing nobles did not care to meet.
So in the year fifteen ninety three, the ruler of Florence, a Medici grand duke named Ferdinando, gave an order.
He sent the butchers and the tanners away, and in their place he put the goldsmiths and the jewellers.
From that day to this, more than four hundred years, the shops on the bridge have sold gold and fine stones.
Picture them now, those little shops shuttered for the night, their bright treasures sleeping in the dark.
The river slips by below as it always has, untroubled, quiet, and slow.
Let that long unbroken patience pour gently into you in the warm dark.
Let your body grow heavier, your breath soft and slow, as the old shops rest above the water.
Now lift your gaze a little, to the top of those small shops, and notice something strange and wonderful.
Running along above them, like a covered passage, is a long enclosed corridor.
It was built more than four hundred years ago by a man named Giorgio Vasari, in the year fifteen sixty five.
The Medici rulers wished to cross the river without going down among the crowds and the bustle of the street.
So Vasari raised this hidden walkway above the rooftops, a private path strung high over the city.
It ran from their great palace on one side of the river, across the bridge, to another palace on the far side.
The grand dukes could pass unseen above the heads of the people, walking quietly between their two homes.
Imagine that hushed corridor in the dark now, empty and still, its small windows looking down on the sleeping water.
No one walks there tonight; it waits, as patient as the bridge that carries it.
There is a deep calm in that quiet height, in a passage made for unhurried and private crossings.
Let that calm gather softly around you, the stillness of a high and silent place.
And let your breath grow slow and deep, as quiet as the corridor sleeping above the river.
Now picture the little shops once more, and lean closer to one of their back walls.
For the shops on the bridge have a secret, leaning out beyond the edge of the stone.
Behind each shop there is often a small back room that hangs right out over the river.
These little rooms are called the retrobotteghe, which simply means the rooms behind the shops.
They are not held up by the bridge at all, but pushed out into the air on wooden brackets and beams.
So a goldsmith working late might sit in a small room that floats above the moving water.
Below the floor, the slow Arno passes by, glinting faintly in whatever light there is.
Imagine resting in such a room in the warm dusk, the river murmuring softly somewhere beneath you.
It is a snug and hidden place, suspended gently between the bridge and the slow dark water.
There is something cradling in that thought, of being held softly above a quiet and moving river.
Let yourself feel held like that now, suspended and weightless in the warm dark.
Let the murmur of the water carry your thoughts gently downstream and away.
And let your breath grow long and slow, as easy as the river drifting under the little rooms.
This old bridge has lived through a great many years, and it has seen the hardest of times.
It has watched floods rise and fall, and rulers come and go, and the city change around it again and again.
And during a great war, long ago in the year nineteen forty four, it faced its sharpest danger.
An army was retreating through Florence, and as it went it destroyed every bridge across the Arno.
One by one the other bridges fell into the river, broken and brought down.
But this old bridge, alone among them all, was spared, and it was left standing over the water.
And so it remains today, as it has remained through floods and wars and the long passing of time.
Picture it now in the deep quiet of the night, dark and patient above the slow and steady river.
It has outlasted so much, and it asks for nothing, and it simply goes on standing there.
There is a great peace in that long endurance, in a thing that has seen everything and still abides.
You do not have to remember any of it, or keep a single word that was said.
Let the bridge and the river and the small lit shops all fade gently into the soft dark.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and there is all the time in the world; let yourself drift, and rest now.

lectures.title: Tower Bridge
lines: There is nothing you need to do now, and nowhere at all you need to be.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, settling a little deeper with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words; let them drift over you like soft rain on a quiet river.
Imagine the room around you has gone dim and warm, and that you are safe within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the soft quiet along your jaw.
There is nothing to finish tonight, nothing waiting, no crossing you have to make.
Somewhere out in the gentle dark, picture a slow grey river, and a fine rain falling without a sound.
Out of that dark rise two great towers, faint and patient, standing quietly side by side.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath out lets you sink a little further, the way mist sinks slowly onto still water.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
Those two towers you are picturing stand over the river Thames, in the old heart of London.
They belong to a famous crossing called Tower Bridge, which rises beside the ancient stone walls of the Tower of London.
It was opened in the year eighteen ninety four, after some eight years of patient building.
In those Victorian days the river below was one of the busiest in all the world.
Tall ships crowded its waters, their masts a moving forest, carrying goods to and from the great port of London.
The city badly needed a new way across the river here, down near the sea where the docks lay thick.
Yet any bridge built so low could not block the path of those tall ships passing beneath.
So the riddle was a gentle one, how to cross the water and still let the great ships through.
Picture that crowded river now, the slow brown water, the rain dimpling its surface in the failing light.
There is no need to remember the names or the years; let them drift past like boats on the tide.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slow and deep.
Feel yourself loosening, settling further into the dark, as the wide river flows quietly through your mind.
The answer they found was a clever and patient one, and it is the heart of the bridge to this day.
They would build a bridge whose roadway could open, parting in the middle to let the tall ships pass.
The two halves of the road were made to lift, each one tilting slowly upward toward the sky.
Such lifting leaves are called bascules, a word borrowed from the French for a see-saw.
And like a see-saw, each great leaf is balanced by a heavy weight hidden away below.
So even these huge spans of road can be raised gently, swinging up as smoothly as a slow breath in.
Out toward each bank, the roadway hangs instead from chains, in the manner of a suspension bridge.
So Tower Bridge is really two ideas joined in one, a bascule in the middle and a suspension at each side.
How fitting it is to design across many years, knowing the work will outlast its makers.
Picture those two great leaves of road rising slowly in the dusk, opening as patiently as a yawn.
There is something restful in that slow, sure motion, in great weight moving without any haste.
Let that ease settle over you now, the calm of something vast that opens gently.
And let your breath grow long and unhurried, rising and falling like the slow leaves of the bridge.
Two thoughtful men are remembered most for shaping this bridge, and it is pleasant to picture them at their work.
One was the architect, a man named Horace Jones, who imagined how the towers should look.
The other was the engineer, John Wolfe Barry, who worked out how the great machine should stand and move.
An architect dreams the shape of a thing, and an engineer makes sure that shape will hold.
Together, dreamer and builder, they brought the bridge slowly up out of the river over those long patient years.
Imagine them poring over their drawings by lamplight, the rain soft against the windows of the room.
Imagine the quiet care of it, the years of small decisions, each one made and then set gently aside.
The bridge they raised was a labour of many hands, of countless workers along the muddy banks.
And it has stood ever since, holding its place over the water while the lamplight long ago grew still.
Picture it now, the work all finished, the drawings rolled away, the great towers standing quiet in the rain.
There is a deep peace in a thing completed, in care that is finally laid down to rest.
Let that peace pour into you, and let your body grow heavier with every slow breath out.
Now let your mind move closer to those tall towers, and see what they are truly made of.
They look like old stone castles, carved and pointed in the grand Gothic manner of the Victorians.
Yet that stone is only a skin, a beautiful covering wrapped around a hidden frame of steel.
Beneath the carved brick and stone, a skeleton of strong steel holds the whole great weight aloft.
The fair Gothic dress was chosen so the new bridge would sit kindly beside the ancient Tower of London nearby.
So the builders gave a modern machine the gentle, familiar face of a much older world.
There is a quiet wisdom in that, in dressing strength in something soft and welcoming to the eye.
Inside, all is iron and steel and machinery; outside, all is calm grey stone in the falling rain.
Picture the rain running down those carved walls, tracing the old shapes, soaking the patient stone.
The towers ask nothing of you; they simply stand in the dark, holding their hidden strength quietly within.
Let that stillness settle into you, the calm of something solid that has nothing left to prove.
And let your breath grow slow and soft, as quiet as rain sliding down old stone.
Now picture, deep inside the bridge, the great machines that once did all the lifting.
When it was new, the bridge was raised by the patient power of water held under pressure.
Engines driven by steam pumped water hard into the works, and that pressing water drove the lifting gear.
Some of this pressure was kept in waiting in great vessels called accumulators, ready for whenever a ship arrived.
Then, when the moment came, that stored power was let loose, and the heavy leaves of road swung slowly skyward.
Imagine the soft hiss and hum of it deep below, the gathered power easing those vast spans into the air.
Today the old steam is gone, and oil and electricity do the quiet work instead.
Yet some of the first great engines have been kept and cared for, resting where they always stood.
They sit there still, patient and oiled and at rest, the gentle giants that once moved the road.
Picture them now in the warm dim, the old machinery sleeping, its long labours softly behind it.
There is a deep calm in tools laid down to rest, in great strength that no longer needs to stir.
Let that calm settle into your own body, the calm of all your day's work finally set aside.
And let your breath grow long and slow, as steady as the engines that breathed beneath the bridge.
High above the road, near the tops of the two towers, run a pair of covered walkways through the air.
They were built so that people on foot could still cross from side to side while the road below was lifted open.
A walker could climb up inside one tower, stroll across the high bridge, and come down the other side.
Imagine being up there in the quiet, the rain on the glass, the slow river far below your feet.
Far downstream and up, other bridges cross the river too, plainer and simpler than this grand one.
One of them, just upstream, is the bridge truly named London Bridge, though it is quite plain to look at.
People often muddle the two, and picture these famous towers when they speak of London Bridge instead.
There is a fondness in that small mistake, the way a much loved face is the one we always see.
Now let the high walkways and the towers and the slow grey river all fade gently into the dark.
You are lying here in the warm dim, and somewhere over a quiet river two great towers stand at rest, as you do.
You do not have to remember any of it, or keep a single word of what was said.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the soft rain is falling somewhere far away.
Let yourself drift, and rest now, the way the river rests beneath the patient bridge.

lectures.title: Brooklyn Bridge
lines: There is nothing for you to do now, and nothing you need to hold in your mind.
Let your body grow heavy where it lies, sinking a little further with every slow breath out.
You do not have to follow the words; let them drift over you like a cool wind off a wide river.
Imagine the room around you has gone soft and dark, and that you are safe and warm within it.
Feel the weight of your limbs, the loosening of your shoulders, the quiet settling along your jaw.
There is nowhere to be tonight, nothing to finish, no distance you must cross.
Somewhere in that gentle dark, picture a great web of thin cables spread against the night sky.
They sweep up and over in long, patient curves, swaying ever so slightly in the dark air.
Let your eyes rest, whether they are open in the dim or softly closed.
Each breath lets you sink a little deeper, the way the light sinks slowly out of an evening.
We are only going to wander together for a little while, until you drift off to sleep.
So let the words be a lullaby, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Rest your weight, and let yourself be held by the quiet of the dark.
The thing you are picturing in the dark is a great bridge, one of the most loved in all the world.
It crosses a wide stretch of water in New York called the East River, joining two shores together.
On one side stands the island of Manhattan, and on the other the streets of Brooklyn.
In those days they were not one city at all, but two separate cities, divided by that broad cold river.
To go between them, people crowded onto ferries that froze fast when the winter ice came.
And so for many years the people on each bank dreamed of a way to walk over the water.
Imagine standing on one shore in the cold, looking across at the lights of the other.
It is a tender thing, that wish to close a distance between one place and another.
The story of this bridge is really the story of two shores reaching slowly toward each other.
There is no river for you to cross tonight, and no far shore waiting in the dark.
Let that wish to be elsewhere loosen and fall away, the way the ferry lights blur and fade.
And let your breath grow long and slow, as you settle deeper into the warm and quiet dark.
The man who first dreamed this bridge into being was an engineer named John Roebling.
He had built smaller bridges before, hung from great cables, and he believed he could span the wide river too.
His idea was to hold the roadway up not on stone alone, but on cables spun from steel wires.
It was to be the first great suspension bridge made with wire of steel, stronger than any before.
Picture it in his mind, a roadway floating high above the water, carried lightly between two towers.
But before the work had truly begun, John Roebling hurt his foot while surveying down by the water.
The wound turned poisonous, and within a few weeks he died, never seeing his bridge rise.
So the great vision was left behind, set down like an unfinished drawing for others to take up.
There is something quiet and human in that, a dream begun by one and carried on by another.
Picture the cables he imagined, still only lines on paper, waiting patiently to be spun into being.
You do not have to remember his name, or any of it; let it drift past like wind over the water.
Let that thought rest lightly, and let your breath grow slower, deeper, softer in the dark.
Feel yourself loosening and settling, as the great bridge waits, still only a dream, in your mind.
To carry such a bridge, the towers had to stand on solid ground, far down beneath the muddy riverbed.
So the builders did a strange and daring thing, sinking great wooden boxes called caissons down into the water.
A caisson was like an enormous upturned box, open at the bottom, pressed down into the riverbed.
Air was pumped inside to push the water out, and men climbed down to dig away the mud beneath.
Picture them working far below the river in that hissing, lamp-lit air, digging toward bedrock.
It was dangerous work, and many of the men came up feeling ill, aching deep in their joints.
We understand now that the pressed-in air had harmed them, a sickness called caisson disease.
The son who had taken charge, Washington Roebling, was struck down by it too, beneath the water.
He never fully recovered his strength, and the river had taken a hard price for its crossing.
Let the picture of that work grow dim and gentle, the men coming up at last into the open air.
There is no depth for you to descend into tonight, no hard labor waiting below.
Let your body grow heavier, your breath slow and soft, as the deep work settles into the quiet dark.
John Roebling had begun the bridge, and his son Washington had taken it up, and now he too was failing.
The caisson sickness left him unable to walk to the site, or even to speak with ease for a long while.
But there was someone else who would not let the great work fall, and her name was Emily Warren Roebling.
She was Washington's wife, and she carried his instructions down to the bridge each day.
More than that, she studied the engineering herself, learning the cables and the mathematics of it.
For years she relayed his wishes to the workers and watched over the site in his stead.
In all but name she helped guide the building of the bridge through its long and difficult middle years.
Picture her crossing the half-built span with her papers, calm and certain, holding the whole vision in her care.
It is a lovely thing, that quiet persistence, a family seeing one dream through across long and patient years.
There is no task waiting for you to carry tonight, no work you must hold together.
You may set it all down now, every burden, the way the day's papers are folded and laid aside.
Let that ease pour through you, and let your breath grow slower as the bridge rises softly in your mind.
At last the two great stone towers stood, and the time came to spin the cables that would hold the roadway.
Four great cables were needed, and each one was made of thousands of thin steel wires gathered together.
Picture a single wire carried back and forth, over and over, high above the river between the towers.
Wire upon wire was laid alongside the last, until thousands had been bound into each thick and gleaming cable.
Spun slowly in the open air, the cables grew strong enough to carry the whole weight of the bridge.
Into the towers themselves the builders cut tall pointed arches, in the old style men call Gothic.
Through those great stone arches the roadway would pass, framed like two windows opened onto the sky.
Imagine standing far below, looking up at those high arches and the long cables sweeping down from the towers.
There is a deep calm in that web of steel, a vast and patient thing made of countless slender threads.
Like the cable, you are gathered together now, every strand of you settling, growing quiet and still.
Picture the wires resting in their long curves, swaying gently, asking nothing of you at all.
And let your breath grow long and unhurried, as steady as a wire laid softly beside another.
Feel yourself sinking deeper, held aloft as lightly as that great web of cable in the dark.
After fourteen long years of work, the bridge was finished, and it opened in the spring of eighteen eighty-three.
When it opened it had the longest span of any bridge on earth, reaching far out over the wide cold river.
Emily Warren Roebling, who had given it so many years of her care, was the first to ride across.
And the two cities that had once been divided by the water were joined at last by a road through the air.
There is an old story that only days after it opened, a sudden fear of collapse rushed through the crowd.
In the panic many were hurt, though the bridge stood firm, exactly as it had been built to do.
To calm such fears, it is said the showman P. T. Barnum later led elephants across the span.
True or not, the bridge stood firm beneath them all, and it stands firm still, far more than a century on.
It carries people over the river to this day, its towers and cables still patient against the sky.
And now there is nothing more to follow, and nothing left to keep in your mind.
Let the towers and the cables and the long years soften and fade gently into the dark.
Your breath is slow now, and your body is heavy, and the dark is soft all around you.
Let yourself drift, held as lightly as the great bridge over the quiet water, and rest now.

lectures.title: Versailles
lines: Let the room grow soft and dim around you, and let your shoulders sink down into the warmth of the bed.
There is nothing to do now, nothing to reach for, nothing to remember or solve.
Breathe in slowly, gently, and let the breath go again like a long quiet sigh.
Your arms feel heavy, your legs feel heavy, your whole body feels held and still.
Somewhere far off, almost too far to hear, water is falling into a basin, over and over, in no hurry at all.
You can imagine wide green avenues stretching away into a soft evening light.
The avenues go on and on, calm and even, leading nowhere you need to go tonight.
Each breath out lets a little more of the day drain away from you.
There is a coolness in the air, and the faint hush of fountains drifting on the wind.
You do not have to follow the paths or look at anything; you can simply rest among them.
Let your jaw soften, let your forehead smooth, let your eyes grow heavy.
You are sinking, slowly, gently, deeper into the quiet.
And as you breathe out once more, you begin to drift, softly, toward sleep.
Long ago, a young king named Louis the Fourteenth looked out over a stretch of low, marshy ground.
It was wet land near a small hunting lodge, not yet grand at all, soft and reedy and plain.
The king dreamed of turning that damp ground into the most ordered garden anyone had ever seen.
He was sometimes called the Sun King, and he liked the idea of the garden as a kind of calm, radiant order.
The thought was that nature, gently shaped, could be made to mirror a sense of balance and peace.
So the work began in the sixteen sixties, slow and patient, over many years.
Marsh was drained, soil was carried in, and the wet ground was coaxed toward firmness.
It would take decades, and the garden would grow a little at a time, like a long, unhurried breath.
You do not need to hold any of this; let the dates and names float by like leaves on water.
Picture only the wide flat land slowly settling into something smooth and still.
Let that image rest softly behind your closed eyes.
And let yourself sink a little deeper, warm and heavy, toward sleep.
The man who shaped these gardens was named Andre Le Notre, a quiet master of the formal French garden.
He loved straight lines, clean geometry, and long views that draw the eye gently into the distance.
In his style, hedges were clipped square and even, and paths ran arrow straight across the ground.
This kind of garden was called the jardin a la francaise, the garden in the French manner.
Its whole idea was a feeling of calm order, of nature softened and arranged into patterns the eye can rest on.
Le Notre worked with the land for years, never rushing, letting the design settle into place.
He understood that a long straight avenue can be deeply soothing, a path the mind can wander down without effort.
Think of the garden as a vast, slow geometry, smooth and even in every direction.
You can let your thoughts drift along one of those quiet lines, with nothing to bump into.
There are no sharp turns here, no surprises, only gentle measured space.
Feel how restful it is to imagine such evenness all around you.
Your breathing slows to match those long, calm lines.
And you drift, softly, a little nearer to sleep.
From the great house, one long central axis runs straight out toward the west.
It points, by the king's wish, toward the place where the sun sets each evening, the garden built around that light.
This was meant as a quiet symbol, the king as the sun and the garden as order gently laid over the land.
Near the house lie the parterres, flat beds where low hedges are clipped into smooth, swirling patterns.
Seen from above, a parterre looks like soft embroidery laid out upon the ground.
Beyond them, the wide avenues, called allees, stretch off between walls of trees.
And tucked among the trees are the bosquets, small hidden groves like quiet green rooms.
Each bosquet is a little secret, a calm enclosed space away from the long open views.
You can wander these in your mind, from open avenue to sheltered grove and back.
There is no need to choose a path; every one of them leads only toward more quiet.
Let the soft green walls close gently around you.
Your thoughts grow slower, your body heavier, as you settle in.
Where the great central axis reaches far out into the garden, the ground opens into the Grand Canal.
It is a long arm of water, about one and a half kilometres from end to end, lying flat and still.
On calm days it becomes a long mirror, holding the sky and the trees upside down in its surface.
In the king's time, small boats and even little gondolas drifted slowly upon it.
People would glide across the water in the cool of the evening, with nowhere in particular to go.
The canal makes the garden feel even wider, stretching the long view out toward the horizon.
Imagine standing at its edge and watching the still water hold the soft colours of dusk.
Nothing moves quickly here; even the boats only drift.
You can let your mind float out across that long, smooth water.
The surface is calm, unbroken, gently reflecting the fading light.
Feel yourself growing as still and quiet as the canal at evening.
And let that stillness carry you down toward sleep.
Scattered through the gardens are the fountains, and these were the hardest wonders of all to make.
To lift and carry so much water, the builders made a vast and troublesome system of pipes and pumps.
The most famous was the Machine de Marly, a great structure that pumped water up from the river Seine.
Yet for all that effort, there was never quite enough water to run every fountain at the same time.
So fountaineers were stationed through the grounds, and they turned the jets on in sequence as the king walked past.
Water would rise ahead of him and fall quiet behind, following his slow stroll through the garden.
Among the loveliest are the Latona Fountain and the Apollo Fountain, with their carved and gleaming figures.
Picture the soft, steady sound of water rising and falling, rising and falling, somewhere out among the trees.
It is a gentle, repeating sound, the kind that asks nothing of you.
You can let it wash quietly through your mind, soothing and even.
Each falling sheet of water loosens you a little more.
Your breath slows, your limbs go soft and warm.
And the sound of the fountains carries you gently toward sleep.
The gardens move slowly through the seasons, as they have for hundreds of years.
In winter, the tender trees in their tubs are wheeled into a great sheltered hall called the Orangerie.
There they wait through the cold, safe and quiet, until the warm light returns in spring.
Through summer the avenues fill with green shade, and in autumn the leaves turn and drift down.
The same long lines that Le Notre drew are still tended and kept to his old design today.
Gardeners trim the same hedges and rake the same paths, season after season, year after year.
Centuries have passed, and still the great axis points toward the setting sun.
There is something deeply restful in that, a calm pattern that simply continues.
You can let the seasons turn slowly in your mind, green to gold to bare branch and back to green.
Nothing here is hurried; everything returns in its own quiet time.
Let that slow turning settle over you like a soft blanket.
Your thoughts are fading now, gentle and far away.
And with one more slow breath out, you let go, and drift down into sleep.

lectures.title: Ryoan-ji
lines: Let the room go soft and dark around you, and let your eyes close as gently as a door easing shut.
There is nothing here that needs doing, nothing to solve, nothing to hold onto for even a moment longer.
Feel the weight of your body settling down, sinking a little deeper with every slow breath out.
Your shoulders loosen, your jaw unclenches, and your hands lie open and still.
Breathe in slowly, and let the breath out even more slowly, as if it were sighing on its own.
Imagine a wide, calm rectangle of pale gravel, raked into long, quiet lines.
A few smooth stones rest upon it, gathered in small and easy groups, going nowhere at all.
Beyond a low wall, the dark shapes of pines move very gently, and the air smells faintly of cool stone.
There is so much empty space here, and the emptiness asks nothing of you.
Let your thoughts drift across that open ground the way light drifts, without settling anywhere.
Each breath out smooths another line into the gravel, softer and softer.
You are growing heavier now, warm and unhurried, content to simply lie here and rest.
And as the quiet deepens, you begin to drift, easily and sweetly, toward sleep.
In the old city of Kyoto, in Japan, there is a Zen temple called Ryoan-ji.
Its name carries the sense of a place of peace, a quiet refuge tucked among trees and ponds.
The temple is most loved for one small garden that lies along the side of a wooden hall.
It is a kind of garden the Japanese call karesansui, which means a dry landscape.
There is no pond here, no flowing stream, only gravel and stone and a little moss.
It is thought to date from the late fifteenth century, in the age called the Muromachi period.
Yet who first laid out the stones, and exactly when, has never been certain.
The garden keeps its own quiet about its beginnings, as though that too were part of the design.
People have come and gone for centuries, and the gravel has been raked again and again.
Imagine kneeling on the smooth veranda, looking out at that still, pale field.
There is nowhere you need to go, and the garden is in no hurry to be understood.
Let that stillness settle over you now, heavy and kind, as you sink toward sleep.
A dry garden is a gentle riddle, where one thing is allowed to stand for another.
The raked gravel is not really water, and yet your eye reads it as water all the same.
Long lines combed into the stones suggest small ripples spreading across a calm sea.
The stones rising from that sea become islands, or perhaps the peaks of distant mountains.
Nothing is labeled, and nothing insists on a single meaning.
The garden offers a map of the world made from only sand and rock, and lets you fill in the rest.
This is the wonder of it, that so little can hold so much.
You do not need to master the image, only to let it float before your inner eye.
An island here, a mountain there, a sea of fine pale grain, all held in a small frame.
Picture the soft gray light lying over it, even and undemanding.
Your breathing slows to match the slow, even raking of the lines.
Heavier now, calmer now, you let the picture blur at its edges.
And the dry sea carries you, without a sound, toward the shore of sleep.
Within that rectangle of gravel there are fifteen stones, set in five small groups.
Some stand alone, and some lean close together, ringed by soft green cushions of moss.
For hundreds of years, people have counted them and puzzled over how they are placed.
There is a much loved fact about these fifteen stones that visitors still test for themselves, for from any single spot along the viewing veranda, you can never see all fifteen at once.
Wherever you sit, at least one stone is always hidden behind another.
Only from above, looking straight down, could every stone be seen together.
Some take this as a gentle lesson, that no single view ever holds the whole of anything.
It is offered as one interpretation, not a settled truth, for the garden leaves its meaning open.
And there is a quiet comfort in not having to see everything at once.
You can let the hidden stone stay hidden, and rest easy all the same.
Let that ease spread through you now, soft and warm, as you drift further down toward sleep.
There is nothing left to count, nothing left to find, only the deepening quiet.
Each day, before the visitors arrive, someone comes to tend the gravel.
With a wooden rake drawn slowly back and forth, the long lines are renewed.
Around each group of stones the rake curves, tracing rings like ripples around an island.
It is patient, repeating work, the kind that empties the mind as gently as it fills the time.
Wind and rain and fallen needles unsettle the lines, and so the raking returns again and again.
The garden is never truly finished, only kept, tended like a small daily devotion.
There is a wonder in caring for something that will simply need caring for once more tomorrow.
Imagine the soft scrape of the rake, even and unhurried, the only sound in the cool morning.
Each pass smooths the field a little flatter, a little calmer.
Let your breath follow that slow rhythm, in and out, back and forth.
You are being smoothed too, your worries combed away into long, easy lines.
And in that gentle, repeating quiet, you let yourself sink toward sleep.
A low wall runs along two sides of the garden, holding it in like a quiet frame.
It was made of clay boiled in oil, and over the long years the oil has seeped and stained it.
Age has mellowed its surface into soft browns and golds, like an old painting left in the sun.
The wall is kept deliberately low, so that it never closes the garden off from the world.
Beyond it, taller trees rise up, and their green is allowed to become part of the view.
The Japanese have a name for this, a borrowed scenery, where the distance is gathered gently in.
So the small garden quietly belongs to the larger hillside, and the hillside to the garden.
Nothing is walled away, and nothing is grasped too tightly.
Picture that warm old wall and the soft trees leaning over it, breathing in the evening.
The light is going golden now, then gray, then dim.
Let the borrowed trees sway slowly at the edge of your mind.
Your thoughts loosen and lean outward, like branches over a low wall.
And softer and softer, you let them go, drifting down into sleep.
Elsewhere on the temple grounds there is a low stone water basin, called a tsukubai.
Carved into its rim are characters arranged around a square opening in the middle.
Read together with that central square, they are often understood as a single quiet saying.
The saying is taken to mean that one already has enough, that what you have is plenty.
It is a small reminder, cut in stone, to be content with the simple things at hand.
And in a way the whole garden whispers the same thing, with its little and its emptiness.
Some have called the raked space a sea, others a tiger crossing a river, others the open sky.
But the garden never says, and that openness is the heart of it, freely given to each visitor.
It is a place made for stillness, where the mind is invited to rest rather than to decide.
You have enough now, in this dark and quiet room, and there is nothing more to seek.
Let the empty raked space spread wide and soft inside you, room enough for your whole tired mind.
Breathe out one last slow breath, and let every line go smooth.
And here, in that gentle and unending quiet, you drift all the way down into sleep.

lectures.title: Kew Gardens
lines: Let the room go soft and dark around you, and let the bed take all of your weight.
There is nothing to do now, nowhere to be, no thought you need to finish.
Outside, somewhere far off, a gentle rain is falling, and you do not have to listen to it.
Feel your shoulders settle, a little lower than you thought they could go.
Let your jaw loosen, and let the small muscles around your eyes grow heavy and still.
Breathe in slowly, and let the breath out even more slowly, like a tide easing back.
Imagine rain on the glass of a great quiet glasshouse, a soft patter spreading wide.
Inside there is only a green hush, the warm stillness of leaves at rest.
Your arms feel heavy now, sinking, as if the whole bed were holding you up.
There is nothing to hold, nothing to carry, nothing to keep watch over.
Each breath out lets a little more of the day drift away from you.
You are warm, you are safe, and you are slowly, gently coming to rest.
You will drift off to sleep soon, and there is no hurry at all.
Beside the wide, slow river Thames, just west of London, there is a garden.
It began long ago as the pleasure grounds of royal houses set among quiet meadows.
In the seventeen hundreds these private gardens were planted and shaped for kings and queens.
The year seventeen fifty nine is often given as the start of the botanic garden there.
What began as a place for beauty slowly became a place for study and care.
Bit by bit, the garden gathered living plants from every corner of the green world.
It grew into a quiet cataloguing of all that grows, a patient map of leaves.
Think of it as a vast collection, lovingly kept, of the living world's many forms.
Where once a few favoured flowers grew, now whole continents of plants were tended.
And you do not need to remember any of this, only to let it settle softly.
Let the names and the years drift past you like clouds you need not follow.
You are sinking deeper now, warm and easy, breathing slow beside that quiet river.
Near the heart of the garden stands a tall, slender tower called the Great Pagoda.
It was raised in seventeen sixty two to a design by the architect William Chambers.
It rises in many storeys, each a little smaller than the one below, tapering to the sky.
For its time it was a marvel, a far-off shape brought to an English garden.
From its high windows you could once look out over the spreading green of Kew.
It was built in an age that loved curiosities gathered from distant lands.
And yet for all its height it has the patience of a thing that simply stands and waits.
Picture it now in the soft grey light, the rain beading along its many edges.
The garden below lies hushed, the paths empty, the air cool and very still.
You do not have to climb it, only to know it is there, quiet and tall.
It has watched over the garden for longer than anyone alive can remember.
Let that stillness move into your own body, into your slow and easy breath.
You are drifting now, lighter and lighter, sinking gently toward sleep.
The garden's most famous building is the Palm House, a great cathedral of glass.
It was built between eighteen forty four and eighteen forty eight, in the heart of that century.
The architect Decimus Burton drew its soaring shape, curved like the hull of a ship.
The ironfounder Richard Turner forged the wrought iron that holds the glass aloft.
Inside, the air is kept warm and humid, a small captured pocket of the tropics.
Tall palms reach toward the curved roof, their fronds spreading in the gentle heat.
It is a jungle kept safe under glass, a piece of the rainforest held in iron and light.
Walking among the great leaves, you breathe warm, soft, green-scented air.
Think of it as the living world kept patiently, gently, behind a wall of glass.
The rain falls on the high panes above and slides away in long quiet streams.
Let that warmth wrap around you now, slow and close, like a blanket of leaves.
Your breath grows softer, your body heavier, as you sink toward a deep warm rest.
Later in that same century, an even larger glasshouse rose, the Temperate House.
It was built for the plants of milder lands, the cooler green places of the world.
It is grander still than the Palm House, the largest of the garden's glass halls.
Within it grow trees and shrubs from gentle climates, kept through the cold English winters.
Each glasshouse is a different held breath of the world, a different green country preserved.
Together they make a quiet archive of the living world, each leaf catalogued and cared for.
Outside, the Pagoda stands tall, and the great glass roofs catch the changing light.
It is all a patient gathering, a map of growing things made real and tended by hand.
And there is nothing here you must do, only the soft work of letting go.
Let the wide quiet of those halls move through you, room after green room.
Your thoughts grow slow and faint, like footsteps fading down a long glass aisle.
You are sinking now, warm and untroubled, drifting closer to sleep.
The garden is not only living plants, but plants pressed flat, dried, and saved.
In a great building called the herbarium are kept millions of pressed specimens.
Each one is a single plant, gathered long ago, dried with care, and fixed to a sheet.
Under the work of directors such as William and Joseph Hooker, the collection grew vast.
Plants were carried back from across the world to be named, studied, and understood.
To name a thing is to know it a little, to give it a place in the green order.
Each pressed leaf is a small held memory, a single page in an endless quiet book.
Think of those long shelves, the folders stacked, the soft paper waiting in the dark.
It is a library of leaves, patient and still, asking nothing of anyone tonight.
You do not have to read a single page, only to rest among the quiet shelves.
Let your mind grow as still as that dim, dry, sleeping room of pressed flowers.
Heavier now, slower now, you let yourself drift down toward sleep.
There is nothing to remember, nothing to hold, only the soft dark and your breath.
In our own time, the garden's care has reached even further into the future.
Kew runs a place called the Millennium Seed Bank, housed out at Wakehurst in the country.
There, the seeds of wild plants are gathered, dried, and kept cold and safe.
They are saved against loss, against the day a plant might vanish from the wild.
Each tiny seed is a folded promise, a whole green future held in a small dry shell.
It is the gentlest kind of keeping, the world's wild plants tucked safely away.
Kew is honoured as a World Heritage Site, one of the great gardens of the earth.
Through the rain and through the seasons, the garden keeps its slow and patient watch.
Spring greens the beds, summer warms the glasshouses, and autumn lets the leaves fall.
And all the while the seeds sleep, and the pressed leaves rest, and the palms breathe on.
Now let yourself be kept just as gently, safe and warm and asleep.
Your breathing is slow, your body still, and the whole green world is at rest.
Let go now, drift down, and sleep, while the soft rain falls and falls.

lectures.title: The Alhambra
lines: Let the room go quiet and dark around you, and let the day fall away.
There is nothing left to do now, and nowhere you need to be.
Feel the weight of your body settling, growing heavier with each slow breath.
Let your shoulders soften, and let your jaw unclench, and let your hands lie still.
Breathe in gently, and let the breath out slowly, a little longer than it came in.
Somewhere far away you can almost hear water trickling through cool, shaded courtyards.
It moves without hurry, a thin thread of sound that asks nothing of you.
Imagine cool stone arches and deep shade, a place made to keep out the heat of the day.
The air is soft here, and the light is dim, and everything is unhurried.
You have arrived somewhere restful, and you are allowed to simply rest.
Let each breath out carry you a little deeper, a little lower, a little further from waking.
Your thoughts can drift loose now, like leaves on slow water.
There is nothing to hold onto, and you will drift off to sleep.
High on a long red hill above the city of Granada, in the south of Spain, there stands a palace.
It is a palace and a fortress at once, set among trees where the air stays cool.
Its name is the Alhambra, and that name comes from an Arabic phrase meaning the red one.
It was named for the warm red colour of the clay and stone its outer walls were built from.
Most of what we see today was raised by the Nasrid dynasty, who ruled here long ago.
They built across the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, court by court, room by room.
From the walls you can look out over the rooftops of the old city and the plain beyond.
Behind it rise the high mountains of the Sierra Nevada, white with snow for much of the year.
The builders set their palace where mountain air and mountain water could reach it.
Think of that quiet hill in the warm dark, the great walls cooling as the night comes on.
There is no need to hold any of this; let the names settle and grow soft.
Let yourself sink a little deeper into the bed, and let the breath slow.
In the garden tradition this palace belongs to, an enclosed garden carries a gentle meaning.
It was meant to be an earthly image of paradise, a small green answer to a dry land.
The idea was that a walled garden, full of water and shade, could echo the gardens promised in heaven.
Many such gardens were laid out in four equal parts, divided by channels of running water.
This fourfold plan was sometimes called the chahar bagh, the fourfold garden.
The four water channels were imagined as four rivers flowing out from a central source.
So the garden became a kind of map, a quiet picture of a more perfect place.
It was a refuge from heat and noise, a cool centre at the heart of a busy world.
To step inside was to leave the dust and glare behind and find shade and the sound of water.
You do not have to believe anything to feel the calm such a place was built to hold.
It is enough to picture green leaves and still water inside cool walls.
Let that picture rest behind your eyes, soft and unmoving.
Breathe out slowly, and let the garden hold you while you drift.
Water was the true heart of the design, more than stone, more than tile.
It had to be carried a long way, down from the snows of the Sierra Nevada.
The builders led it along a channel they called the Acequia Real, the Royal Canal.
That canal ran for miles, gathering mountain water and bringing it up to the hill.
From there it was divided and led into court after court, fountain after fountain.
It filled long pools, slipped along narrow runnels, and rose in soft jets toward the sky.
The faint sound of moving water can be heard almost everywhere within the walls.
It cooled the air, fed the gardens, and gave the whole place its quiet living voice.
Imagine that thin, patient sound, water that has travelled far and asks for nothing.
You can let it carry your attention the way a current carries a leaf.
There is nothing to follow and nothing to do but listen and grow heavy.
Let the slow water lead you gently down toward sleep.
One of the calmest courts in the palace is known as the Court of the Myrtles.
Down its centre lies a long, still pool of water, plain and rectangular.
On either side grow low hedges of myrtle, trimmed and green and sweet smelling.
The pool is kept so calm that its surface becomes a clear mirror.
In that mirror the pale walls and arches above are reflected, doubled and softened.
Looking into it, you can hardly tell the true wall from its quiet twin in the water.
The whole court was made to feel open and serene, a long breath of stillness.
Nothing rushes here; the water barely moves, and the reflection holds.
Picture that smooth dark surface and the soft shapes resting upon it.
Let your own thoughts grow as still as that mirrored pool.
With each breath out, the surface settles a little flatter, a little quieter.
Let yourself lie as still as the water, and begin to drift away.
Nearby stands the most famous court of all, the Court of the Lions.
At its centre is a low fountain, and around its bowl stand twelve carved marble lions.
They are old and worn smooth, patient stone creatures holding up the basin between them.
From the fountain, four narrow channels of water run out toward the four sides of the court.
Those four small streams were meant to recall the four rivers of paradise flowing from a source.
So the garden idea returns here in stone, a quiet centre with water reaching outward.
Around the court rise slender columns, so many and so thin they seem almost like a grove of pale trees.
The light falls between them in soft bars, and the water threads quietly across the floor.
There is a gentle order to it all, a balance that asks nothing and gives rest.
Picture the marble lions in the dark, keeping their long, patient watch over still water.
You do not need to keep watch over anything tonight.
Let the slender shadows lengthen, and let your breath grow slow.
You are sinking softly now, down toward sleep, and that is just as it should be.
Above the palace, a little higher on the hillside, lies a gentler estate called the Generalife.
It was the summer garden, a quieter place to retreat to when the heat grew strong.
Its long heart is a court named the Patio de la Acequia, the Court of the Water Channel.
Down its whole length runs a slim canal, lined on both sides with arcing jets of water.
The jets cross above the channel in delicate arches that catch the light and fall again.
Around them grow flowers and trees and climbing green, kept fresh by all that water.
Everywhere the walls are dressed in fine carved stucco, with patterns of geometry and leaves.
Bands of coloured tile run along the lower walls, and lines of Arabic poetry are carved above.
The poems praise the beauty of the place itself, the water, the light, and the cool green shade.
It is as though the building quietly recites its own loveliness to anyone who pauses to read.
You need not read a single word; you can simply rest in the sound of falling water.
Let the arcing jets blur into one soft hush behind your eyes.
Breathe out, let go, and let the summer garden carry you down into deep, easy sleep.

lectures.title: The Pleiades
lines: Let the room go soft and dark around you now.
There is nowhere to be and nothing to do.
Feel the weight of your body settling into the bed.
Your shoulders loosen and sink a little lower.
Let your jaw unclench and your hands fall open.
Breathe in slowly, and let the breath out even more slowly.
With each breath out, you feel a little heavier, a little softer.
High above the roof, far past the dark, a small misty knot of light is resting in the sky.
You do not need to look at it or name it tonight.
It is simply there, quiet and faint, while you let go.
Your eyelids are warm and heavy and ready to close.
Let your thoughts drift like slow clouds, untended.
You are sinking, gently, toward sleep.
Imagine you are lying out under a clear country sky.
Off to one side rises the cluster people have watched for as long as there have been people to watch.
It looks at first like a small smudge of light, a tiny cloud of brightness.
Then your eye settles, and the smudge resolves into a little gathering of stars.
Most people, looking with the unaided eye, can pick out about six of them.
A few keen eyes on a dark night can tease out seven, or even more.
They sit close together, a delicate dipper in miniature, easy to miss and impossible to forget.
Because most of us see six where stories so often promise seven, a gentle puzzle is built right into the sky.
You do not have to solve it now.
Just let the soft cluster hang there at the edge of your sight.
Your breathing slows to match its quiet stillness.
And you sink a little deeper into the warmth of the bed.
What you are seeing is not a single thing but a whole family of stars.
Astronomers call it an open cluster, a loose company of stars born together.
It holds not seven stars, and not a dozen, but many hundreds, drifting through space as one slow crowd.
Only the brightest few shine clearly enough for the naked eye to catch.
These bright ones are hot, young, blue-white stars, only a small fraction of the age of our Sun.
They are infants as stars go, still glowing with the heat of their making.
Around them hangs a faint blue haze, a veil of fine dust catching and scattering their light.
All of this floats about four hundred and forty light-years away from where you lie.
The light touching your eye tonight left those young stars centuries ago.
Think of that gentle blue glow traveling all that long, quiet way just to reach you.
There is nothing to hold and nothing to chase.
Let the thought soften and blur as your breathing grows slow.
You are drifting now, carried on that ancient, patient light.
Long ago, the storytellers of Greece looked up at this cluster and saw seven sisters.
In their telling, the sisters were the daughters of the titan Atlas and the sea-nymph Pleione.
Atlas, the legend says, was made to hold the sky upon his shoulders forever.
The seven daughters, so the story goes, were placed among the stars to keep them safe.
