Let that warmth settle over you like the dust on the cactus, and let your breathing slow even more.
In old Mexico, in the warm hills around Oaxaca, there were patient gardeners who knew these small insects well.
They tended the cactus with a slow and gentle care, the way you might tend a garden you have known all your life.
When the time was right, they would come with a soft brush and a small basket.
With the lightest of touches, they would sweep the tiny insects from the pads, one careful stroke at a time.
There was no hurry in it, only the long patience of warm afternoons and steady hands.
The sun lay heavy on their shoulders, and the work went on slowly, gently, without rush.
Each soft grey speck was gathered like something precious, and laid quietly into the basket.
It was the kind of work that asks for calm, for a quiet mind and a quiet hand.
Hour by hour the baskets filled, while the warm wind moved across the open land.
Imagine the soothing rhythm of that brushing, soft and slow, over and over, in the golden heat.
Let that rhythm become your own breathing, gentle and unhurried, in and out.
And as you picture those patient hands at their easy work, let your own thoughts grow soft and let yourself drift.
Now here is the secret that lived inside those small grey specks, the secret hidden in the basket.
When the insects were dried in the sun, they shrank to little more than dust, dull and silvery and plain.
You would never guess, looking at them, what colour they held inside.
But when that dust was crushed and stirred into water, something astonishing happened.
Out of the dull grey rose a red so brilliant and so deep that it seemed almost impossible.
It was carmine, a crimson richer than blood, brighter than any berry, glowing like a coal.
So much colour, blooming from so little, from a handful of grey dust no heavier than a sigh.
It is one of those quiet wonders of the world, that the brightest thing can hide in the plainest place.
There is a gentleness in that thought, that beauty can sleep unseen inside the smallest and dustiest of things.
You need not hold onto it, only let it warm you, like a colour glowing somewhere just out of sight.
Let the wonder fade softly into warmth, and the warmth into a deep and easy heaviness.
Breathe out, and let yourself sink another gentle layer down toward sleep.
That brilliant red did not stay in the warm hills where it was found.
It crossed the wide and rolling sea in the holds of slow ships, carried far from home.
And where it went, it coloured the cloaks of kings and the robes of those who ruled.
It dyed the coats of soldiers a red so bold it could be seen from far across a field.
Whole markets rose and fell on the trade of that little grey dust and its glowing secret.
And for a very long time, the true source of the colour was kept a closely guarded secret.
Those who knew where the red came from held the knowledge tight, and told no one the truth.
People across the sea wondered and guessed, never knowing it began with a small soft insect on a cactus pad.
So the secret travelled the world hidden inside its own bright colour, quiet beneath all that splendour.
But none of that is yours to carry tonight, neither the ships nor the kings nor the guarded secret.
You can let it all drift away over the dark water, growing smaller and dimmer and farther off.
Let it go, and let the quiet close softly around you, warm and complete.
Now let the whole long story settle into nothing more than a colour and a warmth.
Red, like the glow of a fire that has been banked low for the night, holding its heat in the dark.
Red, like the soft light behind your own closed eyes, gentle and dim and near.
Red, like the warmth of a safe and quiet room, where nothing can reach you and nothing needs you.
You are wrapped in that warmth now, held in it, carried by it, with nowhere at all to be.
Each breath is slower than the last, and each one lets you sink a little deeper into the soft dark.
The voice is fading now, a low ember of sound, glowing fainter and farther away.
There is nothing left to do, nothing to think, nothing to keep hold of.
Let the last warm glow blur at its edges and melt softly into the dark.
Your breath is slow, your body is heavy, and the whole world has grown quiet and kind.
Let yourself go fully now, down past the warmth, down into the soft and welcoming sleep.
Rest now, and sleep, and let the warm red dark hold you until morning.

lectures.title: The Arctic
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Feel the weight of the day loosen its hold and slip quietly away from you.
Each breath out carries a little more of it off, and you do not need to follow where it goes.
You can let your body grow heavy now, as heavy and as still as drifted snow.
There is a white calm settling over everything, smooth and cool and endlessly soft.
Nothing here asks anything of you, and there is nowhere at all you need to be.
Let your thoughts grow far apart, like flakes falling slowly through quiet air.
If your eyes wish to close, let them close, and let the warmth gather around you.
There is only this gentle drifting, and the long, slow tide of your own breathing.
Sink a little deeper, and let yourself rest, while the words go on without you.
Far to the north there is a place that sits at the very top of the world.
It is not a land at all, but a frozen ocean, a great pale sea turned hard with cold.
Beneath the ice the dark water moves, slow and patient, as it has for ages.
Above it lies a hush so wide and deep that it seems to swallow every small sound.
There is no edge to walk to here, only white going on softly in every direction.
If you stood at the very point of the pole, all the world would lie to the south of you.
Every way you turned, every road and river, would lead gently back toward home.
It is a strange and quiet idea, that you could stand where all directions become one.
The wind moves over the ice without hurry, smoothing it, hushing it, settling it down.
There is a vastness here that does not frighten, only stills you, only slows you.
You can hold that great white calm in your mind like a cool stone in a warm hand.
And as you hold it, let yourself grow quieter, and heavier, and ready for rest.
In this far place the sun does not rise and set the way it does at home.
For months at a time it sinks below the rim of the world and simply does not return.
The long polar night comes down, and the dark settles in like a soft and folded blanket.
But it is never wholly black, for the snow keeps a faint glow, and the stars are everywhere.
They hang close and bright and countless, wheeling slowly across the patient sky.
Then, after all those months, the sun lifts again above the edge and stays.
Through the long polar day it circles round and round and never goes to bed.
The light grows low and golden and lingers, never quite turning to true night.
Between these two great seasons lie the slow blue twilights, neither day nor dark.
The whole sky deepens into one soft and dreaming shade of evening blue.
It is a light made for drifting, for half-closed eyes and slowing thought.
Let that blue twilight gather over you now, and let it carry you toward sleep.
The frozen sea is not one solid thing, but a living skin of ice upon the water.
It grows in the cold of winter, spreading wide across the dark and quiet ocean.
It shrinks again in the gentler season, melting back, drawing in toward the pole.
All the while it shifts beneath the wind, and it speaks as it shifts.
It creaks and it groans, low and slow, a deep and drowsy voice in the cold.
Sometimes the ice cracks open into long dark lanes of water called leads.
The black sea shows through for a while, smooth and still beneath the sky.
Then the cold returns, and the leads close softly, knitting white over the dark again.
Nothing here is in a hurry, and nothing here is ever quite the same twice.
The ice breathes with the seasons, slow in, slow out, like a great sleeping thing.
You can let your own breath fall into that same unhurried rhythm now.
Slow in, slow out, growing heavier, growing stiller, easing down toward rest.
Even in all this cold, there is life, moving softly across the ice.
The great white bear walks the frozen sea on broad and silent feet.
It pads along without hurry, patient and unbothered by the cold.
The seal waits by its breathing hole, rising for air, slipping down again.
Foxes and hares turn white with the season, ghosts that vanish into snow.
They tuck themselves small against the wind and wait the long night out.
Beneath the ice the great whales glide, dark and slow through the dark water.
They sing to one another in long low notes that travel for miles in the cold.
All of it moves gently, sparing itself, keeping warm, keeping still.
There is no rushing in this world, only the soft economy of rest.
Each creature knows how to be quiet, how to wait, how to settle and endure.
Let yourself settle too, soft and warm and still, the way they do.
People have lived here too, on the ice, for thousands and thousands of years.
They learned the cold the way you learn a face you love, slowly and well.
They built warmth where there seemed to be none, and they shared it freely.
A small lamp of oil could fill a shelter with a steady, golden glow.
The sled carried them softly over the snow, drawn by patient dogs.
They learned to read the snow and the sky the way you might read a quiet page.
They could tell the weather coming, and the safe ice from the thin, by long looking.
And among their many gifts was the deep gift of stillness, of waiting without worry.
In the long winter they told slow stories, and rested, and let the season pass.
There was a patience in them as wide and as calm as the land itself.
You carry a little of that same patience now, here in the late and quiet hour.
Let it hold you gently, and let yourself grow drowsy, and warm, and at ease.
So picture the whole of it now, that vast white quiet at the top of the world.
The frozen sea lies smooth beneath the stars, hushed and endless and still.
And high above, the great lights begin to move across the dark.
Slow green curtains of light drift and fold and sway in the cold sky.
They ripple without a sound, soft and unhurried, fading and glowing again.
All beneath them the white world settles, deeper and deeper, into rest.
The bear sleeps, the fox sleeps, the seal drifts down in the dark water.
The ice grows quiet, and the wind lies down, and the long night gathers in.
There is nothing left to do, and nowhere left to go, and nothing to hold.
Let the green light drift across your mind, slow and soft and dimming.
Let your breath grow long, and let your whole self grow heavy and warm.
And let the great white quiet carry you all the way down into sleep.

lectures.title: Antarctica
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Feel the weight of your body settle gently into the bed, heavy and warm and unhurried.
The day is over now, and you can let every small task of it drift quietly away.
There is nowhere you need to be, and nothing you need to do, except to rest.
Imagine a wide white silence stretching out before you, calm and empty and still.
It asks nothing of you, and it holds you the way snow holds the soft hush of a winter night.
Let each breath grow a little longer than the last, and a little quieter too.
Your thoughts can slow down now, like footsteps fading into deep and gentle snow.
Let your eyes rest, and let your face grow soft, and let your jaw fall loose and easy.
You are safe, and you are warm, and you are slowly drifting down toward sleep.
Far away, at the very bottom of the world, there lies a great white continent.
It is a land buried beneath a vast and ancient dome of ice, smooth and pale and endless.
It is larger and stiller than you could ever quite hold inside your mind.
Picture a place so wide and so empty that the eye finds nothing to land upon.
Only white, and more white, curving softly away to meet a quiet grey sky.
This is the emptiest quiet on all the Earth, a stillness that has lasted for ages.
No towns are here, no roads, no busy crowds, only the slow breathing of the wind.
The cold air is clean and sharp, and the silence settles over everything like a soft white sheet.
You can rest in that silence now, the way you might rest in the hush of an empty room.
There is room here for every weary thought to spread out and grow calm and faint.
Let the vastness of it carry you, gentle and slow, away from the small worries of the day.
Let your breathing match its stillness, and let yourself sink a little deeper into rest.
Across this land lies a great sheet of ice, deeper than you might ever imagine.
It began as snow, soft flakes that fell long ago, in winters older than any memory.
Each year a little more snow settled down, and pressed the older snow beneath it.
Slowly, over thousands and thousands of quiet years, that snow was squeezed into ice.
Now the ice lies a mile and more deep, hiding whole mountains far below.
Somewhere down in the dark there are valleys and peaks that no eye has ever seen.
And the great sheet is not quite still, though it seems to be frozen forever in place.
It flows, so slowly you could never see it move, creeping gently toward the distant sea.
Imagine that patience, that endless unhurried drift, and let your own pace soften to match it.
There is no rush here, and there never has been, only the slow and certain passing of time.
Let that slowness fill you, the calm of something that has all the time in the world.
And let yourself grow heavier and warmer, sinking quietly toward sleep.
This land holds strange and gentle wonders, hidden in its great white quiet.
There are dry valleys where it has not rained nor snowed for an unthinkable span of years.
Bare brown earth lies there, swept clean by the wind, dry as the surface of the moon.
Out at the edges, broad shelves of ice float on the dark and patient water.
Now and then a piece breaks away, with a soft, low boom that rolls across the cold.
A new iceberg drifts free, pale and silent, sailing slowly out into the open sea.
On the high polar plateau, the sun hangs low and golden along the rim of the sky.
The light is soft there, and it lingers, painting the snow in faint and tender colours.
You do not have to picture all of it clearly, only let these images drift softly past.
Each one is calm, and each one is quiet, and each one lets you loosen a little more.
Let the soft boom of the breaking ice fade gently into the distance behind you.
And let your thoughts grow as slow and as still as that low and golden light.
Even here, at the cold rim of the world, there is life, hardy and patient and warm.
On the ice through the long dark winter, emperor penguins gather close together.
They huddle in a great soft crowd, sharing their warmth, sheltering one another from the wind.
Each takes a turn at the cold outer edge, and then moves gently into the warm middle again.
Picture that slow, kind shuffle, that quiet sharing of heat against the dark.
On the floating ice, seals rest with their pups, dozing in the pale and gentle light.
Beneath the cold sea drift great clouds of tiny krill, glowing faintly in the dark water.
And the whales come to feed there, vast and slow, moving through the rich and quiet deep.
Life clings gently to this rim of the world, asking little, holding on with patient grace.
There is something soothing in that, in creatures so calm and so warm in the cold.
Let their warmth become your warmth, gathered close and safe beneath your soft blankets.
And let yourself rest among them, dozing, drifting, sinking slowly toward sleep.
Long ago, brave people crossed this ice, walking out into the white and the cold.
They came by ship and then on foot, hauling their sleds across the endless snow.
They mapped a little of the land, and learned a little of its silence, and then went home.
Some of their small wooden huts still stand, frozen and quiet, far out on the ice.
Inside them the cold has kept everything just so, the tins, the bunks, the old worn boots.
It is as if the people only stepped outside a moment ago, into the patient hush.
Today a few quiet scientists keep watch there, in small warm stations under the wide sky.
They read the ice and the air, gently, patiently, listening to what the cold has to say.
There is a deep humility in standing so small before something so vast and old.
And there is peace in it too, in being a small quiet thing in a great quiet place.
Let that humble calm settle over you, soft and warm and entirely without worry.
And let it carry you down, slow and easy, toward the deep rest of sleep.
And so this great white continent lies at the bottom of the world, calm and complete.
Think of it as the planet's soft white pillow, cool and clean and endlessly still.
Its silence is so deep and so whole that it becomes a kind of perfect peace.
The long polar night settles gently over the ice, dark and soft and kind.
Nothing stirs but the slow wind, and even that grows hushed and faint and far.
You are warm now, and safe now, wrapped softly in your own gentle quiet.
Let every last thought grow pale and dim, fading like footprints filling with snow.
There is nothing to hold, and nothing to keep, only this soft and drifting rest.
Let your breath grow slow and easy, slower still, and let it carry you down.
Down into the white, down into the quiet, down into the warm and gentle dark.
You are drifting now, calm and complete, into a deep and peaceful sleep.
Rest now, and let go, and let the long white silence carry you softly into sleep.

lectures.title: Icebergs
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Settle a little deeper into the warmth of where you are lying, and let the whole weight of you be held.
The day is over now, and you can set it down, the way you would set down something heavy you no longer need to carry.
Feel how your arms grow loose and heavy, how your hands have nothing left to hold.
Let a cool blue stillness drift in around you, calm and wide and quiet.
Imagine yourself drifting slowly across that stillness, going nowhere, needing nothing.
Each breath out lets you sink a little further down into the soft dark.
There is no hurry here, and nothing for you to do but rest.
Let your thoughts grow slow and far away, like a tide going gently out.
Let yourself grow heavier and quieter, drifting easily toward sleep.
Far away, at the cold edge of the world, a great wall of ice stands above a grey and patient sea.
For a long, long time this ice has been still, leaning slowly toward the water without ever quite letting go.
Then, somewhere deep inside it, a slow crack begins to travel, soft and unhurried.
A deep groan moves through the ice, low and long, a sound older than any word.
A great white mass leans out over the water, slow as a sigh, and begins to part from the wall.
It breaks free at last, and slides down into the sea with a long and gentle hush.
The water rises up to meet it and folds around it, cool and welcoming.
A new iceberg is born, rocking softly until the sea grows calm again.
It settles into the water as if it had always belonged there, finding its quiet balance.
And then it simply floats, white and patient, going wherever the slow water takes it.
There is no rush in any of this, only the long, easy unfolding of something very old.
Let that slowness move through you too, and let yourself drift a little nearer to sleep.
What you can see of an iceberg is only a small bright part of the whole.
Most of it lies hidden below the surface, far down in the cool and silent water.
Beneath the shining peak there is a vast and quiet bulk you cannot see at all.
That hidden weight is calm and steady, resting deep where the light grows soft and blue.
It is this unseen part that holds the bright peak up, patient and unhurried.
The seen and the unseen rest together, balanced, leaning on each other in the dark.
So much is held below, gentle and still, asking nothing, simply being there.
You do not have to see a thing to be carried by it, and you do not have to understand.
Let yourself trust the deep, quiet weight that holds you now.
Something steady is beneath you, holding you up while you let go.
You can rest your whole self upon it and sink as deep as you like.
Let the hidden depth carry you down, slow and safe, toward sleep.
In the soft light the iceberg shines a clean and gentle white.
Where the sun slants through it, the ice glows the palest, coolest blue.
Deep in its hollows the blue grows richer, like glass, like the sky at dusk.
Here and there a thread of green runs through it, a quiet vein from long ago.
The sun and the slow sea have worked at it for years, smoothing every edge.
They have carved it into soft arches and curving spires and round, gleaming domes.
Some of its walls are smooth as polished stone, cool to an imagined touch.
Inside the ice, tiny bubbles of ancient air lie sleeping, held for a thousand years.
All of this beauty was made slowly, without effort, simply by time and water and light.
You do not have to hold the picture, only let its cool blue colours wash over you.
Let the calm blues and quiet whites fill the space behind your eyes.
Let them dim and soften now, fading gently as you sink toward sleep.
Once it is loose upon the sea, the iceberg begins its long, slow journey.
The deep currents take hold of it below, and the wind leans on it from above.
Together they carry it across the cold grey water, mile after quiet mile.
For years it drifts, in no hurry at all, simply going where the sea decides.
All the while it melts a little, softening at its edges day by patient day.
Now and then it rolls slowly over, turning a new face up to the sky.
With each turning it grows quieter and smaller, and a little more at peace.
It asks for nothing on this journey, and it resists nothing either.
Slowly, slowly, it is returning to the very water it came from.
There is no sadness in this, only a long and gentle homecoming.
Let yourself drift along that same slow current, carried and unhurried.
Let the long, easy drifting carry you down, deeper and deeper toward sleep.
All around the floating ice the polar sea lies deep and still.
If you came close, you might hear the smallest fizz, soft as a whisper.
It is the ancient air escaping at last, tiny bubbles loosed after a thousand years.
The ice gives off a cold, clean breath that hangs gently in the air above it.
Seabirds come to rest upon its pale ledges, folding their wings and growing still.
They settle there as on a quiet shore, needing nothing, simply at rest.
Beyond them the sea stretches away, dark and smooth and endlessly calm.
A deep silence wraps around the iceberg's pale and gleaming walls.
It is the kind of silence that asks nothing of you, soft and complete.
You can rest inside that silence as the birds rest upon the ice.
Let the quiet settle over you like a cool and gentle blanket.
Let the deep hush of that far sea carry you softly down toward sleep.
And so the iceberg drifts on, a slow white traveller upon a wide dark sea.
Little by little it gives itself back, dissolving gently into the water.
Nothing in it is lost, nothing wasted, only changed from one form to another.
The ice becomes the sea, and the sea will rise one day as cloud and snow and ice again.
There is a deep peace in this turning, a long slow circle with no end.
You need not follow it any further now, only let it go.
Let the picture grow faint and soft, fading like mist over still water.
Let your breath grow slow and even, and let every part of you go heavy.
There is nothing left to do, nowhere to be, nothing at all to hold.
Let yourself dissolve as gently as the ice into the warm dark around you.
You are held, and you are safe, and you may let go completely.
Drift down now, soft and quiet, all the way into sleep.

lectures.title: The Tundra
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to do now but settle, nothing to hold and nothing to carry.
Let the weight of the day loosen and slide away from you, like a coat slipping from your shoulders.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Each breath you take can be a little longer than the one before, a little softer, a little slower.
Feel how heavy your body has become, sinking gently into the warmth beneath you.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Around you a wide and open quiet is spreading, smooth and low and endless.
You do not have to follow the words, only let them drift past like a soft wind far away.
Your eyes are heavy, your jaw is loose, and your hands have grown still and warm.
There is so much space here, and all of it is calm, and all of it is yours.
Let yourself sink a little deeper now, down into the easy, drowsy quiet of rest.
Far in the north there lies a vast and treeless plain, wide and low and open under an enormous sky.
This is the tundra, a great flat land at the cold edge of the world, where the forests give way to open ground.
Picture it stretching out before you, smooth and gentle and almost endless, lying patient to the horizon.
There are no tall trees here to break the view, only the long low sweep of the land beneath the clouds.
The sky seems impossibly large, curving down on every side to meet the quiet rim of the earth.
A soft wind moves across the open ground, unhurried, carrying the cool clean breath of the north.
The land lies flat and patient, holding its silence, asking nothing of you at all.
You could walk for a long, long while here, and the gentle horizon would only drift slowly along with you.
Everything is wide, everything is calm, everything is laid out plain and simple beneath the sky.
There is room here for the eye to rest, and room for the mind to grow quiet and slow.
Imagine standing in all that openness, with nothing pressing in and nothing to hurry toward.
Let that vast and patient quiet settle over you now, and let yourself grow soft and heavy within it.
Beneath this open land lies a hidden world, a deep and ancient stillness held within the ground.
Far below the surface the soil is frozen, and it stays frozen all year long, through every season.
This deep and lasting frost is called permafrost, the patient cold that never quite lets go.
Through the short warm weeks only a thin top layer ever softens, while the depths remain frozen and still.
Because the ground stays hard so far down, the roots of trees cannot reach deep enough to hold.
So no great forest can rise here, and the land keeps its low and open shape.
Down in the frozen earth the cold is kept like a memory, quiet and unmoving for ages upon ages.
Above it lies only a thin living skin of soil, a soft surface over a deep and sleeping cold.
The ground holds its stillness gently, as if it too were resting, deep and undisturbed.
Nothing hurries beneath the surface, and nothing there is ever troubled or awake.
Think of that deep frozen quiet, holding still and patient far below your feet.
Let your own body grow that still and heavy now, sinking softly toward a deep and easy rest.
Across the surface of the tundra grow small low plants, keeping close to the ground out of the wind.
There are soft green cushions of moss, gathered in gentle mounds upon the cool earth.
There is lichen, grey-green and crusted, spreading slow and patient over stone and soil.
Tiny flowers tuck themselves low among the leaves, small and bright and modest in the open air.
Even the willows here are dwarfed, creeping along the ground rather than standing tall.
Everything stays low and sheltered, hugging the earth where the wind passes gently overhead.
These little plants grow slowly, so very slowly, taking long quiet years to spread even a little.
Some of the soft cushions you might pass are far older than they look, ancient and unhurried.
There is a deep patience in this low green world, content to grow at the gentlest of paces.
Nothing reaches or strains here, and nothing rushes to become anything more than it is.
Imagine resting your hand on the soft moss, cool and yielding and quietly alive.
Let that slow and patient calm fill you now, and let yourself grow soft and drowsy and still.
For a little while each year the long cold loosens, and a brief bright summer comes to the plain.
The snow withdraws across the land, drawing back in shining patches to reveal the dark soft ground.
The thawing earth softens into a glitter of small ponds, scattered like mirrors across the open plain.
Light dances on all that quiet water, and the whole land seems to wake and shine.
Then comes a sudden bloom of flowers, small and many, opening together in the gentle warmth.
The plain that was so still grows briefly tender and bright, dressed in soft and quiet colour.
And across this softened land move the great herds, the caribou, the reindeer, drifting slowly onward.
They walk in their countless numbers over the open ground, unhurried, following the season.
You can almost feel the slow steady rhythm of so many soft footfalls passing across the plain.
The herds move on and on beneath the wide pale sky, calm and patient and never in haste.
Picture them flowing gently across the bright summer land, slow as a long slow breath.
Let that slow and easy movement carry you now, drifting softly toward sleep.
In that brief warm season the sky fills with birds, come from very far away to nest.
They arrive in great soft clouds, crossing half the world to reach this open northern land.
They settle among the low plants and the shining ponds, raising their young in the gentle light.
For a little while the quiet plain is busy and alive, full of soft wings and distant calls.
But the warmth does not last long, and soon a hush begins to settle back over the land.
The birds gather and rise and turn away south, fading into the wide pale distance.
The great herds too begin to drift southward, moving slowly off across the cooling ground.
One by one the small flowers close, and the ponds grow still, and the light grows long and low.
Then the first snow comes, settling soft and white and silent over everything.
It falls without a sound, gentle and slow, smoothing the land beneath a soft pale cover.
The plain grows quiet again, hushed and calm and ready for its long deep rest.
Let that soft and silent falling snow ease you down now, deeper and deeper toward sleep.
And so the tundra passes into its long quiet winter, lying still beneath the deep and even snow.
The land lies smooth and white from edge to edge, calm and unbroken under the dim northern sky.
The snow is a great soft blanket spread gently over the whole of the sleeping land.
Beneath it the small plants rest, and the frozen ground holds still, and all the world is hushed.
Nothing hurries here now, and nothing stirs, and the long calm night settles in to stay.
The wind moves softly over the smooth white plain, and even the wind has grown gentle and slow.
Everything is at rest, held safe and quiet beneath the patient drifting snow.
There is nothing left to do, and nowhere to go, and nothing at all to hold.
Let that great calm blanket settle over you too, soft and warm and endlessly still.
Feel yourself growing heavier now, sinking down into the deep and gentle quiet.
Let every thought drift away across the snow, fading into the soft white distance.
Rest now, fully and completely, and let the long calm night carry you gently into sleep.

lectures.title: The Monsoon
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Feel the weight of the day loosen its hold and slip quietly away from you.
Your hands grow heavy, your arms grow heavy, and the bed rises gently to meet you.
Each breath out carries a little more of the day into the warm dark.
There is nowhere you need to be, and nothing you need to do.
Let the warm rain of the imagination fall somewhere far off, soft and easy.
You do not have to follow the words, only let them drift past like falling water.
Your eyelids feel full and heavy, and they are happy to close.
Sink a little deeper into the warm hush, calm and held and safe.
Let yourself grow heavy and still, soft and slow and ready for sleep.
Before the rains come, there is a long and patient waiting over the land.
The earth has gone dry and pale, and the dust lies fine upon every road.
The air hangs heavy and still, warm as breath, holding itself in place.
The fields are cracked and thirsty, and the wells have sunk low and quiet.
Across the whole country, people lift their eyes to the wide empty sky.
They watch the horizon in the evenings, listening for something that has not yet come.
The leaves hang limp on the trees, waiting, and even the birds grow quiet.
It is the held breath of the season, the long pause before the turning.
Everyone waits together, patient and slow, in the heat of the gathering days.
There is a hush over everything, a stillness that feels almost like sleep.
Let that long waiting settle over you now, soft and unhurried and calm.
Breathe slowly into the warm stillness, and let it carry you toward rest.
Then far out over the warm sea, the great wind begins to turn.
Each year it changes its mind and swings around to blow in from the water.
It comes heavy and damp, carrying the weight of the whole ocean upon it.
Over the long miles it gathers moisture, growing fuller and softer as it travels.
On the far horizon the clouds begin to build, tall and grey and slow.
They rise in great soft towers, climbing higher and higher into the sky.
The light goes dim and tender, and a coolness drifts ahead of the storm.
From very far away comes the first low roll of distant thunder.
It is a gentle sound, more felt than heard, a soft murmur in the deep.
The wind sighs through the waiting trees, and the leaves begin to stir.
Let that turning wind move through you, easy and slow and kind.
Feel it carry you gently downward, deeper and softer toward sleep.
Then the first rain breaks, and the land lets out a long slow sigh.
Before the water even falls, the smell of it rises from the dust.
It is the warm earthy scent of dry ground waking to the coming rain.
The first fat drops come down slow, one and then another upon the dust.
They strike the warm ground and bloom into small dark stars upon it.
Then the warm downpour opens, drumming soft on the roofs and the leaves.
The sound is steady and round, a gentle thunder that fills the whole evening.
Water runs singing into the gutters and ribbons away down the lanes.
Children run out into it laughing, and the farmers stand glad in their doorways.
Everywhere there is the soft and welcome music of falling rain.
Let that warm rain fall around you now, steady and kind and slow.
Let its drumming soften into a lullaby that carries you toward sleep.
After the rains, the whole land drinks deep and turns slowly green.
The thirsty earth opens to the water and takes it in without end.
The rivers rise and fill, brown and full and moving softly along.
The paddy fields shine like quiet mirrors holding the grey sky.
The young rice stands bright and tender, green upon the gleaming water.
In the cool of the evenings the frogs wake and begin to sing.
The insects hum in the wet grass, and the whole night murmurs softly.
Vines climb and leaves unfurl, and the world grows lush and full again.
Everything that was dry is fed now, renewed and gentle and green.
The land breathes easy again, slow and satisfied and at peace.
Let that green peace settle into you, soft and full and calm.
Feel yourself fed and renewed, growing heavy and quiet and slow.
Then come the long rainy days, settling into a steady and gentle rhythm.
The rain falls soft and constant now, neither rushing nor stopping.
It is a quiet curtain of water, falling and falling all the day long.
The light goes grey and gentle, soft as wool over everything you see.
The air turns cool and clean, washed fresh by the falling water.
Indoors it is warm and dry, and the world feels small and close and safe.
You sit by the window and watch the rain blur the soft grey street.
The sound of it lulls you, a steady whisper that asks nothing of you.
On and on the water falls, even and calm and endlessly kind.
There is nothing to do but listen, and even the listening grows soft.
Let that steady rain lull you now, on and on without end.
Let it carry your thoughts away and lay you down toward sleep.
Now the warm rain falls all through the night, steady and slow and kind.
It falls on the roofs and the leaves and the quiet sleeping fields.
It washes the whole world clean while you lie warm and still.
There is nothing to keep, nothing to hold, nothing to carry into the dark.
Let each falling drop loosen you a little more, soft and heavy and calm.
Your breath grows slow and even, drifting down with the falling rain.
The sound of the water folds itself gently around your tired mind.
You are warm and safe and held, far from anything that asks of you.
Sink down now into the soft dark, easy and slow and deep.
Let the rain go on falling, steady and kind, all the long night through.
There is nothing more to do, only to rest, only to fall softly asleep.
Let go, and let the warm rain carry you all the way down into sleep.

lectures.title: Fog and Mist
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Feel the bed take your weight, and let it hold you, gently and completely.
There is nowhere to go now, and nothing left to do but rest.
Let the day you have lived drift quietly away from you, like a small boat slipping its rope.
You do not have to follow it, and you do not have to call it back.
Imagine a soft grey hush settling over everything, dimming the world to a quiet and gentle calm.
Your thoughts may move slower now, and slower still, until they are barely moving at all.
Let your face grow soft, your jaw unclench, your eyes rest easy behind their lids.
Each breath out lets a little more of you sink down into the warmth.
Heavier and softer with every word, you are already drifting toward sleep.
Picture a fog as a cloud that has come down low to rest upon the ground.
It does not rush, and it does not press; it simply settles and stays.
Wherever it lies, the hard edges of the world grow soft and uncertain.
The sharp corner of a fence post becomes a faint grey suggestion of itself.
Sound goes quiet too, hushed and close, as though wrapped in soft wool.
Footsteps that should echo are swallowed, gentle and near and small.
The far things vanish, and only the near things remain, kind and close at hand.
The whole wide world grows small around you, no larger than a single quiet room.
There is something tender in that smallness, something that asks nothing of you.
You need not see far, for there is nothing far that you must reach.
Everything you need is here, soft and close and within easy arm.
Let that closeness wrap around you now, and let yourself grow still.
Fog gathers most often in the still and cooling hours of the night.
Through the long day, the warm air holds its moisture quietly, invisibly, without a sound.
Then the sun goes down, and slowly the ground gives up its heat to the dark.
As the air cools, it can hold less and less of the water it carried.
There comes a moment, called the dew point, when it can hold no more.
And so the water leaves the air, gathering into countless tiny droplets.
Each droplet is so small and so light that it cannot quite fall.
Instead they hang there, suspended, drifting softly in the quiet dark.
Millions upon millions of them, too fine to feel, too light to land.
They gather slowly, patiently, with no hurry and no sound.
This is the quiet that pools across the fields while you are sleeping.
Let it gather softly around you too, and let yourself sink down.
Imagine walking slowly through the fog on a cool and quiet evening.
A street lamp ahead is not a point of light but a soft round halo.
Its glow spreads gently into the mist, a pale and welcoming bloom.
The trees come toward you one by one, dim shapes resolving out of grey.
And as you pass, they dissolve again behind you, back into the soft nothing.
Your own footsteps are quiet, hushed and unhurried on the damp ground.
The fog touches your face, cool and soft, like the lightest of veils.
It beads in your hair and on your sleeve, gentle and weightless and kind.
Everything near is muffled and calm, wrapped in the same grey peace.
There is nowhere you must hurry to, and no reason to walk fast.
Each slow step carries you deeper into the quiet, deeper into rest.
Let your breathing match those gentle steps, and let your eyes grow heavy.
Every place wears its fog in its own quiet way.
Along the coast, the sea fog rolls in silent over a sleeping harbour.
It moves across the still water and folds the moored boats away.
In the valleys, the mist pools low at dawn, lying soft in the hollows.
It fills the dips and the meadows like a calm white tide.
High in the cloud forest, the mist drifts through the leaves all day.
It hangs in the branches and drips slow and gentle from every fern.
And over a still river at morning, a low haze hovers above the glass.
It softens the far bank to a dream, pale and quiet and dim.
Each of these places is hushed and slow and breathing softly.
You can rest in any one of them, wherever your tired mind drifts.
Choose one now, and let it hold you, and let yourself grow still.
And then, so slowly that no one quite sees it happen, the fog begins to lift.
The sun rises somewhere behind it, a pale and patient glow.
Its light spreads through the mist and turns the grey to softest gold.
The droplets warm, the tiniest ones first, and rise again into the air.
The thick white world grows thin, and thinner, letting the light come through.
Shapes return one by one, gentle and unhurried, in no rush at all.
A hedgerow, a hillside, a quiet roof emerge as if from a dream.
The last wisps curl and drift, lifting away from the warming ground.
The world comes back so softly that it never wakes anything sharply.
There is nothing sudden here, nothing loud, nothing to startle you.
It is only a slow and golden easing, a quiet returning of the light.
Let that gentleness settle over you, and let yourself grow heavy.
Now let the fog come back to you, soft and grey and close.
Let it settle around you like a warm and weightless blanket.
It hides the whole world away, kindly, so there is nothing left to see.
There is nothing to look at, and nothing at all to do.
There is nowhere to be but here, wrapped in this soft grey quiet.
Every edge has gone soft, every sound has gone still and far.
Your breath is slow, your body is heavy, your thoughts are drifting away.
Let them go, one by one, into the mist, and do not follow.
You are held, and you are safe, and you have nothing left to carry.
Sink down now, deeper and softer, into the warm grey hush.
There is only rest here, and rest is all you need.
Let the fog close gently over you, and drift down into sleep.

lectures.title: The Thunderstorm
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
You are safe, and you are warm, and you are perfectly dry, wrapped in the gentle dark of your own quiet room.
Let the day you have carried slip from your hands now, one small weight at a time.
There is nowhere you need to go and nothing you need to do but rest.
Feel how heavy your body has become, sinking softly into the place where you lie.
Each breath you let go grows longer and slower than the one before.
Let your eyes rest closed, and let the room grow soft and far away.
Outside, somewhere far off, the night is gathering itself in a slow and easy way.
But here, where you are, all is still and kind and warm.
So let yourself sink a little deeper, and let the quiet hold you.
The evening had been warm and heavy, the kind of air that settles over everything like a soft blanket.
All day a stillness had been building, a hush as though the sky were holding a long slow breath.
Not a leaf stirred outside, and the trees stood quiet against a deepening sky.
You are tucked away inside, safe behind walls that have kept you warm a thousand nights before.
Far off, beyond the hills, the first low rumble rolls across the distance, soft as a sigh.
It is so far away that it feels less like a sound and more like a memory of one.
There is no need to stir, no need to wonder, only to lie still and let it come.
The warm air rests on your skin, gentle and close and comforting.
Somewhere far off the storm is gathering, but it gathers slowly, in no hurry at all.
And you are cozy here, wrapped warm and dry, with the whole soft night ahead of you.
Let that distant rumble be a lullaby, a sound that asks nothing of you.
Breathe out, and let yourself grow heavier still, sinking gently toward sleep.
Far away on the horizon, the great clouds are slowly building, tall and grand and soft.
They rise like quiet mountains, climbing high into the dimming sky.
From your warm and sheltered place you can see them only as soft shapes in the distance.
Now and then a gentle flicker of light glows within them, low and golden and far away.
It is not sharp or sudden, only a soft pulse, like the slow blink of something sleepy.
The rumble rolls a little closer now, but it stays low and round and never harsh.
It is the sound of something vast moving slowly, with all the time in the world.
There is a grand and easy calm to it, the calm of weather that has done this forever.
You watch the far clouds drift and glow, and your eyes grow heavier with every breath.
Nothing about it asks you to be awake, and nothing about it asks you to be afraid.
Let the slow grandeur of the distant sky settle over you like a warm hand.
And let yourself drift a little deeper into the soft and waiting dark.
Then, softly, the rain begins, the first drops finding the roof above you.
It comes gently at first, a scattering of taps, and then it settles into a steady, soothing fall.
On the roof and against the window it makes a warm and even drumming, close and kind.
You are safe beneath it, dry and held, with the whole storm kept softly outside.
There is such deep comfort in the sound of rain when you are warm and sheltered within.
The air that drifts in is cool and clean now, washed and fresh and easy to breathe.
Each drop on the glass is a small soft note in a long and gentle song.
You need not count them or follow them, only let them blur into one steady hush.
The rain says rest, and rest, and rest again, over and over without end.
Feel how snug and gathered in you are, how far the cold and wet remain.
Let the steady drumming carry your thoughts away like leaves on slow water.
And let your breath fall into its rhythm, slow and soft and deep.
Far across the hills a soft flash lights the clouds, gentle as a candle behind a curtain.
You wait, quiet and unhurried, and the seconds drift by like slow breaths.
One, and two, and three, and then the low roll of thunder finds its way to you at last.
It is a long and rounded sound, soft at the edges, more comfort now than warning.
Each time the light glows, the wait before the thunder grows a little longer.
And each time the thunder comes, it arrives a little softer than before.
The storm is turning away from you now, wandering off slowly across the dark land.
There is something kind in the way it leaves, gentle and tired and slow.
You count the soft seconds without trying, and they only make you sleepier.
Flash, and wait, and a far low roll, each one fainter than the last.
The thunder murmurs its way toward the edge of the world and grows ever more distant.
Let each fading rumble draw you down, deeper and softer, toward sleep.
The storm is passing on now, drifting away beyond the hills and out of sight.
The rain has eased to a soft and tender patter, lighter with every passing minute.
The thunder is only a faint murmur now, far over the dark and distant fields.
It rumbles once more, so gently and so far that it is almost a kindness whispered.
The air around you is washed clean and cool and sweet, settled and at peace.
A great calm is spreading through the night, soft and wide and deep.
You are still warm, still dry, still safe, exactly as you have been all along.
Nothing remains of the storm but its gentle going and the quiet it leaves behind.
The world outside is rinsed and still, breathing slow beneath the clearing sky.
There is such peace in the after of a storm, a hush that asks for nothing.
Let that great washed calm fill you, from your slow breath to your heavy limbs.
And let it carry you down, gently and surely, toward the soft edge of sleep.
Now only the last gentle drips remain, falling soft and slow from the quiet eaves.
One drop, and then another, spaced far apart like the slowing of a sleepy heart.
The deep calm after the storm wraps all around you, warm and dark and kind.
You are safe in the soft dark, held by the stillness of the late, late night.
The faint rain that lingers is the softest of lullabies, asking nothing, holding everything.
Let your breath grow as slow as the last drips falling from the eaves.
There is nothing left to do, nowhere to be, no thought to keep.
The night has washed the world clean and laid it gently down to rest, and you with it.
Feel yourself sinking, soft and warm and safe, down through the quiet dark.
Let the last small sounds of rain blur and fade and let you go.
You are warm, you are safe, you are held, and the storm has long since passed.
So rest now, and let the soft rain lull you all the way down into sleep.

lectures.title: The Trade Winds
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Feel the day loosen its hold on you, slipping away like something you set gently down.
Your body grows heavier with each breath, sinking softly into the warmth around you.
There is nowhere you need to be, and nothing at all you have to do.
Let your hands grow still, let your jaw unclench, let your forehead smooth itself away.
A warm and gentle breeze seems to move somewhere far off, easy and unhurried.
You do not have to follow the words; you can simply let them drift past you.
Every breath out carries a little more of the day away from you.
Let yourself grow soft and heavy and slow, with nothing left to hold.
Rest here a while, sinking deeper, letting the quiet carry you down toward sleep.
Far out across the warm wide ocean, there are winds that blow steady and patient and slow.
Unlike the gusty winds of home, these do not fret or change their minds.
They do not rush in cold from the north, or scatter the leaves, or rattle the windows.
They blow the same gentle way for days, and then for days again, faithful as a heartbeat.
Imagine a breath that never quite finishes, a long warm exhale across the sea.
These are the steady winds of the warm latitudes, the easy breezes of the tropics.
They have been blowing this same soft way for longer than anyone can remember.
There is no struggle in them, no sudden change, only a calm and constant moving.
They ask nothing of the sea but to ruffle it gently and pass on.
Picture that wide blue water, breathing slowly under a sky that holds no storms.
Such a steady wind asks nothing of you either, only that you let it carry you.
Let that thought settle over you now, slow and warm, and let your breath grow long.
Long ago, in the age of sail, these gentle winds were given a kind and useful name.
Sailors called them the trade winds, for they carried ships across the sea to trade.
Before there were engines, a ship had only the wind to lean upon.
And so the sailors learned where the steady winds could always be found.
They would sail out and down toward the warm latitudes, and wait to meet them.
When the trade winds filled the sails, the long voyage truly began.
There was a quiet faith in it, a trust that the wind would hold and carry you onward.
Day after day the same soft wind would blow you toward the far side of the world.
You did not have to make it happen; you only had to let it take you.
Imagine that old and simple trust, the wind that always came, the way that always opened.
There was nothing to do but raise the sails and be carried gently on.
Let that same easy faith settle into you now, and let yourself grow drowsy and still.
Imagine you are aboard one of those ships, far out on the open and untroubled sea.
The sails are filled and steady, leaning into the warm and constant wind.
You feel the breeze against your face, soft and warm and endlessly patient.
The days are long and blue, and one slips into the next without any edge between them.
The ship rolls gently with the slow swell, rising and settling, rising and settling.
Behind you the white wake unspools across the water and slowly fades away.
There is nothing to steer toward and nothing to fear, only the wind and the wide sea.
You have nothing to do but be carried, hour after gentle hour.
The sun is warm on the deck, and the rigging hums its low and easy song.
Time loosens out here, growing soft and shapeless, no longer marked by anything.
You feel yourself being carried, rocked, held by the breathing of the sea.
Let the swell rock you now, slow and deep, and let your eyes grow heavy.
These warm winds touch islands scattered like green stones across the blue.
On the shores, the palm trees lean all one way, bowed gently by the steady breeze.
Soft surf folds itself over pale coral, sighing in and drawing slowly back.
Overhead the clouds march in neat and tidy rows across a turquoise sky.
The wind smells of salt and warmth and faraway flowers carried on the air.
The days here move to an easy rhythm, slow as the tide, soft as the surf.
Nothing hurries on these islands, and nothing needs to be hurried.
The shade is warm, the water is clear, and the breeze is always near.
You can almost feel the warm sand beneath you, holding you up.
The palms whisper their long soft hush above you, over and over.
Let that easy island rhythm slow your breath and loosen your limbs.
Lie back into the warmth of it now, and let yourself grow heavy and calm.
Now the warm day softens into a long and gentle tropical night.
Still the wind blows on, soft and faithful, while the islands fall asleep.
It rustles quietly through the palms, a sound like slow and distant water.
It ruffles the dark sea, ruffles it and smooths it, over and over again.
The stars come out thick and bright above the breathing water.
The wind does not stop for the night; it simply blows on, steady and unhurried.
It asks nothing of you, only blows softly past you in the dark.
You can let your breath fall into time with its slow and patient moving.
There is something deeply restful in a thing that never has to try.
The warm air moves over you like a soft and weightless blanket.
Let that steady wind breathe for you now, in and out, in and out.
Sink into the warm dark with it, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
And so the warm wind carries you gently onward over a calm and quiet sea.
The swell lifts you and lowers you, slow and deep and even.
The steady breeze is a lullaby that never stops and never asks anything.
There is nothing left to hold, nothing left to do, nowhere left to go.
You are carried, and you are rocked, and you are warm.
Let the wind take you wherever it is going; you do not need to know.
Each soft swell rocks you a little deeper toward sleep.
Your breath grows long and slow, falling into the rhythm of the sea.
The warm wind blows on, faithful and unhurried, while you let go at last.
There is only the gentle rocking now, and the soft and endless breeze.
Drift now, easy and weightless, carried on the patient warm wind.
Let it carry you all the way down, into a deep and quiet sleep.

lectures.title: A Drop of Pond Water
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Feel the weight of the day loosen its hold and slip quietly away from you.
Your hands grow heavy, your jaw unclenches, and your forehead lets go of its small frown.
There is nowhere you need to be and nothing you need to do.
Each breath you take is a little slower and a little deeper than the one before.
Let the bed hold you completely, the way the water holds everything that floats within it.
The room is dim and gentle, and the hour asks nothing of you at all.
You are allowed, now, to simply rest and to drift.
Let the words flow over you like warm water, carrying no weight and asking no questions.
Sink a little deeper into the soft dark, and let yourself begin to fall.
Imagine a single drop of still pond water, no bigger than a tear, resting in the light.
To the eye it is only water, clear and quiet, a small round bead of nothing much.
But inside that drop there lives a whole world you could never see on your own.
It is busy and gentle and alive, a tiny universe folded into the smallest space.
Hundreds of small creatures drift and swim there, each one going softly about its day.
They have no idea you are watching, no idea of the great wide world beyond their drop.
Their whole sky is the curve of the water, their whole ocean a single shining bead.
There is something deeply restful in a world so small and so complete.
Nothing in it hurries, and nothing in it worries, and nothing in it needs you.
You can simply float above it, watching from far away, asking nothing of yourself.
Let that little world drift in your mind like a soft and glowing lantern.
And let your breathing slow to match its quiet, unhurried calm.
Look first at the green that fills the drop, soft specks and fine drifting threads.
These are the tiniest of plants, the algae, scattered through the water like loose petals.
Some are single round grains of green, turning slowly as the water turns.
Others are long delicate threads, swaying gently the way grass sways in a far-off field.
They drink the sunlight quietly and turn it into food, asking for nothing more.
This is the meadow of the tiny world, a green pasture too small for any eye.
There is no sound there, only a slow and patient drifting in the watery light.
The green glows soft and dim, like the last colour left in a room at dusk.
Everything moves at the pace of something half asleep, swaying without effort.
Let that gentle green fill your mind, cool and soft and endlessly slow.
Breathe in the calm of a meadow that needs nothing but light and time.
And let your thoughts grow as still and drifting as those quiet threads of green.
Now find the amoeba, a small soft blob of living jelly, formless and clear.
It has no proper shape at all, only a body that flows and folds as it pleases.
Watch it stretch out one slow arm of itself, reaching gently into the water.
The rest of it follows, pouring after, the way warm honey settles into a spoon.
It is the most unhurried of all creatures, never rushing, never anxious, never tense.
When it finds its food it simply wraps itself around it, soft and slow and sure.
It folds the morsel in like a blanket drawn quietly over a sleeping child.
There is no haste in it, no struggle, only this patient, gentle flowing.
It moves the way you are moving now, sinking by slow degrees toward rest.
Let your own body feel that soft and shapeless ease, heavy and loose and calm.
Imagine all your edges softening, your limbs flowing into the warmth of the bed.
And drift, formless and untroubled, deeper into the quiet of the night.
See the paramecium now, a tiny slipper shape gliding smoothly through the drop.
Its whole body is covered in fine waving hairs, too small and soft to count.
They beat together in slow ripples, like a field of grass stirred by a gentle wind.
And so it glides, turning and spinning unhurried, a small slow boat upon the water.
There are others like it too, little swimmers drifting at their own quiet pace.
Some wander in lazy circles, some coast in long and dreamy lines.
None of them is going anywhere in particular, and none of them is in any rush.
They simply go about their quiet day, turning softly in the green-lit water.
Watch them spin and slide, slow and smooth, and feel your own thoughts slowing too.
There is a deep peace in watching something move so gently and so well.
Let that smooth, unhurried gliding carry your mind along with it.
And let yourself drift on, slow and easy, toward the edge of sleep.
Among the smallest swimmers move a few that are a little larger and easier to see.
Here is the rotifer, with a small spinning crown of hairs at the front of its body.
The crown turns and shimmers, drawing a soft current of water gently toward it.
It grazes there in the green light, patient and content, like a creature in a quiet field.
And here is the water flea, drifting and bobbing on tiny rowing limbs.
Its body is so clear that you can almost see the small heart beating within it.
It beats slow and steady, a tiny faithful drum keeping its own gentle time.
These larger ones drift among the green, grazing softly, never hurried, never afraid.
Their whole world is calm, lit dim and green, rocking them as they go.
Let that slow heartbeat and that gentle rocking settle into you now.
Feel yourself swaying softly, held and rocked by the quiet water.
And let the rhythm carry you down, slow and warm, toward sleep.
Now the light over the little world begins to fade, and the drop grows still.
The green threads stop their swaying and hang quiet in the dimming water.
The amoeba folds itself together and settles, soft and shapeless, into rest.
The little swimmers slow their spinning, their tiny hairs growing calm and still.
The rotifer closes its small crown, and the water flea drifts down to rest.
Even the smallest heart beats slower now, slower and softer, sinking into quiet.
The whole tiny world grows hushed, every creature easing toward its sleep.
And you are easing with them, slower and heavier with each long breath.
There is nothing left to watch, nothing left to do, nothing left to hold.
Let the drop go dark and still, and let your own thoughts go dark and still.
Let your breath grow slow and quiet, and your whole body grow soft and heavy.
Rest now, deep and warm, and let the gentle dark carry you all the way to sleep.

lectures.title: Diatoms
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Feel the weight of the day loosen its hold and slide away from you, piece by quiet piece.
Your arms grow heavy, your hands grow still, and the bed seems to rise softly to meet you.
Somewhere far off there is light moving through clear glass, gentle and unhurried.
You do not need to follow it, and you do not need to understand it.
Let each breath out carry a little more of you down into the warm dark.
There is nowhere to be and nothing to do but rest here, just as you are.
If a thought drifts by, let it drift on, the way a leaf drifts past on slow water.
Your whole body is sinking now, soft and easy and content.
Let yourself grow heavier still, and let the quiet hold you.
In every drop of the sea, and every still pond, there are tiny living jewels drifting unseen.
They are far too small for your eyes to find, smaller than a grain of dust on a windowsill.
Yet they are there in their countless billions, more numerous by far than all the stars.
They float in the upper water where the light is soft, neither rising nor sinking, simply adrift.
These are the diatoms, the quiet gardens of the water, scattered through every sea on earth.
A single cup of ocean holds more of them than there are people in all the world.
They have no need of you and ask nothing, drifting on as they have for ages beyond counting.
You could swim through a great cloud of them and never know that they were there.
And all the while they shine, each one a small bright thing turning slowly in the light.
Imagine them now, a hush of glimmering specks suspended in the blue, going nowhere in particular.
There is something restful in a thing so small and so untroubled.
Let that image float, and let yourself float with it, soft and slow and heavy.
Each of these little creatures builds itself a tiny box of clear glass.
It draws the glass straight from the water around it, gathering it grain by patient grain.
From plain seawater it makes a shell of silica, the same glass that windows are made of.
The box has two halves, a lid and a base, that fit together like a little pillbox.
One half slides gently over the other, snug and neat, holding the soft life inside.
No hand could make a thing so fine, not the steadiest jeweller with the finest tools.
The walls are thinner than a whisper, clear as held breath, and perfectly true.
When the diatom grows and divides, each new one carries half of the old box with it.
So the building goes on and on, a quiet craft passed down without a single word.
Picture that small clear shell, smooth and cool, catching the light and letting it through.
There is no effort in it, only a slow and certain making.
Let that gentleness settle over you, and let your breathing grow softer still.
No two kinds of diatom wear the same dress, and the patterns never seem to end.
Some are perfect circles, like the tiniest of plates, ringed and rayed from the center.
Some are long ribbons, some are fans, some are stars with arms held wide.
Others coil into slow spirals, or stretch into slender needles, or join hands in delicate chains.
Each kind has its own design, pricked out in rows of pores too small to truly imagine.
These pores run in neat lines and arcs, finer than lace, repeated without a single error.
It is a museum of jewels that no one made and almost no one ever sees.
Beauty here is simply spent on the dark water, freely and without any reason.
Imagine drifting slowly past one shining shape and then another, each more lovely than the last.
You need not name them or hold them, only let them pass.
Let the endless gentle patterns blur softly into one another.
And as they blur, let your own thoughts blur too, and grow still, and rest.
These tiny jewels live by gathering light, floating near the bright surface of the water.
They turn the sunlight into food, quietly, the way the leaves of a tree do.
From light and water and air they make all that they need, asking nothing more.
And because there are so very many of them, they feed the whole wide sea.
The small fish eat them, and larger fish eat those, and so the ocean is fed from the bottom up.
Half of the fresh breath of the world is made by these specks too small to see.
When the light is right, they gather into a soft green-gold haze that tints the water.
A sailor passing over might see the sea glow faintly, and never guess the reason.
Imagine that warm haze of light spread thin across the calm and rocking water.
There is no hurry in it, only sunlight slowly becoming life.
Let that warmth move through you, easy and unforced.
And let it carry you down, gently, toward sleep.
In time, each tiny diatom finishes its small life, as all things do.
The soft living part fades, and only the clear glass shell is left behind.
And then, with nothing to hold it up, the little shell begins to fall.
It sinks through the water slowly, turning, drifting, taking days to reach the floor.
Down there it lands among countless others, settling into soft and pale drifts.
Over the long ages these shells pile deeper, a gentle snow that never melts.
Layer on layer it gathers, the lightest snow there is, falling for millions of years.
Whole hills of this pale dust have built up where ancient seas once lay.
It is the slowest, quietest falling that the world has ever known.
Imagine that endless soft snow of glass, drifting always downward through the dark.
There is nothing anxious in it, only a long and patient settling.
Let yourself settle with it now, deeper and deeper, into rest.
So let the jewels drift down through the still dark water, one after another, without end.
Each one turns slowly as it falls, catching a last faint thread of light.
There is no sound down here, only the soft hush of the water far above.
Down they go, settling soft and slow onto the pale and quiet floor.
And as they settle, you are settling too, sinking gently into the warm dark.
Your breath is slow now, your body heavy, your thoughts drifting somewhere far away.
Let each small jewel that falls take a little more of your weariness with it.
There is nothing left to hold and nothing left to do, only this slow and easy falling.
Down through the quiet you go, soft and unhurried, carried by the gentle current.
Let the last of the light fade kindly, and let the stillness gather close.
You are safe, and you are heavy, and you are nearly asleep.
Let the drifting carry you all the way down now, into a deep and peaceful sleep.

lectures.title: The Water Bear
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Let the day you have carried slip quietly from your hands, one small weight at a time.
There is nowhere you need to be, and nothing more that anyone is asking of you now.
Feel the bed holding you, steady and gentle, the way the ground holds everything that rests.
Let your jaw loosen, let your hands grow heavy, let your thoughts wander somewhere far and dim.
Each breath out can be a little longer than the last, soft and unhurried and easy.
You do not have to follow these words, only let them drift around you like warm air.
If your mind floats away, that is good, for floating away is exactly where you are going.
Let yourself grow pleasantly heavy, sinking just a little deeper with every slow breath.
There is nothing to do now but rest, and let the quiet settle gently over you.
Far below the world you usually notice, there lives a tiny and very gentle creature.
It is so small that it would vanish on the tip of your finger, smaller than a grain of sand.
People who love it call it the water bear, or sometimes, more tenderly, the moss piglet.
It is plump and round, with a soft rolling body that looks a little like a sleepy little bear.
It has eight short and stubby legs, each ending in tiny clinging claws.
When it walks it does not hurry, swaying and ambling with a slow and patient gait.
It trundles along through its tiny green world, in no rush to arrive anywhere at all.
Imagine it bumbling softly over the leaves, pausing, then bumbling gently on again.
There is something deeply restful in a creature so small and so wholly unbothered.
It asks nothing of the wide world, and the wide world asks nothing of it.
Picture it now, round and soft and slow, padding through the quiet on its little legs.
Let its unhurried walk slow your own thoughts, and let yourself grow still and calm.
The water bear makes its home in a place you have walked past a thousand times.
It lives in the soft green cushion of moss, or in the pale crust of lichen on a stone.
To you these are small and quiet things, but to the water bear they are an entire world.
Inside the moss there clings a thin film of water, fine as breath upon a window.
In that film of damp the little creature swims and ambles and feels perfectly at home.
The moss is a soft and dripping jungle to it, towering and green and full of gentle shade.
It grazes there, sipping at the juices of the plants, taking only what it needs.
It wanders the wet green hollows, content, asking for nothing more than this.
All around it the world is damp and cool and hushed, a sheltered little paradise.
Think of that secret garden tucked into a single patch of velvet moss.
Let yourself shrink gently into that softness, surrounded by green and quiet.
And let the calm of that small damp world settle warmly over you as you rest.
But the little world of the water bear does not stay wet forever.
The sun warms the moss, and slowly, slowly, the thin film of water begins to fade.
For most creatures this drying would be the end, but the water bear has a quiet gift.
When its small pond shrinks away, it does not struggle, and it does not come to harm.
Instead it gently draws in its eight little legs, tucking them close against its body.
It curls itself down into a tiny rounded barrel, small and snug and still.
And then, softly, it lets itself fall into a deep and dreamless sleep.
All the busy life inside it slows, and slows, until it is the faintest whisper.
Its breathing nearly stops, its little heart of activity grows quiet as a held note.
It becomes a tiny seed of sleep, waiting in the dust of the dried moss.
There is no fear in this, only a soft and trusting letting go.
Let yourself learn from it, curling inward, growing still, and giving in to rest.
In that dry and curled up sleep, the water bear can wait for a very long time.
Not just a night, and not just a season, but years upon quiet years.
The heat may come, and the cold may come, and the long still days may pass.
Through all of it the little barrel rests, untroubled and patient and calm.
It does not fret about the time, for time has gently loosened its hold.
It dreams of nothing at all, and nothing at all is a wonderfully peaceful thing.
The wind may carry it far, or it may lie tucked in the same soft crack for ages.
Either way it simply waits, perfectly content, perfectly at peace.
Imagine resting so completely that the years drift by like clouds you never count.
No worry can reach it there, no hurry, no weight, no need to wake.
It is the deepest and most trusting rest that any small thing has ever known.
Let that endless quiet seep into you now, and let your own waiting be just as calm.
Then, one day, after all that patient waiting, something tender happens.
A drop of rain falls, or a little dew gathers, and the moss grows damp once more.
The water finds the tiny curled up barrel and soaks it softly through.
And slowly, the way a flower opens, the little water bear begins to soften.
It unfurls its stubby legs, one by one, stretching out from its long sleep.
Its body fills again with the gentle film of water it had been waiting for.
And then, as if no time had passed at all, it takes up its slow walk again.
It ambles off into the green, unhurried, unharmed, entirely itself once more.
The long sleep did not take anything from it, but gave it back whole and well.
Rest had carried it gently across the dry years and set it down good as new.
Imagine waking like that, restored, soft, and perfectly at ease.
Let that promise of gentle waking comfort you, and let yourself sink deeper still.
So now, like the little water bear, you can let everything slow down.
There is nothing more for you to carry tonight, and nowhere you must go.
Let your breath grow long and quiet, slowing the way its small life slowed.
Curl yourself soft and safe, here in the warm dark, held and unbothered.
Let the day dry gently away from you, and feel no need to hold it at all.
You are small and safe in your own patch of quiet, tucked away and at peace.
Let your legs grow heavy, let your hands grow still, let your thoughts grow dim.
Sink down into the deep restoring sleep that asks nothing of you in return.
Trust, as the water bear trusts, that rest will give you back whole and well.
There is nothing left to do now but drift, softly, gently, down and away.
Let the last of these words dissolve into the hush, and let them go.
Sleep now, little one, deep and calm and safe, all the way down into rest.

lectures.title: Pollen
lines: Let your shoulders soften and your breath grow slow, here in the warm hush of the late hour.
There is nothing to learn tonight, and nothing at all to remember.
Let the voice become a low and distant murmur, a sound you no longer have to listen to.
Feel the day loosen its hold, slipping away from you like a tide going quietly out.
Your body is growing heavy now, sinking a little deeper into the warmth that holds you.
There is nowhere you need to go, and nothing you need to do, in this soft golden quiet.
Let your jaw unclench, let your hands fall open, let the small cares of the day drift off.
Imagine a warmth in the air around you, as soft and as fine as faint golden dust.
It asks nothing of you, only that you rest, only that you let yourself be still.
Each breath out carries away a little more weight, until you feel almost weightless.
Let the words wash over you like warm air, and let your thoughts grow slow and dim.
Sink down now, gently, into the soft and heavy hush, and let yourself begin to rest.
Deep within every flower there is a quiet gold, a fine and gentle powder waiting.
It gathers at the heart of the bloom, soft as dust, soft as a sleepy thought.
This is pollen, the golden dust of flowers, scattered through the meadows of spring.
It dusts the back of the drowsy bee, and it dusts the fingertip that brushes a petal.
If you have ever touched a lily, you may have worn a little of that gold on your skin.
It is the quiet color of summer mornings, of buttercups held beneath a chin.
Whole fields are softly powdered with it, a faint warm glow upon the open air.
It lies in the cup of the poppy and the throat of the rose, hidden and patient.
There is so much of it, and it is so light, that the meadow seems to breathe gold.
You need do nothing with this, only picture it, soft and warm and far away.
Let that softness settle over you, fine and golden and endlessly gentle.
Let it dust your heavy eyelids closed, and let yourself drift a little deeper down.
Each grain of pollen is far too small to see, smaller than a speck, smaller than dust.
And yet, were you to look very close, you would find each grain is a tiny jewel.
Every one is a small perfect sculpture, shaped with a care that no eye ever sees.
Some grains are round and smooth, like little golden moons polished by patient hands.
Some are covered in soft spikes, like tiny stars, or gentle drowsy sea creatures.
Some are netted with delicate lace, a pattern finer than any thread you could spin.
Some have little wings, or hollows, or ridges drawn in faint and curving lines.
And here is the quiet wonder of it, that every kind of flower has its own design.
The pine and the daisy and the grass each carry a secret shape, all their own.
A whole hidden world of jewels rests in a single dusting of that gentle gold.
You do not need to hold these shapes in mind, only to let the wonder soften you.
