Now let the journey begin to fade, like a gentle tide drawing back.
Let the grey dust and the black sky soften and grow dim.
Come slowly back to the quiet weight of your own body.
Feel the warmth of your bed, the softness of your pillow, the safety all around you.
Your breath is slow and easy now, rising and falling like a calm sea.
Far overhead, the still Moon keeps its silent watch, and all is well.
You are safe here, and you are held, and there is nothing left to do.
Let the words grow faint, and let them drift away from you.
Let each thought loosen and dissolve, like mist upon the morning.
There is only the breath now, slow and soft and warm.
Let yourself sink down, gently, into the deep and welcome dark.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Onsen
lines: Welcome, and let yourself arrive here, just as you are.
There is nothing left to do now, nothing to fix or finish.
Let the day go, the way you would set down a heavy bag at the door.
Feel the bed holding you, and let it take all of your weight.
Soften your shoulders, your jaw, the space between your eyes.
Let your hands grow loose and warm where they rest.
Let your breath grow slow, a little longer on each gentle out-breath.
Tonight you do not have to go anywhere or be anyone.
Tonight, in your mind, you sink into a warm spring high in the mountains of Japan.
This is an onsen, a hot spring fed by the quiet warmth of the earth.
Let the word settle over you like steam, soft and slow.
And if you fall asleep before the end, that is perfectly fine.
Far beneath these mountains, the earth is restless and warm.
Japan is a land of islands shaped by fire deep below.
Down in the dark, old stone holds a slow and steady heat.
Rainwater and snowmelt sink down through the ground, year upon year.
There, in the warmth, the water is gently heated, far out of sight.
It gathers minerals from the stone, a quiet gift of the deep.
Slowly, patiently, the warm water begins to rise again.
It finds its way upward through hidden cracks and channels.
And at last it reaches the surface, steaming softly into the cool air.
The restless fire of the earth has become something tender and kind.
You do not need to understand it, only to feel its warmth.
Let that deep, ancient heat rise gently toward you now.
Before you enter the water, there is a small and gentle ritual.
You step into a quiet washing room, warm and full of soft steam.
You sit down on a low wooden stool, close to the floor.
Beside you waits a little basin and a stream of warm water.
Here you rinse yourself, slowly, with no hurry at all.
You wash away the dust of the day, every trace of it.
You let the warm water run over your shoulders and down your back.
With each rinse, something tight inside you loosens and lets go.
This is how you enter the shared pool, already clean and calm.
It is a small kindness, to the water and to yourself.
By the time you rise from the stool, the day feels far away.
You are ready now, soft and quiet, to step toward the warmth.
You move slowly to the edge of the pool and lower yourself in.
The heat wraps around you at once, holding you from every side.
Steam rises from the surface and curls into the mountain air.
Your shoulders drop, sinking down below the gentle warmth.
The heat seeps into tired muscles you did not know were tired.
Your arms float, your legs grow heavy and soft and free.
You feel almost boneless now, melting into the water itself.
This bath rests outdoors, a rotenburo open to the quiet sky.
Above you the stars are clear, and the cold air is sweet.
Snow may drift down and touch your face, cool against the warmth.
Yet your body stays warm, cradled and safe within the spring.
There is nowhere else to be, and nothing to hold at all.
In one such valley live the wild monkeys of Jigokudani.
They are the snow monkeys, with thick fur and calm dark eyes.
Long ago, in the deep cold, they found the steaming pools.
One by one they learned to slip into the warm water.
Now, through the white winters, they bathe as you do.
They sit together in the heat, peaceful and unhurried.
Snow gathers softly on their heads and shoulders as they soak.
Their eyes grow heavy, half closed, lost in the warmth.
They do not rush, and they do not worry over anything.
They simply rest in the warm water while the world turns white.
Imagine sitting near them, quiet, sharing the same gentle heat.
Let their stillness become your stillness, slow and deep.
When evening comes, the little onsen town glows softly in the dusk.
Wooden inns line the narrow streets, their windows warm with light.
These inns are called ryokan, old and quiet and welcoming.
Guests wander slowly along the lanes in soft cotton robes.
These robes are called yukata, loose and light and gentle.
Wooden sandals make a slow, soft sound upon the stones.
Steam drifts from the bathhouses and rises among the rooftops.
No one is in a hurry here, and no one needs to be.
The soak before sleep is part of the rhythm of this place.
You wander back toward your room, warm and pleasantly tired.
A soft bed waits for you, low to the floor and inviting.
Here, in this town, sleep comes easily and without weight.
Now let the town and the mountains begin to fade away.
Let the snow and the steam grow soft and dim and distant.
There is only the warmth now, deep within your own body.
Your breath moves slowly, in and gently out, all on its own.
Your arms are heavy, your legs are heavy, your whole body is held.
You are warm, and safe, and carried, like water carrying water.
Let the words grow quiet, drifting somewhere far behind you.
There is nothing to follow, nothing to hold, nothing to keep.
Let each thought dissolve like steam into the dark.
Sink down into the warm heaviness, soft and slow and deep.
You are held, and you are warm, and all is well.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Pamukkale
lines: Welcome, and thank you for letting yourself arrive here.
There is nothing left to do now, and nowhere else you need to be.
Let the day you have carried settle gently to the floor, like a coat slipping from your shoulders.
Feel the weight of your body sinking softly into whatever holds you.
Let your jaw loosen, let your shoulders fall, let your hands grow quiet and still.
Breathe in slowly, and let the breath out even more slowly, as if you were sighing the day away.
With each breath, you grow a little heavier, a little warmer, a little more at ease.
Tonight, you do not have to listen closely, and you do not have to remember anything.
We are going to wander together to a quiet hillside in Turkey, a place of warm white pools.
It is called Pamukkale, a slope of gleaming stone where soft warm water rests in shallow basins.
We will go slowly, and you may drift off whenever you wish.
If sleep comes before the end of the story, that is perfectly fine; you may simply let go.
Picture a wide hillside in the warm south of Turkey, glowing white under a soft sky.
From far away, it looks as though snow has fallen on only this one slope and nowhere else.
The people here gave it a gentle name long ago: Pamukkale, which means the cotton castle.
And it does look like cotton, like soft white cloth laid in folds down the hill.
Yet it is not snow, and it is not cloth at all; it is pale stone, smooth and bright.
Deep beneath the ground, warm water gathers in the dark, slowly and patiently.
The earth itself warms this water, and the water dissolves a whiteness from the rock as it waits.
Then, in its own slow time, the warm water rises, climbing up toward the light.
It reaches the top of the hill and spills gently over the lip, carrying its hidden whiteness with it.
The water is warm to the touch, soft and mineral and faintly sweet in the air.
You can imagine it welling up quietly, with no hurry at all, simply doing what it has always done.
Let your breath rise and fall as gently as that water, in no hurry to be anywhere.
Here is the quiet wonder of this place, told softly so you may drift while you hear it.
As the warm water flows over the edge and slows, it cannot hold all its whiteness anymore.
So it lays a thin trace of pale stone down, finer than a whisper, and flows on.
Each day the water comes, and each day it leaves behind another faint layer of white.
One day's gift of stone is far too thin to see, thinner than a single breath.
But the days gather, as days do, into seasons, and the seasons into years beyond counting.
Over an age so long the mind cannot hold it, the thin layers rise into ledges and shelves.
Shelf builds upon shelf, slowly, softly, until a whole hillside of white stone has grown.
This pale rock is called travertine, and it has been shaped by water alone.
It looks for all the world like a waterfall that paused mid-fall and turned gently to stone.
A frozen white cascade, made not in a moment but across uncountable patient days.
There is no rush in any of it, and there need be no rush in you tonight.
Now picture the shape that all this slow building has made on the hill.
The white stone has gathered into terraces, shallow pools set one below another.
Each pool has a soft curved rim, rounded and smooth, holding the warm water within.
They step down the slope in tiers, like a wide gentle staircase made of cloud.
Each basin brims with still water, warm and calm, barely moving in the light.
Where the water is shallow it shines almost white, and where it deepens it turns a soft turquoise.
The pools catch the sky and hold a pale blue and green glow against the gleaming stone.
In the sunlight the whole hillside dazzles, bright and soft at once, like snow that is warm.
The water spills so slowly from one pool to the next that you can hardly see it move.
It is the stillest, gentlest staircase you could imagine, made of warm water and white stone.
Let your mind step down those soft tiers, one quiet pool at a time, sinking lower with each one.
With every step down, you grow calmer, heavier, and closer to sleep.
Imagine slipping off your shoes and stepping out onto the warm white stone.
Beneath your bare feet the surface is smooth, with soft low ridges where the water has shaped it.
The stone is warm from the sun and the warm spring beneath, gentle against your skin.
You walk slowly, with no need to hurry, feeling the firm soft floor hold each step.
You lower yourself into one of the shallow pools, and the warm water rises around you.
It comes only to your ankles, perhaps your knees, soft and clear and soothing.
You sit, and the warmth wraps your legs and loosens everything it touches.
From here you look out, and far below the green valley stretches away in the soft haze.
Trees and fields lie quiet in the distance, hushed and small and far away.
The warmth rises gently through you, easing your back, your shoulders, your weary hands.
There is nothing to reach for and nothing to hold; the warm water holds you instead.
You let your eyes grow heavy as the warmth carries every last bit of tension away.
High on the heights above the white pools, there once stood an old and gracious city.
Its name was Hierapolis, and people came to it from far away to rest beside the warm springs.
Long ago, Romans and many others made the long journey simply to bathe and to be still.
They believed the warm waters could soothe a tired body and quiet a restless mind.
They built bathing halls and shaded courtyards, and they lingered in the gentle heat.
After their bathing they would rest, just as you are resting now, soft and unhurried.
Much of that city is quiet ruins today, pale stones lying open beneath the wide sky.
Fallen columns rest in the grass, warmed by the sun, keeping their old patient silence.
The crowds are long gone, and a deep stillness has settled over the ancient stones.
Yet the same warm water that drew them still rises and still flows, just as it always has.
It does not remember and it does not hurry; it simply keeps its old, slow, gentle way.
And you may rest in that same warmth now, across all those quiet years, soft and safe.
Now you can let the white hillside soften and grow dim, fading like mist at the edge of sleep.
Let the pools and the warm stone drift away; they will keep themselves without you.
There is nothing more to picture, and nothing more to follow.
Come back gently to the simple warmth of your own resting body.
Feel how heavy and warm you have become, sinking softly into the place that holds you.
Your breath moves on its own now, slow and easy, in and softly out.
You are safe, and you are held, and you have nowhere at all to be.
Let the words grow faint and let them blur, like warm water slipping over a soft white rim.
Each breath carries you a little deeper, a little further into the warm quiet dark.
There is nothing left to do but let go, and sink, and rest.
Let yourself drift now, soft and warm and safe.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Blue Lagoon
lines: Welcome, and let yourself arrive here, with nothing left to do tonight.
You can set the day down now, the way you set down a heavy bag at the end of a long walk.
There is nowhere else to be, and no task waiting that cannot wait until morning.
Let your shoulders soften, and feel them sink a little lower with each breath.
Let your jaw loosen, and let the small space behind your eyes grow quiet and dim.
Breathe in slowly, and let the breath out even more slowly, like steam rising and fading.
Tonight you are floating in a wide, warm lagoon, far away in Iceland, milky and blue.
The water holds you gently, warm against your skin, while the cold night air rests on your face.
You do not have to swim, and you do not have to move, only drift and be held.
Each breath carries you a little deeper into the warmth, a little further from the day.
There is nothing to follow and nothing to remember, only the warm water and the cool air.
It is perfectly fine to fall asleep before the end, so let yourself drift whenever you wish.
Let your mind sink down now, past the surface of the warm water, into the dark ground below.
Iceland sits on a place where the crust of the earth is thin and quietly restless.
Far beneath you, the rock is warm, and warmer still the deeper you imagine going.
Down there, water moves through the stone, and the heat of the ground passes gently into it.
Slowly that deep water grows warm, then warmer, and begins to rise toward the light.
It travels upward through the dark, patient and unhurried, carrying the warmth of the earth.
By the time it reaches you, it is soft and warm, like a bath drawn just for you.
You are floating on heat that began far below, in the quiet engine of the land.
There is no fire to see, only the steady warmth that the ground has given freely.
Let that thought settle you, that the warmth holding you comes from deep and far away.
It asks nothing of you, and it has been rising long before you ever arrived here.
Breathe it in, and let the warmth of the deep earth hold your whole tired body.
Now let your eyes rest on the colour of the water all around you.
It is not clear like glass, and you cannot see the bottom through it.
Instead it glows, a soft and milky blue, pale as the inside of a shell.
The water is full of a fine white mineral called silica, carried up from below.
The silica drifts in the water as countless tiny specks, too small to ever see.
When the daylight falls into the pool, those specks scatter it softly back to you.
The blue light lingers and spreads, while the rest of the light melts away.
So the whole lagoon seems to shine from within, luminous and gentle, like an opal.
It is the colour of calm itself, soft and cool to look upon, though the water is warm.
You could cup the water in your hands and watch it turn clear and ordinary.
Yet all around you it stays that dreaming, milky blue, glowing quietly in the steam.
Let that pale blue fill your mind, soft and endless, with nothing sharp anywhere in it.
Now feel the wider place that cradles this warm and glowing pool.
All around the lagoon lies a field of old black lava, dark and still.
The stone was once melted and flowing, and long ago it cooled into rough, quiet rock.
Against that black ground, the pale blue water glows even softer and brighter.
Steam rises everywhere from the warm surface, drifting up into the cold, clear air.
It curls and lifts in slow white ribbons, then thins and vanishes into the sky.
Imagine wading in slowly, the warm water climbing gently up your body as you go.
Above the surface the air is cool and fresh, and it touches lightly on your cheeks.
Below the surface you are wrapped in warmth, soft and steady and complete.
That is the whole feeling of this place, warm water below and cool air above.
Your body floats in the middle of it, held between the warmth and the cold.
Let yourself rest in that gentle contrast, perfectly comfortable, perfectly still.
At the quiet edges of the lagoon, the white mineral gathers and settles.
It forms a soft pale mud, smooth and cool, as soft as fresh cream.
People scoop a little of it up and smooth it gently over their faces.
It dries slowly to a soft white mask, cool and calm against warm skin.
You could do the same, with the lightest touch, only if you wished to.
Or you could simply float and watch, letting your hands rest in the warmth.
All around you, other bathers drift slowly through the rising steam.
They are half-hidden, soft grey shapes that move without any hurry at all.
No one speaks loudly here, and the quiet seems to belong to the place itself.
Now and then a face appears in the steam, calm and pale, and fades away again.
Everyone here is doing the same gentle thing, drifting, warm, and slow.
Let their slow drifting carry your own mind even slower, even softer.
Now let the sky above the steam open wide and dark and clear.
Sometimes a soft snow falls here, or a fine rain drifts down through the cold air.
The flakes or the small drops touch the warm water and melt away at once.
You float on your back, warm to your chin, and feel them land lightly on your face.
Each one is cool for a heartbeat, and then it is gone, leaving only warmth.
On a clear winter night, something else may slowly wake in the sky above you.
Pale green ribbons of light begin to shimmer and sway across the dark.
This is the aurora, soft curtains of colour drifting high over the lagoon.
They brighten and fade, fold and unfold, in a silence you can almost hear.
So there is warmth below you, and quiet wonder far above you, all at once.
And you are held in the middle, floating, safe, with nothing you must do.
Let the green light drift, and let your breathing drift along with it.
Now let the lagoon begin to fade, softly, the way a dream loosens its edges.
Let the colours blur and the steam grow dim, and let the words fall quiet.
What stays is only the warmth, holding your body the way the water held it.
Your limbs are heavy and warm, sinking gently into the soft place where you lie.
Your breath is slow now, slower than the falling snow, slower than the drifting steam.
There is nothing to picture and nothing to follow anymore, only rest.
You are warm, and you are floating, and you are completely safe and held.
Each breath out lets you sink a little deeper into the warmth and the quiet.
Let the lagoon go, let the night go, let even these words go now.
There is only the warm dark, soft all around you, asking nothing of you.
Drift, and let yourself be carried gently down into sleep.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Roman Baths
lines: Welcome.
There is nothing left for you to do now.
Let the day go, the way a tide lets go of the shore.
You can feel the bed beneath you, holding all of your weight.
Let your shoulders soften, and let them grow heavy.
Let your breath grow long and slow, with no effort at all.
Tonight you will step softly into an ancient Roman bath.
It is built around a warm spring, a gentle gift of water that has flowed for ages.
There is nowhere to hurry, and nothing to remember.
Each breath out lets a little more of the day dissolve.
You are simply here, warm and quiet, settling deeper.
And it is perfectly fine to fall asleep long before the end.
Imagine a place where warm water rises out of the deep earth.
It has risen here day after day, age after age, long before anyone was watching.
The water comes up faintly steaming, soft and warm against the cool air.
People long ago felt that such a thing must be a sacred gift.
They could not understand it, so they loved it, and they called it holy.
The Romans came and built a great green pool around the steaming water.
They lined it with smooth stone and ringed it with tall columns.
Lamplight rests on the surface, swaying gently with every ripple.
The room breathes with a low warmth, and the air feels kind.
You can almost hear the quiet lap of water against the worn stone.
The warmth seems to rise up and meet you, asking nothing in return.
You let yourself believe, just for tonight, that the water is glad you came.
The bath is not one room but a slow journey through many.
You leave your clothes at the door, and with them, the weight of the day.
You smooth warm oil over your skin, and it begins to glow.
First you move into the warm room, where the air is soft and mild.
Your muscles, one by one, begin to remember how to rest.
Then you step into the hot, steamy room, the caldarium.
Here the steam wraps around you like a thick, gentle blanket.
You feel the long day rise out of you as warmth and breath.
After the heat comes a cool, clear plunge, bright and quieting.
Then a slow scraping clean, unhurried, drawing the tiredness away.
Stage by stage, your body comes unwound, like a knot loosening in warm hands.
There is nothing to do but follow the warmth from room to room.
The Roman bath was never only a place to wash.
It was a place to rest, and to be among people, slowly.
Friends meet here in the warm half-light and speak in low voices.
There is quiet talk, soft laughter, and the steady echo of water.
No one is hurrying, and no one expects anything of you.
The cares of the day are set down at the door, like sandals.
Some float in the warm pool, eyes half closed, saying nothing at all.
Some sit at the edge, letting their feet trail in the water.
The sounds blur together into a soft and drowsy hum.
You are part of this gentle gathering, held by the same warmth.
Time moves slowly here, the way it moves in a dream.
To be in the bath is simply to be allowed to rest.
The warm spring had a goddess, and her name was Sulis Minerva.
The Romans believed she lived in the steaming water and listened.
Bathers would lean close and whisper their hopes into the rising warmth.
They spoke of small worries, and quiet wishes, and people they loved.
Then they dropped little coins and tokens into the gentle water.
Each offering was a way of trusting the spring to hold their words.
The warm water received it all without judgment, and kept it safe.
Imagine handing your own small cares, one by one, into the steam.
You do not need to carry them through the night.
Let the warm spring take them, the way it has taken so many before.
The goddess of the water asks for nothing but your ease.
So you whisper your last small wish, and let the warmth keep it.
There is something deeply comforting in how constant the spring is.
The same warm water still rises today, long after the Romans are gone.
Their voices have faded, their lamps have gone dark, and yet the water comes.
It rises faithful and warm, just as it always has.
It is as if the earth keeps a small fire burning far below.
A quiet fire, tended by no one, kept only to comfort us.
Through every winter and every silence, the warmth keeps coming up.
You can rest on that constancy, the way you rest on the steady ground.
Something warm and old is still flowing, gently, even now.
It has outlasted every hurry, every worry, every long day.
And it will still be rising, warm and patient, while you sleep.
The earth is keeping its small warmth, and it is keeping it for you.
Now you can let the old bath begin to fade.
Let the columns soften, and the lamplight blur, and the voices grow faint.
The steam thins, the words drift apart, and only the warmth remains.
Come back to the warm heaviness of your own body, here in your bed.
Feel how heavy and safe your arms and legs have become.
Your breath is slow, and long, and easy, all on its own.
You are held, exactly where you are, warm and quiet.
There is nothing more to follow, and nothing more to know.
Let the words dissolve like steam into the soft dark.
Let the warmth carry you down, gently, with no effort at all.
You are safe, and you are warm, and you can let go now.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Crystal Cave
lines: Welcome, and let yourself arrive here, with nothing left to do.
The day is behind you now, and you can set it gently down.
Let your shoulders soften, and let them sink a little into the warmth beneath you.
There is nowhere to go, and nothing to reach for, and no one needing anything from you.
Feel the weight of your body, held and resting, heavy and safe.
Let your breath grow slow and long, easy as a tide that asks for nothing.
With each soft breath out, let a little more of the day melt away.
Tonight, in your mind only, you will go down into a hidden cave deep beneath the earth.
It is a quiet room of giant crystals, far below the ground, made for no one to see.
You do not have to picture it perfectly, only let the words carry you down.
If you drift off before the story ends, that is perfectly fine.
Sleep is welcome here, and you may let it come whenever it wishes.
So let yourself sink, slow and unhurried, down through the warm dark of the earth.
Far below the busy world, deeper than roots, deeper than rivers, there is a hidden room.
The earth made it long ago and sealed it away, a secret kept in the quiet stone.
Inside, the air is still, and the dark is soft and complete.
And rising out of that dark are crystals, great beams of pale stone taller than a person.
They are made of selenite, a clear and gentle form of the soft mineral called gypsum.
Some lean like fallen pillars of glass, crossing the room in long, calm angles.
Others rise like smooth blades, leaning together, resting one upon another.
They are cool and translucent, and the dark seems to glow faintly within them.
Nothing hurries here, and nothing stirs, and the silence is wide and kind.
You feel how old this room is, and how patiently it has waited.
Let your breath slow to match its stillness, soft and unhurried and deep.
These great crystals did not appear; they grew, slowly, over an unimaginable depth of time.
For ages beyond counting, this chamber was filled with warm, still, mineral-rich water.
The water held a dissolved mineral, unseen and patient, drifting in the quiet dark.
And atom by atom, grain by tiny grain, that mineral settled onto the crystals.
Each beam grew the way a thought grows in sleep, too slowly to ever be seen.
A single hair of growth might take longer than you could ever imagine.
There was no hurry in it, none at all, only the long and gentle patience of the earth.
While whole ages turned above, the crystals lengthened by the smallest of breaths.
Layer upon layer, the soft mineral gathered, and the pale beams grew vast and tall.
To stand among them is to stand inside a piece of time made visible.
Let that slowness settle into you, the calm of something growing without rush.
Breathe out, and let your own thoughts grow as slow and soft as the crystals.
Now let the room grow quieter still, and let yourself rest within its stillness.
Imagine a faint and gentle light, soft as candleglow, drifting across the crystal faces.
It slides along the smooth pale beams, slow and quiet, touching one and then the next.
Where it meets the clear stone, it sinks in, and the crystal seems to hold a small glow.
Here and there the light scatters, and the dark fills with soft and drifting glints.
Each face is smooth as still water, cool and clear and endlessly calm.
The light asks for nothing, and the crystals answer only with a quiet shine.
This is a warm and silent room the earth made for no one at all to see.
And yet it is beautiful, gleaming softly in the dark, simply because it is.
There is no sound here but the sound of your own slow breath.
Let the soft glints drift behind your eyes, gentle and slow and dim.
And feel the deep peace of a place that has been still for so very long.
Let your gaze move slowly now across the great shapes of the cave.
Smooth angular blades rise on every side, long and pale and calm.
Beams lean and cross one another, like fallen columns laid gently down.
Some are clear as ice, and the dark shows softly straight through them.
Others are milky and pale, glowing faintly like the moon behind a cloud.
They grow in every direction at once, leaning out, reaching across the quiet.
It is as though a burst of light was caught here and slowly turned to stone.
A frozen flowering, an unhurried star, spread wide and held in stillness.
Nothing here is sharp or hurried; every shape is smooth and broad and calm.
You could rest your hand on the cool clear stone and feel only stillness.
Let these gentle shapes drift through your mind, soft and pale and slow.
And let your breath grow softer still as you rest among the quiet crystals.
Think, softly, of how long this room has kept its quiet secret.
Sealed away in the warm dark, it grew while whole ages passed far above.
Forests rose and fell, and seas came and went, and still it waited, unseen.
Grain by patient grain, the crystals lengthened, asking nothing of the world.
No eye watched them, and no hand touched them, through all that endless time.
It is a jewel-room of the deep earth, made slowly and kept in silence.
There is wonder in a thing so beautiful that grew with no one near to see it.
It simply was, and is, gleaming patiently in the dark beneath your feet.
Let that quiet patience hold you now, steady and slow and kind.
You have nothing to finish, and nowhere to be, and all the time in the world.
Like the cave, you may simply rest, and grow soft, and be still.
Breathe slowly, and let the deep calm of the patient earth settle over you.
Now let the cave grow dim, and let its pale shapes gently fade.
You do not need to hold the picture any longer; let it drift away.
Come slowly back to the warmth of your own resting body.
Feel how heavy and soft you have become, sinking into the place you lie.
Your breath is slow now, and long, and easy, moving all on its own.
There is nothing to do, and nothing to keep, and nowhere left to go.
You are safe, and you are held, and you are warm in the quiet dark.
Let the words grow soft and far away, dissolving like light into stone.
Let each slow breath carry you a little deeper toward sleep.
Heavy, and warm, and held, you may let go completely now.
Let everything soften, and fade, and grow still.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Glow-Worm Cave
lines: Welcome, and let yourself arrive here, just as you are.
There is nothing left for you to do tonight.
Let the day go, with all its small noises and its tasks.
Feel the weight of your body settle into the place where you rest.
Soften your shoulders, and let your jaw grow loose and easy.
Let your breath lengthen, slowly, with no effort at all.
Each time you breathe out, you sink a little deeper.
Tonight you will drift in a little boat through a dark and gentle cave.
Above you, thousands of tiny living lights will glow, soft and cool.
There is nowhere to go, and nothing to reach for.
You only need to float, and to listen, and to let go.
It is perfectly fine to fall asleep long before the end.
Imagine a quiet hillside, green and folded, far from any town.
Beneath it lies a cave of smooth, pale limestone, older than memory.
A slow river runs through it, dark and cool and very still.
You walk down a gentle path, and the daylight fades behind you.
The air grows cool against your skin, soft and faintly damp.
Everything quiets, until the loudest sound is your own slow breath.
At the water's edge waits a small, flat boat, low and steady.
You step in, and it holds you with an easy, rocking calm.
Someone unseen draws the boat forward by a hand along the rope.
You glide out onto the black water, slow and smooth and silent.
The world above you is forgotten now, far away and unimportant.
There is only the dark, the water, and the gentle drift onward.
As your eyes soften to the dark, you begin to look up.
High above you, the cave ceiling opens into a wide, dim hush.
And there, scattered across it, are thousands of tiny points of light.
Each one glows a soft and tender blue-green, cool as moonlight.
They do not flicker or rush; they simply shine, steady and calm.
It is like a whole galaxy spread close above your upturned face.
A private night sky, hidden deep beneath the quiet hill.
The lights gather in soft drifts, like clouds of distant stars.
Some hang alone, faint and far; others cluster, bright and near.
You feel very small, and very safe, beneath this gentle sky.
Your breath slows further as you gaze up into the glow.
There is nothing to understand, only this quiet wonder to receive.
Each of these little lights is a living thing, small and patient.
It is a glow-worm, the young of a small and harmless fly.
It rests along the cave roof within a thread of soft silk.
From inside, it makes a cool and gentle light of its own.
The light asks nothing of you; it simply glows in the dark.
Down from each glow-worm hang fine silk lines, delicate as dew.
Tiny beads of moisture cling along them, catching the faint shine.
They drift down like the slenderest of fishing lines, barely there.
Small insects, drawn upward toward the glow, wander gently near.
And so the little light feeds, quietly, in its patient way.
You need hold none of this; let the knowing drift past you.
It is enough to float here beneath the soft and living stars.
Now let your gaze drift down, toward the water you float upon.
The river lies glassy and black, smooth as polished glass.
Not a ripple stirs it, save the slow passing of your boat.
And there, in the dark water, every light is doubled.
The whole glowing sky is mirrored softly beneath you.
You seem to float between two skies, one above and one below.
Stars above your face, and stars in the quiet deep beneath.
You hang, weightless, in the still space held between them.
The hush around you is so complete it feels almost soft.
Somewhere, a single drop of water falls, and you hear it clearly.
The small sound spreads, and fades, and the silence returns.
You breathe it in, this perfect quiet, and let it hold you.
The boat drifts on, slow and smooth, through the gentle dark.
Overhead, the soft constellations turn, easy and unhurried.
New drifts of light come into view as you glide beneath them.
Each is a small calm sun, shining only for this quiet cave.
You do not steer, and you do not hurry; you simply go.
The deep quiet wraps around you, warm as a soft blanket.
Your body grows heavier, sinking into the steady, rocking calm.
Each breath out lets a little more of you melt away.
The lights above blur softly as your eyes grow tired and slow.
You are carried, gently, with nowhere at all to arrive.
The river knows the way, and you may safely let go.
Drift, and float, and let the soft stars carry you onward.
Now let the cave begin to soften and fade from your mind.
The little lights blur into a warm and distant glow.
You no longer need the boat, or the river, or the dark.
There is only your body now, heavy and floating and still.
Feel how deeply you rest, held safe within the quiet.
Your breath moves on its own, slow and easy and low.
There is nothing to hold, and nothing left to do.
Let the words grow faint, and farther, and softer still.
Let them dissolve, like ripples fading into calm water.
You are safe, you are held, you are carried into sleep.
Drift down, gently, into the warm and waiting dark.
Rest now.

lectures.title: Stalactites and Stalagmites
lines: Welcome, and let yourself arrive here, in this soft and quiet place.
There is nothing left to do now, and nowhere else you need to be.
Let the day you have carried slip gently from your shoulders.
You can set it down like a heavy coat beside the door.
Feel the weight of your body sinking softly into the bed beneath you.
Let your jaw loosen, let your hands unfold, let your forehead grow smooth.
Draw a slow breath in, and let an even slower breath ease its way out.
With each breath, you grow a little heavier, a little calmer, a little more still.
Tonight, in your mind, you step gently into a quiet cave deep underground.
It is hung with slow stone icicles, built drop by patient drop.
We will wander there together, in no hurry at all.
And it is perfectly fine to fall asleep long before the end.
Picture a single drop of rain, far above the cave, falling on a quiet hill.
It lands in the soft soil and soaks slowly downward into the dark earth.
As it sinks, it gathers a faint breath of the air, a gentle trace of acid.
This makes the water just barely able to soften stone, the lightest touch.
Down it trickles, threading through the pale limestone beneath the hill.
As it goes, it dissolves a whisper of the rock, carrying it along.
The stone does not vanish loudly, but melts a little into the moving water.
Patient and unhurried, the drop finds its slow way through tiny cracks.
It travels for a long time in the cool and silent dark.
At last it reaches the roof of our quiet cave, far below the world.
There it seeps through and gathers, hanging as a single bright drop.
It trembles for a moment in the still air, holding all that it has carried.
Now watch what the hanging drop leaves behind before it lets go.
As it rests on the ceiling, it gives back the faintest ring of stone.
The ring is thinner than a thread, barely there at all.
Then the drop falls away, and another slowly gathers in its place.
That drop too leaves its own delicate ring of mineral behind.
Ring settles upon ring, each one resting softly on the last.
Over a patience too vast to picture, the rings begin to reach downward.
Slowly, slowly, a slender stone icicle takes shape on the ceiling.
This is a stalactite, growing down toward the floor far below.
You can remember its name, for it holds tight to the ceiling above.
It hangs there in the dark, gleaming faintly, growing as you breathe.
And still the drops keep coming, one after another, never in a rush.
Follow the drop that loosens and falls from the tip of the stone icicle.
Down it drifts through the quiet, and lands softly on the cave floor.
There, too, it leaves behind its small gift of dissolved stone.
Drop after drop falls gently to the very same spot below.
Each one adds the thinnest layer to a gentle, rising mound.
Where the icicle points down, a matching shape begins to climb up.
This rounded mound is a stalagmite, reaching slowly toward the ceiling.
It might reach up mightily, you can tell yourself, to recall its name.
One grows down from above, and one grows up from below.
They are made by the very same patient drops of falling water.
Above and below, the cave is quietly building itself in the dark.
And all of it happens without a sound louder than a gentle drip.
Imagine waiting beside them for an immense and unhurried reach of time.
The icicle above grows a little longer, drop by patient drop.
The mound below grows a little taller, gift by gentle gift.
Slowly, the space between them narrows in the dark.
The tip reaching down and the tip reaching up draw closer.
After ages beyond counting, the two may finally meet and touch.
Where they join, they grow together into one smooth pillar of stone.
It stands like a quiet column between the floor and the ceiling.
Think of it as a slow handshake between below and above.
Neither one hurried, neither one knowing that it would arrive.
Yet here it stands, joined and whole, in the patient dark.
You can rest your eyes upon it and feel how unhurried the world can be.
Consider how slowly all of this unfolds in the cool and silent dark.
Many of these stones grow only a hair's breadth in a long human life.
A whole lifetime might pass while a single icicle thickens that little.
The cave does not measure time the way you do.
It keeps a slower clock, one counted out in ages rather than years.
Every soft drip in the dark is one quiet tick of that ancient clock.
Drip, and a whisper of stone is given to the icicle above.
Drip, and a whisper of stone is given to the mound below.
The cave you stand in has been forming since long before your birth.
It will keep forming long after this quiet night has passed.
And still it asks for nothing but the next slow, falling drop.
Let that endless, gentle ticking carry you deeper into rest.
Now let the cave grow soft and dim, and let the stones fade from your mind.
There is nothing more to follow, and nothing more to hold.
Let the words begin to blur and drift, like drops in the far dark.
Feel again the gentle weight of your body, heavy and at ease.
Feel the slow rise and the slower fall of your quiet breath.
You are safe here, held and warm, with nothing left to do.
Let each thought soften and dissolve, the way stone dissolves in rain.
Heavier now, and slower, sinking deeper with every breath.
The drip fades, the dark grows kind, and you let it all go.
Down and down, gently, into a soft and dreamless quiet.
Sleep is near, and you may step into it whenever you wish.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Painted Caves
lines: Welcome, and let yourself arrive here, just as you are.
There is nothing left to do tonight, and nowhere else you need to be.
Let the day you have carried slip from your shoulders, soft and unhurried.
Feel the weight of your body settling down into the place where you rest.
Let your breath grow a little slower, a little deeper, all on its own.
With each gentle out-breath, let something small be set down and released.
Soften your forehead, your jaw, and the quiet spaces around your eyes.
Let your hands grow heavy, and your shoulders melt away from your ears.
Tonight we will step softly together into an ancient cave, deep in the rock.
Long ago, by the light of small fires, people painted animals upon its walls.
There is nothing you must remember, and nothing you must follow or hold.
It is perfectly fine to fall asleep long before the end.
Imagine a hillside in an age of ages, and a low opening in the stone.
You step inside, and the cool air of the cave breathes softly against your skin.
The daylight thins behind you, and the passage leads gently down into the dark.
Far from the sun, the world grows quiet, hushed, and wonderfully still.
You carry a small stone lamp, a hollow cradling a little pool of animal fat.
A single flame floats upon it, warm and golden, no bigger than a leaf.
By its tender light the walls glow honey-gold all around you.
The shadows lean and sway, breathing with the flame as you move.
Your footsteps are soft, and the silence wraps around you like a blanket.
The air smells of cool stone and the faint sweetness of the burning lamp.
Here, deep in the earth, time itself seems to slow and gently settle.
You feel safe in this small ring of light, held by the quiet rock.
And then, where the lamp light touches the wall, the animals appear.
A great herd of horses flows across the stone, manes lifted as if in wind.
Wild bulls and aurochs stand among them, broad and calm and strong.
Deer step lightly past, their antlers branching like slender winter trees.
Bison gather close, heavy-shouldered, lowering their shaggy heads.
Here and there a lion moves, quiet and golden, and a woolly rhino looms.
They are drawn in flowing lines of black charcoal, dark and sure.
Warm red and yellow ochre fill them with the colour of earth and sun.
The lines are soft and certain, laid down by a patient, loving hand.
Nothing here is quite still, for every creature seems caught mid-stride.
The whole wall feels alive, a herd forever moving and never tired.
You watch them drift past in the lamplight, gentle and unafraid.
Look closer, and you see how cleverly the painters used the rock itself.
The wall is not flat, but swells and hollows, rounded here and dipping there.
Where the stone bulges outward, a painter set the flank of a galloping horse.
So the curve of the rock becomes the curve of a living, breathing side.
A hollow becomes the soft of a belly, a ridge becomes an arching back.
The animals are not painted upon the wall so much as drawn out of it.
And as the flame wavers, the shadows shift across every swell and dip.
In that moving light, the herd seems to surge and ripple along the stone.
A horse appears to leap, and a bison seems to turn its great slow head.
The painters knew this, and gave their creatures the breath of the fire.
You stand quietly, watching the whole wall stir and settle and stir again.
It is the oldest of moving pictures, alive in the warm and patient dark.
Among the animals, you notice something smaller, and very tender.
Here and there upon the wall are the soft shapes of human hands.
Someone pressed a hand flat to the cold stone, fingers gently spread.
Then they blew a soft cloud of powdered colour all around it.
When the hand lifted away, its shape remained, pale upon the wall.
A hand like yours, with the same five fingers, reaching out of the dark.
It is a quiet greeting, soft as a whisper across an age of ages.
It seems to say, simply and gently, I was here.
You could almost lift your own hand and rest it against that shape.
Two hands meeting across all that time, palm to faded palm.
There is such tenderness in it, small and human and kind.
You feel how near they are, those people of the long-ago firelight.
After the painting was done, the people went away, back to the sun.
In time the caves were sealed, and the dark closed softly over the walls.
And there the animals rested, untouched, in a silence beyond counting.
An immense span of seasons passed above, while the herd slept below.
No wind, no rain, no light reached them, and so the colours stayed fresh.
The red stayed warm, the black stayed deep, the gold stayed clear and bright.
Through an age of ages the horses waited, mid-gallop, in the patient dark.
Then, long ago and far from now, someone crept in through a narrow way.
They lifted a small light, just as you hold yours, and slowly looked up.
And there, all at once, the great herd rose out of the shadows to meet them.
Across all that time, the first artists and the new eyes met, face to face.
You feel that meeting now, gentle and astonishing, in the soft gold light.
Now let the cave grow dim, and let the animals drift quietly out of mind.
Let the small lamp soften, and the warm walls fade into the dark.
There is nothing more to see, and nothing more you need to hold.
Come back now to the simple weight of your body where it rests.
Feel how heavy and how easy your arms and your legs have become.
Let your breath move slowly, in and then out, all on its own.
You are safe, and warm, and gently held in the quiet of the night.
Let the words grow faint, and let them dissolve like wisps of smoke.
There is nothing to follow, and nowhere at all you need to go.
Let yourself sink down, soft and slow, into the deep and easy dark.
Sleep is near now, and it welcomes you with open arms.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Tortoise
lines: Welcome, and let yourself settle into this quiet hour.
There is nothing left to do now, nothing to fix or to finish.
Let the day you have carried slip gently from your shoulders.
Wherever you are lying, let the bed take your whole weight.
Soften your forehead, your jaw, the small muscles around your eyes.
Let your hands grow heavy, your feet grow heavy, your body sinking.
Draw one slow breath in, and let it out even more slowly.
There is no hurry here, and there is nowhere else you need to be.
Tonight you keep company with the tortoise, the slowest of all wanderers.
It moves through the world unhurried, content with each unrushed step.
Let its gentle pace become the pace of your breath and your thoughts.
And if you drift off to sleep before the end, that is perfectly fine.
Picture the tortoise now, somewhere warm and green and quiet.
It begins to walk, though walk is almost too quick a word.
It lifts one round foot, slow as the hour hand of a clock.
It sets that foot down upon the soft earth, in no hurry at all.
Then another foot rises, and the great shell sways just a little.
It moves at a pace that lies somewhere beyond patience.
There is no race in its mind, no place it must reach by nightfall.
Each step is complete in itself, asking nothing of the next.
You can feel your own breathing slow to match that gentle rhythm.
In, and out, the way the tortoise lifts a foot and sets it down.
Nothing pulls it forward, and nothing chases it from behind.
It is simply here, moving softly through a long and easy day.
Upon its back the tortoise carries a home it can never leave.
Its shell is a smooth dome of bony plates, fused into one piece.
This dome is both its armour and its house, always close around it.
Imagine carrying your own quiet shelter wherever you happen to go.
When trouble comes, the tortoise does not run, for running is not its way.
Instead it draws its head softly inward, and folds its legs away.
It waits, sealed within its own calm room, until the danger drifts past.
There is great peace in knowing you carry your safety with you.
You too are wrapped tonight in your own warm and sheltering quiet.
The blankets are your shell, the dark room your patient dome.
Nothing can reach you here that you must answer or attend to.
You may simply rest inside, the way the tortoise rests inside its own.
The tortoise lives a life longer than almost any creature you know.
The giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Aldabra are slowest of all.
They can live longer than the oldest of people, by many quiet years.
A single tortoise may outlast a whole human lifetime, and then more.
It watches generation after generation come and go, while it grazes on.
Children grow grey, and still the tortoise wanders its same green hill.
There is no panic in such long days, no fear of running out of time.
When your years are counted so slowly, an afternoon is a small thing.
Perhaps this is why it never hurries, for hurry has no meaning for it.
Let that vast and unhurried patience settle softly over you now.
Tonight there is more than enough time for everything, and for nothing.
You can let the minutes stretch and soften like a long warm afternoon.
The tortoise lives by the gentle rhythm of warmth and of light.
It is a cold-blooded creature, and the sun is what stirs it awake.
In the cool of morning it lies still, waiting for the first warm rays.
Slowly the sun climbs, and slowly the tortoise begins to glow with heat.
Warmed at last, it ambles out to graze on grass and tender leaves.
It crops each mouthful slowly, tasting the green of the morning.
It finds water and drinks deep, in long and patient swallows.
When the day grows hot, it seeks the shade and settles down to rest.
Its life is measured not in minutes but in seasons and in suns.
There is no clock it must obey, only the slow turning of the light.
Feel your own body settle into that same warm and easy rhythm.
Warm, fed, watered, and resting, with nothing left to want.
You may remember the old story of the tortoise and the hare.
The hare was quick, and boasted, and darted far ahead.
The tortoise only walked, slow and steady, never once stopping.
The hare grew tired of its own speed and lay down to sleep.
And the tortoise, step after patient step, walked quietly past.
When the hare awoke, the slow one had already reached the end.
Slow and steady carries you through, the old fable gently says.
You do not need to rush to arrive where you are going.
You do not need to be quick to be sure, or to be kind.
There is a deep wisdom in moving softly through your days.
Let the tortoise teach you that arriving is not the point at all.
The slow walk itself is the whole of the gift.
Now let the tortoise wander on, slow and untroubled, into the dark.
Let its shell and its gentle steps fade softly from your mind.
There is nothing more to follow, nothing more to picture or to hold.
Return now only to the heaviness of your own resting body.
Feel how deeply your limbs sink into the warmth beneath you.
Your breath moves on its own now, slow and quiet and sure.
You are safe, you are held, and you are wrapped in the soft dark.
Let the words grow distant, like a voice heard across still water.
Let them blur, and soften, and dissolve into the quiet.
There is nowhere to go and nothing to do but breathe and sink.
Drift now, gently, the way a tortoise eases down to sleep.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Snail
lines: Welcome, and let yourself arrive here, just as you are.
There is nothing left to do tonight, and nowhere else to be.
Let the day you have carried slip gently from your shoulders.
You can set it down now, all of it, and let it drift away.
Feel the weight of your body sinking softly into the bed.
Let your jaw soften, and let your hands grow loose and easy.
Breathe in slowly, and let the breath out even more slowly.
With every breath, you are sinking a little deeper into rest.
Tonight, we will follow the snail, in no hurry at all.
It carries its home upon its back, and it is never late.
There is nothing it must rush toward, and neither is there for you.
If you fall asleep before the end, that is perfectly fine.
Picture a snail in the cool green hush of a quiet garden.
It does not walk, for it has no feet at all.
Instead it moves upon a single smooth and muscular foot.
Along that foot run slow and gentle waves, soft as ripples on a pond.
Each small wave carries the snail forward, a little at a time.
It glides, rather than walks, smooth and unhurried and calm.
There is no effort you can see, only a quiet flowing on.
Watch how patient it is, content to take its time.
Behind it lies a faint and shining trail, like silver thread.
You can breathe in time with that slow and gliding motion.
In as it gathers, and out as it eases gently forward.
Let your own pace soften, until you too are gliding into rest.
Let us follow that silver trail a little further now.
As the snail glides, it lays down a thread of slick and cooling mucus.
This soft trail smooths the path before it, wherever it must go.
Upon it, the snail can cross a rough edge without any harm.
It can even pass along the very point of a thorn, unhurt.
Nothing sharp can reach it, for it carries its own gentle road.
And in the early light, that trail begins to shine.
It catches the morning sun like a thread of woven moonlight.
A quiet ribbon of silver, looping softly across the leaves.
What a gentle thought, to lay down softness as you go.
You, too, may smooth your own way with each easy breath.
Let the silver thread shimmer, and let your thoughts grow still.
Now let your gaze rest upon the shell that it carries.
This is the home the snail has grown entirely on its own.
It is a perfect spiral, coiling round and round and round.
Each turn winds inward, smooth and even, toward a quiet centre.
Wherever the snail wanders, its home goes softly with it.
It never has to leave, and never has to find its way back.
And should it wish, it can withdraw completely inside.
There, in the curl of the shell, it is wholly and truly safe.
No cold, no noise, no trouble can follow it within.
Imagine carrying such a refuge always close to you.
Your own warm bed is just such a shell tonight.
Curl into it, safe and held, and let yourself rest.
The snail loves the soft and gentle hours best of all.
It comes out after rain, when the world is cool and damp.
It wanders in the dew of evening, glistening on the grass.
From the bright and dusty heat of midday, it quietly hides.
It tucks itself away in shade until the cool returns.
Its world is a small and tender one of moisture and green.
Dim leaves, wet stems, and the deep hush beneath them all.
There is a softness to that world, a coolness like evening air.
Feel that same cool hush settling gently over you now.
The room grows dim, and the air grows soft and kind.
Like the snail, you seek the quiet and the shade of night.
Let the cool darkness fold around you and hold you close.
And when the world turns dry, or the long cold comes, the snail sleeps.
It draws itself deep within the spiral of its shell.
Then it seals the door with a thin and papery lid.
Behind that gentle door, it rests in perfect stillness.
It may sleep through a whole long season in this way.
No hurry stirs it, and no worry breaks its calm.
It simply waits, patient and untroubled, deep in dreamless rest.
It is waiting for the rain to call it softly out again.
And the rain will come, in its own quiet time, and wake it.
Until then, there is only stillness, only the long and easy sleep.
You may sink into that same deep stillness now.
There is nothing to wait for, and nothing to do but rest.
Now let the little snail drift softly out of mind.
Let the garden fade, and the silver trail dissolve.
There is nothing more to follow, and nothing more to know.
Feel only the heaviness of your body, sinking deep and warm.
Feel the slow and easy rhythm of your breath.
In, and out, slower and softer with each gentle wave.
You are safe here, held and quiet, like a snail within its shell.
Let the words grow faint, and let them fade away.
Let them blur, and soften, and slip beyond your hearing.
There is only warmth now, only stillness, only rest.
Let go, and drift, and sink into the quiet.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Manatee
lines: Welcome, and let yourself be just where you are.
There is nothing left to do tonight, and nowhere else to be.
Let the day go now, the way warm water lets go of the shore.
You can feel your shoulders soften, and let them drop a little lower.
Let your jaw loosen, and let your hands grow heavy and still.
Each breath you let out can be a little longer than the one before.
Breathe in slowly, and breathe out even more slowly.
Tonight you will drift with the manatee, the gentle sea cow.
You will float beside it in warm and shallow water.
There is no hurry here, and there is nothing you must remember.
If you fall asleep before the end, that is perfectly fine.
Let the words carry you down into rest.
The manatee is a large and round and gentle creature.
People call it the sea cow, for it grazes slow and calm.
It moves through the warm water without any hurry at all.
Its face is soft and whiskered, with small and kindly eyes.
It has never hurt a single thing in all its quiet life.
It carries no claws, no teeth to fear, no sharpness anywhere.
It simply drifts through its days, unbothered and at ease.
Nothing about it is sharp, and nothing about it is quick.
You can picture its broad grey body, smooth and rounded as a stone worn soft.
Imagine resting a hand on that warm and gentle back.
It would only turn its whiskered face to you, slow and unafraid.
Let its gentleness settle over you like a warm and quiet blanket.
Below the manatee lies a wide green meadow of seagrass.
The soft blades sway in the slow and easy current.
Here the manatee grazes for hours, calm and unhurried.
It crops the tender green blades gently, one mouthful at a time.
There is no rush to finish, and no reason to look up.
It browses through the warm shallow bay the way clouds drift through a sky.
Sometimes it wanders into a slow and winding river to graze.
The seagrass meadow gives all that it could ever need.
You can hear, very faintly, the soft tearing of the gentle blades.
Each slow mouthful is enough, and then it takes another.
It is a peaceful grazer, content in the quiet green.
Let your own breath slow to the rhythm of that easy grazing.
Out over the meadow, the manatee hangs almost perfectly still.
It neither sinks toward the sand nor rises toward the light.
It simply hovers, weightless, held by the gentle water.
Now and then it paddles once with its broad and rounded tail.
That single slow stroke is enough to carry it along.
It rolls over slowly, turning in the water like a leaf in no wind.
Nothing holds it down, and nothing pulls it up.
It is the very picture of floating ease.
Feel how your own body grows weightless as you imagine this.
Your limbs are heavy, and yet you seem to float.
You hang in soft warm water, neither sinking nor rising.
Let yourself drift, the way the gentle manatee drifts.
Every few minutes, the manatee rises softly to breathe.
It lifts its nose just above the surface, slow and quiet.
It takes one long and easy breath of the warm air.
Then it sinks back down, gently, to rest among the grass.
There is no gasp and no struggle, only one slow breath.
Even while it sleeps, it rises to breathe and drifts back down.
Up it floats, a single breath, and down it sinks again.
You can let your own breathing follow that same slow rise and fall.
Breathe in as the manatee lifts its nose to the air.
Breathe out as it sinks softly back into the deep green calm.
Slow, and easy, and unhurried, breath after gentle breath.
There is nothing to do but rise, and breathe, and sink, and rest.
The manatee loves warm water above all else.
When the open sea grows cool, it seeks out the warmth.
It drifts toward the mild flow of the warm springs.
There the water rises gentle and clear and warm from the earth.
Many manatees gather in those warm and quiet pools.
They cluster close together, drowsy and content.
They rest in the soft heat, paddling barely at all.
It is a slow and sleepy gathering in the gentle warmth.
You can imagine that warmth wrapping softly around you too.
It spreads through your chest, your arms, your heavy legs.
You are warm and held and wholly at ease.
Let that drowsy warmth carry you closer toward sleep.
Now let the warm springs and the seagrass slowly fade.
Let the gentle manatee drift quietly out of sight.
You no longer need to hold any picture at all.
There is only your body, heavy and floating, soft and still.
There is only the slow and easy rise and fall of your breath.
You are safe, and you are held, and there is nothing to do.
Let the words grow faint, and let them dissolve away.
Let each breath out carry you a little deeper down.
You are floating in warm and quiet water, weightless and calm.
Let go of this thought, and then the next, and then all of them.
Drift down, gently, into warm and dreamless rest.
Rest now.

lectures.title: The Koala
lines: Welcome, and let yourself arrive here.
There is nothing left to do now but rest.
Let the day you have carried slip quietly from your shoulders.
You can set it down, all of it, and leave it for the morning.
Feel the weight of your body sinking softly into the place where you lie.
Let your breath grow longer and slower, easing out like a tide going gently away.
Soften your forehead, your jaw, your hands, and let them all be still.
Tonight you will settle high in a quiet tree, in a fork of warm grey wood.
There you will rest beside the koala, the dozy, drowsy dweller of the gum trees.
It is the sleepiest of companions, and it asks nothing of you but to be calm.
If you drift off before the end of this, that is perfectly fine.
Sleep is the whole point, so let it come whenever it wishes.
High in the tree, the koala is already asleep.
It sleeps for the larger part of every day and night.
It drowses away nearly all of its hours, curled snug in the fork of a branch.
Few creatures on the earth sleep as deeply or as long as this one.
It is one of the sleepiest animals there is, and a perfect friend for a sleepy listener.
While the world hurries below, the koala simply rests.
Its round, soft body settles into the wood as though the tree were made to hold it.
Its eyes close, and its breathing slows to a quiet, even rhythm.
There is no rush in it, no worry, only the long, gentle business of resting.
You can let your own breath fall into that same slow rhythm.
In and out, soft and unhurried, like the koala dozing above you.
There is nowhere to be and nothing to chase.
You might wonder why the koala rests so very much.
The answer is gentle, and it lives in the leaves it eats.
The koala feeds on the leaves of the gum tree, the eucalyptus, and on almost nothing else.
These leaves are tough and stringy, and they hold very little energy inside them.
They even carry a faint trace of something a little like poison.
So the koala has learned to live carefully, spending its strength as slowly as it can.
It rests almost all the time, and it digests its quiet meal slowly and patiently.
By sleeping so much, it keeps what little energy the leaves can give.
There is a deep wisdom in this, a calm and unhurried way of living.
It teaches that rest is not idleness but the body quietly tending itself.
As you lie here, you are doing that same gentle work.
You are saving your strength, slowing down, letting your body restore itself in the dark.
See how the koala sits in its tree.
It wedges itself snugly into the curve where two branches meet.
It holds on with strong, sleepy arms and broad, rough-padded paws.
Those paws grip the bark softly, so the koala never has to grip hard or strain.
It is perfectly balanced, perfectly at ease, settled like a cushion in the wood.
High above the ground, it is safe, and it knows it is safe.
Nothing can reach it there, and so it lets go of all watchfulness.
It dozes with its chin tucked down and its body rounded and warm.
Feel how your own body is held, just as surely, by the bed beneath you.
You do not have to hold yourself up or keep yourself together.
The earth is carrying you, the way the tree carries the koala.
You can let every muscle soften and trust that you will not fall.
Now let the air around you change.
The forest is full of the scent of eucalyptus, sharp and clean and cool.
It is a fresh green smell, calming and clear, like a slow breath of evening.
The long leaves are grey-green and narrow, hanging quietly in the warm air.
A soft breeze moves through them, and they rustle, the gentlest of sounds.
That rustle rises and falls, rises and falls, like breathing made of leaves.
The koala breathes it in, slow and deep, and sinks a little further into sleep.
You can breathe it in too, that clean and quiet scent of the gum trees.
Let it fill you softly and then let it ease away.
With every breath the forest grows calmer and the light grows dimmer.
The warmth wraps around you like a thin and gentle blanket.
There is only the leaves, the breeze, and the slow rise and fall of rest.
Lower in the same tree, another koala is resting too.
She is a mother, and she carries something small and precious.
Tucked in her warm pouch is her baby, a tiny koala called a joey.
It is very little, and it sleeps almost without waking, snug against her warmth.
It rides there safe and hidden as she dozes through the long, slow days.
When it grows, it climbs onto her back and clings softly to her fur.
There it rests against her, rocked gently whenever she shifts in the wood.
She is calm and patient, and the baby learns that the world is a safe and quiet place.
Nothing hurries them, and nothing troubles their long, warm rest.
Imagine being held like that, so completely, with nowhere else to be.
That same warmth and safety are around you now, here in the dark.
You are held, you are warm, and you can let yourself be small and safe.
Now let the tree begin to fade, and the koala with it.
Let the leaves and the breeze grow faint and far away.
You do not need to picture anything anymore.
Let the words grow soft and start to blur together.
Come back, gently, to the weight of your own body.
Feel how heavy and warm your arms have become, how still your legs lie.
Feel your breath, slow and quiet, moving on its own without your help.
You are safe here, and you are held, just as the koala is held by its tree.
There is nothing left to do and nowhere left to go.
Let the last of the words dissolve into the dark.
Let yourself sink down, soft and slow, into sleep.
Rest now.
